If I may be permitted to make a suggestion I shall first advise him to have [DOT] the manufacturers surrender to the Government one half of the hundred million profits they have realized during the war. In fact, it is a shame to see that while the small industries and even the workingmen are being taxed, people like Mr. Flavelle and others are permitted to accumulate fortunes. Let us cut down the number of the ministers. We have about twenty of them. I believe that, with a better distribution of the work, ten would be quite sufficient. Let us do away with all the Commissions which have been appointed and the incumbents of which are granted salaries equal to those of hon. ministers; let us practice economy, and let us be satisfied 271
that, by such means, we shall be in pocket many millions.
Sir, before I resume my seat I would like, a,s did the hon. members who preceded me to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in answer to the speech from the Throne, for the able manner in which they have discharged their duty; but I do not wish to congratulate the Government for having departed from the old custom prevailing in this House and which consisted in having the address seconded in French. It seems to me that it would have been easy enough to find, among the hon. members sitting to your right, a gentleman who was conversant with the beautiful French language, and if no such scholar could have been found, then a well gifted gentleman might have been selected among them and set to the task of learning French.
How I deplore and regret the disappearance of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier! He was a great statesman, he was for the liberal party a great chieftain, he was the idol of his compatriots and was for me, personally, a great friend or rather a great protector. As a public man, I shall strive to conform to his wise teachings and to adopt this motto which was his own: "First a Canadian, always a Canadian."

It is with feelings of extreme consternation that we must now contemplate what would have happened to the whole civilized world if these pernicious doctrines had become consummated facts. If Canada had withdrawn from the Empire who can say that her example might not have been followed by other colonies? If our form of Government had been changed and if the British Empire had gone to pieces, is there any sane person who would have the temerity or hardihood to suggest that it would have been found possible to stop the terrible Hun in his ruthless and unchristian attempt to conquer the world? Thank God the true situation has been clearly demonstrated and the stability, foundation and principles of our form of Government have been firmly established.	_
~ The Empire has stood the test of the greatest war of history and has come through triumphantly, stronger aim greater than ever. Long live the King! God bless him! Under him and his advisers, the great and powerful British, Empire was able at a moment's notice to fly to the assistance of courageous little Belgium and of noble France both of which were being ravished and destroyed by the inhuman foe. Under him the silent British navy cleared the seas of enemy ships and shipping and made the transportation of troops and foodstuffs possible. Under him the nation was able to materially assisit our valient allies in bringing the Bosche to his knees. The world is safe once more. It is with feelings of intense pride and admiration that we must contemplate His Majesty's personal record during the war as well as the record of the whole royal family. They placed the cause of freedom and humanity before everything else and nobly did they play their part.
As Canadians we may be doubly proud that His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales attached himself to the Canadian army and shared with them the hardships and dangers of the fight. I am told that he endeared himself to the Canadian troops all* of whom will agree that he is what soldiers call a good head. Perhaps I might also be permitted to suggest that even the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) will agree that the whole British aristocracy, with all their titles and other encumbrances, did magnificent work and that 
we as Canadians must make our acknowledgments to them.
It is hardly necessary for me to say that Canada has been singularly fortunate in the high standard of the men who have been sent to us in the capacity of Governors General. In the case of the present incumbent the high traditions of the office have been maintained.
The speech from the Throne on this occasion will live long in Canadian history if for no other reason than that it contains a well deserved acknowledgment of the splendid conduct of the soldiers of Canada. Every Canadian must have a personal sense of pride when he reads the reference to our Canadian soldiers:
In the notable victories leading to the glorious issue accomplished by the arms of the Allies, none of the forces engaged bore a more valorous or heroic part than those of Canada, whose achievements throughout the entire war have won imperishable renown for their country. It is most gratifying to be able to state that, in the final and decisive stages of the mighty struggle, our divisions in the field were maintained at over strength, and equipped in the highest degree with all the requirements of modern warfare.
I would call particular attention to the final sentence of this paragraph:
The appreciation and gratitude of the nation cannot be too earnestly and sincerely expressed to the gallant members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, whose sacrifices, sufferings and heroism have played so effectual a part in vindicating the cause of world liberty and civilization.
Personally, I feel that the problems affecting our returned soldiers, their dependents and the dependents of those who will not return, should receive our first consideration. However, with the kind indulgence of the House, I will refer to that subject later on.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my constituents, I would like to add my tribute to the memory of the late, lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier. So much has been said, and so well said, in this connection that I feel that in anything I might say I could add nothing to our veneration for the memory of this wonderful man. In British Columbia the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was held in high esteem by both Liberals and the old time Conservatives. His memory will always be kept green, and I believe for all time to come he will be considered as having been one of our greatest Canadians. ^	'
I would also like to be permitted to add my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech. I think it was singularly fortunate and appropriate that the mover and seconder should both be returned soldiers,

men who had taken a part, and had done their share in defending the liberty of the world. I congratulate these hon. gentlemen on the manner in which they performed their duty in this House, and I believe that it is in strict accordance with the work they did overseas.
I would also like to add my congratulations to those already extended to the new Leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). He has some qualifications which appeal to me, viz: He is a Presbyterian, he is Scotch, and he is a lawyer, surely a combination which cannot be surpassed; and I hope that the future will show for him a record which will stand side by side with the record made by his illustrious predecessor.
I sincerely regret that there has been some criticism from the hon. gentlemen on the Opposition benches, as to the absence of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) at the Peace Conference. I have been wondering why these hon. gentlemen should worry so much that the Premier is away at this particular time. I have been wondering if perhaps they think that the majority on this side of the House is not large enough, or perhaps whether they have been thinking that the Prime Minister and his absent colleagues might be induced to follow the "light in the window," which no one else on this side of the House has yet been able to perceive. I would like to ask seriously if these hon. gentlemen really think that Canada should not be represented at the Peace Conference, and should not be represented there by the Prime Minister? Why should not the Premier be absent from this House when he has such a splendid substitute to leave in his place? I remember when I first saw Sir Thomas White. It was at Osgoode Hall in Toronto in 1899 and 1900. He was then the Big Boy of the School, Gold Medallist, prize debater, and so forth. I am glad to see him once more as the Big Boy of this school of statesmen. We must all appreciate the splendid record the Acting Prime Minister made as Finance Minister during the war. He had big problems to solve, he had big work to carry out, and he was big enough to do that work in a manner satisfactory to the great majority of Canadians.
Leaving out of consideration the many other matters in which Canada is interested at the Peace Conference, if the Prime Minister and his colleagues who are attending that Conference can assist in having the Kaiser brought to justice for his many crimes against humanity, their
time will not be wasted. The Kaiser should not be allowed to escape. History will no doubt record that he was responsible for this terrible war. He was responsible for the violation of Belgium, the poison gas, the mustard gas, the liquid fire, and all other fiendish devices of hell; the crucifixion of Canadian soldiers, the air raids and the unnecessary deaths of so many defenceless women and children, and the wanton destruction of property, the sinking of the Lusitania, the murder of Nurse Cavell and Captain Fryatt, the ruthless submarine warfare, with the murderous shelling of lifeboats; and everything that is low, mean, contemptible, barbarous, inhuman and cowardly in modern warfare. The Kaiser should be brought to justice, he should have a fair trial-no doubt he will get a fair trial-and if it is shown conclusively that he personally was in any way responsible for any of the terrible crimes mentioned, he should be punished as he deserves. There are other fiends and archcriminals among his advisers who should also be prosecuted.
I am not one, Mr. Speaker, who thinks that the ministers of the Crown should spend all their time in Ottawa. As a matter of fact I believe that their departmental duties should be lessened to such an extent that they will be able to pay frequent visits to other parts of this great Dominion. The people of British Columbia appreciated the visit of the Cabinet Ministers last fall. It put the ministers in touch with conditions in British Columbia, and let the people see and hear them, and I can say, Mr. Speaker, that they made a good impression upon the people of that province. We had the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell), the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), the Minister of Militia and Defence (Maj. Gen. Mewburn), the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid), and the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White). The latter paid his visit during the Victory Loan campaign. Possibly the most important from the standpoint of my constituency was the visit of the Minister of Public Works. Previous to his visit to my constituency that hon. gentleman did not have a very clear idea of the conditions there, such as a man must get by actually being on the scene.
The first time I met the Minister of Public Works was in Ottawa during the early part of the last session of Parliament, f went to see him about some further improve-

ments in the channel of the Fraser river. He said to me: " Now, look here, McQuar-rie, there is no use in your talking to me about trying to make a ship channel on the Fraser river. You cannot do it; it is impossible; there are too many things to contend with, and I do not propose to spend very much money on it." I said to him: " Mr. Carvell, have you been on the Fraser river?" He said: " Yes, I have been at New Westminster and I have seen the Fraser river, but I must say that I have not actually taken a trip down the Fraser river from New Westminster to the gulf." I said: " Will you promise me that when you visit British Columbia you will come to New Westminster and spend some time on the Fraser river?" He said that he would, and I said that I was satisfied. I remarked further: " Mr. Carvell, after you have seen what kind of river we have out there and what the conditions are, if you repeat your assertion that you do not care to spend any money on trying to improve that ship channel, I shad have nothing further to say; but I have too much respect for your judgment to think that you will take that stand."
Now, we were fortunate in having the Minister of Public Works spend a considerable time on the Fraser river. He is a man who wants to see for himself. You may lay engineers' reports and ad that kind of thing before him, but he wants to see for himself what you have and to find out whether the goods are there or not. That is the kind of man we like; that is the kind of man we want to have visit us. Although his time was rather limited, the minister spent two days and a half on the Fraser river. We have quite a big river there; those of you who have not been out there do not understand what a great river it is. The Fraser is one of the greatest rivers in Canada; it is one of the greatest rivers in the world. It has two branches, one running to the west, which is called the North Ann, and the other to the south, which is called the main channel, the latter being the larger.
The minister spent a half day on the North Arm, and was able to see the conditions there. If we are going to have any considerable industrial advancement in British Columbia, it must be on the Fraser river. The peninsula on which Vancouver, New Westminster and the intervening municipalities are situated is practically identical with Ifew York City so far as its geographical situation is concerned. There the great industries are on an island, which is similar to what we have, and there is the

flat land along the river, which is the proper land for industrial sites.
The minister spent a whole day on the main channel. We took him up to one of the largest and most up-to-date saw mills in the world, that of the Western Canada Lumber 'Company. We took him down the river and showed him sawmill after sawmill, industry after industry, and we showed him the dredges at work at the mouth of the river. The river at New Westminster is something like three-quarters of a mile wide; the distance from New Westminster to the gulf is something like eighteen miles. There is deep water, forty or fifty feet, right at the docks at New Westminster. There is deep water all the way down, a good channel until you get to the sand bars at the mouth of the river.
The minister spent another day going through the upper reaches of the Fraser river. We were able also to give the minister certain information. We were able to tell him that on the Fraser river there were still remaining something like eight billion feet of timber belonging to the Provincial Government and something more than eight billion feet of merchantable timber belonging to the Dominion Government, and that if the present stumpage rate was continued the Dominion Government would receive from that timber in stumpage no less than $4,000,000. We were able to tell him that we had saw mills on the Fraser river, at and near New Westminster, with a capacity of 500,000,000 feet. We were able to tell him that we had shingle mills on the Fraser river close to New Westminster turning out 300,000,000 shingles a year. We were able to show him that something like 8,000 men were employed in these industries, and that indirectly the. whole population of that district was affected. We were able to tell him that there was an investment in mills and timber of something like $100,000,000, and we were able to show him that we did business with the whole world. We ship lumber all over the world, Mr. Speaker.
Our ships are already plying between Canada and many foreign countries, but unfortunately because of the lack of sufficient depth in the channel at the present time, we are unable to accommodate the larger class of ships which wish to do business with us. We have at present a depth of some twenty-four feet, but we want to get a depth of thirty feet. We explained all these matters to the Minister of Public Works and at a little meeting that we had afterwards with him, he stated that he had been mistaken about the Fraser river. He was a big enough man to admit that

the information which he had had was not altogether correct; that he had had an idea that the Fraser river was a very turbulent stream; that it was very difficult of navigation; that there were all kinds of difficulties to be contended with, and that from an engineering standpoint, successful navigation of the Fraser river was impossible of accomplishment. He told us also that he had had an idea that we were trying to build up a port in New Westminster to compete with the port of Vancouver which was a port of sufficient capacity to look after all the shipping that we might ever expect to have on that part of the Pacific. There is a splendid harbour at Vancouver. Everything that the Minister of Public Works said about it is quite true. At the meeting to which I refer, he said: " Gentlemen, I find that you do not wish to build up a port to compete with Vancouver. What you wish is to have a channel out to the sea which will enable you to send out to "the world the products -which you manufacture. You are entitled to that, and I -am going to do everything I can to assist you to get it."
The problem is, to a layman, not a very difficult one, but I must say that, unfortunately, there has in the past been a great deal of bungling and a great deal of money thrown away in connection with the work on the Fraser river. We do not like that. It does not do us any good. It does not bring the results that we want. We want a channel and at present we have not a channel. The reason is that the whole proposition has not been undertaken intelligently. To my mind, the present Minister of Public Works is the first one who has viewed the situation in an intelligent manner. We have been fighting for years to get an engineer on that work who will do nothing but look after the dredging of that channel, who will have entire charge and authority to see that the work is done properly. Formerly, it had been done under the control of the department and there had been some supervision, but no properly qualified man was on deck all the time to see that the work was carried out in an intelligent manner. We put this situation up to the Minister of Public Works and an engineer was put in charge of the work. My information is that during the last year more and better work has been done than in any previous five years. We found that the department had been endeavouring to keep dredged a circuitous channel, one that was full of turns and curves, so that when you dug it out in one place it would fill up in another and you could
never, in the world, expect to have a proper channel. We explained to the Minister of Public Works what we wanted; we said that we wanted to get a straight channel out to the sea, so that the current of the river would wash out the sand and silt which is deposited from above and thus keep itself more or less clear. We showed him our plans. He said:	"That appeals
to me; I am going to try it out." He is trying out this plan and I have no doubt that, under the guidance of the Minister of Public Works, we are going to have a channel down to the sea of sufficient depth to look after our requirements. I think that is what we are entitled to have. If Canada is going to be built up, she must be built up by her commerce and her industries and we, on the Pacific coast, expect to share in the advancement in those respects which is bound to come to Canada.
We had also, as I said, a visit from the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid). We in New Westminster are interested in railways as well as in other matters. We also had visiting us the managing director, the assistant managing director, and, I think, pretty nearly all the directors of the Canadian Northern Railway. They saw for themselves what the conditions were and they ascertained what our requirements from the Canadian Northern were. The original plans of the Canadian Northern Railway contemplated the construction of the main line through New Westminster to Vancouver. This company, which has at the present time a railroad of about 3,000 miles in length, is in this unfortunate position, that for the last twelve miles of that distance it has to run over the tracks of a foreign railway. Such a thing is a disgrace to Canada. If we are going to construct a railroad 3,000 miles in length, surely we can finish up the last twelve miles of it so as to have our own tracks. The city of New Westminster, in accordance with an arrangement with the Canadian Northern Railway Company, who were then in control of the road, made an expenditure of $500,000 in widening Front street which is close to the river, for the purpose of allowing the Canadian Northern to run through the city. The Canadian Northern purchased lands in New Westminster and contiguous thereto on which they spent something like $2,000,000. Those lands were purchased for the purpose of running the line through New Westminster to Vancouver. I have had the matter up with the minister and also with the managing director and his assistant,

and I believe it is the intention, as soon as the necessary finances are available, to carry out the original plan.
I wish to congratulate the Government and the Minister of Eailways and Canals upon their ^election of the men to take charge of the Canadian National railways. In the West, both Mr. Hanna and Mr. MacLeod are very well thought of. We think they are very big men and quite capable of taking charge of a big proposition like this. They have the respect of the community, and I think they will get results. The men who took over the control of the Canadian Northern railway for the Government had a very big problem on their hands, because the Canadian Northern had a bad reputation,-a very bad reputation in British Columbia. There we have close to us the famous townsite of Port Mann, and I can say without fear of contradiction that Port Mann was one of the biggest steals ever perpetrated in the history of Canada. It is a disgrace to Canada that any one, to use a Western phrase, should be allowed to pull off a thing like that and get away with it. Port Mann did more than anything else to give the Canadian Northern a bad name. The road had also a bad reputation with the banks. I know as a matter of fact, that the banks refused to do business with any one who was looking to the Canadian Northern for payment. I am reminded of a conversation I had on my way to Ottawa last session with two business men of British Columbia, one a banker, and the other a millman. They said: " Now that the Government has taken over the Canadian Northern, it is a strange thing that they do not do something to put it on a proper financial basis. Do you know that one of the largest banks in Canada has refused to advance money to any one on the strength of a contract with the Canadian Northern?" They gave me particulars, and the first man I met in Ottawa happened to be Mr. Hanna. I said to him: " This is a nice kind of railroad you are trying to run. It appears to be discredited with the banking institutions of this country." And I told him of the conversation I had had on the train. He asked if he was at liberty to use that information, and I said, " Yes, I will give you the names of the gentlemen and all details." He said, "All right. There is going to be some fur flying in a very few minutes," and he set off down the street. I am glad to say that under the present management the financial reputation of the Canadian Northern has been very much enhanced. There is a great future for this 
road. I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. D. L. Redman (Calgary East) for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, resumed from Wednesday, March 12.
Mr. WILLIAM G. McQUARRIE (New Westminster) (resuming): Mr. Speaker, I

was saying when the House adjourned yesterday, that there was a great future before the Canadian National railways if properly managed. The transcontinental line running through the West, formerly the Canadian Northern railway, is a very important one from our standpoint, and I believe that that railway is going to become a great asset for Canada. With railways the most remunerative part of the business should be the haulage of freight, and in this connection, the railroad having the best grades has a great advantage. I believe I am correct in saying that the Canadian Northern Railway transcontinental line has better grades than any other transcontinental railway in the whole of America. The following comparison with the Canadian Pacific railway exemplifies this situation very clearly: The Canadian Pacific can only haul a train of sixteen cars from Vancouver to Calgary through the mountains, whereas the Canadian Northern can haul, with one engine, fifty cars fully loaded, from Vancouver to Quebec. When the grain of Alberta and Saskatchewan flows westward this will be an important factor in the success of the Canadian Northern. A very considerable portion of the grain from these provinces is bound to go out through the Pacific.
In considering the transportation of grain, or any other product for that matter, where rail and water are both to be utilized, an important feature.to be taken into account is to get the shortest rail haul to satisfactory water transportation. This will be accomplished by using the Fraser river route. We expect some day to see grain elevators on the Fraser river. We have miles and miles of excellent sites for elevators from Port Coquitlam to the gulf and when the Minister of Public Works completes the channel of the Fraser river there will be a sufficient depth of water for great freighters to dock at any of these sites.
We have four important railway lines running into New Westminster now-the Canadian Northern, Canadian Pacific, the Great Northern and the Northern Pacific. The Canadian Pacific has already intimated that it will, when the proper times comes, build elevators at Port Cbquitlam and use the Fraser river route thereby cutting down its rail haul about 25 miles. It has acquired a lot of land at Port Coquitlam and will have lots of room. to handle the cars without congestion. The Canadian Northern also owns a lot of property at, and in the vicinity of, New Westminster. Why not follow the lead of the Canadian Pacific and use the Fraser river route for the vast quantity of grain that is bound to be hauled? Perhaps we might even get in ahead of the Canadian Pacific and establish our elevators first. I would advise the management of this railway to consider the ad-visibility of building elevators on the Fraser river without delay and let others do the following. If the Canadian Northern carries out its original plan of building its line from New' Westminster to Vancouver it will save the $2,000,000 it has invested in New Westminster and vicinity. It will also get the business at North Arm, Lulu Island, Burnaby and South Vancouver. Many additional miles of splendid industrial sites will be opened up and much good will result to the whole country.
I think the new management will make good. When the Government took over the line, the Canadian Northern was trying to do business without equipment and without credit. Contracts of the Canadian Northern were not recognized by the banks as security for advances. Since coming under Government control all that has been changed. One hundred and fifty engines and 16,000 cars have been added to the equipment and financial aid has placed the Canadian Northern in this position:	(1)
No shortage of cars; (2) no shortage of pow'er; (3) trains running on time; (4) the public looking to do business with the Canadian Northern instead of the Canadian Northern running after the public; (5) good credit.
When the minister was out in New Westminster, we pointed out to him, among other things, the necessity of having a British Columbia man on the Canadian Northern directorate and I believe that this will have his favourable consideration. Personally, I think that every province should be represented on the Board of the. Canadian National Railways.
The minister had quite a busy time in British Columbia, and we consider that he is the right man in the right place. I would also like to pay my respects to the deputy minister: he is a good man and doing good work. The other Cabinet Ministers were also very busy during their visit to British Columbia. They discussed many matters with the members of Parliament for the province, met many delegations and addressed a number of public meetings. We were glad to have them with us, and we only hope they will come again soon and that other members of the Cabinet will visit British Columbia. There is one minister, Mr. Speaker, who did not come to British Columbia, although he received a very pressing invitation to do so. I refer

to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I am very sorry indeed that he did not find it convenient to come to our province. All the signs point to trouble in connection with the British Columbia fisheries. In connection with those fisheries we have had Royal Commissions, we have had International Commissions, we have had investigations of all kinds; but the situation does not appear to have yet been cleared up. Now it is alarming to see the depletion in such an important industry as the salmon, and I think it would be a good thing for the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to give a matter of that kind very serious consideration.
There is another factor in connection with the fisheries of British Columbia, which to my mind requires and demands the attention of the minister, and that is the fact that the great majority of fishing licenses in British Columbia are issued to Japanese, and the great part of the remaining licenses are issued to other foreigners- Austrians, Greeks, Norwegians, Swedes, and so forth. Now I have here some figures which I will give in that connection. This is a letter which I reoeived from one of the fishery officials and is dated 6th of January, 1919:
It is quite true that so far as gill net fishing is concerned, the Japanese hold the majority of licenses. For instance on the Fraser River, during the season just closed there were 473 whites, 86 Indians, and 1,023'Japanese. In 1917 834 whites, 272 Indians, and 1,521 Japanese. In 1916, 605 whites, 198 Indians, and 1,437 Japanese. In the northern part of the province, where in 1918, 2,216 gill net licenses were issued, 1,211 were of Japanese nationality. In salmon fishing the Japanese are restricted to gill net licenses, and there is not a salmon drag, or purse-seine license issued to any one of this nationality. It is quite true that some of the white licensees employ Japanese to operate their seining licenses, but this is a matter over which the department has absolutely no control. True also, certain Japanese acted as buyers of salrffon on the Fraser River for American firms, and this, of course, we cannot control.
Now, I have nothing to say against the Japanese, but I do not think it is a proper condition when we find that the majority of the licenses are being issued to men from a foreign country. Perhaps this may not appeal to hon. gentlemen as being a serious matter, but I wish to assure them that it is a very important matter, from the standpoint of British Columbia at least. When you consider the fact that in a normal year the pay-roll to the fishermen on the Fraser river only is something like a million dollars and when you see the greater part of that million dollars going to foreigners, you must realize that something should be done to remedy that state of affairs.
Could they not get white men to take their places?

That is the unfortunate part of it; the white man cannot compete with the Oriental in fishing, because these two classes of people do not live in the same way. The Japanese can live much more cheaply than the white man. The

Japanese is a good fisherman, and we have plenty of white men who are good fishermen, but they cannot compete with the Japanese. I have watched this situation for something like thirty years. I have seen the Japanese menace to the fisheries increase from year to year until now these people have the monopoly of that natural resource. I remember the time when a good run of fish meant prosperity to that district, but now the money received by the fishermen goes out of the country and helps not to build up Canada, but to build up a foreign country.
The International Commission to which I have referred was formed because of the fact that our neighbours to the south were doing absolutely nothing to protect the fish. We had, hatcheries, we had close seasons, we did everything we could, according to the best judgment of the men in charge of the department concerned, to conserve the salmon; but the Americans did nothing but take the fish. On the other side of the line they had large traps in which thousands of these fish were caught which otherwise would have come up to the spawning grounds in the Fraser river. It is unfortunate that those who had to do with arranging the boundary between Canada and the United States in the early days _ did ' not take these circumstances into consideration. The condition is an unnatural one that should not have been permitted to ' exist. However, we are face to face with it; and now we have this International Commission.
My point in referring to this commission is that, according to reports in the press, it has recommended that the number of licenses on the Fraser river be limited to
1.800.	Up to the present time any one who wanted a license has been able to get one. But if the number of licenses is limited to
1.800,	are we going to allow the Japanese to have the whole of them or shall we so arrange it that they will get only a fair proportion of them? One of my constituents has asked me to see if it would be possible to get the Government to make some kind of regulation cutting down to fifty per cent of the total the proportion of licenses to be issued to the Japanese. It seems to me that that suggestion is along the right line, but under present conditions its adoption is out of the question. The Government and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will have to consider what is to be done for the future; will have to consider whether foreigners are to be allowed to have all our fishing rights.
Why are foreigners accorded fishing rights in the Fraser river?

We call these men foreigners, but as a matter of fact they are not foreigners. According to the law, they are naturalized British subjects. Now, you know what that means; anybody who lives in British Columbia knows what that means. These men are citizens of this country only in name and only for the particular purpose of securing a fishing license. They take the oath of allegiance to His Majesty the King, but remain loyal subjects of their own emperor.
I have referred to investigations. As a matter of fact, an investigation is now being conducted in British Columbia by Mr. Justice Eberts, one of the judges of the Supreme Court of that province, under a Royal Commission. Many charges have been made in connection with the administration of the fisheries in British Columbia-charges of graft, corruption, waste, destruction, and so on. Some of those charges have been made by men who have been rash in their statements and very unfair to the fisheries officials and to the Government. A member of the British Columbia Legislature, a returned soldier with a distinguished record in the war, made what I consider to be rash and uncalled for statements. I refer to Major Richard Burde, D.S.O. He made these charges in the Provincial Legislature and also at a public meeting. I have in my hand an extract from the Vancouver Daily Province of February 7, 1919, which reads as follows:
Big Graft Ring in Fish.
Major Burde Used Strong Language in Legislature Thursday.
Gives Details of Difficulty in Getting an Inquiry at Alberni.
Victoria, Feb. 7.-Calling the Fisheries Department a standing disgrace to Canada, "smelling of fish but of a rotten brand," Major Richard Burde, of Alberni, scathingly indicted '/.e Federal Administration for what he described to the legislature yesterday as its absolute disregard of citizens of this province.
"There never was a bigger graft in Canada than there is in the circle where one must wait to-day for a fishing license," he said. "The very fact that an application for a seine-net license is made in private to the Chief Inspector of Fisheries and the public does not know anything about it must make any one of a penetrative mind smell graft.
"You can sell a fishing license any day in a real estate office for $3,000 or $4,000. Our fisheries in this province are being depleted. The sockeye salmon has gone to the museum and the herring would soon be in the same class, but for an inquiry which we now have instituted in the district of Alberni. Herring packers have recently gone into that territory, and fishing for them are more Japanese than I believe have

any right to be in British Columbia. These men are employed to the exclusion of the whites, although Ashing might well be considered a good employment for returned soldiers. In Alberni we procured thirty affidavits to prove that there had been almost enough herring wasted by the seine-net ringsters to feed Canada for three or four years. The bottom of the harbour is silvery carpeted with dead herring. Yet, when we press for an inquiry, the Dominion member for the district, the chief inspector of Asheries and his satellites met us with chips on their shoulders. Our charges by inference involved the chief inspector, but when we asked Ottawa for an inquiry we were told that it would be made by this official. We replied that we would prefer to have -the Federal department send a man down to investigate the inspector rather than have that official take up our charges. The reply from Mr. Desbarats, Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, was that our message was impertinent, and that if we persisted in that course we would not get any inquiry at all. But we persisted and public opinion forced a probe. Now we have a situation where a Dominion department reluctantly consents to granting us an investigation it should have -made long ago itself. This department has apparently outlived its usefulness. I am told that the seine-net Ashermen impound about 150 tons of herring in each drive. Sixty per cent of them are smothered and dead by the time the other forty per cent are loaded. The dead Ash drop to the bottom of the harbour, and thus the terrible waste goes on. It seems to me, and in fact I have that admission from the chief inspector of Asheries, that hundreds of Japanese working for these herring concerns have no right to engage in the occupation because they are not naturalized. But somehow or other they produce naturalization papers when called on. People say that the canneries hand out the naturalization certiAcates to the Japanese whenever they wish to employ them. The Japanese going home to the Orient leave their certiAcates behind, and the Japanese contractors apparently sell them to the new-comers or to the canneries."
The speaker went on to say that the Japanese put up tons of immature herring and ship them via Tacoma to Japan, in this way robbing British Columbia of one of its most valuable assets. The question was one which the province should take up with* Ottawa and fight the matter through with the Dominion, he considered. The administration of the fisheries of British Co-, lumbia would well be in the hands of the province itself. It might be urged, of course, that to seek to bar the Japanese would be to raise an issue with an ally, but it seemed to Major Burde that if the Empire owed a debt to Japan then the Empire should pay rather than ask British Columbia to meet the whole price of the alliance.
Major Burde was not content with making a statement in the legislature involving the chief inspector and other officials in the Department of Fisheries. At a-meeting held in Alberni he made further charges, involving also the Federal member for that constituency. I have here the Vancouver Daily

Sun of February 22, 1919, from which I purpose reading this extract:-
Major Burde Alleges that West Coast Fisheries are Controlled by Graft -Ring.
Port Alberni, Feb. 21.
Major Dick Burde, M.L.A., made a Aghting speech here to-night, at a meeting of Ashermen and citizens attacking the cannery men, H. S. Clements, M.P., Chief Inspector Cunningham, of the Fisheries Department and Al. Hager of the New England Fish Company, Vancouver. The provincial member was wildly applauded by the crowd when he repeated the charge that the West Coast Fisheries were controlled by a Graft Ring and urged the Ashermen to stay with their Aght. He contended that the scope of the inquiry should be extended, and that Mr. Cunningham should be put on the stand. If this was done, some sensational evidence would come [DOT]out, he said. "There was a graft ring in Ash bigger than the Yukon whiskey ring," he asserted. "I believe it because I can smell it."
With regard to Mr. Hager, Major Burde said he had heard that Hager told certain men at the Hotel Vancouver that "Burde is a liar; if we get him on the stand we will make dog meat out of him."
In answer, the major said "if Hager said he will make dog meat out of me, I'll make dirty, rotten Ash meat out of him."
Referring to the Fisheries Department, Major Burde said it was the Department's business to start the investigation, not that of the Ashermen. He said this was to the disgrace of Clements and the Department. "We are up against a bunch of brigands," he said. 'We must not start anything we can't Anish."
I will now take up the investigation. The investigation was held and Mr. Cunningham, chief inspector of fisheries, went on the stand and was examined and cross-examined at length, denying each and every one of these charges of graft 'and incompetency that had been made. At that investigation not one thing was proved in the way of graft or dishonesty or anything of that kind against the member for Alberni, the chief inspector of fisheries, or any of the officials of the department, and, strange to relate, Major Burde, although requested to give evidence himself, did not see fit to do so. It seems to me that when a man, whether he is a returned soldier or not- and I give Major Burde all credit for his service at the front-make such charges in the legislature, he should know that his charges are going to be substantiated, and that when an investigation is held, when the country is put to the expense of thousands of dollars to hold an. inquiry of this kind, the man who makes the charges should, if he is not able to come and give evidence himself to prove his charges, produce the men upon whose statements he relief when making his charges. This kind of thing is bad for everybody concerned in it. It is bad for Major Burde; it is bad for the

fisheries officials; it is bad for Mr. Clements. It does harm because people see the first reports of those charges and think there is something in them, and they do not see the last reports, which show that the charges have been absolutely exploded. The situation in connection with the fisheries of British Columbia is, to say the least, very unsatisfactory. The control and management of the fisheries is vested absolutely in one man-the Chief Inspector of Fisheries. It is absolutely a one man affair, and if that appeals to the minister as proper, I can tell him that it certainly does not so appeal to me or to a great many others. No matter how honest and capable this one man may be who has the control of licenses and all details in connection with the fisheries of British Columbia, dissatisfaction is bound to exist. The Chief Inspector is managing director, as it were, of the fisheries, with full power. It is only natural that a man who is refused a license should be dissatisfied and think there is something wrong with the man who refused him the license. This gives rise to suspicion and rumours, and rumours nearly always result, as they have done in this case, in charges and insinuations. It will not do. No one man is big enough to have full control of the fisheries of British Columbia, and I am glad to know that the acting minister is considering the appointment of a Fisheries rsoard for British Columbia, composed of no less than three men with a thorough knowdedge of the fisheries and whose awards will be accepted by the people of the province.
I have another complaint to make in connection with the fisheries of British Columbia, and it is with regard to the removal of the office of the ohief Inspector of Fisheries from New Westminster, wnere it had been for fifty years, to Vancouver. I do not care to discuss this matter in the absence of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), as I may have an opportunity on some other occasion to go into the matter fully. There is a question of principle involved which I shall then discuss. After what I have said I think the House will agree tnat I was quite correct in saying that all signs pointed to trouble in connection with the administration of the fisheries of British Columbia. I regret very much indeed that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did not see fit to go to British Columbia in connection with the fisheries. I trust that he will be back in his seat before long and will bring down legislation to remedy some of the evils I have mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, many splendid speeches have been made in this debate on various matters by men much more competent than I am to discuss them, but as I have come almost three thousand miles I hope the House will bear with me while I express a few Western ideas in a Western way. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) has told us that we have to raise millions and millions of dollars and that there will have to be an increase in the income tax; there was nothing else for it, he said. I would suggest to him and to the Government that before increasing the tax an effort should be made to collect the taxation imposed by the present Act. I have here a clipping from the Vancouver World dated February 14 last, -which says that according to an official statement from Ottawa:
The returns to date from the Income Tax Act of 1917, which applies only to incomes in excess of $3,000 in the case of married persons and $2,000 in the case of unmarried persons, show that about 30,00*0 assessments have been made, of which 19,000 are paid.
The first question I would ask is, why have the other 11,000 assessments not been paid? Secondly, why have only 30,000 assessments been made when there should have been at least twice that number? I will tell you the reason, Mr. Speaker. It is because a great many persons liable under the Act have not filled out the returns which they received from the tax collector, but have simply torn them up and thrown them in the waste paper basket, saying: "We shall simply be making trouble for ourselves if we fill these in." I have been told that it is a regular joke in the clubs the way men are tearing up these forms. The statement has also been made to me by men of financial standing that a great many of the returns that have been sent in are not altogether correct. If my information is correct, certainly something should be done to remedy this state of affairs. Everyone liable under the Act should be made to pay, and a return that is at all events reasonably correct should be insisted upon. I think that if that were done it would perhaps be unnecessary to increase the income tax. We should get the money that we require, in an equitable manner, and not, as we have received it heretofore, from some and not from others who were entitled to pay. I am not attaching blame to the men who have charge, in the different provinces, of the collection of the income tax. I know that in our province we have a good man. He has done his work well, but he has not a proper staff. He has not the proper clerical assistance which he

should have to enable him to perform his work in the way in which it should be done. I think that the collectors in the different provinces should be afforded the necessary assistance to carry out their work more satisfactorily.
In regard to the Business Profits Tax, there seems to be a general impression that the Government intends to discontinue this tax. I do not know whether that is correct or not. In this connection I may read an editorial-a short one-which appeared in the Vancouver World of February 19, of this year:
A Tax That Should Continue.
The Business Profits War Tax, it is said, will not be renewed for 1919. If this be true Parliament ought to have a word to say about it.
The Federal Cost of Living Commissioner, in his report for last month on stocks of products in cold storage, points out that profiteering is still going on and strongly recommends that the order limiting profits should be restored and "rigidly enforced." He advocates special measures for the "protection of all Canadians for the period of reconstruction."
One such protective measure is the Business Profits War Tax. It tends to reduce profiteering and at the same time goes some distance towards allaying the labour unrest throughout the Dominion. Besides this, Canada has a huge bill of the war costs to meet and those who have made money out of the war or out of the conditions that will follow the war are the logical persons to bear the heaviest share of this debt.
Public opinion should make itself felt at Ottawa. The profiteers should not be allowed to have it all their own way.
With the sentiments expressed in that article, if the facts are correct, I entirely concur. It seems to me that this is a tax which might very well be continued; it is a tax which has produced a good deal of money. The returns under the Business Profits Tax appears to be very satisfactory, certainly a large amount of money has been collected in that way. According to information which I gather from the press, the assessments under this tax have aggregated $65,000,000, of which $59,000,000 have been collected. The balance will probably be received within the next two months.
I come now to the question of highways.
I am pleased to note that the Government intends at last to do something towards assisting in the construction of highways; but I am afraid I cannot altogether agree with the manner in which this assistance is proposed to be given, as outlined in the resolution standing in the name of the hon. ' Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. J. D. Reid); and I hope that before it is finally disposed of, the resolution will be con-

siderably amended. I think we need, not so much the expenditure of money as the obtaining of results. We need to have assistance from the Dominion Government in the building of highways which will be of some use to the people of Canada. Now, we have in British Columbia a highway which we consider is important enough to receive assistance. I am referring to what is known as the Pacific Highway, which runs from Vancouver to San Diego, California, on the border of Mexico, a distance of some 2,000 miles. It is an international highway passing through the States of California, Oregon and Washington. In those states the counties all along that road are at present hard-surfacing it. Every county is doing its share, and the state is assisting; so that that highway of 2,000 4 p.m. miles down the Pacific coast will have a hard surface practically all the way. In British Columbia there is about thirty miles, to connect up with that splendid international highway. Thirty miles is all we have to do to complete our portion of the work; twelve miles has already been done. The road from New Westminster to Vancouver is a splendid one, a beautiful pavement,-one of the best in Canada, and one of which we are justly proud. Only eighteen miles remain to be done. I think-and I am supported in this opinion by the people of British Columbia, the Good Roads Associations, and all other organizations interested in roads-that that is a road which should receive assistance from the Dominion Government. Now, we have heard from various hon. members on both sides of the House of the necessity for effecting national unity, encouraging the national spirit, and with those sentiments I am in entire agreement.
I think we in Canada are too provincial; we know our own provinces and no others. We do not know what the rest of Canada consists of. Take British Columbia, for instance. Do we, in British Columbia, know anything about the province of Quebec, except what we read in newspapers, and observe casually on trains passing through that province? What do we in British Columbia know of the great provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, which are right at our doors, Manitoba, Ontario, and the Maritime Provinces? We know practically nothing.
The hon. member for Westminster District (Mr. Stacey) the other day, advanced in splendid words, a beautiful plan for promoting the spirit of national unity. I have another plan to suggest and it seems to me-

stages rather than to look after it later on. Epidemics are started because cases are not attended to as they should be at the first. There should be free medical attendance for those who wish to take advantage of it. At the present time all the machinery for carrying out a system of free medical attendance is in existence. You know, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has medical officers and has hospitals to look after the returned soldiers who require medical attendance. These men are supplied with medical attendance, drugs, medicines and so on.
In due time, and I hope in the not far distant future, the soldiers will be discharged from the hospitals, and there will be no further work for those institutions or for the medical men who are looking after them. Why not continue those hospitals and those medical men in the service of the country, and give free medical attendance to the people who want to take advantage of it? I hope that the new Department of Public Health will consider that question, because I believe, and am convinced, that it is very important.
Now as to the high cost of living. I got a letter from my wife yesterday, and she said: " I hope you people down there in Ottawa will try and do something to bring down the cost of living. That is about the most important business that you can think about." That is the way all the women in this country feel at the present time. I do not see anything about this subject in the speech from the Throne, but I think some action is contemplated in the programme of the Government. Mr. Speaker, we must consider the women more than ever now under present conditions

Seme hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

-and if they demand that the cost of living be brought down we shall have to comply with that demand. How it is going to be done I do not know, that is something that will have to be worked out.
As to the Civil Service Commission, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the criticism of that body, and I hope that patronage as in the old days will never be restored in Canada. Personally I do not wish to have anything to say about any of the appointments which are to be made in connection with the Civil Service. At the same time, however, I think that the Civil Service Commission can stand some remodelling, it is not working out very satisfactorily. I am not saying that with any desire to criticise any member of the Civil
I Mr. McQuarrie.j
Service Board, I think they are trying to do their best, but the existing system needs improvement. It is all new, and the needed reforms will have to be worked out. My experience with the 'Civil 'Service Commission has been something like this: I have not heard anything from the commission since I have been a member, neither have I communicated with it, but a rather remarkable thing has happened in that connection, and that is what I want to call attention to. As a matter of fact a great many of the applicants for Civil Service positions from my constituency gave my name as one of their references. I do not know whether it was right or not for them to do so, but at any rate they did so, although not at my request. Now, the peculiar part of the proceeding is that never on one occasion have I had any reference to me from the Civil Service Commission as to any of these applications, and no appointment, so far as I know, has been made by the commission of any one from my constituency. We have good men in my constituency, just as other hon. gentlemen have in their constituencies, but they do not seem to have been recognized by the commission. Whether it is that their applications were refused and thrown out immediately the commission saw that a member of Parliament's name was given as one of the references, or not, I cannot say, but the fact remains that no reference was ever made by the commission to me. Neither am I aware whether any reference was made to any of the other gentlemen who were on the applications or not. I think it is a strange thing that before making appointments the Civil Service Commission should not communicate with all the references given on the applications. I think the Civil Service Commission will be all right if it is given time, but I do hope that patronage will not be returned to the members of Parliament.
With regard to immigration, we have to consider it as a problem-one of -the greatest problems of demobilization. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) speaking on this subject, as reported on page 220 of Hansard said: " The first thing is to get population." Again, as reported on page 221 he said: First of all get population, get people with money." I can hardly agree with the hon. gentleman that money should be the only qualification. I would say, get population, but get the right kind.
Sir SAM 'HUGHES:	Hear, hear.
Hear, hear.

To my mind there
are certain classes of population that we do not want in this country. The first class is one which includes people who cannot readily be assimilated. Among this class are, the Chinese, the Japanese, the Hindus, and other Eastern races. So far as the Chinese are concerned, we get them in British Columbia. The unfortunate thing is that when you speak of the number of Chinese in Canada you practically have reference to the number of Chinese in British Columbia. I only wish the Chinese would come down here in large numbers, and that you would employ them as you think they would be useful to you. I know how you feel about it here in Ontario. You have no sympathy with us, when we speak against Oriental immigration. You say:	" These Chinese will be very useful
to us, we want cheap labour." I want to tell hon. gentlemen that when you get the Chinese you do not get cheap labour. The Chinaman, like everybody else, has become educated, and he is not going to work for any cheap wages. Although there is an overabundance of Chinese in British Columbia at the present time, yet they demand big wages. What would you people in Ontario think of paying $60 to $70 a month to an ordinary farm labourer, when down here you probably pay about $25, or $30?
Oh, no.

I venture to say you pay consideraljly less than $60 to $75 a month for good farm labour. In British Columbia you cannot get a Chinaman who is any good to w'ork on a farm for less than that wage. You cannot get a Chinaman, who is any good, to work in a house or residence, for less than $50 a month and board. If you want to get a good one, you must pay $75, $100 or $125 a month. Talk about cheap labour; you do not get it with the Chinese. I am safe in saying that there are too many Chinese in British Columbia, because I have no less an authority for it than the Chinese Consul at Vancouver. Conditions are so bad that he has found it necessary to go to the Vancouver City council and make representations in the matter. In speaking of these Orientals, the Chinese, Japanese and Hindus, I am referring, of course, to the coolie classes. The Chinese Consul has asked the Vancouver City council to make
representations to the Dominion Government with a view to restricting Chinese immigration. I have here a copy of the written statement made by Koliang Yih, the Chinese Consul, in the Vancouver City Council chamber on February 7, 1919. It is as follows:
Although there is only one Chinese to every 3,000 Canadians in this country, yet labour conditions here, aggravated by the large number of returned soldiers, whom we all honour, make it advisable that no more Chinese labourers be allowed to come at present, unless they are returning Chinese or bona fide exempted class, pending a gentleman's agreement between the governments concerned to abolish the head tax and to limit the number of immigrants.
I understand that some 2,000 alleged students, paying $500 head tax each, have come to Canada during the past few months without expecting the war would end so suddenly, and that head tax has been received here and elsewhere on more than 1,200 alleged students who have not yet left China. I think you should petition your Federal Government and suggest that these head taxes be returned to those paying same and those who arrived at Canada three months before the armistice was signed, if they desire to return. I will do my part in requesting my government to allow no Chinese labourers to come here without applying for government's passport, properly vised by a British Consul.
Many Chinese already in this country are finding difficulties in making a living at present, and the stand I am taking now is for the pro-tecton of their immediate interests as well as those of the Canadians.
Between the period of 1906 and 1917, no less than 30,000 Chinese have paid their head tax to the amount of more than $15,000,000 to your Federal Government. Many Chinese, finding that the conditions, both economic and social, were unbearable to them, have since returned to China, and this statement can be proved by the fact that according to the last census taken, there were less than 30,000 Chinese throughout the whole Dominion. Those unfortunate fellows who paid in the tax and went away elsewhere have certainly found themselves between the devil and the deep sea, without being driven to the latter by others.
The Chinese who are planning to come to Canada know little or nothing about the true situation caused by the sudden end of the war, and it is only right for your Government to refund the tax when it knew itself that 50 per cent of the so-called students applying for admission are unable to go to school at all. Your Government should be more rigid in examining these alleged students and more lenient in dealing with other exempted classes. But once the Chinese are admitted they should be entitled to every right and protection as any citizen or subject from other countries enjoying the most favoured agreement. I have heard so much of the Britisher's traditional sense of justice and I hope it will show itself in this case.
After all, this big question should be amicably settled by the government concerned while we are here simply to express our own points of view. I therefore suggest that the question brought up by the representatives from Fairview and Grandview be not considered by this council, and that the less talk about the Oriental immigration to mislead the public the better.
