The question of Oriental immigration must be considered from thq standpoint of the returned soldier, and I believe the returned soldiers' organizations are rather exercised over present conditions. This is an extract from the Vancouver World of February 27, 1919, which reflects the feeling fairly well:
In considering the problems dealing with the repatriation of returned men, some attention must he given to the Asiatic question, Captain P. C. Brown, of the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment Commission told the Kiwanis Club, on Thursday, in making an appeal for co-operation in behalf of the men who are now coming back from the front. During the months of January and February, no less than 3,000 men were brought back to this city and discharged, and of this number 1,700 are still without employment. In seeking the solution of this condition of affairs, he urged that earnest consideration would have to he given the Asiatic problem in this city, declaring that in some parts of Vancouver, one would never realize this city was not an Oriental city, to watch the passers-by and listen to the language being spoken. South of Granville Street bridge.

he mentioned that no less than seven Orientals were in business for themselves, and said that he had been informed by white merchants In competition with those Orientals that if they did not have to meet that competition they could employ more returned men. It was all very well to talk about those Orientals being Allies, he said, but it has also to he remembered that they did not go away and fight for the country.
He said there seemed to exist in the minds of some business men fear that the returned men would have to be discharged again if given employment, and in this connection put forward a plea for more consideration to he shown the returned man, pointing out that the man who had been through the thickest of the fighting at the front was usually the most difficult to get back to civil life again. He urged business men not to forget the service such a man had rendered his country and to keep up the spirit of gratitude.
I have stated that the Japanese have already obtained practically a monopoly of the fishing industry. They are now going out after other industries. They are commencing to take up small farming, and there is a feeling that if this movement goes on, they will, in a very short time, monopolize small farming in British Columbia. I have not one word to say against the Japanese. The Japanese are a fine people; their men are industrious, hardworking and sober. But still they come within the class to which I have referred, namely, those who cannot readily be assimilated. In this class, we have also the Hindu. I need not say anything more about the Hindu except that so far as I can see the Hindus who are being sent to this country are some of the very worst who could possibly be got together. In any event, they are not suitable for the country; they may like the country, but the country does not like them. With all this class, the same thing prevails, namely, they cannot readily be assimilated and they will always exist as an Oriental settlement in our midst. They send a great deal of their money back to their respective countries; they do not spend it in this country. They do not help to build up this country. They take away from, rather than give, to Canada something that is worth while. There is another class which 1 think should be kept out. That is a class of people who might be readily assimilated, but who are of such moral fibre that we do not want them just at present. I refer, of course, to our enemy aliens. We do not want any Germans, Austrians, Turks, in this country until they are so changed in their ideals that they will be able to look at things as we do, until they reach such a stage of mental development that they will make decent and respectable citizens of this

country, that is, if such a thing ever comes to pass. I notice that practically all the other Allied countries are deporting enemy aliens as fast as they can. China has despatched several boatloads of them. They are being deported from Belgium, France, England. Canada seems to be rather slow in getting rid of'her share. I agree with the previous speakers who have said that we should send the alien enemies out of Canada as soon as possible. If it is necessary and advisable to do that, surely we do not want to bring into Canada other people of the same class.
The third class of people that we should keep out of Canada is the Bolsheviks. We do not want them in this country. After hearing the splendid exposition made by the president of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) of the doctrines of the cult of Bolshevism, I think we will all agree that we do not want any Bolsheviks in this country.
There is a fourth class that we must keep out of Canada, and which is pretty nearly as bad. I refer to the I. W. W's., and included in that class are the labour agitators. I can speak from information which has been given to me as to conditions in British Columbia. During the last year, hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of damage has been done by the I. W. W's. in British Columbia.
Their doctrine is to destroy everything that is of value. They destroy timber by starting fires in the forests, reservoirs by blowing up the dams, machinery by letting the water out of boilers, and all that kind of thing. They destroy anything and everything, and during last year they have certainly destroyed a whole lot in British Columbia. I do not know what destruction they have been guilty of in other parts of Canada, but certainly we do not want these men in this country, no matter how much money they have. I class with the I. W. W. the professional agitator. He is the cause of all the trouble in labour circles at the present time. If you go back far enough you will find that every strike in Canada during the last few years was caused by two or three or half-a-dozen agitators. We should not let men of this sort come into the country, and we should drive out those already here. I agree with the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) that we need population in this country, but we want population of the right kind, and our immigration officials should be very careful as to the class of immigrant they admit. It is better to get along with our present population rather
than have it increased by any of the classes to w7honi I have referred.
I wish to say a word on behalf of the returned soldier. I am afraid there is a tendency already in this country to forget what the returned soldier has done for us.
I have heard it said that he is asking for too much, that he is unreasonable. I do not believe it. I do not believe that the men who had the interests of this country and of the civilized world sufficiently at heart to go over there and offer up their lives, if necessary, would make unreasonable demands on the people and resources of this country on their return home. All the returned soldier wants is a square deal, and he is certainly entitled to that. We should not forget his wonderful record in this war, and the great changes that have been brought about during the last four years by his fighting for us. Great mon-archs, like the German Emperor and the Czar of Russia, have lost their thrones and their governments are being reorganized. Other crowned heads have fallen, and the map of Europe, of Asia, Africa and other places is being made anew. Nowadays we talk of millions and billions without winking an eyelash and I think it is about time we changed our ideas of what should be done for the returned soldier. Never in the history of any country has the returned soldier got a square deal or been treated as he deserves. I am glad to see that the Government will bring down legislation on behalf of the returned soldier, in the way of increased pensions, for instance. I hope this Parliament will do a whole lot for the returned soldier. We certainly cannot do too much for him.
Mr. Speaker, you have borne with me very patiently. I trust that my remarks will bear fruit and that this Parliament will evolve means to solve the serious problems that now confront us.

Mr. Speaker, one day in the British House of Commons after the Rt. Hon. Walter Long had been speaking for three hours, Mr. Balfour's desk-mate whispered to him, "When is he going to finish?" Mr. Balfour answered, "He has finished long ago, but does not know how to stop." Without wishing to be discourteous to my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) I must say that I was reminded of that incident in the British House while he was speaking.
Mr. Speaker, the second session of the thirteenth Parliament of Canada opened

under very remarkable circumstances-circumstances which all those then present will never forget as a blending of joy and grief, of hope and distress. Joy, at the news that the monster of war that had been threatening humanity for four years had finally been vanquished and overthrown. Grief, at the death of the most prominent member of this House. Hope, that the treaty of peace would free humanity forever from sanguinary, contests. Distress, at the thought that the voice of the premier representative of Canadian statesmanship and patriotism would never again be heard in this House.
Mr. Speaker, I should be unworthy of the solicitude and kindness which the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier always showered upon me if my first utterance this afternoon were not a word of respect and admiration for the memory of one who, though dead, yet lives and will always live in the heart of every true 'Canadian. Sir, the achievements of his illustrious career have already been eloquently referred to by the church, the state, and the press. His wisdom, his brilliance, his loftiness as a statesman, his magnanimity, his magnetism and eloquence, indeed, the entire devotion of his life, from his first public utterance in the early sixties, up to a few weeks before his death, to the interests of peace, fraternity, and unity of creeds and races in this country will fill the noblest and brightest pages of Canadian history. But, Sir, he will especially be remembered and cherished on account of his kindness of heart and his generous courtesy even to the most humble. " I am ' glad Sir Wilfrid Laurier did not die while he was Premier of Canada," was the remark I overheard at the funeral of the great statesman. This remark was made by a modest, unknown citizen. "Why?" I venture to ask. "Well, sir," he said, "if Sir Wilfrid Laurier had died while he was Premier this tribute of admiration, and all the expressions of sympathy which have been made in regard to him from every part of Canada, would probably have been attributed to his high position in the state. But look at these enormous crowds lining the streets of the Capital and bearing visible signs of grief, people from every part of the country; they are not lamenting the death of a premier, they are mourning the sudden and final cessation of a heart whose every throb was alive for his country and his people."
The impressive ceremony could not fail to remind me of Tennyson's immortal words:-

The dark crowd moves and there are sobs ana tears,
The black earth yawns, the mortal disappears Ashes to ashes, dust to dust,
He is gone who seemed so great.
Gone, but nothing oan bereave him Of the Force he made his own Being here, and we believe him Something far advanced in State,
And that he wears a truer Crown
Than any wreath that man can weave him.
Speak no more of his renown;
Hay your earthly fancies down,
And in his peaceful rest leave him.
God accept him, Christ receive him.
Mr. (Speaker, I heartily join in the congratulations which have been showered on the mover and the seconder of the Address, in such profusion that it would have made the hon. members blush with confusion had they not been accustomed to more severe bombardments, and although I believe that the honour conferred upon them had the effect of making them rather eulogistic ot the Government, their effort on the whets was very creditable.
I may, however, express regret at the fact that the well established custom of having the seconder's speech delivered in French >
was departed from in this instance. This departure is surely not an indication of progress towards racial unity in Canada. The official excuse given was that the Government, having exhausted last year their French-speaking talent in the person of the hon. junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chabot) were not in a position to follow the custom. Now, I think that this action on the part of the Government is an emphatic and uncalled for ejectment from the Unionist party of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Mackie), who speaks French very fluently, and, I may add, eloquently, and who, as the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) has said, could not possibly have mutilated the beautiful language of Moliere and Racine. Be that as it may, I concur entirely in the sentiments expressed by the hon. gentlemen who moved and seconded the Address and other hon. gentlemen who have spoken, in their .plea for a better understanding be-
5 p.m. tween the races and creeds in Canada.
I have carefully preserved all the printed references which have been made to our late departed chief by hon. members of the House and by the press, and have pasted them in a scrap book, already containing articles emanating from the same gentlemen, and the same press during the campaign of 1917. It will be an edifying and instructive page of history for my son to

read when he shall have attained the age of fifteen.
Mr. Speaker, the first part of the speech from the Throne I cannot but concur in, that is the expression of relief at the cessation of hostilities, and the victory of the Allies. The happiness which our brave boys will bring back with them will be marred only by the memory of those who Will never return, and who are now sleeping their last sleep in the blood-stained fields of France and Flanders. This victory is not a victory of one of the Allies, but of all the Allies. Little Belgium held the enemy for a few weeks at a tremendous sacrifice. France, by the indomitable courage of her troops and the genius of her generals, held the foe until relief could be sent. The British Empire, with her watchdogs of the sea and her army always increasing, stopped the invader. Italy, buckled up Austria, and our neighbours to the south, although arriving late, delivered a crushing blow. Mr. Speaker, when the history of this war is written, it will be shown that it was not a victory of any one of the Allies, but that the victory could not have been achieved without the co-operation of each and all of them.	.
But, thank God, this butchery is over, and we read in the speech from the Throne that, prior to the armistice, plans had been made for the return, demobilization and reestablishment in civil life after the close of the war of our soldiers and their dependents overseas. I am not thoroughly acquainted with the work of the department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, but it seems to me that the word " prior " at the beginning of this item is not very accurate in reference to the resignation of the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) and the official cause of his withdrawal. The news of the conditions, and the riots at Kinmel Camp, seems to confirm our belief that the chairman of the Repatriation Committee was perfectly right when, in the first part of his speech, he repeated three times that the armistice took him by surprise. I am informed from a reliable source that the conditions at the camps are intolerable. A returned man of the 42nd, who enlisted in 1914, arrived at the camp on the 27th December last and stayed there a month. Nearly all the men at this camp are invalids and have been wounded. The officers in charge force them to work and assign them to all kinds of hard and dirty jobs. The officers do not take into account the length of service of a man when the question of
return comes up and many men who have been in Europe for a few months are returned before those who had been fighting in France since the beginning of the war. The men are only told a few hours before their departure. The returned man who gave this information started from the camp at 12 p.m. He had to walk five miles to the station. No care was taken of the crippled, the wounded, the sick or the invalided. The officer ordered these men to take their kits on their backs and it took them two hours to reach their destination. Some of the men were totally exhausted. These men, I am informed, had asked for motors, or carriages, for their transportation and they were refused.
I heard from another man who enlisted as a private in 1914, and who arrived a few days ago. He had been over there since the beginning. He was promoted to a lieutenancy on the battlefield and he had been wounded three times and invalided. He was booked to return at the beginning of January last. He prepared himself to come back, but he was notified on the eve of his departure that an officer who had only been in London for three months attending pink teas, was taking his place and the wounded and invalided man had to wait another month.
In a beautiful booklet artistically printed by the minister and distributed by the Repatriation Committee, we are told that since the armistice the men have been classified in order to their better civil re-establishment. Since the armistice? Why, Mr. Speaker, this work had been done for the soldiers of France, England and the United States months prior to the armistice. This situation is a disgrace to this country and shows an incompetency on the part of the department and of the authorities in charge which cannot be too strongly criticised and denounced.
There are many other items in the speech from the Throne which will need our careful consideration. Amongst them is the question of prohibition. I am not prepared to give my view of this legislation before it is brought down in a more concrete form, but I wish to warn the Government of one thing. If it is their intention to have total prohibition, I hope the measure which they will introduce will not be a law of exemption like the Ontario Temperance Act. The remark made the other day in this House by my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), that in Ontario men are not valued by the amount of wealth they have but by the amount of liquor they possess

is perfectly true. A few months ago I happened to spend a week in Toronto one Sunday and I asked to be shown the beautiful residences of the city. The taxi driver, when I inquired of him who was living in such-and-such a beautiful place, told me: This is Mr. So-and-So; he has $50,000 worth of liquor in his cellar.
Sir, some of my hon. friends were surprised the other day at the -threatening menace of Bolshevism in this country. No wonder, with such measures as the Ontario Temperance Act. Why should the man of wealth, the profiteer, be allowed to gather regular warehouses of liquor and drink as much as he likes, while the working man of modest means, not being able to mobilize his meagre capital, will be sent to jail if he dares attempt to indulge in the very limited consumption of a glass of beer with his meals? Is it fair for the returned man to hear when he comes hack, that while he was fighting overseas, those for whom he was risking his life were " stocking up," and at the same time framing and passing a law to restrict his liberty and deprive him of legitimate enjoyment? There are, Mr. Speaker, sincere and deserving people preaching prohibition, deserving apostles of prohibition, and I entertain a most profound respect for them; but there are also hypocrites, and I want to know where they are. If total prohibition is passed, let us clean the cellars, let us publish a list of all those who have liquor in their houses, or, if my suggestion is better, let us pass a law-
An Order in Council.

Or an Order in Council which will force the hypocrites to wear a badge or a button, with a yellow star for every case of liquor they possess; then, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that some of the most vituperous prohibitionists will look like Indians. Mr. Speaker, prohibition-I mean total prohibition-does not seem to be very popular nowadays. Let me read you a few extracts from this week's issue of the Toronto Saturday Night. I quote:
Out in Alberta the Stewart Government has, in utter desperation, abolished the Commission created to enforce the Prohibition Act, and has "passed the buck" to the Hon. John Boyle, Attorney-General. In turn the Attorney-General also takes a pessimistic view of the situation. For instance, in a speech on the floor of the Legislature the other day, he remarked that out of the 100,000 estimated male adults of the province 60,000 of them were guilty of some infringement of the Liquor Act during 1918. That the violation of the Liquor Act in British Columbia is the chief form of popular amusement in that province Is too well known
fMr. Al'chambauit.]
to require further comment, other than to remark that it is estimated by British Columbians of unquestioned standing that fully eighty-five per cent of the male adults in that neck of the woods have in some form or other broken the prohibition enactments.
Oh, oh.

Now let us come to a province geographically nearer to us. The paper says:
In centres like Toronto we were promised that when prohibition was in force crime would decrease until there would actually be no use for jails or police. What has been the result? According to the annual report of Chief of Police Grasset, of Toronto, 25,714 persons were apprehended for crime in the year 1917, as compared with 28,206 in 1918, an increase of 2,492 for "dry" 1918. The Chief goes on to state the obvious: "There is no reason to believe that the morals of the people are improving."
Among the members of the Ontario House there are gloomy forebodings. When prohibition is mentioned a chill runs up and down the spines of the members, and more particularly Government members. They are all wondering how the prohibition cat is going to jump. They look back to the half score byelections and their pedal extremities seem colder than the mild winter warrants. In a word, they are in a "blue funk." The other day Colonel H. A. Machin, who sits as Conservative member of Kenora, had his first opportunity since returning from overseas, to express views on the subject. In speaking of the growth of Phariseeism in Ontario, the gallant Colonel referred to the "sin hound" who spent his time trailing people who wanted to live their own lives in their own way, and he reminded his hearers that Canadians had gone "over there" he among them, to fight for democracy and human liberty, and they came back to find their own liberty as British subjects taken away from them. The Colonel made it clear that he did not wish the return of the bar, but he did believe that the present wave of fanatical Puritanism had led the Government into taking unwarranted steps, and in so doing had trampled underfoot the rights of the individual.
I would say furthermore, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to have total prohibition, let us have machinery that will enforce the
law, so that dynamite whiskey-to use some expressions from the West-squirrel gin, or rot gut, sold in blind pigs will not ruin the health of those who are not millionaires or profiteers.
I was astonished, Mr. Speaker, upon reading the speech from the Throne, to find that it contained not one line about the high cost of living. After a few moments' reflection, however, I found out the reason. I discovered again the hidden hand of the masters of this Government, the profiteers, who will not permit any attempt at the deflation of the cost of -the necessities of life. The Labour Gazette of last month shows no relief in the matter of the price

of these necessities-meat, eggs, milk, etc. And, Sir, the profit on these things goes not to the producer or to the farmer, but to the food king.
Perhaps the House will be interested to know the profits of the milling companies for 1917-and I am told that those for 1918 are even higher. The Ogilvie Flour Mills in 1913 made $470,000 in profits, and in 1917, $2,100,000. Their reserve fund in 1913 was $473,000; it is now $2,690,000. Up to 1916 their dividend had been 8 per cent; in 1916 it was 12 per cent, and in 1917, during the war, when everybody was told to be economical, it was 26 per cent, war taxes paid.
The Lake of the Woods 'Milling Company made $385,000 in profits in 1913 and $700,000 in 1917. In 1913 the dividend was 10.7 per cent; in 1916, 14 per cent, and in 1917, 18 per cent. Although the company redeemed $800,000 of bonds from 1913 to 1917, its actual reserve fund is now a million dollars more than it was in 1913.
The Maple Leaf Milling Company made $241,844 in profits in 1914 and $1,763,000 in 1917. After deducting $1,000,000 a year for depreciation, it still had $1,100,000 by way of net profits in 1917.
The Western Canada Flour Mills paid a war tax of $35,000 in 1917, but this did not prevent their profits, which were $445,000 in 1913, from climbing to $840,000 in 1917, to say nothing of an important amount paid up to their sinking fund.
Other milling companies of less importance made a brilliant showing. For instance, one of these which had a deficit oi $62,000 in 19l3 had a surplus of $138,000 in 1917. The result is that we have to pay an exorbitant price for bread, 7i to 8i cents a pound. Mr. Speaker, I could go on giving you figures on the same scale in respect to practically every necessity of life
Were the increased profits of the millers the result of an increased turnover or an increase in the profit per barrel on flour?

I am not prepared to answer my hon. friend now, but I will tell him this: When the people are paying more and more for bread and the millers are making more excessive profits every day, something is wrong somewhere. That is common sense.
Our food control is a joke. We have another very artistic booklet. The Government is evidently in the printing business for good, and is flourishing at it, as you have noticed by the report of the commission appointed to inquire into conditions at the Printing
Bureau and the present strike of employees in that institution. What do we find in this booklet? We find that the revenue derived from food licenses "was $531,719 last year, and that it cost the people of Canada $491,000 to collect that amount. Is that good business, Mr. Speaker. Is that good management? No wonder the speech from the Throne did not touch this question. Imagine what the returned hero, who for four years has been risking his life at the front, will say when he finds his wife driven to despair and his children starving on account of the prohibitive prices of foodstuffs.
Another omission from the speech from the Throne was any reference to a matter which recently was of but minor importance, but which last year, through the action of the prime (Minister of Canada, developed into a matter of great importance. I refer to the question of titles. I was surprised that there was no mention of that subject in the speech from the Throne. You will remember, Sir, that last year, when the House was practically unanimous on this question, the Prime Minister came into the House armed with his whip and threatened to resign if the members on your right did not swallow all they had said and vote against their opinions. The Prime Minister gave as his principal reason for his action at that time, if I remember well, the fact that His Majesty's Government had asked that the proposal be stayed until the holding of the Imperial Conference, when the matter would be settled. He intimated that the action of the Conference would be recorded before the next session, and that in the meantime no titles would be granted. The member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) stuck to his guns and to his honour. The member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan), and the member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden) gave their support to the Government on the express condition that the matter would be discussed at the Imperial Conference and that in the meantime no titles should be granted. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) wanted to withdraw his motion, and when he could not withdraw it, on account of the objection of the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe), he declined to support the amendment he himself proposed. The hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) did the aeroplane act and flew out of the room. The crack of the lashes of the Prime Minister's whip is still ringing in my ears, and I still see the hon. members crouching before their master. What happened,

what was done	at the	conference?The speech from the Throne should have enlightened	us	on	this subject, but it does not, and I am therefore not in a position to know what was done. But what I know, and what every hon. member knows, is that a few weeks after this slavish incident, contrary to the solemn promise of the Prime Minister, titles were conferred on three persons, one of them being the Minister of Trade and Commerce who must have known what was coming to him when he defended the titles a few days before with a voice trembling with pathos and tears.

Who were the others?
Mr. ARCHAMiBAULT: If I am correctly informed, one of them was the brother of the Prime Minister and the other was the Clerk of the Senate, formerly, private secretary of the Prime Minister.
Then there was a gentleman from London.

A question close. ly connected with the high cost of living is the labour question to which the speech from the Throne makes no reference. Is it possible that the Government is so blind that it does not see the tidal wave of labour unrest and legitimate revindications threatening to invade and flood our political and social institutions? Is it the intention of the Government to wait until these institutions are swamped without hope of rescue, before they wake up to realities and shake off their criminal indolence? Is it not time that the barons of finance, the industrial and railroad kings should not be given the powerful liberty of imposing upon the country their political wishes and of exercising on Canada an arrogant and unjustified dictatorship? In these times of the rejuvenation of the world, the workingman is no longer satisfied to be the material instrument producing wealth for the profiteers, without receiving any share of the comforts of life for himself and his family. Unless the workingman has confidence in his employer and is given for his own protection and welfare, a reasonable control in the management of industries, we are bound to see this peaceful country become the prey of dangerous agitators. In England, the Government has decided to apply the Whiteley system of giving the workingman a share in the management of Government workshops and yards. I hope this Government will see fit to adopt a similar measure and at the same time to provide old age pensions for the workingman.

Of all the speeches made by hon. members on your right, Mr. Speaker, the one which impressed me most was the eloquent address of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder). But after it was all over, I tried to relate to a friend of 'mine what the minister had said, and although my memory is fair, all that I could remember when the noise had ceased, and the western tornado had passed, was, first, that hostilities had ceased very suddenly; secondly, that hostilities had ceased much sooner than had been expected; thirdly, that the end of the war came suddenly, and fourthly, that he was still a Liberal; that no person could make him anything else, and that no one could drive him out of the Liberal party. Not relying upon my memory, I waited until the next day and on reading his speech in Hansard, I found that my remembrance was right.
As to the first three points, unpreparedness, unpreparedness and unpreparedness I would respectfully suggest to the Acting Prime Minister that a new department be created and called the Department of " Lack of Foresight " with the Minister of Immigration at the head of it, As to the fourth point, the minister seemed to be the porte-parole and premier exponent of a certain number of hon. members on the other side, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) included. I wish to ask a few questions of the minister, and I am very glad to see him now in his seat. I do not insist that he should reply immediately to my questions; but I wish he would spend just a few minutes of his valuable time on them, and see if the answers to these questions are quite satisfactory to his political conscience. First of all, what is Liberalism? Is it an association composed of members who are at liberty to belong to it when they wish, who can join when they want to, who can be expelled from it, no matter what their ideals or principles are; or is it a creed, a faith, a group of fundamental principles? Is it not repugnant to reason and to the teachings of political history that no matter what are his principles, his ideals, nay, his	company, a man can always
call himself a Liberal and be an	adept exponent of Liberalism.
I quite agree with the hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder)-I was almost going to say the Minister of Unpreparedness-that no one has the authority to rule him out of the Liberal party. He has a perfect right to call himself a disciple of Liberalism as long as he wishes, but I submit that his assertion, in order not to

be in conflict with the truth, must be supported by his principles, by his ideals, and by his company. I refer, of course, to his political principles and ideals. Let us see whether his principles and ideals are those of Liberalism. What is Liberalism? I have read somewhere that Liberalism is, in essence, the problem of realizing liberty. It seeks the setting free of the mass of the people in regard to self-government, trade, religion, education, and industry in all the manifold ramifications of society. The opposite to Liberalism is restriction, and means the centralization of government in the governing classes, the setting of the brakes on social progress and liberty. The aim of Liberalism is the common good: the aim of those opposed to Liberalism is the individual good. Gladstone said that the principle of Liberalism is, "Trust in the people, qualified by prudence." The principle of Unionism is mistrust of the people, qualified by fear. Mr. Asquith has said that "Liberalism is a living faith, a spirit, an attitude of mind, a form of political temperament and genius, a temperament, which, whenever it sees a wrong, would redress it absolutely, and wherever it discerns a cause for grievance anywhere^ would pluck that cause out by the roots." In three words I will give you, Mr. Speaker, my own conception of Liberalism: Masses versus Classes.
Now that we know what Liberalism is, let us see if the hon. Minister of Immigration has lived up to Liberalism. As a minister in the Unionist Cabinet, he is responsible constitutionally for all the acts of the _ Government, and constitutionally again, if he wishes to relieve himself of this responsibility his only course is to resign. Not having done so,-and there are no signs that he intends doing so-I logically surmise that all the measures of the Government have his approval.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to put my questions. Is the voting against a measure abolishing titles in Canada included in the Liberal doctrine? Will my hon. (friend pretend that the War-Time Elections Act, breaking faith with thousands of citizens and dragging the honour of Canada and its fair name in the mud, is a Liberal measure? Is it the opinion of the minister that the Military Voters' Act, especially in view of the purpose for which it was used in the last election, is imbued with pure Liberalism? Was not the campaign of racial and religious prejudice carried out by the Government to which the hon. gentleman sticks like a leech anything but Liberalism? Is the consolidation of the financial ring of Toronto, erstwhile denounced by my hon. friend, an action that he could call Liberal? Is the companionship of food profiteers end the benevolent paternalism of bacon earls fit foi any one who still calls himself a Liberal? Are the instructions to the military officers to disregard the orders of the established courts in accordance with Liberal principles? Is the exemption of Victory bonds from taxation, which is nothing less than a camouflage enactment to protect those who have enriched themselves during the war from paying income tax, a Liberal measure? Can my hon. friend state, without wincing, that the censorship of the press and the gagging of independent opinion is pure Liberalism?	Is not
the censorship on publications, which goes so far as to make it a criminal offence ^ for any one to have in his possession Plato's Republic, anything but Liberal? Is the wholesale buying of the press of this country for political purposes a Liberal measure? Is the incompetency and indifference to the welfare of the masses, a,s evidenced by the present high cost of living with no relief in sight, true Liberalism? Is my hon. friend aware that Liberalism stands for a just share by the working man in the profits of industry? Does ^ my hon. friend believe that militarism in its most truly Prussian form can be regarded as an offspring of democracy? Will my hon. friend dare to contend that the forcible sending of men to Siberia without authorization of Parliament is in accordance with Liberal ideals? I should also like to know whether it was a Liberal sentiment which prevented representatives of the people from being called into counsel during the most momentous nine months in our history?
Does the flagrant abuse of the War Measures Act, passed at a very critical time, appeal to the Liberalism of my hon. friend? Is the Government of the people by Orders in Council, even when Parliament is sitting, considered by my hon. friend a Liberal measure? Did my hon". friend ever consider that the passing of Orders in Council, with retroactive effect, is in direct violation of the liberty of the citizen? Can the hon. minister contend that the operation of the War Measures Act,^ three months after the war is over, to . liquidate a railway company, is up to Liberal standards?

Mr. Speaker, before recess I was in the middle of ail argument regarding the Liberalism of the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization and that section of the Government who hold his views and still believe that they can logically call themselves Liberals, and remain on your right. I had, to the best of my ability, given to the House my opinion of Liberalism, and the definitions of such men as Gladstone and Asquith. I then proceeded to put certain questions to the minister, and I had a few left when six o'clock arrived. I now beg leave to proceed with them. Did my hon. friend ever consider that the passing of Orders in Council with retroactive effect is an entire violation ol the liberty of the citizen? Can the minister contend that the use of the War Measures Act, three months after the war is over, to put a railway in liquidation is up to the Liberal standard? Is my hon. friend of the opinion that the handing on a plate of a parliamentary seat to a friend of the Government, distrusting at the same time the judicial authority of the Supreme Court of Canada, an action derived from the best examples of Liberalism? Does the minister believe that secret Orders in Council are not against Liberal doctrine? Well, Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand an extra of the Official Gazette of 7th February last, in which nine Orders in Council passed at different dates, one as far back as the 28th September, 1917, are published for the first time-seventeen months after they were passed. To prove my assertion I will cite pages 24 and 25 of the Canada Gazette of 7th February last. The introductory passage says:
The nine following Orders in Council were first published in the Extra of the Canada Gazette dated the 7th February, 1919.
The first Order in Council is dated 28th September, 1917; the second, 4th October, 1917; the third, 24th December, 1917; and the next, 8th day of January, 1918. But, listen to this. The next one is dated Wednesday, 1st May, 1918. Government by Order in Council is bad. It is contrary to constitutional Government and must only be resorted to with prudence and in cases of extreme urgency. But government by secret Order in Council is surely the limit

of autocracy. Yet, Mr. Speaker, it is not the limit to the Kaiserism and Czarism of the present Government. There is one of these Orders in Council passed 1st May, 1918, and published for the first time on 7th February, 1919, to which I especially wish to direct the attention of the House. It contains the following enactment:
Any person who makes default in the performance of a duty imposed upon him by this paragraph shall be liable on summary conviction to imprisonment for three months with hard labour or to a fine of $100 or to both.
The fact that a man might be sent to prison for not obeying a regulation adopted in secret by the Government and never made known, even to the limited class that reads the Canada Gazette line upon line, shows to what lengths governments may go when allowed to be, as the present Government were, more or less, a law unto themselves. Surely the Liberalism of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization is the Liberalism of the Middle Ages when men were sent to dungeons by lettres de cachet at the will of the autocrat. His ultra Liberalism leads him to pass a law creating an offence punishable with imprisonment at hard labour and enabling him to jail a citizen for an offence that he could not possibly have committed. If my hon. friend has the ability, or the elasticity of political conscience to reconcile such measures with Liberal principles he will have well deserved the surname which was given to him of being "the Bob Rogers of the new Administration."
It is useless for me to take up any more of the time of this House in order to show that the company that my hon. friend is keeping is only, as my revered departed chief said last year, Toryism with a little veneer. However, I submit that the only way in which the Minister of Immigration and Colonization can make good his claim that he is still a Liberal is by answering the questions that I have put to him. If his answers satisfy the Liberal party, I will say no more, I shall be satisfied; but if the hon. gentleman's answers should not satisfy the Liberal party then how will he stand with the Unionist party at whose christening he is understood to be anxious to officiate? It is not for me to answer that question, but I have no doubt that his Unionist colleagues would like to hear from the hon. gentleman a full report about ' his visit to Quebec a short time ago, as to whom he met and what was discussed. Lastly, when the hon. gentleman has studied

all these questions, will he not say that he is trying to clothe himself in the livery of Heaven to serve the devil?
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) made a statement last night against which I desire to register my most vigorous protest. After indulging in n remarkable eulogy of b'rance he spoiled his tribute of respect by saying that last year France was ready to ciuit. Sir, France has never quit; France cannot quit; France cannot die because she is immortal. My hon. fiiend cannot phnt to one incident in the whole history of France in which she did not finish w'hat she had started. She did. not even quit in 1870, when she was left alone and defenceless to fight the Prussian invasion; and if last year France made some remonstrances it was because some public men amongst her Allies were not willing to adopt the only policy which enabled us to beat the Hun -unity of command. My hon. friend from Springfield also seems to be a very ardent supporter of the Government, and although he has painted a most vivid and pathetic picture of the battlefields of France-for which he has my entire endorsation-the cause of his admiration and devotion to this Government may not be strange to the treatment which he received over there.
I wish my education in English would allow me to introduce into my description of the feasts he attended, the slangy expressions and phraseology with which he has decorated his address; but not having had the opportunity that the hon. gentleman had of associating with the distinguished people using these expressions, I am only going to give the House a report of one incident which happened while my hon. friend was attending one of the many banquets tendered to him while in England. I am quoting now from a British paper;
R. L,. Richardson, M.P., is extremely fond of grapes. He attended a Guildhall banquet recently as a member of that expedition of Canadian editors which has been irreverently termed "Beaverbrook's printers' picnic," and being seated immediately in front of a huge fruit-basket filled with the luscious hot-house product, he proceeded to gratify his cravings with the same nonchalance as if he were in Canada. Famished Englishmen who noted his fine work estimate that at the current price (about 7 cents a grape), the Editor of the Winnipeg Tribune put away some eleven dollars' worth.
Mr. Speaker, while listening to my hon. friend Tuesday night, and hearing him state that he never believed in the sincerity of the Liberal party regarding the tariff
I could not but call to memory the Macdonald election, when the hon. gentleman told the electors of that constituency the unmistakable faith he had in the Liberal party on tariff matters-that was in 1912, was it not?-and his unequivocal belief in the insincerity of the Premier of Canada, and I could not do otherwise than recall the banquet where, like Noah of old, he showed a propensity for the product of the vine, and my natural conclusion was that the eleven dollars' worth of grapes which he introduced into his anatomy some months ago have fermented and produced the spirit of affection which he displayed for the Government on Tuesday night.
I am coming now, Mr. Speaker, to a much graver question. Of course the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) had to have his usual attack on Quebec, otherwise he would have been censured at the next meeting of his lodge, as the hon. member for Toronto was last year. But I submit, Sir, with all due respect to the brethren, that the hon. member for Frontenac was not particularly happy or convincing in his argument. The hon. member gave us some figures about the number of men who joined the Expeditionary Force from the different provinces, and although he has not indicated the source of his figures, or whether they are official or not,
I have no doubt he acted in good faith when he gave them. But, even supposing, for the sake of argument, that the hon. gentleman's figures were correct, I cannot agree with his conclusion. As the basis of his argument to indicate the number of men who enlisted from" different counties of the province of Quebec, he took the official return of the elections in 1917, showing how many soldiers voted in each constituency. He said, for instance, that in the constituency of the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) only fifteen soldiers polled votes and he concludes that only fifteen soldiers left that constituency. Sir, after the debate on the military votes last session no one can seriously contend that the return of such votes can constitute a sound basis to determine the number of soldiers who enlisted in each constituency in the Dominion. The votes of the soldiers were placed at will by the "democratic" agents of this "democratic" Government in the constituencies where they would be most useful. This, Sir, was proved beyond a doubt, and was even openly admitted at the judicial inquiry at St. Johns into the military vote, where soldiers and officers did not conceal

the fact that their purpose was to vote, not in the constituencies where they came from but in the constituencies where their votes would be most useful to the Union Government. The member for Kamouraska informs me that a great number of the military electors of his constituency were forced to poll their votes in the constituency of Cumberland, N.S. May I digress a moment to request the Government not to forget, when they carry out their housing scheme, to provide homes for the six hundred odd officers and men of the Engineer Training Depot at St. Johns who swore that they had no residence in Canada.
As to the other figures given by the member for Frontenac, although I believe in his good faith I am inclined to think that his elaborate calculation about the number of men who should have enlisted in proportion to the population is utterly unfair. Let me remind him and the House, Mr. Speaker, first, that the number of persons engaged in agriculture in Quebec is much larger in proportion to the population than it is in Ontario; second, that the male population under eighteen is about five times as numerous in Quebec in proportion to population as in Ontario or in the other English-speaking provinces; third, that the number of married men in Quebec between the ages of eighteen and thirty-five is about five times as great in proportion to population as in Ontario and in the other provinces; fourth, that the British-born in the English provinces are about twenty times more numerous than they are in the province of Quebec.
Another basic element in connection with this matter which, I believe, has not been discussed in the House, was brought to my attention by an article published in Toronto Saturday Night. I was surprised to read such an article, and before I communicate it to the House, in order that my sentiments shall not be distorted, I wish to state that 1 have the utmost admiration and respect for the men who went overseas and who made sacrifices in so doing. Nothing is too good for them and their dependents in this country, and the Government should provide with the utmost care and diligence for their welfare and civil re-establishment. Having made these preliminary remarks, let me read the article to which I refer:
You have seen what a real hero looks like. Thank Heaven he is plentiful enough to be recognized! Now take a squint at the other sort. Here he comes down the street. Observe him closely, for he is a type, and in his own person sums up all the charges that can be made against the wrong kind of returned hero. 
Before the war he was one of our "unassimilated population.'' He worked in spots, and the spots were not many. He never liked work here or anywhere else, then or now. He never had a job that demanded more than a twelve-year-old boy's intelligence, but now that he has come back he wants a clerical job, "no manual labour" if you please, and a gentleman's salary. He has become one of the leisured class, and fancies no labour harder than lifting his envelope once a week, or once a month, or whatever the term of loafing may be. His idea is to live on the Government, which will make a job for him even when there is no job and he isn't fit for it anyway.
The chances are that he is not a hero at all, that he never got farther than Shorncliffe, that he was an unfit or a bad 'un and was sent home for cause. But take him at his own value and give him the once-over. Cap on the back of his head, no shave, tunic unbuttoned,
belt missing, trousers rumpled, shoes dirty_____
looks as if he had slept in the back-yard of a livery stable all night. He went to the war to get a "trip 'orae,'' and now that he is back without having seen anything of the war nearer than Folkestone, he brings a grouch .with him.
Sir, this article gives me another reason why the figures of the member for Frontenac are not sound. It is this: In Quebec we have not the type described in Toronto Saturday Night. In Quebec, every French Canadian who left made a sacrifice. In Quebec, not a French Canadian left to make a "trip home;" his only home is Canada. In Quebec, every French Canadian who went overseas left behind him dear relatives, often feeble and poor. In Quebec, not one French Canadian who left could be classed as one of our "unassimilated population." I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that the member for Frontenac has given this opportunity of finding why the enlistments in some provinces were large while in Quebec they were not. I repeat that I would not have discussed this matter again had not the member for Frontenac resorted to his bad habit of attacking Quebec every time he addresses this House. Let us hope that he has done so for the last time.
Sir, the union, harmony and fraternity between the two greatest races in the world, the French and the British, have been cemented forever on the battlefields of Europe, and I cannot find a more appropriate way of ending my remarks than by repeating the words which were uttered in this House by my revered and departed leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, during the Boer-War. He said:
Men representing both elements of the Canadian family have been fighting shoulder to shoulder for the same cause and under the same flag.
Some of them have made the supreme sacrifice, their bodies rest in the same grave, in a

fraternal clasp, until the end of time; are we not allowed to hope, aract this will be my last word, that in this grave will toe touried forever the last remnants of our strifes and differences.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words this evening, and while I have not trespassed upon the time of the House before,
I shall make my remarks very brief, because this debate is drawing to a close, and I am sure the members and the public in general are not anxious to hear a rehash of all the arguments which have been put forward. At the outset, I wish to offer my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the Address and to add my congratulations and approval to their efforts, which are especially pleasing to me because they are both men who have served their King and country overseas. It is a matter of special gratification to me because the seconder of the Address is a member of my own profession.
We, in Canada, I am sure, all rejoice in the grand and glorious termination of the war. We are proud of the part that Canada has taken and played in this titanic struggle. We are also proud of the imperishable fame which our Canadian boys have brought to Canada.
We are now face to face with the problem of getting some three or four hundred thousand men re-established in civil life. This is not an easy task, and the country has this and many other problems of great importance to deal with. Let us consider, for a moment, what this means. During the past four years, our whole machinery has been untilized towards the developing of a fighting programme. We are now bound to bring ourselves back once more to conditions of peace. The man who has been in the army for one, two, three or four years, has had some one to think and provide for him. He did not have to worry where his next meal or his next suit of clothes was * coming from. Everything was provided for him, even medical attendance in case of sickness or accident. When he returns, he will be thrown on his own resources and will have to provide all these necessities for himself. In many cases he is not the same man as he was when he left our shores. He has many times gazed into the jaws of death, and it is not to be expected that he should be the same man mentally and physically as he was when he went away. I want right here to sound a warning to employers of labour on this man's behalf. Since coming back to Canada I have, in connection with medical boards, come in contact with these men appearing for medical examination with regard to
pensions. I have, as a medical man, observed that these men are not the same mentally or physically as when they went away. I have watched them come back and get employment in Canada. I have watched them try one job after another, become dissatisfied with one job, throw it up and try something else. Many of them are not able to give one hundred per cent of service. All I ask for them is that the employer shall be a little patient with the returned soldier and in a short time he will be as good as he was when he left.
I am sure the Government is to be congratulated on the energetic manner in which they are dealing with these problems which are new and with which no country has had to deal with before. The huge programme of expenditure which the Government have in view will go far towards providing employment for all, and I- was glad to hear the Acting Prime Minister state that in a few months there would be no unemployment in Canada. We must all recognize that we have a duty to perform in this matter, and we must not throw the burden of responsibility from one to another, or as the common phrase seems to be " pass the buck." The Government of this Dominion has a great duty to perform in providing employment for these men. The governments of the different provinces, the municipal authorities, and so on all down the line, must bear their share of the burden. During the past four years public expenditures have been reduced to a minimum. Public works have gone into disrepair. The time has now come when these public works must be put into a proper state of repair and proposed public buildings which have been left in abeyance must be erected. This will take care of a great deal of the excess of labour.
One thing in the speech from the Throne with which I am very much pleased is the statement that the Government have finally decided to constitute a department of public health. I consider this one of the most important pieces of legislation, if not the most important, to be introduced in this House at this session. We take great pride in conserving all our natural resources, but I consider the greatest asset or resource which we possess is our national life. This should be taken care of and fostered, and right at the outset I would say, not that a medical man should be in charge of this department, but that, to get the best results, a medical man must be in charge of this department. The duties of this department would, amongst other things, be to regulate immigration, to protect child labour, to deal with tuberculosis, venereal

diseases, contagious and infectious diseases, such as typhoid fever, etc. It seems to me -and I am sure it is a fact-that the country and the people in general do not appreciate the seriousness of the ravages of tuberculosis.
The statistics for 1916, which are the latest I have, show that in that year the deaths from tuberculosis were as follows: Ontario 2,559, or 92 out of every 100,000 people; Quebec 3,327 or 150 out of every 100,000; Saskatchewan 323, or 45 out of every 100,000; British Columbia 413, or 108 out of every 100,000; Nova Scotia 921, or 181 out of every 100,000; Manitoba 484, or 96 out of every 100,000. There probably is no disease which can be cured more readily than tuberculosis if treated in the early stages. During the latter stages, of course, the deaths are practically 100 per cent. When the disease is recognized by medical men in the early stages and the patient put under proper treatment, at least 90 per cent of these cases can be restored to health. This is a matter of vital importance to the people of Canada. In 1916, 8,027 deaths occurred in this Dominion from tuberculosis, and I am sure that if we had proper housing conditions and sanitaria conveniently situated throughout all the provinces where people attacked by the disease could receive proper treatment, the great majority of these people-would be living to-day and be an asset to this country. But the trouble now is that we have not sufficient sanitaria to take care of these people, and sometimes the responsibility is shifted from one province to another. A doctor in the East, for instance, will recommend a patient suffering from tuberculosis to go to British Columbia because the climate there may do him good. The patient may arrive in British Columbia in the latter stages of the disease and if the authorities there have not hospital accommodation for that man they may say,
" You do not belong to us but .to Nova Scotia or New Brunswick; go back there." Now that condition of affairs is not right and I trust that when the Department of Public Health is established it will turn its attention first to this great'problem of tuberculosis and inaugurate and encourage the building of sanitaria throughout this Dominion. The sanitaria should be built and supported by the Dominion because the responsibility for the lives of the people of this Dominion rests upon this Government.
I have looked into some of the Government's plans for settling our soldiers on the land, and although in a matter of this

kind one is bound to proceed rather slowly I am pleased to see that .splendid progress is being made. In the province of British Columbia we have in our valleys land as fertile as can be found in any other place in the world, and thousands of the soldiers who enlisted from that province will take up land and go on the farm. Many thousands also will be attracted from the other provinces by our climate. The province of British Columbia probably offers a brighter prospect for the farmer than any other province in Canada, because the farmer there has a market right at his door. In the year 1917, we imported into the province $20,000,000 of farm and dairy products, and it practically took every dollar of gold, silver, copper, lead and zinc which we mined to feed ourselves. So I am glad that the Government is holding out inducements to the men to go on the land, and I am sure those who settle in British Columbia will meet with every success. One difficulty in British Columbia is the cost of clearing -the land, and I would suggest that the Department of .Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment make provision for additional assistance to men taking up land in that province to help defray the cost of clearing.
I am sure we are all glad the war is over. The wives and the sisters and the mothers of our soldiers are thankful to have their men home once more. We are all proud of our soldiers for the immortal fame they have brought to this country. We trust that the Peace Conference now sitting in Paris will achieve the object for which the war was fought, which was to make it impossible for another war such as this to occur in the future. In 1860, Tennyson looking into the future spoke of aerial combat and the aeroplanes " raining down their ghastly dew," and went on to say that the battle flag would be furled in the Parliament of Man, the federation of the world. May Tennyson's prophecy come true, and may the Peace Conference be successful in its deliberations and bring about a condition where there shall be a Parliament for the World, to which all disputes can be taken and each case decided on its merits.	-
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette): Mr. Speaker, if the incertitude and unexpectedness in the trend of human events were still to be proved, the history of the past year would serve to establish them. Less than twelve months ago, on the 18th day of March, the first session of the thirteenth Parliament opened. Shadow's of doom and forebodings of evil were then prevailing in

our minds; for we lived in anticipation of the dreaded and boastfully heralded German attack on the Western front. Three days after the opening of the session-on March 21st-the attack was launched with an incredible fury such as the world had never before witnessed in warfare. In less than three days the Germans had destroyed the Fifth English Army and had advanced to a depth of more than thirty miles from their starting point. So great was our despair and our peril that, in the confusion of our minds, it seemed to us that the war was already lost. We all know what followed. We know of the prodigious efforts of the Hun, of the masterful strategy of the Allies, and of the ultimate crushing defeat of the enemy. The rapidity of these events, from impending defeat to complete victory, has been one of the happiest surprises of this war, so full of wonders.
The speech from the Throne refers to the successful conclusion of this greatest of all wars, and we are all happy to unite with the Government in devoutly thanking Providence for deliverance from so awful a peril. This session of Parliament, therefore, was summoned under the most favourable auspices. But suddenly, like a thunder bolt on a day of sunshine, a national calamity threw our country into mourning and deep sorrow. I refer to the death of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It had been announced that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) and the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) would share the honour, on this side of the House, of paying a tribute to Canada's Grand Old Man. I hope I may be pardoned if I, too, following the example of hon. members on both sides of the House, take the liberty of adding my quota of admiration to the memory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I shall not speak of Sir Wilfrid Laurier as a nation-wide, or even as an empire-wide statesman. By so doing I might possibly do him injustice by exaltations which would not adequately 9 p.m. describe his virtues. What has been spoken, written, and done throughout Canada since the hour of the death of the master, speaks for itself, and is sufficient to immortalize him. But in the name of the people of my race I wish to deposit one more crown of unwithering laurels upon his grave. Our national poet, Mr. Louis Frechette writing about the great compatriot, Louis Joseph Papineau, says:
II fut toute une gpoque, et longtemps notre race N'eflt que sa voix pour glaive et son corps pour cuirasse.
When one ponders the sad event of the past few weeks, these words of the poet seem vividly to apply to our hero. Lover of liberty, defender of the oppressed, he always made himself the champion of the rights of the minority, and unfortunately it so happened that the minority which were so attacked were the people of his own race. The chant of the poet, eminently adapted to Sir Wilfrid Laurier under the present painful circumstances, will forever find its echo in the hearts of the men of his race.
The war is over. Reconstruction has begun; and racial and religious prejudices are vanishing. Generation will follow generation, and history will write the life of Laurier; and when in the years to come pilgrims from all over this country shall travel to the grave of this great man, our children and our children's children, remembering his noble work in the interests of his race, will repeat:
II fut toute une gpoque, et longtemps notre race N'eut que sa voix pour glaive et son corps pour cuirasse.
As to hon. members on this side of the House, his disciples, .1 can find no expression better capable of adequately and justly describing our affliction than this text fi'om the Holy Book: "I will smite the shepherd and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad." The shepherd, Mr. Speaker, has been smitten with an invisible hand, an inevitable hand, and the sheep of the flock, bewildered by the suddenness of the shock, have been scattered abroad with wailing and lamentation. But the flock have assembled anew. They have chosen a new leader, a new shepherd,- good, kind, and devoted-in whom they have placed their esteem and confidence.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to contribute to the numerous expressions of congratulation of which the mover and the seconder of the Address have already been the objects. Their quite apparent sincerity, together with the broadness of the views they have expressed, goes a long way, indeed, towards the bridging of the gap which now separates the two main racial elements in Canada. Let these hon. gentlemen and other hon. members of the House rest well assured that the gallant move which is now being made to unite and consolidate the divers elements in our dear country will not pass unheeded by the generous French-Canadian race, who are ready to go the full half way to meet their English compatriots and heartily shake hands with them. It was with no little pleasure that I listened the other night to the hon. mem-

ber for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) paying an admirable tribute to the French-Canadian people of Quebec. I am not able to quote the words of the hon. member verbatim, but I have them in my heart, and if I understood him aright, he spoke about as follows:
The people of the province of Quebec are good and generous; the people of the province of Quebec should be known better by other elements in this country ; I am sure that if closer relations should exist between the people of Quebec and the people of the other provinces the sentiment which of late has not been what it should have been perhaps would be improved greatly not only to the benefit of the people of Quebec but of every other province and of the whole Dominion. Those were the words, or that was the sense of the words which were used the other night by the hon. member for *Springfield. I want on this occasion to take the opportunity of offering my thanks to the hon. member and to all the other members of this House who think as he does and from what I can see there are a good many of such hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. This country is too great, its possibilities' are too immense that any of us should be allowed to divert its energies from the course which Providence has set before us or to destroy these energies in the furnace of racial and religious conflict. I believe that in so speaking I express the views not only of the members of this House but of the majority of the people of this country. However good and sincere our dispositions may be I am sorry to say there are still left in this country unrepentant sinners whom I cannot help but mention in relation to race and religious conflicts that greatly grieve me. I may be wrong in my judgment. Pehaps ll am wrong as to this matter that I have reference to but I for one felt that I should not allow this article that I am going to mention now go unchallenged.
On the 20th of last month while our hearts were bleeding freely because of the death of the great man a Toronto newspaper whose principal aim appears to be to insult everything Catholic and French *Canadian was addressed to me and apparently to all the members of this House.
I am referring to the edition of the Orange Sentinel of February 20. What was the object of having that paper addressed to us in the hour of our deep sorrow if not the malicious intent of digging deeper the ditch which unfortunately separates the English from the French by exasperating the latter race. At a time when every

citizen is turning his thoughts more and more towards the unity of Canada, this paper has made it its object to work in an opposite .direction. Looking at the heading on the front page of this paper I read the following:
The tragedy of Quebec, and the great failure of French-Canada in the war.
What a great English newspaper says about conditions in Quebec where the people are held in bondage to the black robes.
The lengthy article which follows and which is presented as the expression of the Saturday Review is nothing short of a web of falsehoods and misrepresentations of the most libellous character. I am convinced that the article must have been contributed by some one on this side of the ocean who is a regular contributor to the -Sentinel because I cannot believe that any one in England with even the most superficial knowledge of Quebec could ever have written so false an article.
Evidently " the black robes " of Quebec are the enemy and as a consequence the French Canadians are singled out to bear the wrath of those who speak through the Sentinel. I feel very sorry that the education of those people has been so neglected that they should not know of the work of " the black robes." Ever since Canada was discovered, are they not aware that it was " the black robes " who followed, step by step, the first colonists of this country? And that the second largest river in the world, the Mississippi, was discovered by one of those black robes, Father Marquette, together with Joliette? Are they not aware that these black robes were equal in every sense to the martyrs of the first ages of Christianity in sacrificing their lives, many of them dying under torture by Indians in order to implant in this country the ideals of Christianity and civilization? Are they not aware that during the rebellion of 1837 the black robes remained faithful to the English Crown, against the people of their own race and religion, notwithstanding the injustices of which, as history has since recognized, these people had been the object? To speak of more recent times, are they not aware that the black robes of Quebec, for many years, were the supporters of Sir John 'Macdonald, an English Protestant and an Orangeman? They followed him against one of their own faith and race. Who will say after this that the black robes of Quebec are bigots, that they are being led in politics by religious influences largely, or that these black robes are not rendering justice to every class and to every political party in this country? They have

supported Sir John Macdonald against Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I would not repeat an incident of that kind if it were not an historical fact. My friends should also be aware that, in turn, Sir John Macdonald always had the greatest consideration and respect for the black robes of Quebec. The apostles of the Sentinel should at least, if they are Tories, respect those whom Sir John Macdonald respected, lest they would pretend to be more loyal than Macdonald himself. If they are Liberals let them respect those whom Sir Wilfrid Laurier respected, lest they should appear to teach a lesson to Laurier. But I do not think these people should belong to either the Conservative or the Liberal party, because they appear to be unaware of the principles which have always guided the two great leaders whom I have mentioned. They are people belonging rather to a class of their own and I do not know how to qualify them better than by saying that they are, perhaps, more to be pitied than censured. Looking at the front page of this paper, I read:-
Our watchword: One School, one Flag, a united Canada.
I wish to draw the attention of the House to these three words and try and find out what they mean as they appear on the front page of this paper.
This motto, appearing in a paper of this kind, is certainly worth noting, as it constitutes one of the finest examples of contradiction and mockery which can be found. "One flag." Every one, I understand admits the desirability of this-even the black robes of Quebec, and it is a surprise to me that this loyal Ontario paper should have as a watchword a proposition which no one in Quebec would ever think of discussing for a second. Are we to believe that there are in Ontario, where the loyalty of the people is unquestioned, people whose faith in the flag is so staggering that it has become necessary for the Sentinel to read them a warning of this kind? " One school." If this means anything, it means that, according to the ideals of those people, there should be throughout Canada one class of schools only, and that is the English nonreligious schools. Again I have to tell my friends: You are forgetting the most elementary principles of British institutions, otherwise you would be aware that in Canada, Egypt, South Africa, and every other country in the world which has been conquered by the British, they have made it a principle to leave to those whom they have conquered the free and unmolested use of their language, faith and institutions. With-29
out these principles, the British Empire would never have become what it is today, and the devotion and love for the flag and the conqueror would never have been implanted in the hearts of the conquered. During my whole life, I have been taught to believe that I should be proud to live under the British flag because of the freedom and liberality of its institutions. Not only have I been taught to believe this, but I have believed it and I do believe it now. For generations my people have been taught to believe the same principles. Not only have they been taught to believe it, but they do believe it now. And yet to-day there is a newspaper published in loyal Ontario with a watchword calculated to destroy, with one stroke of the pen, what has been the immutable principles of British liberty and freedom for the last two hundred years, and which have contributed more than anything else to make the British Empire what it now is. And yet .these people of the Sentinel proclaim themselves loyal subjects. They think themselves empire builders. Empire builders are they? No, they are empire destroyers, and it is fortunate that this class of people are not more numerous throughout the Empire, for they would do more to tear it asunder and destroy it than the Hun himself could ever have done.
A united Canada-this is the third proposition of the watchword. It is hardly necessary to say that this proposition is a fallacy and a mockery in the mouth of those for whom the Orange Sentinel speaks. While these people proclaim a united Canada, they are doing everything in their power to disrupt and antagonize the diverse elements which people this Dominion. I have never seen so illogical a proposition, and L can not explain it otherwise than by saying that the minds of these people have been obscured to such an extent as to deprive them of the happy faculty of common sense. If it be true that there are still in the province of Ontario people so narrow as to find delectation in the reading of absurdities such as those contained in this edition of the Sentinel, give these people their daily bread, but in the name of truth and common sense, strike out from the paper these words "A united -Canada," and replace them with the words, "The disruption of 'Canada," for no one is contributing to a greater extent than they are in the nefarious work of disuniting and rending the component parts of Canada.
Sir, I think perhaps I have been led to discuss this last subject at too great length,



and I feel rather sorry that I have done so, convinced as I am that it is not worth while speaking so long and occupying the time of the House to such an extent, trying to answer propositions such as those we see in the Sentinel. I promise the House that I will never again enter upon a consideration of a subject of this character, because to insist any more upon the views which I have expressed would he to inflict upon hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House what I would call a grave injustice, because it would tend to make other people believe that perhaps large numbers of members in this House share the ideas which are taught in this paper the Sentinel, whereas I am fully convinced that the good thinking English people of Canada reprobate these articles just as much as we reprobate them ourselves.
Now, Sir, a very important question has been more or less discussed by the speakers who have taken part in this debate-I refer to the question of indemnity. In opening up this question I think we may be allowed to ask ourselves, "What shall Canada get from this war?" We have contributed five hundred thousand men-in fact the figures show that nearly six hundred thousand have been enrolled, either voluntarily or under the Military Service Act.
