We have spent for war purposes nearly two billion dollars. The war is over, we have triumphed, but I think it is reasonable for every Canadian citizen to ask himself, "What shall Canada get from it?" I can imagine my hon. friends on the other side quite ready to ask me: Are you so far behind the times that you are not yet aware of what Canada is getting out of this war? To my mind what we are getting is of a two-fold character. There is first the moral question, and this is the one to which my hon. friends opposite would refer if I had been interrupted on this point. The moral result. That is the good that Canada-in fact all civilized peoples and humanity at large-has derived from this war. If we examine this proposition, I would say to my hon. friends than (Janada has benefited immensely from the war because it has helped to save civilization and democracy in this world. So that from that point of view we have won tremendously. But we have not a monopoly of the moral gain; it is shared by all the other Allied nations. We are, therefore, all on the same footing so far as moral gain is concerned; we are satisfied within ourselves that we have done our duty in helping the Allies to win the war.

But there is another question that we should examine; it is that of material gain. We have spent large sums of money in carrying on our part in the war, and our debt now amounts to $2,000,000,000. If I understand rightly the speech delivered by the Minister of Public Works (Hon. F. B. Carvell) the Government does not at this juncture see its way clear to pay this debt, or even the interest on it. How are we to make up the $100,000,000 that we are short? Let me make a comparison. France has helped to save civilization; she is on the same footing as we are in that regard. But France will receive a material indemnity as a result of this war. France will gain the coveted provinces of Alsace and Lorraine and will obtain other territories, the particulars concerning which have not yet been adjusted. France will gain something of immense value in the way of future guarantees, and she will be able to maintain' an army much smaller than heretofore and spend very much less upon armaments than she was spending before the war. Consequently, poor France, sorely tried as she has been, is getting material gain out of this war.	,
Now, let us take England. England has new possessions that she did not have before the war. She has Palestine; so far as we can judge, she can have the Dardanelles if she wants them; she can control Asia Minor. England has seen the removal of the German menace against her colonies. Egypt and India are no longer threatened; South Africa will no longer be bordered by German colonies. England has established the supremacy of her navy. England will obtain great advantage in the unparalleled development of her trade. Before the war Germany was the great competitor of England in trade and commerce; after the final conclusion of the war by the signing of . peace Germany, as a competitor in this regard, will have disappeared.
I have heard people say that England went into this war for the gain that she expected to derive from it. Sir, I should be ashamed of myself if for one moment I supported a view of that kind. If England had gone into this war simply to obtain some material object and had spent hundreds, of thousands of lives in accomplishing that object, she would no longer deserve the respect of the world. England did not enter the war for that reason. But, actuated as she was by a sense of justice, by her responsibilities in respect of treaties she had signed, and by her desire to protect Belgium, it is nevertheless true that England will derive immense material bene-

fit from the successful conclusion of the war. Italy also will have her gains; she will have her lost provinces on the Adriatic and other lands in the Balkans or in northern Africa.
That brings us to the inquiry: What is Canada getting out of this war in a material sense? Canada is not getting a dollar's worth of material benefit out of this war. Canada has sent her men and spent her money, but is getting no material recompense. Even if the indemnity to be paid by the Germans is sufficient to pay only a part of the debts that have been incurred, I submit that it would be reasonable for Canada to have a justly distributed proportion of that indemnity. I go further; even if the indemnity is sufficient to pay only 25 cents on each dollar of England's war debt, Canada should get more than that, because England is obtaining numerous, material benefits out of the war while any indemnity paid to Canada would be the only material gain that would come to our country.
I read in the Montreal Gazette of March 8, the following despatch:
London, 'Sat, March 8.'-According to the Daily Mail's Paris correspondent, the powers have agreed to distribute the German warships among themselves, but the United States and Great Britain are in accord regarding the necessity for sinking their respective shares.
"According to this despatch, the ships handed over by Germany will be divided among the Allied nations, but England and the United States are going to sink their shares. Certainly we have nothing to do with England or the United States sinking their shares. But it is admitted that Canada is not getting any material compensation in respect of her part in the war, and Canada needs ships. Canada needed ships in 1911; our party was defeated at that time partly on a programme of building warships. We shall need these ships after the war just as much as we needed them in 1911; the time is not far distant when this Government will be called upon to build a Canadian navy. If England sinks her share of the ships surrendered by Germany, it is quite possible that immediately after that is done Canada will begin to build battleships.
I cannot understand a policy of this kind. I can very well understand that, by reason of the competition between England and the United States, because neither wishes the navy of the other to be increased, the navies of neither of these two powers should be augmented and that the ships that are allotted to them should be
destroyed. But instead of destroying the ships that are allotted to England, why should she not distribute them - amongst her colonies? The United States would not be jealous of that. The United States would be jealous if England were to get too many ships and England would be jealous if the United States were to get too many, because rivalry will not end with this war. But what wrong would there be if the Dominions overseas, instead of having to build warships with their own money when their resources are exhausted, were to have distributed amongst them that part of the German navy which will be allotted to England? This is only a suggestion of mine, and I am making it for what it is worth, but at first sight, it appears reasonable to me.
Another question which has been very little dealt with in the course of this debate is that relating to defaulters. How many defaulters there actually are in this country, -1 do not know. Perhaps there are twenty thousand, perhaps thirty thousand, perhaps forty thousand. I have no idea as to the number, and I am sure the Government does not know what the number is. But we are sure of one thing, namely, that these defaulters do not all belong to the province of Quebec. In every province of the Dominion there are thousands of defaulters. What is the Government going to do with those people? We have a debt of $2,000,000,000. We have taxes to meet. We have the question of reconstruction facing us. We need men to cultivate the farms and to develop the industries of this country. We need help from all around. Now that the war is over, now that every one in this country is eager to work in order to unite Canada and make it a great and prosperous country, are we going to take these defaulters by the thousand and send them to jail? It is about time that the Government should let its policy on this point be known, not that I am so eager to hear it, but in order that we may know what we have to do. Not any later than the day before yesterday I was called upon to advise one of these defaulters who has been arrested and brought to Montreal. I quite understand that every man who is an outlaw is liable to be arrested and brought before a court of justice or a military tribunal and tried for his offence. But what is going on throughout Canada? Until recently, we have seen defaulters being punished with fines ranging from $5 upwards, or terms of imprisonment up to a maximum of ten years. The

Government has recently passed an Order in Council fixing the amount of the fine, if I am- not mistaken, between $250 and $5,000. But this does not settle the question. The Government should take the matter in hand at once and should adopt a policy in regard to these people. And I feel confident that when the Government adopts a policy, it will be a liberal policy towards these people. We all know that at all times during all wars there have been defaulters. Such men are what we term political criminals; they do not belong to the ordinary class of criminals. Now, that the war is over, what is the object in going after these people? What is the use of the Government paying officers to go through the cities, towns and villages of this country in order to arrest these defaulters, bring them befoie a judge and have them tried? Such a course is simply spending unnecessarily the public money. The Government need money too much to keep in their service hundreds and hundreds of detectives for this work.
I do not think I should pass over this subject without quoting what I would call a reliable authority on the matter. Everybody in this House knows the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) well, and I think every one will agree with me that the hon. member has no feeling of kindness towards defaulters. This is what the hon. member said not any later than March 6:
I will tell you why I object to placing these men behind prison bars. They have been guilty of a breach of the Military Service Act. You take a man and place him in prison or in the penitentiary. Apart from the fact that he has not responded, as he should have responded, to the service of his country, he has shown no criminal instincts whatever. Is it a wise thing to take a man who has given no evidence of criminal instincts and put him in prison along with men steeped in crime? Is that wise from the national standpoint? What chance has that man to come out after two, or five years' incarceration alongside of the worst criminals tne country may have produced and play the part of a man? For that reason, and not because I think they should be exempt from punishment, I believe it is a mistake to place these men behind prison bars in our penitentiaries and jails.
I always thought that the hon. member was very far advanced in his ideas in regard to punishment for military offenders. Consequently, I wish to ask the Government to follow the good advice given to them by one of their followers.
It is no more right to fine the defaulter than to put him in prison. The fine now ranges from $250 to $5,000. For the rich

man the fine means nothing. The rich man can go before a judge, be fined $250, $500,	$1,000,-it does not matter w-hat
amount-and he will pay the fine. But what are you going to do with the poor man? He will not be able to pay the fine and will, therefore, have to go to jail. Consequently, if this question is to be settled by imposing a fine, the rich man will escape and the poor man will go to jail.
Can we afford at this juncture to put thousands and thousands of men in jail? For no one will deny that if the defaulters are to pay a fine, of $250, half of them or perhaps one-third-I do not know just how many, but at all events, a large proportion of them-will not be able to pay the fine and will have to go to jail. I say that it would be unjust to send to jail the man who cannot pay and let go scot free the man who is able to pay the fine. It would be equivalent to allowing a man to purchase his release from military service. We all know that it has been proved that some have purchased their release from military service. But the war is over now, and the Act is no longer in force, and if the Government persists in this policy it will fall very heavily on the poor man who is not a whit more guilty than the rich man. The poor man may have had to stay at home to support his parents and dependents, while in many cases there was nothing to prevent the rich man fighting for his country. I humbly request the Government to suspend these prosecutions, at least for the time being, until they have formulated a definite policy with regard to defaulters, because the question the Government have to decide is extremely important as it will affect between twenty and forty thousand people in this country.
I listened- with keen interest the other day to the excellent speech of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). He is a veteran of this House and a man of recognized high culture, and while I would not have the temerity to engage in combat with him, I find it hard to avoid attempting to answer certain statements in his speech. The hon. member spoke as follows:
On the question of tariff, in my humble judgment-and I have tried to inform myself

those who represent what was formerly the Liberal party occupy a less advanced position than did the whole Liberal party of a quarter of a century ago, so far as their political policy has been stated up to the present time.
Mr. Speaker, to say that I differ in opinion with my hon. friend would be but a weak answer, but the statement that my

hon. friend here expressed, an opinion quite different from his action of less than two years ago is worthy of the attention of this House. I will try to make good my statement and prove that the hon. member spoke in contradiction of his action of less than two years ago, not on the question of conscription, but on this very question of the tariff. On the 29th of May, 1917, when my hon. friend, then a Liberal, and still a Liberal according to his own profession of faith, was sitting on this side of the House, on the motion of Sir Thomas White that the House go into Committee of Supply, Hon. Frank Oliver moved in amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" In the motion be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"In the opinion of this House it would be in the public interest if the Customs Tariff Act were so amended as to provide:
1.	That wheat, wheat flour, and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list.
2.	That farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery, and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
3.	That staple foods and food products (other than wheat flour), domestic animals and foods therefor, be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of, any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty.
i. That substantial reductions be made in the general tariff on all articles imported into Canada, excepting luxuries.
5. That the British Preference be increased to fifty per cent of the general tariff.
After discussion a vote was taken on this amendment, the details of which appear on page 1790 of revised Hansard. Among the yeas I find: Bourassa, Buchanan, Clark (Red Deer). So my hon. friend voted for the amendment, and the vote, so far as I can judge, was a straight party vote. Sir Robert Borden, Sir Thomas White, Sir George Foster and Messrs. Cochrane, Doherty, Meighen, Reid, and so forth, voting against the amendment. Those of the Liberal party who were then present voted for the amendment and the Conservative party voted against it. The amendment was negatived. Therefore, after having given his support to the fiscal policy of this party less than two years ago, how can my hon. friend get up to-day and declare that the Liberal party occupies a less advanced position than it did twenty-five years ago? If it be true that the Liberal party in the course of the last twenty-five years has followed a retrograde movement, why has the hon. member followed this party all his life save for the last eighteen
months or so? To say that the Liberal party has retrograded is equivalent to the hon. member's admitting that he himself has followed a retrograde movement. But on the merits of the case is it accurate to say that the Liberal party has not retrograded-not for one minute. To prove my assertion I need only say this: If the amendment of 1917 which I have just quoted was moved again this year and a vote taken on it, who would vote for and >who against it? I think I am safe in saying that the hon. members on this side of the House would vote for the amendment and the hon. members opposite against it; at least, the majority of them would. How would the hon. member for Red Deer vote? I am sure he would have to leave behind his friends of to-day and vote for the amendment. Otherwise, he would come in conflict with his own principles in the most flagrant way. I could not for one moment entertain the idea that the hon. member should have changed his principles in regard to the fiscal question in less than two years; and I am quite sure that he would still support the amendment if it were put to the vote; otherwise he would be voting against himself and against the principles he professed less than two years ago. If the hon. member voted for the amendment, then he would be giving a vote of confidence to the party which sits on this side of the House, and against the party on the opposite side. The Liberal party has not followed a movement of retrogression, as is suggested. I may have been mistaken when I understood the hon. member to say that the Liberal party was not what it was twenty-five years ago. I cannot understand how the hon. member could support the fiscal policy of the Liberal party less than two years ago, and today say that this party is following a retrograde movement, notwithstanding the fact that its policy is precisely the same as it was at that time.
Now, Sir, with great literary taste and a fine sense of humour, in my opinion, the leader of the Opposition concluded his address with the parable of the light in the window; and since then a dozen speakers on the other side have devoted their talents to the discussion of the allegory which it contains. I was really surprised at this, for it never appeared-to me that my leader, by placing his little light in the window, was offering any kind of provocation comparable to the challenge of the toreador waving his red flag. Nevertheless the hon. member for Red Deer has made an effort to

extinguish the light in the window. Foi what purpose I do not know. I can see no reason why so much labour has been expanded on the other side of the House to put out this light, so inoffensive, and so flickering in the opinion of my hon. friend, if it is not their fear that that light may possibly be harmful in the way of dissolving some of the heterogeneous elements which compose the governmental majority. Why this exaggerated fear on- the part of my friends? Is the Government which they support so vulnerable, that a wee
10 p.m. light in the window should be capable of perturbing it? Our friends are giving us every reason to answer the question in the affirmative. Of course, the light is not the only frightful device. The latch string is another. Is the latch string dangerous? I do not think so. What is a little latch string in comparison with the formidable lasso which the hon. the Prime Minister made use of in the formation of his Union Government?
The attitude taken by the hon. member for Red Deer leads one to believe that the sect of the Pharisees is by no means extinct. Like the biblical personage, my hon. friend sits in a conspicuous place in the temple and tenders his thanks to God that he is not like the publican sinner, my leader. We need not Ise surprised, after this, to hear my hon. friend speak of a little shack, as he called it, as representing the home of the light. If the ideals in the materialistic mind of the hon. member do not rise higher than the roof of a shack, no one but himself should be held accountable for the deficiency. To me, the light in the window has a very different significance. I look figuratively to it as to a grain of mustard seed, " which a man took and sowed in a field; which indeed is the least of all seeds, but when it is grown it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof."
The light in the window, small but steadfast, is the symbol of those small heavenly stars which serve faithfully to guide the mariner to his port; while the light which my hon. friend and his associates followed when they crossed over to the other side, may justly be compared to the dazzling and treacherous fires lighted by the vengeance and craft of the Trojans to entice upon the reefs the vessels of the Greeks returning from the siege of Troy.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the House I do so with considerable diffidence, and were it not for the fact that I occupy a somewhat unique position, largely representing the agricultural interests of the country, I should have refrained from addressing myself to this question during this debate. I cannot but realize the wonderful difference there is between the meeting of the House at this time and that which took place twelve months ago. At that time the nations of the world were in the throes of the mighty conflict which has just closed. We in Canada were greatly interested in the issues involved in that conflict, and we scanned the papers for news from across the sea with intensest interest, wondering what would be the issue of the next hour. Things have changed wonderfully since that time. The forces that were struggling for liberty and righteousness, justice and democracy as we see it, though they felt the strain of the conflict at that time to be intense, yet their arm was sufficiently strong and their courage sufficiently great to carry them through to victory. Democracy was saved, freedom was secured, and the small nations of the earth were accorded the satisfaction of knowing that they would be free to work out their own destiny in their own way. The war is over. An important conference is dealing with the aftermath of the struggle and preparing for conditions which, we hope and pray, will usher in a peace that shall fill the earth. We hope that the Peace Conference will be wisely guided and that its decisions will mean the end of all wars.
Coming to the issues that affect us in connection with the circumstances bringing us together in this session of the House, I may be permitted to express my views with regard to one or two things. We were impressed by the magnitude of the problem which the war presented and the energy which the people of this country put into the struggle in order that victory might be achieved. But, Mr. Speaker, while the war is over, while the fighting is done, while we hope the last drop of blood has been spilt, the problems of the war are not settled. The gathering up of the results of the war has yet to be attended to. That which is necessary to secure, out of the war, conditions which will bring peace to the peoples of the world has yet to be attended to. The responsibility resting upon the Government while the war was on in connection with marshalling our forces and despatching them overseas was very great but yet I claim that the problems confronting this

Government to-day are more intricate and difficult of solution than those which already have been solved. I have an anxiety that the men who are at the head of affairs in this country shall be wisely guided and that their hands may be strengthened in every possible way in order that we may get safely through the aftermath of the war.
This brings me to make another statement. The people of Canada elected this Government as a war Government to deal with the war. I believe that I rightly interpret the mind of the people when I say that dealing with the war means dealing with all the issues of the war until normal [DOT]conditions obtain. Therefore, the obligations assumed by this Government continue until reconstruction is attained and the repatriation of our men has taken place. If the people by the pronouncement they made a year ago last December declared that the Government should assume the responsibility of carrying the war through to its conclusion I claim that they demand of the Government that they stay with their job until their task is completed.
With regard to the administration I feel fairly satisfied with the conduct of the affairs of the country by the Government during the year that has passed. I do not mean that the Government has not made mistakes. A government that is traversing new ground, dealing with new issues and new problems and which has not history to fall back upon, unless it is too fearful to amount to anything, is sure to make some mistakes. A government that is progressive and courageous, and that is seeking to grapple with important questions, will push forward, will carry the issues through and it is just possible that some mistakes will occur in connection with its work.' But, it is better to make mistakes of a minor character and go through, than it is to fall down in the great and important work which has been undertaken.
Some criticism has been made in regard to the War Measures Act. I would like to express an opinion in regard to that Act. Like some hon. members of the Opposition, and I have no doubt this is the opinion of members on this side of the House as well, I will say that we do not require, and would not tolerate, a War Measures Act except under peculiar and very special circumstances. Some of us believe that the circumstances were such as to demand that an extraordinary measure should be made use of and the War Measures Act, we believe, was made use of as an extraordinary measure to meet the exigencies of the case.
Why was it made use of? We had been operating under certain regulations in gathering up the men who were to arm themselves and go overseas to fight our battles. We remember very well that in connection with the Militia Act the great majority of the boys responded heartily and readily to the call. But there came a time when more men were needed and the call became more urgent. There was not that hearty response there ought to have been; at least some felt that that was the case. To overcome the difficulty that confronted us at that time other methods had to be resorted to and the introduction of those methods brought serious opposition. When these methods were made use of, people who were not so very free in coming forward under the old Militia Act became very active in propagating the idea that the old Militia Act was all that we needed.
However, the men were not forthcoming, and because of that conscription was brought into force. We come a little further down, and it came to the matter of putting into operation this new Act, The people were looking about for a government that would give effect to the law, and we find the same difficulty confronted the people. Those who said in the first place that the Military Service was good enough, but were not attempting to apply it and to use it to the best advantage, were utterly opposed to the new Act when it , came into force. Therefore when the people were seeking for a government who would enforce that law, and an appeal was made to the country, the Union Government was brought into existence. That Government took hold of the enforcement of the Act, and succeeded in obtaining the men that were needed. At all events the army was brought up to the strength which the Premier of this country had pledged, and it was maintained at that strength. The material essential for the equipment of the army was also maintained in the requisite quantity. Canada was carried safely through the war, and the Government has fulfilled its pledges to the people in that connection. The people are now looking for the carrying out of what I may call the aftermath of the war, and it seems to me we may reasonably expect that the Administration which carried the country safely through the war will have the public confidence in dealing with these other questions. The Government succeeded in getting our troops together, and in training and equipping them and' transporting them Overseas. Now that the war has been won,

the people expect that the same Government will be able to take care of our troops, bring them back again, and reinstate them in civil life; and the Government will not have discharged its full duty until it has accomplished that work.
One of the speakers this afternoon enunciated his conception of the principles of Liberalism. I did not catch all his definitions, but I would like to make reference to one or two of them. I heard the hon. gentleman in question make use of the term "Freedom" as a term that would express what Liberalism means. He propounded certain questions to the minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Cal-der) and asked how he would square his line of action with the great principles he enunciated. The inference was that the adherence to those principles was entirely on the Opposition side of the House, and that an hon. member seated on this side could not claim those principles in any way. While this hon. gentleman was making his argument I could not but think of some of the men in the past who had advocated the principles that the hon. member referred to, and how they stood up for them. I could not help but think of the men who sacrificed life and all they held dear in defence of these very principles. Then my mind reverted to some of the utterances made by certain hon. gentlemen sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker, when the cry came from our gallant boys at the Front, who were fighting for freedom and liberty, to send them assistance. The question was then plaintively asked by some of these hon. gentlemen: "Has not Canada done he? share?" The suggestion was that we should let the rest of our boys stay at home until some other people had sent forward a quota equal to our own. There were our lads overseas, sending back messages to us, and asking: "What are you doing that reinforcements are not coming?-you placed us in this struggle, and you are not behind us." And yet in Canada the declaration was being made, "Canada has done her share, let other people do theirs." Were the people who talked in that way the defenders of freedom? Mr. Speaker, I think that any man possessing a spark of love for freedom, could not have given expression to such sentiments. It was because the Government wanted to stand shoulder to shoulder behind the boys overseas that they took the step they did at that time. Moreover, it is because they wish to see the war problems satisfactorily settled, pro-

vision for our war indebtedness made, and our boys safely brought back and taken care of that the supporters of this Government stand shoulder to shoulder to-day. And they intend to do so, no matter what is said about "a light in the window" on the Opposition side. Mr. Speaker, those who legislate in the interests of the Dominion in the future will be men who have-quit talking about Gritism and Toryism, and all that sort of thing, playing with party politics, men who stand for the principles of democracy.
Coming now to deal with some of the matters referred to in the speech from the Throne, I wish first to make a few observations with regard to the creation of the proposed Department of Public Health. I would rather that the wider appellation had been used of "public welfare," because it would express more fully, I think, what is in the minds of the people.
I hope that in the carrying out of that idea this wider meaning will be kept in mind, and that all matters pertaining to the welfare of the people will be taken care of in that way. Canada is big enough to realize that her greatest asset is the country's manhood, and that she will be strong only in so far as she preserves that manhood in the highest state of efficiency. I haye no doubt that when this matter comes up for consideration such conclusions will be reached and such arrangements made as will meet the case and produce satisfactory results.
I wish to express my appreciation of the statement in the speech from the Throne that the Order in Council referring to the liquor question is to be taken care of and that legislation is to oe put into euect that will hold conditions as they are until the boys are *safely returned. And when they are safely returned I know that there is democracy enough in this House to cause us to say: We will face the issue, we will submit this matter to all the voters who will then decide what Canada's future policy shall be.
Representing as I do a rural constituency, I wish to direct the attention of the Government to the Daylight Saving Act. Someone has said that "God's time is good enough for me." I believe that the vast majority of the people of Canada are of that opinion. The Daylight Saving Bill has served its time; it has ended its pilgrimage upon which it was started by this Parliament a year ago, and has been quietly buried; let us hope that there will be no resurrection. As far as I understand it,

the people, particularly those in the rural districts, are utterly opposed to it and do not want any more of it. I think that until there is a very strong demand for it, the Government would be well advised to leave it quietly alone.
With regard to Reconstruction, the Government has a very important task to perform. I hope that when this Parliament's work is completed, arrangements will have been made to distribute the economic burdens of the country as equitaDly as possible upon the shoulders of uie people. Previous to the war there was a good deal of talk about the burden of taxation imposed for carrying on the business of the country. If it was an important matter to provide the money necessary in pre-war days to take care of the interest on our national debt and provide for the carrying on of the Government surely, naving regard to the responsibility that rests upon us to-day, it will require the united effort and the best thought of this Parliament to devise proper means for our carrying the burden that will fall upon us in those coming days. I am not a pessimist by any means; I believe that with the natural resources which Canada possesses and with the energy and industry of our people devoted to this task, if our forces are united and the burdens of the people are equitably distributed, we shall overcome our difficulties and come out into a successful future.
This is an opportune time for the Government to consider matters that will have to be dealt with in the later sittings of the House and for members from the different constituencies to voice the views of the people on important issues in order that they may receive consideration before the Budget is brought down. So I wish to direct attention to a question that affects very vitally the great interest of agriculture. I refer to the trade policy that is to be inaugurated in connection with the carrying of our indebtedness and the meeting of our expenditures.
The people in rural life believe that the economic burdens of this country have not been equitably distributed. They believe that in connection with a certain economic policy that was introduced in Canada, privileges were obtained and certain classes of the community were able to take advantage of the position in which they were placed by these privileges and to escape the full share of their economic responsibilities and duties.

Hear, hear.
Mr. HENH'BRS : I hear some member on the other side of the House say "hear, hear." I wish to call attention to the fact that when these burdens were imposed upon and were being borne by the people, that same kind of cry was heard from tne Opposition for a good many years. Hon. gentlemen characterized these burdens in very unmistakable terms, such as "legalized robbery," and so on.
I quite agree with the terms that were then made use of, but before hon. members opposite say " hear, hear," too loudly, I want them to remember this, that the people who -made very strong use of these terms in the past and who declared their intentions as to what they would do, should they come into a position where they would have to deal with these conditions, were not so loud in their decrying of these principles after they came into power as they had been before. We have not very much to hope for or to expect if we are to be governed by the teaching of either of the old parties when we come to deal with this question.
I am looking to the Union Government-
Mr. DUFF. You have great faith.
Mr. HENDERiS:	I am looking to the 1
men who are not tied to any of the traditions or [DOT] records of the past, because those records contain nothing flattering

I am looking to the men of the Union Government, having completed the duties and responsibilities before them, regarding the war, to undertake the responsibility of framing a fiscal policy that shall be to the advantage of the people of Canada, and after they have formulated that policy, in due time to appeal to the people of this country for their endorsation. I make this statement to them to-day, that as soon as they formulate that policy-and it must be this session-then some of us who hold strong view's on this question, will declare where we are going to stand with regard to it. From what the Government has done since they came into power, I believe that we can safely look to them to open a way into the future and to give us a policy that will be in the interest of the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish, at the outset of my remarks, to join with the members of this House who have preceded me in extending my 'felicitations to the mover and the seconder of the Address for the manner in which they have acquitted themselves. I also wish to join with the other members of this House, and especially do .1 wish to do so on behalf of my constituents,

in saying a word of tribute to the memory of the late, departed leader of the Opposition, iSir Wilfrid Laurier. It may truly be said of this world-renowned statesman that by his passing a vacancy is left in the political life of Canada that cannot easily be filled. It may also be said that in his passing a life has closed that was full to overflowing of all the elements that go to make for a true democracy, a life so refulgent in its beauty and brightness that it will cast a radiant light down the future ages of this country that will lead the way and enable future leaders to attain to a higher standard in democratic ideals than they could ever have expected to. attain had Sir Wilfrid Laurier never lived.
I do not intend to follow closely the argument of the hon. member (iMr. Henders). As regards his reference to the controversies that have come between the two parties in the last two years, I will just refer to them in this way-and perhaps it may be interjecting a little of a personal reflection, but I feel it is my duty to do so. When I was elected to this Parliament a little more than a year ago, I took this ground; I knew my electorate, and my electorate knew me; and the policy on which I stood was a straight and staunch supporter of the principles of Liberalism as known, announced and worked out under the leadership of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The members of this House all know the disturbed state of mind among the electorate on that occasion, being in the midst of the great war and with all the questions which were put to them. My stand on that occasion was that I reserved from all bias of party affiliation my free right as a citizen of this country to vote for any measure, from whatever source it might emanate, that might, in my judgment, assist in bringing the war to a speedy and successful conclusion. I can say to this House to-night that I maintained my stand to the highest point and never on any occasion was it necessary for me to deviate from the leadership of the late Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. In the short time that has passed since our late lamented leader has departed, I firmly believe, from the records so far of his worthy successor, that I can . maintain the high commission given to me by my electorate and, at the same time, be a loyal supporter of my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) who now heads the Opposition.
Coming more directly to the matter contained in the speech from the Throne, I wish to express my approval of, and to concur in, that part of the Speech which tenders the gratitude of the nation to the gal-[Mr. J. E. Sinclair.!
lant members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force for the suffering they underwent and for the endurance they exhibited in fighting the battles of liberty and freedom across the seas. I wish also to express my feelings of sympathy and condolence for the sisters and brothers, the wives and sweethearts, and especially the parents, of those brave boys and nurses who made the supreme sacrifice, laying down their lives on the fields of France and Flanders that liberty and civilization might be vindicated and truth and justice prevail.
Reference is also made in the speech from the Throne-and perhaps I am now entering upon matters that will be of more contention during this session of Parliament-to the intention of the Government to grant from the Dominion Treasury substantial aid to the different provinces to aid in the building of permanent highways. It is well kfiown that this question has been discussed at great length in former Parliaments, and I wish to say that, so far as it indicates the intention of the Government to render assistance from the Federal Treasury to the various provinces, that intention will meet with my hearty approval. But from the information contained in the Notice of Motion, I feel that the method employed in granting that assistance to the provinces is not being wisely considered. We have been told time and again that the control of public roads is vested in the provincial governments, and what strikes me most forcibly in the Government's proposed legislation is the fact that the Federal Government will be interfering with and overlapping the work of the provincial governments. This overlapping or dual authority is causing a great deal of waste of money and energy in the different departments of the Government to-day and has been doing so for many years, in some cases even since Confederation.
The speech from the Throne foreshadows a proposal to establish a Department of Public Health in Canada. To illustrate my point I shall make reference to other departments of the public service at the present time. I mention the Department of Agriculture, not because I wish to criticise that department any more than any other department of this Government, but simply to show how the duplication and overlapping of work leads to waste of public money, and to raise my voice in protest against further departments of Government being organized on the same principle. It is a condition that has prevailed in the Department of Agriculture for a very long time, and was probably brought about by

a lack of foresight on the part of the Fathers of Confederation. Under this Department of Agriculture we have a condition of affairs which is not wholesome or conducive to getting the best results for the money expended. We have the Federal Department of Agriculture directing its energies to the marketing end of agriculture, while nine provincial departments are taking care of production. This may seem to the casual observer to be a fair distribution of labour, but in practice it is working out in a very different way. To attain a uniform standard of excellence for Canadian produce from the Atlantic to the Pacific requires a productive organization with a single purpose, with unity of action, and kindred ideals everywhere. It must be truly Canadian, and in all its departments it must have co-operation, co-ordination, and unanimity. It must have one head, and its activities in Canada must be directed from a common centre and towards a common end. In every province we have an agricultural policy that differs essentially from the policy of any one of the other eight provinces. Examples of overlapping of work, discord among officials, and clashing of policies may be found everywhere. It would seem that the haphazard hit-or-miss propaganda of the provincial departments depends largely on the initiative of a few individuals in provincial affairs. Provincial policies thought out by men trained to think in terms of a province are somewhat narrow and wholly provincial. This must be so, because they are working to a provincial end. It will be said that precisely at this point the Dominion Department of Agriculture comes into operation and takes up the work where it is laid down by the provinces. This is what was intended, but the intention is far from being realized. Our Dominion department is failing in the duty it owes to the Canadian nation. Here we have the organization that should have scope and vision and power to achieve. We have also the men unhampered by provincial atmosphere and restriction, who ought to be able to stand out and give direction to the affairs of the country in a manner befitting the trustees of the nation. They should be able to coordinate the work done in the several provinces into a complete Canadian system. But upon analysis we find that the power which logically and rightfully belongs to these men and their organization has been vested in the representatives of the provinces. This leaves the Dominion department to a certain degree powerless. It simply marks time and haggles away at the edge of things
while provincial organizations without either the knowledge, the incentive, or the ideal, work along in a vain attempt to frame the policy of the country. It works out wrongly. It is like trying to dress a man in a boy's suit. Whole battalions of officials are struggling to get Canada into a suit of clothes cut to fit Ontario, Quebec or one of the other provinces. The Dominion officials follow up, taking what is left for them to do, and very kindly see that nothing is left out or forgotten by the provincial brotherhood, while down in the country the public is asking questions that no one can answer.
This, then, is the kind of production policy that is in existence. It is upon such a superstructure that a system of selling associations is to be built that will emancipate the farming community from the dilemma of markets, and guarantee to both producer and consumer an efficient business system and equitable prices in the distribution and sale of the country's foodstuffs. This is a short description of the method employed to encourage agricultural production in our national agricultural policy, and I have given it simply to show the waste of money that such a policy entails.
The war has drawn public attention to the waste in production and marketing. The demand for food controllers has shown that when the nation is under stress, waste and profiteering are intolerable. As a sound economic principle, it may be stated that any public service that can be carried on by the people in the public interest should not be handled by private enterprise for private profit. In the past, deplorable waste has taken place and the business of marketing has been carried on for private profit. The Markets Branch has undertaken to assist agricultural development by organizing the sale of farm produce on the co-operative plan as a means of eliminating these two evils. Until the system of co-operative selling organizations is complete, every production organization in the country will remain handicapped. Marketing is the final process of the farm, and is purely and essentially the farmer's business. This being so, the ultimate success of the whole agricultural machine depends on the Markets Division. The Markets Division in turn depends for its very existence on the disjointed efforts of a producing organization having nine different heads throughout the Dominion. Each of the nine organizations works independently of the others, and all work without a common ideal or a national viewpoint. This,

and my constituents of the measure known as the War-time Elections Act. While I have no intention of anticipating what may be affixed to the Franchise Act, from the opinions expressed by some h in. members seated on your right hand, Mr. Speaker, we may expect that a selective franchise will be offered to this House at this session. In this connection I wish to refer particularly to the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Mclsaac), who, speaking on alien enemies, said:
I, for one, sincerely hope that the Government will exercise its utmost powers in carrying out whatever regulations may he enacted to drive these people out of the country. They have no rights here, and they-have done much harm; X hope the Government will leave nothing undone to suppress them.
I cannot interpret that as the true sentiments of the citizens of Canada towards the people who are termed alien. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden), in his eloquent speech, referred to alien enemies and said that we would not be true to our soldiers who went overseas to fight in France and Flanders if we did not send these people home. In justification of his statement he went on to say who these alien enemies were and what constituted alien enemies. The proof which he cited simply showed that the men whom he called alien enemies had made certain statements to the effect that they were not Canadians. I have no brief to defend alien enemies. I have always taken the ground of a common citizenship and encouraged in every way possible our people to be loyal. But, if those who are termed alien enemies were to be approached in accordance with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Kings and the hon. membeT for Brandon, you could only expect to get the worst and basest principle of their nature brought to the surface. And, Sir, if we are to give a lead-a proper lead-to our people we must not use expressions that will set one class against another. We must propound and carry out a policy in this Parliament that will lead all classes-a policy that they can follow, and follow as a unit. In regard to this matter, I desire to place myself on record in this House, that so far as my influence and voice will go, I will stand for a common citizenship and a universal franchise as the only means of leading Canada towards her proper position in relation to the different colonies of the Empire and the nations of the world.
In conclusion, Sir, permit me to say, that our motto must be: "Let us all be

Canadians in the broadest and truest sense of the term."
"Let us be Canadians."
" Let us be broad Canadians."
" Let us all be Canadians."

Consideration of the motion of Mr. D. L. Redman (Calgary East), for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session resumed from Thursday, March 13th.
Lt.-Col. CYRUS WESLEY PECK, V.C. (Skeena):	Mr. Speaker, I had hoped
not to intrude upon the notice of the House at such an early date because, in the presence of so many experienced Parliamentarians and debaters, I thought it might be more modest for a new member like myself to wait a while. At the same time I felt that there were some subjects being discussed on which I might be particularly qualified to speak, and being a new member and not very familiar with the rules of the House, I thought that in the debate on the Address I was less liable to get out of order; because, Sir, I have noticed from the remarks so far made by hon. members that there is an extraordinary wide range of topics which may be discussed in this debate, and one may speak about almost anything under the heavens, provided he does not talk too strongly upon those subjects which really matter.
Now, Sir, there are one or two things I am going to speak about and they relate to things which really do matter. First of all I desire to allude to a certain statement which appeared in the morning paper. I understand that when imputations are cast upon the character of hon. gentlemen the opportunity is afforded them of rising to a question of privilege. I do not wish to follow that course, or to cause any unpleasantness; I merely desire to say that the statement in the morning paper representing me as being a lawyer is absolutely and entirely untrue.
I wish to thank the House for the exceedingly kind welcome it accorded me on my arrival, and also to all hon. gentlemen on both sides for the very cordial way in which I have been received in this Chamber. I likewise desire, Sir, to thank the staff of the House for the courtesies which they have extended to me during the short time I have been here, and which, I can assure you I reciprocate in the very greatest degree.
il desire especially to thank the hon member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) for the very kind remarks he made concerning
me when I entered the House and to extend my thanks to the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) for his very kind references to hie. I am exceedingly sorry that I shall have to take sharp issue with the latter hon. gentleman on some of the statements which he made during his contribution to the present debate.
I join all the hon. members of the House who have so far spoken in paying my tribute of respect to the illustrious statesman who so long adorned the benches of this House, and who has now gone forever. I was exceedingly impressed with the touching and noble eloquence of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) in the speech he made the other day, when he spoke of the personal charms and personal character of the late great Leader of the Liberals. It will be well indeed if the Liberal party-I do not know the present leader of the Liberal party very well-all I know is to his credit because his name is associated with the tartan which I have worn for a long time upon the battlefield- the Liberal party or any other party will do very well indeed if they get a leader of the same fine mould, the same high character, the same lofty ideals, and who will be followed with the same devotion, the same enthusiasm and the same abiding faith, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier was followed in this House and in the country.
It is not my intention, in the few remarks I shall make, to enter upon the general subjects of politics which have been very fully covered by other hon. gentlemen who have spoken. I have not been too conversant with the ordinary subjects of politics, and if I may be excused for so saying during the last four year®, to quote from the poet.
Little of this great world can I speak
More than pertains to feats of broil and battle.
I was very grieved indeed, Sir, on my entry into this House to hear the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) make certain statements which I deem to be of the utmost gravity. He made statements with respect to the leaders of the Canadian Corps in the field which pained me very much. I was exceedingly pained, because I felt that those statements might revive the grief felt by hundreds, nay thousands, of people in this country, who have lost their dear ones in the war. There are thousands of bleeding hearts in this country to-day, Sir. Thousands of hearts that will never be healed; thousands of mothers, sisters,

wives and sweethearts are listening in vain for that footfall upon the garden path that will never sound again; and I say that any man who says anything to cause these wounds to bleed afresh should have behind him the most indisputable facts, should be able to guarantee his statements to the utmost, and should be absolutely convinced that what he says is absolutely necessary to be said in the public good. The hon. member for Victoria, whose redoubtable character I respect, in his statements in this House said that the lives of a great many Canadian soldiers had been sacrificed in vain to serve the idle ambition of the leaders of the Canadian Corps, sacrificed for no useful purpose. The hon. gentleman said: "I know Cambrai well, and General Mewburn has seen Cambrai." I do not know whether the hon. Minister of Militia wishes to associate his reputation as a tactician with the hon. member for Victoria, ' but that is what he said. The hon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) further said:
I know Cambrai well. It is a dirty little one-horse town that is not worth the life of one Canadian soldier.
I do not know what the hon. gentleman's religion is, but I rather imagine from his speech that he is a spiritualist, because he seems to have a supernatural knowledge of things that have taken place on the battlefield. As a matter of fact, I think his medium must have been out the night before he made his address, because what he says is absolutely at variance with those things which we who were actually upon the ground saw take place. He says that Cambrai is a little one-horse town, not worth the life of one soldier. Now, I have here two maps, one a German map showing the town of Cambrai on a large scale, and the other one of our own maps showing the town on a smaller scale in its relation to the rest of the country. I wish hon. members could see this map; I shall be glad to show it afterwards to any member who wishes to see it.

Perhaps the hon.
gentleman could tell us the population of Cambrai.
Lt.-Col. PECK, V.C.:	I do not know
the exact population, but I do know that it is far from being a little, one-horse town. Cambrai is a town of from 30,000 to 50,000 inhabitants.

27,000.
Lt.-Col. PECK, V.C.: Very well; that is near enough to it. But the question is not so much the population of the town as the
[Lt.-Col. Peck.]
relation which it bears to the rest of the front. If hon. gentlemen will look at this map they will see that six or seven great national highways lead into Cambrai; that several great double-track railways run into the town; that single-track railways and hundreds of roads lead into.it. They will see also that a great canal system runs through the town; so that however you consider it- from an administrative point of view, as a road junction and railway centre Cambrai is a place of the utmost importance and was of the greatest strategical value on that front. Moreover, if you look at this map you will see that the German army commander whose army held Cambrai and the high ground to the north would naturally rest his flank on the La Sensee canal. That canal is a very much more formidable military obstacle than it appears to be as shown on this map, because miles of the surrounding country have been flooded by the Germans. So that the German commander would have on that canal a safe and secure flank and would have a very comfortable feeling indeed. But if he lost the town of Cambrai and that high ground he would at once find his right flank to be tremendously involved in the canals and rivers that lie northeast of Cambrai, and he would have to beat a very hasty retreat -as, indeed, happened when the Canadians a,nd the British corps got through.
It must have been the opinion of the generals of the British army that Cambrai was a very important point; otherwise, why should so many military enterprises have been attempted against it throughout the war? And, Sir, such was the opinion not only of these generals, but also of the German general staff. Perhaps you remember a statement made by Ludendorff or Hin-denburg, I forget which, before Cambrai fell, in which he tried to cheer up the drooping spirits of the German people and to belittle the efforts of the Allies. The statement said: "They have really gained nothing, but when the British get into Lille and Cambrai they may begin to talk, for our situation will be serious indeed."
The hon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) tried to paint a vivid picture before members of the House with regard to the town of Cambrai, and if you looked into the background of that picture you would see the villain of the piece: Sir Arthur Currie, the cold, machiavellian leader, who he says was willing to throw away the lives of all kinds of Canadians to gain a little transitory glory.

Now, the action of Cambrai was not at all a local Canadian action; it was part of an enormous military enterprise which extended over a vast area of *country for days and weeks and which was only a part of what was taking place on the great western front. From the time when Foch struck his first blow, on the twenty-first of August, he continued to strike that front like a pugilist, striking here, there, and everywhere, always with relentless determination, always with consummate judgment and skill, no one knowing where the next blow would fall. The German prisoners used to say; "We live in constant terror; we never know where we are going to be attacked." He kept pounding away until he wore down the German army, demoralized the German defence, broke the heart of the German people, and made the German Government sign the most humiliat- ' ing armistice ever signed in the history of nations. So, Sir, if the battle, of Cambrai was 'Wrong, it was not the fault of Sir Arthur Currie or the higher command of the Canadian corps, it was the fault of the British general staff, and had the concurrence of Field Marshal Foch, the generalissimo of the Allied armies and the greatest military genius of the age.
The hon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) said in his speech,-I thought I had the Hansard here to quote from, but I have not, -that Cambrai should not have been attacked by suburb or street fighting; and he quoted the words of an American officer, addressed to General Buller at Colenzo, to show that the only way is to " go around the darned thing." Well, Sir, that is what actually happened.

One week later.
Lt.-Col. PECK, V.C.: Hold on; we will find out about that. I fought in two phases of the battle of Cambrai in which I did not see the town; that shows" what a "tremendous event the enterprise was. The [DOT]Canadian corps were a long way ahead of Cambrai on the northern flank and the British corps were a long way ahead on the south. The reason why they did not actually take the town by storm was because they did not want to cause undue casualties. We had known for a long time that Cambrai was doomed; it was only a matter of time. We can generally tell from the tactical situation what is going to happen, and we knew what was going to happen in this case. So finally these corps closed in and Cambrai fell. As far as I know, there was "very little, if any, street fighting in Cambrai. Our Third division went through the town, and the boys of the Canadian battalions, with their usual enthusiasm, marked on the doors of some of the buildings: " Captured by such-and-such a battalion." The British, I have heard, were rather annoyed about this; they said that our boys had gone over too far into their territory; and as I shall prove later, the centre of the line ran through Cambrai. At any rate, I am acquainted with all the officers in the various divisions, and I never heard that there was any considerable street fighting on that occasion. Of course, there may have been a little; but I question whether it amounted to anything.
The hon. gentleman tried to make it appear that this was a minor and local event with the Canadian corps, and that Sir Arthur Currie or the leaders of the Canadian corps were sacrificing human lives in this last attempt to gain glory.

Wherein do I show that it was a minor event of the Canadian Corps?
Lt.-Col. PECK, VjC. : I am using my privilege as a member of Parliament to defend the leaders of the Canadian Corps, because they are not here to defend themselves. I have no objection to answering any question put to me by the hon. gentleman, that I can, but he will have plenty of time in this House or in the country to reply to anything that I shall say.
Not only was this not a local event of the Canadian Corps, but there were two corps employed in the capture of Cambrai, which as I said, extended over many days. Further than that, if my memory serves me aright-and I will bank more on my own memory than the hon. gentleman will go on his-, not only was this a division between two corps, but it was the division between two armies, because we were fighting on the right of the first army and a British corps was fighting on the left of the third army. One does not have to be a great strategist to see that this was not a local event which was ordered merely for the purpose of gaining glory for the Canadian leaders. I think the casualties were reasonable considering the strategical importance of that point. Cambrai fell and the great German army commenced a rapid retreat going helter-skelter up the roads that lead to southern Belgium.
I want to say this-and perhaps this may be the most important part of anything 1 shall say about the casualties-our orders were to this effect: that we should press forward with all possible vigour, but that

have been attributed to him that have not been creditable and that have absolutely no connection whatever with Colonel John A. Currie.
To whom, Sir, could that allusion refer? What commander was at St. Julien of the name of Currie of sufficient importance to attract the eloquence of the hon. gentleman? I do not know any commander of that name who was present at that battle of St. Julien except Brigadier Ge leral Arthur Currie, who commanded the 2nd Canadian Infantry Brigade, and I should be very glad if the hon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) saw fit to stand up in this House and deny that he meant to refer to that man.

I mean Sir Arthur Currie, and I shall take the fir^t fitting opportunity in this House to say that it is Sir Arthur Currie and to tell what happened.
Lt.-Cbl. C. W. PECK, V.C.: I have heard that this campaign of infamy is to be continued, and if so, I certainly deplore the fact. It will be unfortunate for the reputation which the Canadians have won for themselves, and which should be cherished in the heart of every true citizen of this country. This truth should forcibly appeal, I think, to every honest Canadian.
The hon. member has asked me a question. May I ask him one?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Is it fair that Col. John A. Currie should go through this world under aspersions, without being vindicated?
Lt.-Ool. PECK, V.C.:	I am not at all
discussing the character of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that, returning from the battlefield and being received so cordially by the Parliament of the nation, I should consider it the last thing in the world I would desire to discuss or even to question the courage of any hon. gentleman; and anything which I have said has been said only from a high sense of duty and because I know what has actually taken place. And because, further, I wish to defend the reputation of those who cannot defend themselves. I beg to say that if this campaign is continued much longer-I earnestly pray that it may not-I shall tell some things of which I know, and there will be some gentlemen who will curse the day they were born.

I rise to a question of privilege.
