speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is not in order in rising to a question of privilege. The hon? member for Skeena (Col. Peck) has the floor. He may be interrupted only with his permission, and only to be asked a question.
Lt.-Col. PECK, V.C.:	I am not a sufficiently experienced parliamentarian to deal adequately with these interruptions; but I freely state that I have the highest possible admiration for the redoubtable character of the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), and I am not one of those who think that he made a million dollars out of the Ross rifle. I have always had the greatest admiration for him, and therefore I think the statements he has made in the House are unworthy of his redoubtable character.
Now, Sir, an important subject has come up lately to which I wish to refer, namely, the discipline of the Canadian troops. We have all read the astounding intelligence of the riots that recently occurred at Rhyl, Wales. I will not for a moment attempt to condone those riots. On the contrary, I believe that if similar unfortunate events are repeated they will seriously impair the great reputation which has been won by the splendid Canadian army in the field. I shall refer to an article that appeared in one of the leading London daily newspapers. The newspaper despatch reads:
The Daily Express in its main editorial to-day says that a most unfortunate state of feeling has arisen among the Canadians owing to the view they take of their recent treatment by the British Government and the British press. They say that, while British military troubles here and in Prance were minimized the Canadian camp disturbance was given full publicity. We would point out, says the Express, that this is only true of what happened in Prance. There the censor simply stopped the news crossing the channel, but what happened at Folkestone or Victoria Station and at Bow Street on Sunday was fully reported. None the less it is true that the blame attaching perhaps to 600 Canadians was placed on 19,000 completely innocent men, and that one or two comments were foolish and unsympathetic.
Now, Sir, that brings the British press and the British public into court, and I very much regret to strike a jarring or discordant note, as I feel I must do to-day. But I am bound to say that a certain portion of the British public and the British press have not dealt with the discipline of our Canadian troops with due tolerance and sympathy. As the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) no doubt knows, when the first Canadian contingent was in England, everything was said to exaggerate the slightest irregularity on their part. Now,

it is impossible to have several hundred thousand full-blooded young men assembled together without an occasional violation of what we call military law. Military law is altogether different from civil law. For instance, if a man fails to get in in time, under military law he is arraigned in the morning, tried for a crime, and probably found guilty; while under civil law a man may return home at four or five o'clock in the morning, and make the fact a subject of mirth at his club the next day, discussing the wonderful time that he had the night before. If a man is drunk, military law imposes on him a very severe sentence; whereas in civil life, if he has imbibed too freely at the club, the good boys take care of him, see him safely into a taxi, and he goes home a hero to his friends. So that there is a very wide difference between! civil and military law. But, Sir, the great test, you will find, of the character of our soldiers is the esteem in which they are held by people with whom they have come in contact. You may go to-day from Ypres to the Somme, across southern Belgium and even in Germany, and you will travel through nothing but a swath of abundant good will on every hand towards the Canadian corps. Now, you cannot make people believe that men are bad who are not so in fact; and that the Canadians are good men is the general opinion of the warm-hearted noble French people whom we admire, the gallant people of Belgium,-aye-and even the people of Germany. My battalion-which, of course, you know, is the greatest battalion that ever served in the field-left Lindlar, twenty-five miles east of Cologne, and the German people got out and lustily cheered them. You can have no more striking evidence than that of the opinion which is universally held of the Canadian soldiers.
We marched up to the Rhine on the 13th of December. The First Division crossed on the southern bridge in Cologne and held the northern bridgeheads of the Rhine to the extent of twenty-five miles east of Cologne. The Second Division crossed at Bonn and held the bridgeheads in front of Bonn. From the first [DOT]moment of the time we were in that vicinity, we found the British authorities very unsympathetic and, as the saying is, " They had it in for the Canadians." They asked that the Canadians might be debarred from Cologne, but Sir Arthur Currie refused to do that. After a while there was some trouble in Cologne, sufficient to furnish the British authorities with an excuse to exclude the Canadians
from that city. I may say that the British Military Governor of occupied Germany was Sir Charles Ferguson, and from the outset, as I have said, the British authorities were unsympathetic. And when this trouble occurred in Cologne they put the Canadians out of bounds, and sent a most insulting message to the Canadian corps, saying, that on account of the continued misbehaviour of the Canadians they would be excluded from Cologne.
I am very proud to say that we had commanders in the field who resented that order. I myself saw a copy of a letter which was written by Sir Arthur Currie and also one by General Sir Archibald Macdonell, commander of the First division, which division held the bridgeheads at Cologne and in front of Cologne, in which they replied to the order of the commander of the Second army. Sir Arthur Currie said, in a letter which was characterized by its vigour and dignity: "We can only consider that order, from the way in which it is couched, as insulting." Sir Archibald Macdonell very soon had his Highland spirit stirred and he wrote a letter, of which I saw a copy, to the British army commander in which he called upon him to produce the proof that the Canadians had been unduly obstreperous in Cologne. Sir Charles Ferguson wrote and made certain charges which were very grave. Sir Archibald Macdonell, that doughty Scotchman, made a scientific and searching investigation of the thing and he found that the number of Canadians who * were charged-not convicted-but charged in Cologne was very much lower than the number that would be ordinarly charged amongst a similar number of men during a like period.
When the First Canadian division at last, after four years of warfare turned its weary footsteps backward to return to the rear areas and to their homes in Canada, it did so with with the insults of Sir Charles Ferguson, the military Governor, ringing in its ears.
I want to say	one word about
the character of 'Sir Charles Ferguson and then 1	shall have done with
a subject which is a very unwelcome one to me, because this is the last thing that I should like to bring up. Sir Charles Ferguson is married to a woman of Cologne and that may account for some of his strange sympathies for the inhabitants. Sir Charles was in command of the 17th. Corps at Arras when the Canadian Corps was rushed down there to save that flank of the British army. I leave to history what was going on "in the south-Sir Charles Fergu-

son was very invidious in his references to the Canadians. Sir Charles Ferguson said to one of our officers:	"We never
had any trouble here until the Canadians came," and our officer answered: "Yes, that is what the Germans say."
'Sir Charles Ferguson was the man who gave up Monchy which was one of the points of vantage and which was really, in a sense the key to Arras because from Monchy, you could observe Arras and you would also observe a portion of the Lens salient. Who retook Monchy? The Canadian Corps. Sir Charles Ferguson gave up Monchy and several officers of the 15th Scottish division said to me that it was the most disgraceful moment of their lives when they had to walk out of Monchy and leave a perfectly good position, one of the finest on the front and give it up to the Germans.

About what date
was that?
Lt.-Col. PECK, V.iO.: Just about the *end of March.

In the retreat of
March?
Lt.-Col. PECK, VjC. :	Yes. Why do
I say all this? I will tell you. When I was standing before my grand old battalion at Lindlar, 25 miles east of Cologne; standing before those brave fellows with whom I had been associated for nearly four years, the grandest, the noblest, the finest men that it had ever been my privilege to be associated with, I said: " When I go back I am going to bring these matters to the attention of the House of Commons." I did not mention these things that Sir Charles Ferguson had said because they might have mobbed Sir Charles, or done something of that kind had they known. But I said: " I will go back to the House and defend the character of the Canadian army before the Parliament and people of Canada," and I mean to do everything I possibly can to make the name of Sir Charles Ferguson stink in the nostrils of all honest and patriotic Canadians. *
A lot of things happened in the British army that you never heard a word about. I rode into a town in 1917-there were 40,000 British troops in open insurrection, and they had taken 3,000 or 4,000 Canadian troops, not one of whom ever made any trouble, and put them to guarding railways and bridges, which I suggest was 4 p.m. an invidious duty. Things of this kind occurred and they never mentioned a word of it. The war is [Lt.-Col. Peck.]
still on and I am not going to mention things that happened this year, but there have been things of the most serious character that have happened on the continent, but nothing is ever said about these things. But when a Canadian does anything it receives the utmost publicity in a certain portion of the British press.
Now, I come to the question of demobilization. I am not going to discuss it at any length because I find that I have taken up more time than I intended. Most people do not seem to understand this question. I was very much impressed by the fine speech of the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn) the other day. Very few people seemed to know that demobilizing a volunteer army is a greater task than organizing that same army and sustaining it in the field. The great object for which the armies have been striving has been achieved and our men naturally wish to get back to Canada and to resume their ordinary ways of life as quickly as possible. I am not here as an apologist for the Government I do not mean to do anything of that sort, Sir, but we wish to be fair. Therefore, I repeat, I was very much impressed with what the minister said. He said that the people seemed to think that their duty had ended.
If there was one thing that served as a comfort and sustenance to us in the field it was the knowledge that we had behind us a strong, vigorous, generous and chivalrous people. It was the knowledge that every day men of different creeds and different points of view were meeting together and striving in an honourable emulation to do those things that were necessary to support us in the field.
I am sure that we must all make due acknowledgement to the hon. Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) for bringing to bear on the great question of finance his undoubted talents, and to all those workers who directed the energies and encouraged the enthusiasm of the Bed Cross workers and doing all those things necessary to make more effective the work of different organizations which contributed so greatly to the support of the troops in the field.
We owe an especial debt of gratitude to the fair women all over the land who met day after day in their little guilds and societies to organize the work of preparing and forwarding those comforts and parcels of wonderful things that we received in the field and which were so cheering to us in

those ghastly moments of warfare. That was the greatest comfort we had in the field in all those long years; it was like the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
And now I wish to appeal to this House and to the country not to think that our labours are done. Having given of your blood and treasure as you have so loyally and generously, I appeal to you to join in this colossal task of demobilization, and to help in getting this wonderful and magnificent army of ours settled back into the avenues of peace and into the field of production, so that they may be able to feel that they have the gratitude of a generous people.
I wish to allude at this point to a statement which was published in the Canadian press of yesterday or the day before. The statement in question originated from the Canadian Associated Press and was to the effect that the soldiers at Rhyl had broken into the girls' quarters-that is the nurses- that they (the girls) cowered under threatened) violence, and that the soldiers otherwise misused them. I desire to point out that Colonel Colquhoun, the commander of the camp at Rhyl, declared that the men had never gone into the girls' quarters and had behaved with the utmost chivalry towards them. I think the Government should investigate this report, and if the Canadian Associated Press is found to be circulating news in this country reflecting on the honour of our glorious soldiers it should be promptly repudiated.
Now, Sir, I come down to the affairs of mundane politics. There is one matter as to which I shall no doubt be out of order if I do not deal with it, and that is the matter of the latch string which has been so much referred to. The hon. leader of the Opposition has done two notable things in the last two weeks: he has become the leader of a great party, and he has coined a phrase. There was a great man who once said, " I would rather make an epigram than rule a nation." You can therefore see that the achievements of the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) are quite considerable.
I am one of those who are considered by the hon. gentleman as having wandered from the fold. I do not agree with that. I was overseas for four years fighting for the principles of Liberalism, and if the Liberal party has not kept up to the scratch it is no fault of mine. The reason I supported the Unionist Government, and the reason the great bulk of the Canadian troops at the front did so, was because we had no faith in the Liberals getting on with the
war. In the fall of 1917 our position at the front was desperate and precarious. We had had some successes that year, but we had only advanced at any point about two or three miles, except in one locality where probably an advance of five miles was made. We had only accomplished this by desperate fighting and after very serious losses.
I am now speaking of the British army. We knew that the Germans were preparing an attack upon a vaster scale than had ever before preceded the assault of an army. We knew that the U-boats were making great inroads into the commerce of Britain, and it was just nip and tuck-from all the information I have gathered iiTwas just nip and tuck from the way the U-boats were sinking vessels-and we knew that before the Americans could bring any considerable force into the field it would be very late in the following autumn. We knew that in the spring, whatever happened, we would be fighting with our backs against the wall for the very existence of the Allied armies, and for the very existence of the cause of liberty and civilization. Is it any wonder, then, that we turned to somebody who had a definite policy?
Now, Sir, I studied whilst overseas with the greatest possible attention the actions and th6 speeches of the members of the Liberal party as now constituted, and I could get no comfort-their policy was as the shifting sand. But, Sir, the Unionist Government at least offered us a definite policy, and a policy which gave us confidence that they would prosecute the war with all vigour. To whom should we turn therefore except to a Unionist Government, especially when we saw that their ranks comprised some of the most able and eminent Liberals in the country? Now, Sir, that is my position. When the Liberal party can show me that they have a more progressive programme than the Coalition, or any other party, and when they convince me that they are going to follow that policy, I will be prepared to support them. But I want to say this one thing: I am not going to go around in the darkness of the evening and gaze into the kitchen window, I am going to walk boldly in through the front door at high noon.
<1 am a Free Trader.

Hear, hear.
Lt.-iCol. PECK, V.C.: I am very much gratified, Sir, to hear the cheers of hon. gentlemen opposite, and I only wish that they had evidenced the same enthusiasm during the last twenty years.

Cheer now.
Lt.^Col. PECK, V.C.: Like the hon. members for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), and Springfield (Mr. Richardson), I had been a supporter of the Liberal party for some time, but I have at last come to the conclusion that there is very little difference between the two parties. Free trade and low tariff may, in certain sections of the country be very good planks to ride into power on, but our administrators always seem to find protection the best policy to keep in on, and it does not seem to matter which policy is carried on so long as they can stay in power and bask in the sunshine of office. In that respect both parties seem to be pretty much on the same footing.
Now, Sir, I was elected an Independent and soldiers' candidate, to support the war policies of the Unionist Government, and I wish to say that I certainly mean to do so until I see something better. I think we should give the Unionist Government a chance, and I must say that not only here but in the Old Country, I found the members of our Unionist Government were honestly and sincerely trying to grapple with this great question of demobilization to the best of their ability. I think we should give the Government a chance, and therefore I appeal to hon. gentlemen on both sides to be charitable in dealing with this question. It is all very fine to make a grandstand play in the House, and to read a letter from some soldier who may have had rather a hard time. At the same time 1 know that hon. gentlemen opposite do not wish to take advantage of mean political tactics, and therefore I appeal to them to show a spirit of charity in their attitude towards the Government. I can assure hon. gentlemen they will find that I will take an independent stand on questions. I do not hold a brief for the present Government, but until we get a better Administration I mean to support them.
In connection with the taking over of the Grand Trunk Pacific by the Government, I hope that the Government will institute a vigorous policy in regard to that road. I am told that there is quite a feeling throughout the country that if we leave this thing long enough under Government control the people will get sick of it and go back to private ownership. But I do not think that is a good view to take. A great friend of mine who was a well-known statesman in this country-I deplore the fact that he has since gone-once said: "You cannot build railways without imagination." Well,
I am afraid that you cannot run the Grand rLt.-Col. Peck. 1
Trunk Pacific for a short time without imagination. But the Grand Trunk Pacific runs through a tremendously rich country in the northern part of Canada and taps the great hinterland that lies to the north of all the other railroads. If a vigorous policy is put in force in this connection it would only be a short time before the Grand Trunk Pacific becomes one of the best paying roads in the Dominion. It has the lowest grades and should compete, I think, in every way with the other railroads. I notice the Minister of Railways (Hon. J. D. Reid) looking the other way. I hope that when the season opens up in the spring, a fast, modern, comfortable daily train will be put on between Quebec and Prince Rupert; I am sure that in time it would pay. I hope, 4oo, that steamship connection will be established with the Orient, because through the saving of thirty-six hours at sea and in going over the easy grades of the Grand Trunk Pacific, we can haul the rich cargoes of China, Japan and India, to the great markets of eastern Canada amd the United States much more advantageously than the other roads can do it. It is only a matter of the Government prosecuting the business with vigour and with a proper outlook, and keeping it free from graft and politics.
In closing, may I just say this. In the trenches we have no politics. It does not matter whether you are English-born or French-born, Roman Catholic, or Protestant, or anything else; you are the same as any other fellow in the trenches if you are a good soldier-and all our boys are good soldiers. In the trenches we were one grand brotherhood. Unless you are a soldier you cannot understand the espirit de corps that prevails. It is the next thing to the family feeling; it is a great and wonderful love for your fellow man. As I saw these fellows perform their duties in the avenues of death, under conditions of the greatest peril, without a murmur, always with the greatest cheerfulness, I used to think what a contrast it was when I read in Canadian newspapers accounts of some of the squalid, sordid political quarrels that take place in connection with Dominion, provincial, and municipal politics. I used to say to my officers that when our men got back to Canada, we should surely have a better national life. If we do not have a higher and nobler national life when these men-who have never quailed or faltered on the field of battle, who have shown that they possess every human virtue that men can have-return to Canada and are in-

corporated into our national life, then, Sir, I think that our sacrifices shall have been in vain and our time lost indeed.

speakeroldname: Hon. WILLIAM STEVENS FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
one of our old parliamentary forms is that which allows us, on the motion for the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne, to discuss a very wide range of questions. I think it is a wise provision in the old rules because it enables members at the very beginning of the session, if they so desire, to give expression to their views concerning the public affairs of the country. Sometimes when the debate is protracted, as this has been, outside critics find fault and tell us that, wo had better quit nonsense and get down to business. Sometimes, I suppose, the practice and the rule are abused; but there is another side to this good old form. There have been cases-far be it from me to say that this is one-when the Government, not being too ready with its business, or possibly waiting for somebody who is away to come back-may find it agreeable to allow two or three weeks to be spent at [DOT]the beginning of the session in the harmless occupation of passing the Address. Even that, however, has something to be said in its favour.
Then, there is a further and more serious aspect of the matter. Every government naturally and properly desires to form its policy in harmony with the recognized wish of Parliament, and when at this stage of the session we have this free-for-all discussion, the Government have the opportunity of learning public opinion from its various angles; and perhaps in the end the debate is helpful to" the business of the session and not, indeed, a waste of time.
In a debate of . this kind it is almost unavoidable that there should be a considerable amount of repetition; we deal with the same subjects and the same thing has to be said often. That I may avoid that as far as possible, may I be permitted, without dwelling on any one of the points, to say that I desire to have myself associated very cordially with many of the things which have been said by the hon. gentlemen who preceded me. I should like to be associated with the well deserved compliments that were paid to the hon. gentlemen who moved (Mr. Redman) and seconded (Mr. Manion) the Address; with the expression of gratification that we all feel upon the splendid triumph of the Allies and the apparent termination of the war; with appreciation of the triumphant and
heroic services of the Canadian soldiers and sailors; with reverence for the memory of those who have given up their lives; with resolve that those who are spared to come home shall have every consideration from a generous and grateful people.
I should like also-need I say-to be associated with the many eloquent, earnest and touching tributes offered from both sides of the House to the memory of our great Liberal leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who has passed away, a man who was honoured and admired by all and loved by those who knew him best.
To me it is a satisfaction-I believe it is to all of us-to feel that we have associated with us here in Parliament, in the work which we are undertaking as representatives of the people, so many gallant soldiers who served the Empire at the front and have won honour for themselves and for Canada. We are especially honoured by the presence and association of these men as fellow-workers in the discharge of our duty; and it will be no disparagement to others if I speak of the particular pleasure which we have all shared to-day as we listened to the voice of the gallant Colonel (Lt.-Col. C. W. Peck, V.C.) who wears on his breast the proudest honour that any soldier can have.
The subjects touched by the speech from the Throne are numerous. There used to be a time when, criticising speeches from the Throne both here and in our Provincial Legislatures, men were in the habit of saying that the Speech was more remarkable for what it did not contain than for what it did contain.
It is about the only thing that I have not heard said so far about the speech, and we cannot say that thbre is any lack of material.
The speech touches on many subjects of importance, and it sets forth a considerable bill of fare, promising a very busy session. There are some things that I suppose we shall be glad to have more information about. The overshadowing question before us to-day is one upon which we can at this stage hear but little. I refer to the financial question. The overshadowing question with us must be in regard to the tremendous burdens which are to fall upon us at the clo.se of the war and in regard to how these burdens are to be met. That they must be met intelligently and courageously, we shall all agree. We cannot at present expect any information respecting those. That stage has not yet arrived. Indeed, we do not need much information, for the thing is so big, the figures are so

colossal, that we can easily realize the tremendous burden we shall have to face, the awful debt that is accumulating, the tremendous obligations that we shall have to provide for. All that we know almost as well as when the Minister of Finance will give us the information in greater detail. We must be content to-day with the glimpse we have had of those things from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Car-vell). The figures, even in the hurried form that he gave them to us, axe startling. We know, however, that they will have to be given to the House in greater detail later on. In the speech of the Minister of Public Works, there were one or two sentences which contained a meaning beyond what he intended. He dwelt, once or twice in his speech, upon the fact that his department, in determining upon expenditure on public works, would have re- gard, not so much to the good of the community, as to the necessity for guarding against unemployment. I thought he dwelt too much on the unemployment and too little on the usefulness to the community. The two things should, I think, go hand in hand. There is in Canada no need, for the sake of guarding against unemployment, to engage in the construction of works which are valueless or of doubtful value. Canada is still a comparatively new country, comparatively undeveloped, and in every part of our Dominion useful public works can be constructed, if we have the means to do so, where we can combine the guarding against unemployment with the service to the whole community. I hope the minister will think more of the good of the community, although I am quite sure we all sympathize with him in his desire to guard against unemployment.
There is one question that we must all think of a little as we look at the vacant chairs, when we recall that there are five ministers of the Crown who are absent from their departments, and absent from their seats in this House. One of those gentlemen, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), has, we have learned with great regret, been laid aside by a very servere illness. We rejoice to know that he is in a fair way to recovery, and we shall all be glad to welcome him back to his seat in this House, we hope, at an early date. As respects the others, the explanation is not so clear. The Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), the Minister of Trade and 'Commerce (Sir George Foster), the (Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and tlxe Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton) are

absent. We are glad to know that they are not ill. 'It is a great pleasure to know that. * We know that they are in Paris. That is rather a pleasant place to be in if you have nothing particular to do. But what they are doing there, that is to say, what business they are doing, that is to say, what Canadian business they are doing in Paris, is one of the things that no fellow can very well understand. The Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) endeavoured to give us a little explanation; the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) gave us a little more, but whatever impression it made upon others, I must say that their contribution to the discussion led me to believe that they were just as much in the dark as we were. What in the world are these gentlemen doing away from their seats at the present time when there is so much to demand their attention at home? Ah, but you will say; are we not interested in the Peace Conference? Surely, the whole world is interested in the Peace Conference. Canada is interested in the Peace Conference. If Canada had never spent a dollar nor sent a man to the war, slxe would still be deeply interested in the Peace Conference, because it is dealing with world problems. I admit all that, but still the question remains: What interest has Canada in the Peace Conference that is not her interest in common with the Empire at large? If I did not know the hon. member for Halifax as well as I do, if I did not know him to be a loyal member of an ultra loyal Government, I would feel some cause for suspicion in his remarks, because he absolutely ignores the fact that Canada is a part of the British Empire. He gave us to' understand that if our ministers had not crossed the seas, Canada would not he represented. I cannot admit that for an instant. I am too good an Imperialist-an Imperialist of the right stripe, mark you-to admit what I would regard almost as a reflection on British statesinen. When Mr. David Lloyd George, Prime Minister of Great Britain, and Mr. Arthur Balfour, Foreign Minister, take their seats at the council board in Paris, Canada is represented, because Canada is a part of the British Empire. Unless it can be shown that Canada has some interest separate and apart from the British Empire, there is no particular reason why we should be represented there. P have enough faith in Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. Balfour to believe that if we had not sent a minister across the seas, the interests of Canada would not have been sacrificed.

There are times when Canada has an interest in public affairs somewhat apart, an interest of her own, an interest not at variance with the interest of the Empire, but an interest specially of her own. In that case it is undoubtedly a wise provision that Canada should be specially represented. In the past there have been numerous cases in which it has been desirable that Canada should be represented. I notice that in the speech from the Throne we are informed that our ministers are " attending " the Peace Conference. I think I can congratulate the Government upon the happy choice of that word. There are some hundreds of officials over there attending the Peace Conference, but attending the Peace Conference does not necessarily imply that they are doing any very large part of the business, and I have not been able to see that we have had there any Canadian business which calls particularly for their presence.
There is overseas a commercial mission which we should distinguish from the political mission. We have sent across the seas several prominent business men who form a commercial mission. Their object is to extend the trade of Canada. Prom all that I can learn they are not as successful in the matter as we would wish them to be, but whether they succeed or not, is, after all, not the question. The object in view is an excellent one, and I commend the Government for sending the Trade Mission. That mission has work to do; we know what it is those gentlemen are trying to do. But we cannot understand what in the world is the Canadian work that our ministers are doing in connection with the Peace Conference. I want again to emphasize the fact that Canada, as a part of the British Empire, would be represented if those gentlemen had not gone to the Peace Conference at all. I admit at once, as I said a moment ago, that there may be occasions when Canada has a special interest and at such times Canada should, of course, have her own representatives. What Canadian interest is before the Peace Conference in Paris to-day? We have no territorial axe to grind. We are not seeking any extension of territory, are we

She had a question of territorial expansion to be considered, so there was that excuse for Australia having special representation. She does not appear to have made much out of it, by the

Her special representation has accomplished nothing, and she could not have been any worse off if Mr. Hughes had stayed away, because the wishes of the Australian Government-I am sorry it was so-have been set aside. But Canada has no such ground for being there. We are seeking no expansion of territory, we have no islands to gather in; in the matter of expansion of territory we are absolutely without any claim.
What then? Indemnity? If we have a claim for indemnity, in all seriousness what in the world can we do but make out the bill and send it to Mr. Lloyd George? What more could anybody do? We cannot by any act of ours induce the Germans to pay us an indemnity. If there is to be an indemnity at all it will go to the British Empire, and I am loyal enough to believe that the British Empire will give us our share if we demand it. But it appears mat we do not want any indemnity. Some of the information we get from Paris we have to look on rather doubtfully perhaps, but now and then we get some information which has an official look. I have in my hand an extract from the Montreal Star's own correspondent, Mr. H. N. Moore, who in a cable from Paris dated February 10, says:
Canada will make no special claim. A certain responsibility was assumed during the war, and that responsibility will be carried to the end. If indemnities are claimed by Britain, if one of the terms of peace is that Germany must pay not only the bill for reparation and restitution, but must also shoulder the entire cost of the war, Canada would undoubtedly receive her share. But the delegation is not pressing for this. In fact, one might assume fairly that any such proposals would be deprecated*.
So we have no territorial expansion to seek, we do not want any indemnity, and in all seriousness il wish somebody would tell me what is the Canadian question which is at this time engaging the attention of the Peace Conference. There is a glamour, I suppose, about this idea of Canada having special representation. There is something fascinating about it, and many people who I think ought to be wiser are magnifying its importance and trying to make something out of it. The question is asked in Holy Scripture, "Which one of us by taking thought can add one cubit to his stature?" It was a hard question in Bible days. It was a question which was asked for the purpose of showing that the thing could not be done-but that was before the days of the Peace Conference. Mr. Speaker, some people seem to think that practically by taking thought, by passing some petty

Canada-and if there was any business to do over there that concerned Canada and that needed explanation, no man could do it better than my friend Mr. John W. Dafoe, of Winnipeg. But you cannot make bricks if you have neither straw nor clay; and as there was no Canadian business to transact, what in the world could Mr. Dafoe do? .Day after day he sent telegrams explaining this, that, and the other thing, and the very multitude of his telegrams became confusing. Well, we got occasional glimpses from other sources. Among the gentlemen who have been in Paris in connection, not particularly with the Peace Conference, but with various surrounding matters, a couple of gentlemen were sent from among the hard-headed farmers of Western Canada, to look after the wheat business. One of these gentlemen was Mr. Norman Lambert, the secretary of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, a very capable man. As far as I can see, he is an absolutely disinterested witness. I do not see that he can have any possible object in picturing things other than they really are. My friend the President of the Privy Council has tried to paint a picture of the grandeur of this work in which our ministers are engaged over there. Well, he has not been over there himself, and consequently must take things on hearsay. I desire to read a passage or two from the pen of a man who has been on the other side, a capable and reputable witness. I have not the pleasure of knowing Mr. Lambert personally, but I believe he is a gentleman of absolutely good repute. He has referred, in a public letter he wrote not long ago, to this story of the Council of twenty-five-the body that does not meet. He says:
" This spendld vision of a council of Twenty-five, however, suddenly vanished, and out of it sprang the indomitable Council of Ten, comprised of the Prime Ministers and Foreign Secretaries of the five great allied powers, in reality the .Supreme War Council of Versailles. No meetings of the Twenty-five have 'been held "- that is the body on which we do not get any representation; but if we have no meetings, we need not cry over the absence of our members.
" No meetings of the Twenty-five have been held, and the great Britannic Commonwealth has been represented entirely by Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. Balfour. As one crestfallen Canadian delegate expressed himself to me "-
Mark you, a Canadian minister.
" As one crestfallen Canadian delegate expressed himself to me, the proposed Council of Twenty-five was just so much eye-wash."
I would like it to be observed, Mr. Speaker, that the word " eyewash " is not 
mine; it is not even a word of the correspondent whom I am quoting. It is the word of the Canadian minister, the crestfallen minister, given to the correspondent.
Mow, if we have to rely upon our English dictionaries for an explanation I admit that there may be some difficulty in quite understanding the application of the word "eye-wash" to this particular state of affairs. But I believe I am correct when I say that the word "eye-wash" is French for camouflage. Mr. Lambert proceeds-
The reason for such eye-wash-
Camouflage.
-is not quite clear as yet to anybody outside the Ten, least of all to the Overseas Ministers.
So, Mr. Speaker, I hope you will see that I am giving you a fairly good authority for the picture I am trying to present to you of the true inwardness of this Canadian representation at the Peace Conference. He says that the thing is not satisfactory to the Overseas Minister and he goes on:
In order that the members of the British Peace Delegation from Overseas and the delegates from the nineteen small nations should have something to do, the Conference very graciously appointed them to a number of investigating commissions and special committees.
I described that to you a moment ago.
The Hon. A. D. Sifton, for instance, was made the principal British delegate on the Commission to report on international claims in connection with ports, rivers, and railways. Sir Robert Borden was asked to be a member of a commission to go to Prinkipo to deal with the Bolshevists, and also to join another body in determining the claims of Greece to greater territory. Hon. C. J. Doherty was named as a member of the British Sub-Committee on the League of Nations, but for some unexplained reason, no meeting of Mr. Doherty's Committee was ever called. He finally issued a statement to the press setting forth his views on the organization of a League of Nations, and thus was able to let the world know that the representative from Canada at Paris at least was thinking about the League of Nations.
In that little picture of our busy ministers overseas we have taken into account the Prime Minister, with his eyes towards Prinkipo, we have Mr. Doherty showing that he is thinking about the League of Nations, we have Mir. Sifton who seems to be looking after claims in connection with ports, rivers, railways and various other things which are not ports, rivers and railways over here. But there is a missing man. What in the world has become of our good friend the'Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster)? The only explanation I can offer of it is

that our good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was too old a bird to be caught with chaff of that sort. I think that when he came to size up the situation he said to himself: " Now, I think that instead of waiting around in the anteroom of the Conference Chamber for something to turn up I had better go down and take a stroll on the boulevard, have an occasional sip of pink lemonade and watch the passing show." If the Minister of Trade and Commerce did that, I commend his judgment, for I think it would be more profitable as well and more agreeable than sitting around the Conference Chamber doing nothing. I have said that this humbug became really so patent that it could no longer be concealed. I have shown you what the opinion of Mr. Lambert was. Now, let me look at Mr. Dafoe's official correspondence. Mr. Dafoe made a brave effort to put the best face on the matter and I commend him for ito He is a master of the art of making much ado about nothing. But he said: We cannot keep up the game any longer, the Canadian people will see through it, and so one day he sent out this despatch-I have not the date of it but it is some time in February:
There is undoubtedly a good deal of feeling at the concentration of the Conference powers in the hands of a small committee of the Great Powers, and it is also a fact that this feeling is shared to some degree by the Dominions which recognize that the assumption of the right of control by the Council of Ten has limited their participation in the affairs of the Conference, as provided by the original plan of organization. This feeling found expression at the last Conference and there is likely to be further evidence of it at the coming meeting.
They could not keep up the game any longer, they had to admit that all this was humbug and they entered this protest. I have not the date of that despatch but on the 19th February I find a later telegram from Mr. Dafoe. You will remember that the 19th February was only a short time ago and that our ministers have been away since November last and have been in Paris days, weeks, months, looking after the Peace Conference. On the 19th February Mr. Dafoe says:
For the first time a representative of the Overseas Dominions has served on The Supreme Council of Ten, the governing body of the Peace Conference. The British Empire's representatives at this afternoon's sitting were Mr. Balfour, the British Foreign Minister, and Sir Robert Borden.
So you see that after long and weary delays, after days and weeks and months sitting around looking for a chance to do something, at last, long last, Sir Robert
Borden is asked to go in that day, that sunny afternoon, on the 19th February. Of course, this was a great day! Of course, some great big thing was going to be done, some grand thing, something of importance to Canada, and that is why Sir Robert Borden was invited to be present! Now, listen:
The matter before the Council was Serbia's claim for enlarged territory.
Far be it from me to underestimate for a single moment the talents of our respected Prime Minister. We all know him here as a gentleman who is well equipped, a lawyer of high standing, and we all know that if there is anything to do, any real business falling within the scope of his professional attainments, he would do it and acquit himself well. But, is it any discourtesy to him to say that if anybody was needed to consider the boundary lines of Serbia there are twenty clerks in the British Foreign Office who could'do it better than the Prime Minister of Canada? Surely all this pretence of Canada having a great part in this Conference is largely humbug. When Canada accomplishes anything in the way of constitutional reform we should be glad to know it and to express our gratitude to those who bring it about. If Canada should acquire any dignity anywhere we should be pleased to know it, but, seriously, does it bring any dignity to Canada to be nominally connected with the Peace Conference under the circumstances described in these statements which I have presented to you- not my statements but information coming direct from headquarters in Paris? No, sir.
If my feeble voice could reach those gentlemen over there I would dare to say to them: " Good friends, come home; there is real business to be done in Canada. If it were not so, we would not hurry you. You Ministers are a hard worked lot; we would not begrudge you a holiday amid the pleasant surroundings of gay Paree, but there is too much real work to be done at home." If the Prime Minister still hungers for the society of the Bolsheviki down at Prinkipo, I would suggest that he read the description of them given by the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) the other day. My hon. friend pictured them very eloquently indeed and told us what kind of people the Bolsheviki are. Although I have no right to speak for the House generally on many things, I am going to assume that I will have the right on this, question to say to Sir Robert Borden: " In the name

of the Parliament of Canada do not have any truck or trade with those Bolsheviki." And if anybody is needed to settle the bounds of Serbia, or any other question of that kind, important as it may be to some people, there are a hundred persons over there who can do it much better than our respected ministers, and so I would beg them, " Come home, come home, there is lots of Canadian business to be done."
This idea of Canada being a nation seems to have seized the imagination of some people. They like to talk about it, they usually get the notion into their heads that it is a great big thing, that it is elevating Canada. Now I am not able to see it in that light. There is too much talk about Canada being a nation, loose talk; there is too much disposition to magnify our own importance without just cause. There was a report laid on the table of the House a week ago, a remarkable report, giving us some information as to the management of a large branch of the public business of Canada, and in that report the Commissioners said: " The art of doing nothing and making it look like real work seems to have been highly cultivated." Well, Sir, I think that somewhere in the departments here there must be a school of instruction for that sort of thing, and I think our ministers when they went overseas must have been taking lessons in that school, because ever since they have gone, there has been an effort to make it appear that they are doing wonderfully big things, and making of Canada a big nation, when, if X may dare to quote the words, the classic words, of a .Canadian statesman no longer with us, " There aint nothing to it." Canada a nation! There is a sense in which Canada is a nation. The British Empire has been happily described as a galaxy of nations, and in that sense Canada is a nation. But in world affairs Canada is not a nation, and I for one am not inclined to look with great joy when I find the ministers over there setting forth a claim that hereafter Canada is to be known as a separate state-. I quote these words from Lord Curzon, speaking in the British House of Lords. In his statement he uses the words that the place of the Dominions in the Conference was afi admission that these countries were henceforth, to be regarded as separate states by themselves. By themselves! That is to say that the Canadian ministers, and the other Dominion ministers, have put forth the claim that these Dominions are separate states. I do not like that, Mr. Speaker, I think it rather makes more for the separ-fMr. Fielding.]
ation that we used to be warned against than for the unity which we all desire. If our present state of affairs is not satisfactory-I know there are men who tell us occasionally that it is not-I would like to say to those who have any change to propose, " Give it to us in plain terms and let us see what it is." Imperial federation is a magnificent dream, and we are all better for dreaming it. I cling to the hope that one day-I do not know by what process- not by radical measures, not by revolution, but by that process of evolution under which the British constitution has developed "Where freedom broadens slowly down from precedent to precedent," by that process I hope and believe we will bring about some closer union between the Mother Country and the various portions of the Empire. There is an Imperialism and an Imperialism. There is an Imperialism which has been happily described as "jingoism," an Imperialism which blows the horn, and beats the drum, and waves the flag, and shouts about its own loyalty and questions the loyalty of other men who do not agree with it. If that is Imperialism, from it, good Lord deliver us all.
But there is another, and I think a truer Imperialism, to which I am proud to subscribe. If to be a loyal subject of the Crown-at this time when crowns are tumbling all around-if to be proud of British citizenship; if to feel that the British Empire is the greatest force, under divine Providence, for the spread of freedom and the extension of civilization throughout the world; if to desire all portions of that grand empire to come into harmonious co-operation, and into as much unity as is consistent with the maintenance of our own autonomy-if that be Imperialism, then I am proud to call myself an Imperialist. But I would earnestly beg that those who want change, those who are dissatisfied, will tell us plainly and squarely what their grievance is. I know of no grievance that Canada has. Canada has no difficulty in regard to her foreign relations. She has no need of asserting herself as a separate state-I am quoting again the words of Lord Curzon that these Dominions now claim themselves to be separate states. We have had occasion to deal with international affairs, but we never up to this moment had any minister of our Dominion set forth the claim that we were to be a separate state. We have long, Sir, had the right, with the cooperation of the British Government, to deal with international affairs when they concerned Canada. Go back a few years

to 1872, to the time of the Treaty of Washington. Go back earlier. No doubt in the olden days there was a time when Canada was not consulted; when the colonies were not consulted, when the colonies had not advanced to the status which they have since obtained, when treaties were made by Great Britain and they bound the empire whether we liked them or not. But that has all passed away. By the legitimate, constitutional development of Canada we long ago acquired the right to be heard and consulted in our international affairs. In 1872 when the Treaty of Washington had to be negotiated, Sir John Macdonald went to Washington along with the Imperial Commissioners. He did not say, "I come as representing a separate state." He said, "I come as representing the British Empire." And when, a little later, the fishery question came up, and when Mr. Joseph Chamberlain and (Sir Charles Tupper went to Washington to deal with matters from the Canadian point of view, the Canadian representative did not set up any claim that Canada was a separate state; he went there as a commissioner of the Empire, empowered by the British Government. A little later a small treaty, not a big treaty- a lopsided and unfair treaty, by the way- was made at Paris on behalf of Canada by Lord Dufferin, the British Ambasador, associated with Sir Charles Tupper, then High Commissioner for Canada. But Sir Charles Tupper did not put forward any plea to be considered as the representative of a separate state; it was enough for him that he represented the British Empire. Come down a little later. It fell to my lot to be associated with my friend-not now in politics-now Mr. Justice Brodeur to negotiate what I believe we may call the ' most important commercial arrangement with a foreign country that was ever transacted on behalf of Canada-the Franco-Canadian Treaty of 1908. Well, Sir, when my friend Mr. Brodeur and I went to the conference, went to the office at Paris, the very place where the Council is meeting to-,day, the Foreign Office at the Quai d'Orsay, we were received with respect as the representatives of Canada, because our French friends knew we had come to do Canadian business. But I do not hesitate to say that we were received with greater respect, and whatever we had to say and do had very much greater weight, because my colleague and I were able to place before the Government of Mr. Clemenceau-for the old Tiger was then as now Premier of France-and because we 31
were able to place in the hands of Mr. Pichon-who was then and is again to-day, in the whirligig of French politics, Foreign Minister-because we were able to place on the table of the Foreign Office at Paris our credentials as the plenipotentiaries of His Majesty, signed by King Edward. That was the thing that gave us weight, and strength, and power, in addition to whatever power and authority we had as ministers of Canada. That is the way these negotiations have been conducted in the past. What more could we ask? What more can we ask by way of liberty from the British Government than we have to-day? I do not hesitate to say, Sir, I can think of no change that we can ask in our relations to-day which will be at the same time of advantage to the Empire, and acceptable to our Canadian people. There have been schemes of Imperial federation devised, worthy, I am sure, in their purpose, devised by people who are very patriotic and thought they were doing good, but which one of these schemes has ever been found acceptable to the Empire, or even to the Canadian people? Not one of them, Sir, down to this moment.
The President of the Privy Council (Hon. N. W. Rowell) said the other day that the present condition was intolerable, inconceivable; that we could not go on as we are. "Inconceivable"-Sir, the word is not new; there is a familiar ring about it. For a generation and more men have been telling us that things could not go on as they were; that conditions were intolerable, inconceivable. Fussy but well meaning men in the Mother Country have been devising schemes for reorganizing the constitution of the Empire and have been telling us that it is intolerable and inconceivable that things should go on as they are. But the thing which was inconceivable and intolerable persisted in going on. When the South African war came, hundreds and thousands of Canadian boys volunteered and went to South Africa to fight for the flag; out of the intolerable and inconceivable conditions sprang the splendid movement which brought honour to Canada and honour to the flag. Then, we had the same cry; things were intolerable, inconceivable. And what happened? The great war came on. We had been told by these worthy but well-meaning people that if their particular fad or constitution were not adopted, the British Empire would go to the "demni-tion bow-wows." But when the great war came on, without any demand from anybody, by the free voice of the Canadian



people supported by the Canadian Parliament, we raised half a million men to fight for the flag. Intolerable? No, Sir; these things are not intolerable; they are not inconceivable.
True, there is an anomaly in the position. I grant you at once that if we had been obliged to take part in the war, having no voice in the making of it, the condition would be inconceivable and intolerable. But under the principles of our constitution the only power which in reality could carry Canada into the war was the power of this Parliament; and I see nothing inconceivable, nothing intolerable, in that situation so long as the thing that we do is the result of our free voice. I have said that I should be glad if some scheme of closer union could be devised. So far, I have not seen any, and until some better scheme is devised may it not be wisdom that we should rather "bear the ills we have than fly to others that we know not of"?
What is it that Canada wants that she had not to-day? I do not think that Canada has any grievance in her relations with the Mother Country, and I see no particular reason why we should distress our souls over the situation. I fear that out of this glamour of a separate nation, out of this glamour of Canada playing a part of her own, will come some scheme by which we shall grasp for the shadow of a vague imperialism and lose the substance of the autonomy which we already possess.
I want to touch now on a more material question, that of the tariff. We have heard a great deal about it; no doubt we shall hear much more about it in the days to come. There is alarm and surprise in Canada on the part of a large section of our respected fellow-citizens, the manufacturers. They are very much alarmed at the outlook, especially in the West. There is just cause for their alarm. When they see the movement in the West; when they see these many meetings of agricultural organizations; when they see the legislatures of Manitoba and Saskatchewan unanimously passing resolutions demanding great tariff changes; when they find hon. gentlemen on your right, Mr. Speaker, demanding great tariff changes in general terms; when they find hon. gentlemen on your left declaring that there is no line of cleavage between them and the West and that they are prepared to act with the West-then, there is a very grave situation, and the manufacturers may well be alarmed.. For their alarm there
TMr. Fielding.]
is much reason; for their surprise there is'' none. The situation which meets the manufacturers to-day is one which any reasonable man might very easily have anticipated. At times there are great movements of which you cannot get warning; there are tides which come without warning. I was much impressed by a passage in the speech of President Wilson at New York a few days ago when he was warning his people against some of the dangers which were presenting themselves to his mind. He said:-
And I want to utter this solemn warning, not in the way o>f threat. The forces of the world do not threaten ; they operate. The great tides of the world do not give notice that they are going to rise and run. They rise in their majesty and overwhelming might, and those who stand in the way are overwhelmed.
These are wise words, wise in their relation to many things in ovir country and in all countries to-day. But of the tide that is rising in our western country there was no lack of warning.
What was the condition of the western country and of Canada _ generally a few years ago? Shall il dare speak of the year 1911? Generally, Canada was prosperous, more than prosperous in her western territory. While the whole country was doing pretty well, a careful observer might have noticed that the greatest prosperity was coming to Canada in the West; that the greatest growth of Canada was in the West, and it would, not have required very much wisdom and sagacity to look ahead and see the consequences which were to follow from that condition. Unfortunately, our manufacturing friends did not seem to see it. I should not apeak of manufacturers generally, because there were many sane exceptions-I will not be invidious and say honourable exceptions, because they were all animated by what they believed to be their own interests. I am making no reflection on the motives of any, but the manufacturers were solemnly warned. I am going to read to you some words-they are worth something, though the one who spoke them may be of no significance-from an address that was delivered in the midst of the manufacturers in Montreal in March, 1911. The speaker was a Liberal, supporting reciprocity. He made an allusion to a speech that he had made on a previous occasion, and then proceeded to enlarge his idea. He said:-
I ventured to point out to the manufacturers of Canada-
That was in the previous speech.

-that it was a mistake for them to array themselves in antagonism to the people of the Western Provinces. That opinion I want to express again to-day. There is the danger that East and West may be brought into antagonism. The danger is not to be found in Reciprocity itself, but the danger is that the manufacturing interests of this country and their allied moneyed interests will array themselves in hostility to the growing feeling of the Western farmers. Don't make any mistake about it-the day is within sight of the younger men here, and of some who are not so young, when there will be more people [DOT]west of the Great Lakes than east of the Great Lakes. The West is going some day to dominate Canada and we, who live in the East, if we are wise, may as well look ahead and see this. What kind of a West is it to be? Is it to be a wise and prudent and sympathetic West; or is it to be a rash and reckless and dangerous West? The answer can be made by the manufacturers of the Dominion and the allied moneyed interests to-day. I do not hesitate to say that with proper care, with fair treatment, with reasonable argument, we can bring the Western farmer to be sympathetic and to be willing to work in harmony with the people of the Eastern country, who have done so much for the building up of the West.
And further on, the speaker continued:
But suppose you do not do that. Suppose the manufacturers should organize to-day with their money to defeat this agreement. I want to tell you, my brethren, that there will grow up in that western country a dangerous feeling. Don't make any mistake about it. I beg the manufacturers of this country-I always talk frankly to them and I am doing so now-I beg them not to range themselves up against the farmers of the West. The manufacturers are not hurt; they are more frightened than hurt. I give it to you as my opinion, worth much or worth little, that if by the forces of the manufacturers this agreement be destroyed, there will grow up in that western country a feeling that will be dangerous to the manufacturing interests of Canada and dangerous to the welfare of this Dominion.
Whose words were these? I did not catch the name.

I do not think that is of importance. The words are of value; it is of no importance who spoke them. The very condition that is spoken of in those words is facing us to-day. It did not require any great sagacity to make that prediction; it was the observation of the signs of the times. In the West we find that every prediction made at that time is coming true. The manufacturers, who were looking out for number one, unfortunately did not observe what was coming. I do not blame them for looking out for number one. I am not questioning their motives; I am questioning their wisdom. A person has to look out for number one to a certain extent, because if a person does not look after his own interests, nobody else will look after it for him. But there is an intelligent selfishness and a clumsy selfishness,

and I think our manufacturers indulged in a clumsy selfishness when they ranged themselves against that reciprocity agreement. What is to be the outcome of all this? We have seen in the meetings in the West; we have seen in the resolutions of the legislatures of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and we see elsewhere all through the West, the evidence of a deep feeling of unrest, of discontent, a determination that the West will no longer allow itself to be dominated by the East. We see it in the expressions of hon. gentlemen here to-day who, in their earnest desire to help the Government, are refraining from saying things that they would like to say. What is going to be the outcome of it all. Some of our Liberal friends from the West have, somehow or other, had the besetting sin of failing to adequately recognize and appreciate the measure of tariff reform that they received from the former Liberal Government. If you consider only the saving of money by way of taxation at the Custom house; that is to say, if you .look at what was paid in Customs taxes during the period of the

If my hon. friend can tell me that as an independent man so-called, he could get through this House any measure of great importance without the intervention and support of the Government, he will give me a valuable piece of information. I want to say in all sincerity to my farmer friends that if they want to accomplish anything in this great work they must look over the ground and see which of the two great political parties- and there are going to be two; I am not speaking of immediate action-comes nearest to his views. I would say, with all deference to those advising them to keep out of politics, that until they are able to pursue that course they will accomplish nothing.
