Mr. Speaker, just before the Deputy Speaker left the Chair at six o'clock, I was endeavouring, necessarily in a somewhat hurried way, to present a review of the tariff policy of the Laurier Government, particularly in reference to the western country, and with some reference to the future tariff policy, and particularly as to the manner in which any great reform must be accomplished in this country. I do not wish to enlarge on that subject now. It is enough to say that I realize that it is a question of very great importance and'that upon whomever may fall the responsibility of dealing with the question, he will have to approach it with a sense of its immense importance in relation to a great many interests in this country.
There is only one point I care to add. I have noticed a revival of the movement to establish what is called a permanent tariff commission. Several years ago the Conservative Government introduced a measure to appoint such a commission. The meas-

ure failed to pass the Senate, and for the session it was abandoned. The Government did not revive it. I judge from that fact that on further consideration they came to the conclusion that the policy was not a wise one. If that was their conclusion I desire to endorse it very warmly, because I am persuaded that the appointment of a tariff commission is not the best way of dealing with tariff affairs in the Dominion of Canada. There is such a commission in the United States, it is true, but the methods of dealing with these things in the United States are not the same as in our country. I need, hardly remind the House that in the United States members of the Government have nothing to do practically with the tariff question. The tariff is dealt with by a ' committee of Congress. The argument in favour of a tariff commission is that members of the Government cannot, with the thousand and one things they have to do, understand fully the tariff question and deal with it in the best way. Therefore, it is argued, they should have a body of experts to deal with it. I noticed quite recently in the Montreal Gazette, a very influential Conservative paper, revival of the argument in favour of a tariff commission. I want to quote a passage from that article in order that I may answer it. The Montreal Gazette of March 5 says:
What a permanent tariff commission may recommend, and what the Government may accept, are not necessarily the same thing, and, in any event, Government, and not the commission, must stand or fall by its tariff policy.
That is a very plausible statement, Mr. Speaker, but when we come to analyse it it absolutely fails to carry conviction. See what the situation is. We are told that there ought to be a tariff commission because the minister, the members of the Government, with the thousand and one things they have to do, cannot sufficiently attend to the tariff question. In other words-I do not say it offensively-the theory is that the Government, and the Minister of Finance, who is usually the officer of the Government dealing with such matters, are incompetent to deal with the tariff question. 'Therefore, they say, vve will appoint a tariff commission which is competent. Then, we are told, after the tariff commission has reported, it is for the Government to say whether it will or will not adopt the recommendation. See how strange the situation would bej, The Government are, according to the argu-
[Slr. Fielding.]
ment, incompetent to deal Nvith the question; therefore, you appoint competent men, and after your competent men have been sitting in judgment and have made a report and decided what we ought to do, you are going to leave it to the incompetent men to decide that they shall set that report aside. The thing is preposterous.
Under our system of government responsibility for the tariff, the greatest taxing machine we have, must rest with the Government and for it they must be responsible to Parliament. Under the custom of our Government the Minister of Finance becomes the proper person to deal with that question. It is certainly to be desired that he shall surround himself with competent help. If he has experts to-day, by all means let him have the benefit of help. If they are not the right ones he will get others. If he needs more help get it by all means; let him surround himself with the best possible help and advice he can get in order that he may do justice to the tariff question as a whole. When that has been done let him take that advice and apply it as he thinks best, bring down his measure to Parliament, but not try to set up any tariff commission between himself and the Parliament of Canada. With that I shall pass away from the tariff question, although it is a very broad and inviting one.
So much has been said about the evils of party politics that I want to say something of the good of party politics. So many hon. gentlemen have told us of the dreadful things that have been done by party politicians. Well, the party system is not perfect. When you say that you only admit that it is a human institution. I am persuaded that those who say that have not fully realized the purpose of the party system. Undoubtedly you can point to harm that has come from party government, but on the other hand, after coming to a calm judgment upon the question, I say you can get better results from party government than from any other kind of government except under certain special circumstances, such as, I frankly say, have existed very lately.
I am going to ask the House to permit me to indulge for about three minutes in a little personal reference. I do not like to intrude my personality upon the House. But I have frequently seen in the public press references to the circumstances under which I had the honour of being elected to this House, and the statements have not always been quite accurate. It seems to me that the point is not important, but if it is

worth while discussing in the press at all perhaps we might as well have the information correct. I was nominated by a Liberal convention. If that is not clear enough and you want something more explicit, I was nominated by a straight Liberal Convention. I was nominated by the same kind of convention, and largely by the same men, as those who had honoured me with nominations for many years before. There was no Unionist convention held or called. My Conservative fellow-citizens held a convention at the same time. They nominated a gentleman as their candidate, and he de-dined to run. I am advised, and I think I am correct, that they then nominated another gentleman, and he declined to run. Then the convention adjourned. A few days later two gentlemen prominent in the Conservative party did me the honour of calling upon me, and they said that they had been instructed by their party to say that they would be glad if I would agree to accept a nomination from them. They knew that I had already been nominated by my Liberal friends, but they proposed that I should be the nominee of both parties. T told them that it would not be wise that I should accept the suggestion. I appreciated very much their courtesy in intimating that they were not likely to oppose me. We take our politics pretty seriously in Nova Scotia, but however seriously we take our politics down there I am glad to say that in all the years I have had the honour to represent that same constituency my personal relations with my Conservative friends have always been agreeable and I have received a great many courtesies from them. I confess that I was pleased with the intimation I received from them, that they were not likely to give me' any opposition. For that courtesy I gave them my warmest thanks, which thanks I repeat here to-day, but I told them that I thought it was best, as I had already been nominated by the Liberal convention, and had accepted the nomination, that I should stand by it. That is the whole situation. Before I was nominated, and after I was nominated, and before I accepted the nomination, I had a heart to heart talk with my Liberal friends. I told them that I was obliged to differ with my leader and with a great many of my friends of the Liberal party on the question of conscription. I told them, whether I was wise or not in doing so, that I supported conscription and that I must take the same position then. I told them that while I thought Union Government had come too late to effect most
of its purposes, I realized the difficulty they had in appreciating the situation. While I felt that Union Government would have been much better if it had come three years before, yet, now that it had come, I was disposed to give it an independent support, especially in all matters in any way dealing with the war. One friend of mine in the convention, with that desire for clear and explicit information which I think is characteristic of Liberals, rose and said: "Mr. Fielding, I want to ask you a question: suppose when the elections are coming on -and, of course, this was before the elections-"it turns out that there is a pretty equal division of the parties up there, and the leader of the party moves a vote of want of confidence in the Government, what will you do?'' I said, "I will vote against that motion. I feel "it to be my duty under the circumstances to give the Government a fair chance to bring forth their measures." That was the situation, Sir, under which I left my constituency. That was my position then, and that is the position which I desire to take to-day. I think the time has not come to bring about a change of Government in this country. I am prepared to-day to play the part of an independent supporter of the Unionist Government. How many hours, days, weeks or months that condition may continue I do not presume to say; but I think I have good reason, satisfactory to myself, why it would not be wise to press for a change of Government at this moment.
In the first place, Sir, the Unionist Government has brought forth a large number of measures designed to meet the conditions which the country is obliged to face. I am willing to admit, Sir, that these gentlemen are honestly and sincerely endeavouring to make the best they can of these arrangements. I do not for a moment believe that these gentlemen have any other desire than to do the best they can in the face of the difficulties which present themselves; and for that reason I would not desire at present to have a change of Government take place. On the various questions that may come up in the House I desire to hold myself free to vote according as my judgment may lead me, and according to the merits of the issue presented. But I say now that unless some new conditions present themselves, unless there is some new situation not visible at this moment, no vote that I shall give will have for its object the turning out of the Government at the present time. There i3

another reason which I desire to give. I think it not advisable to make a change of Government now, because I take it for granted that a change of Government will involve a general election, and I do not think it is in the interest of the country, or of any party, that we should now have the strife of a general election. We are too near the last election to permit us to indulge in the hope that an election to-day would be carried on quietly and smoothly; the echoes and the passions of the last election would remain; we would have a bitter contest, and I am not prepared to say which side would win. I do not think, even for the interests of my friends of the Liberal party, that it is wise for them to press to-day for a change of Government. If my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) or any of his friends should to-day move an amendment to the Address I should be obliged to vote against the amendment; I should take the ground that the Government are entitled to carry their Address. That is the first step to be taken in the management of the affairs of the country, and I should be willing to have that done, and to give them a chance to produce their measures.
Another reason, Mr. Speaker-not the highest reason, not the noblest reason-is that I do not think my Liberal friends have yet brought about that degree of unanimity and unity in the party which I believe to be essential to success. Now, I believe that unity is necessary for any party; a party naturally wants unity in order to carry on its organizations; I am sure that desire must be in the minds of my Liberal friends. Surely, we will all agree in that? Then there is a further reason. With all due respect to my Conservative friends-and I speak of them with great respect, because although we differ from them we try to differ as becomes men- I am persuaded that in the conditions which exist to-day, or which will exist very soon, while any Government will have a troubled time, the only Government which can have any hope of meeting the progressive spirit of this country will be a Government dominated by the Liberal party; and that being the case my desire is that we should bring about that unity which seems to me to be essential for all good ends. We will all agree on either side, I am sure, that that unity is desirable. How is it going to be brought about? I have no special prescription to give as to how it may be done, but perhaps I can be helpful in offering some suggestions how not to do it. Unity in the
	<
Liberal party is not going to be brought about by the men of either section-for there are two sections-throwing rocks at the other, or calling the other names. Unity in the Liberal party is not going to be brought about by either party assuming towards the other a holier-than-thou attitude; nor by either section assuming that they are in exclusive possession of the ark of the covenant of Liberalism, and that all who do not agree with them are worshipping at the shrine of Tory idolatry. None of these things will bring about Liberal unity.
Lastly, may I say that unity in the Liberal party is not going to be brought about by any kind and generous offer to give Christian forgiveness to the wandering brother. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition made a speech which was admirable in its tone, and moderate throughout; there was hardly anything in it that anybody could take exception to. If I had to take any exception at all it would be to the passage which has been so much talked about, as to the light in the window and the latch string hanging out. My hon. friend I know extended that invitation in the true spirit of Scottish hospitality, but if he will read it carefully again he will find that there is running through it that note of Christian forgiveness to which I referred, as though he were saying, "Poor wandering boys, we are sorry you made such a huge mistake, but if you will come back-we do not say, like the Master, go and sin no more, we say, come and sin no more; and if you will just be good and not do this thing any more you will be welcomed back to the old home". Well, Sir, although I admit that this is all done in the kindest [DOT]spirit, it jars upon the ears of some of us. If there was a suspicion of something of that kind in the speech of my good friend the leader of the Opposition, there was more than a suspicion of it in the remarks of two or three other hon. gentlemen who spoke. Now, Mr. Speaker, the men who wandered away, if that is the phrase, we are not sure they did wander away; but these men who, for conscience sake, for empire's sake, for what they believed to be right, separated themselves from the friends with whom they were associated, separated themselves from the leader whom they loved

these men are not asking any forgiveness; they have no apologies to offer, they have no regrets to express. They felt that they were right; they feel now that they were right. But I do not wish to insist that they alone were, right. They recognize that the question of conscription was a large

one upon which men might differ. They realize that the men who supported conscription and the men who apposed conscription might be equally loyal and patriotic. We who supported conscription did not for a moment, and do not now, question the loyalty or the patriotism of the men who opposed conscription. They were within their rights. If we give them that credit, and do not for a moment question their loyalty or their patriotism, is it too much to ask that similar consideration shall be given to the others? Is it too much to ask now that we shall consider. that question one upon which men may honourably differ, and no longer feel that it should be a cause of quarrelling between us? If some of my Liberal friends want to proclaim that the man who supports conscription cannot be a Liberal- and I have heard that almost said in the course of the discussion-then we shall be obliged to point out that if we erred in that respect we erred in good Libera! company. We have already been reminded that we supported conscription along with Mr. Herbert Asquith, the distinguished leader of the Liberal party in England. We supported conscription along with Mr. David Lloyd George, who, though he may be criticised to-day, has surely been a large contributor to the upbuilding of Liberalism in Great Britain. We supported conscription along with five-sixths of the Liberal party in the British House of Commons. We supported conscription along with Lord Crewe and Lord Bryce-James Bryce as we know him better-and all the Liberals in the House of Lords.
We have supported conscription, Sir, in common with the great mass of the Liberals of the Mother Country; we have supported conscription along with the most distinguished figure in the Liberalism of the world to-day, President Woodrow Wilson. If we are able to point to these examples; if we are able to show some reason for what we believed to be right, though we do not insist that we only were right; may we not ask my hon. friends of the Liberal party to revise their judgment on some of these questions? May we not ask them, not to admit that they were wrong, but simply to admit the possibility that the other fellow inay have been right; that there may have been two sides to the question? And when my hon. friends invite us to return to the home, when they tell us that the latch string is hanging out, perhaps they would do well-the Scripture says:	"Let a man examine himself"-
to give a little consideration to the question whether or not the home to which they invite us is really the old homestead; whether it may not be that they, rather than we, have wandered away. The point is worth considering; and with a very old and hackneyed story, which is very appropriate, I will close this portion of my remarks. It is the story of an Indian who was found wandering in the forest. A passer-by stopped him and said:	"John,
what is the matter, are you lost?" " Lost?" was the answer; "No, Indian not lost; Indian here-wigwam lost."
The speech from the Throne, Mr. (Speaker, deals with several matters which, strictly speaking, are of local concern. Legislation is foreshadowed with regard to technical education, to housing schemes, to highways and to public health-all matters which are largely, if not entirely, within the field of the local legislatures. Some of my Liberal friends feel so strongly on the question of provincial rights that they have objected to the Government legislating on these subjects at all. Well, I do not care to go quite so far as that; il would rather have these things done with the help of the Dominion than not have them done at all. The (Fathers of Confederation, who are often so highly praised, especially by those who know least about their work, made a sad mess of the financial relations between the Dominion and the provinces. For years efforts have been made to straighten them out, but even yet these relations are hardly satisfactory. The provinces gave up to the Dominion the power of taxation in respect of customs and excise. There is this curious difference between the eastern and the western provinces: the western provinces were created by the Dominion, whereas the eastern provinces created the Dominion; the provinces are the fathers in the East, the Dominion is the father in the West. The eastern provinces, then, surrendered their right of taxation, thus enabling the Dominion to gather into the Federal treasury enormous sums of money. The theory of the scheme was that there was a reservation of a sufficient sum to enable the provinces to carry on their work efficiently. Time very soon proved, Sir, that the provision made for the provinces was entirely inadequate. For some years nothing was done; Sir John A. Macdonald was so proud of the Confederation scheme that he would not permit any change of it, he would not listen to any suggestion of change from the provinces. When the old chief passed away and other people came to the front, somehow or other they listened to the claims of the provinces and once or twice material

changes have been made by which the provinces have been put in a better position to handle their affairs. But, even as it stands to-day, the provinces have not sufficient means. If, then, technical education is desirable; if housing is desirable; if the public health improvement is desirable; even if roads and bridges are desirable, I say at once that while I regret that the provinces are not able to do these things, I am prepared to help the Dominion Government do them rather than have them
not done at all. _____
As to the question of highways, there is a danger. The matter has been before the House in time past, and the impression has seemed to grow that the Dominion Government wished to get control of the highways for party purposes. All I care to say about that is this: if the Dominion Government are to provide money for any given purpose and are to put it in the hands of the local governments, the Dominion Government may reasonably ask assurance that the money shall be applied to that particular purpose. That is a fair provision. If the Dominion Government are to provide money for roads, they should require of the provincial governments the assurance that the money will be spent on road schemes. Beyoud that, I do not think that the Government should interfere; they should let the province handle the business and be responsible for it.
And that same principle would apply to other things. In regard to public health, may I say a word? I do not know whether the project of the Government contemplates the creation of a department of public health with a minister at the head of it. We have a good many ministers now; we have been splitting up departments in order to appoint more, and I rather think the Government could arrange this thing without increasing the number of ministers. However, the argument is commonly used that a department of public health will be created at the head of which an eminent medical man will be placed. There are on both sides of this House quite a number of eminent medical men; I have no doubt that there are a dozen men here any one of whom would honourably fill the position of head of a department of public health. At the beginning, then, you would get your medical man. But how long would he continue as head of the department? Unfortunately, we have not arrived at that condition of unity in Canada which enables us to select a man for a department of government irrespective of race, of creed, of province or of division. A vacancy occurs in the cabinet. The question is not, who is
[Mr. Fielding;. 1
the best man for the position? It is: who is the best man for the position within the ranks of the party-necessarily he has to be of the same party-and within the particular division from which he comes? The vacancy may be in respect of a position- I am speaking very frankly-that had been held by a gentleman of the Roman Catholic faith-when you come to fill his place and you are inclined to put a Protestant in the position, you discover that the balance of power would be disturbed if you did that. It may be a case where a vacancy exists out in the western country and there is a medical man somewhere down East, where the wise men come from, whom you would like to put there. But you discover that his province is already occupying all the space it can in the Government;-so you cannot take him in. The truth is that under your scheme of putting a medical man at the head of a department of public health, you would have him at the beginning, you might get him once or twice, but by-and-by you would discover that the head of the medical department was probably some respectable fanner, or, more likely, some lawyer-who, 1 hope, would be respectable.
Now, names do not always mean what they seem to imply. We have a Minister of Agriculture; how often has he been a practical agriculturalist? For many years the Department of Agriculture was presided over by excellent gentlemen who had no particular connection with agriculture. We have a Department of Railways; but when was there a railway engineer at the head of it? Never. These names mean nothing, and the result in this case will be that although you start in with an eminent medical man, in a few years, owing to conditions of party politics, divisional politics, racial politics, religious politics, you will have great difficulty in keeping that man in. It seems to me that if you want to have an eminent medical man preside over that department, the better plan would be to have him act as the head in some other form-as deputy minister, for instance- then he can be there and give the country continuous service. If you put him in as minister of the Crown he may be there a few months, and then he may pass away altogether. I offer that suggestion to my hon. friends in all good faith.
Now I am going to say something on a thorny question-prohibition. I may be told by my friends on your left, Sir, that this is a thorny question which the Government will have to worry over, and that we had better let them do the worrying. I have no desire to treat the question in that way; I would rather be helpful and constructive.

if I could, in the matter. What is the situation to-day? By an Act of the Parliament of Canada-because the Order in Council is equivalent to an Act of Parliament of Canada-supplementing the Acts of the provincial legislatures, we virtually have prohibition over the Dominion to-day. We have actual prohibition in all the provinces save one, and in that province I understand we shall have prohibition on the first day of May. I think it never was, and is not now, the duty of the Government and of this Parliament to take any initiative in legislation on the question of prohibition.
I think that is a question on which we might have due regard to the principle of provincial rights. In the olden days, just before Confederation, there were grave difficulties over the form which our constitution should take. There were men who held that we should have a legislative union, one centralised power at Ottawa, whereas, the other side of the question was that we should have a federal union wherein each province should have its own legislature. This idea of a centralized union was a very fascinating one, and I am not surprised to learn, as I do ifrom various sources, that Sir John A. Macdonald, that masterful man, wanted to have a centralised union. He wanted to have everything here at Ottawa under his own thumb. I have rather a liking for that suggestion of a one-man power, under certain limitations, the putting of one man into some central place to do something, taking care to see that you get the right man and then supporting and helping him. That is the way to get things done, that is the way in which the war was won, when Marshal Foch was made the one-man power for the whole of the Allies. So, I rather like this notion within certain limitations. It would, however, never do in Canada. Our territory is too vast; you cannot undertake to deal with all the affairs of this country from the centre at Ottawa. Moreover, there are the differences of race and creed and other things. So the Fathers of Confederation, in their wisdom, determined that we should have a federal union. I think it is right that the question of prohibition should be viewed largely from a provincial standpoint. It was not and is not the duty of this Government to take the initiative in legislation on that question, but it was and is their duty to supplement the legislation of the provinces by such measures as will make the prohibition thoroughly effective. We have at present a Dominion law which provides that prohibition shall exist until the end of
the war which, I presume, means until peace is signed, and for one year later. We are told that the Government are now considering what they will do after that. There is a current rumour as to what they intend to do. It is because I think that is a mistake that I am going to venture and presume to offer them advice not to do it. Punch's advice to those about to marry is good here, " Don't." It is presumed that the Government intend to have a referendum or a plebiscite. That statement is not made in the speech from the Throne; we do not have it in any official form; it comes to us by way of leakage, I suppose, from the caucus; and I know leakage from the caucus is very unsafe as basis for argument. But one or two members of the House, perhaps unconsciously, have disclosed the fact. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden) and, I think, the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) told us that we are going to take a vote on the subject, so we really know what the Government is contemplating. But as the Government have not yet really committed themselves to it, perhaps there is still time for the thought I am offering for their consideration. My view of the matter is that we should not take the responsibility of initiating legislation, but that we should recognize the rights of the provinces. There is a strong movement amongst our temperance friends everywhere to induce the Government to bring forward very stiff legislation. I have no doubt all the members of Parliament have received various circulars on the matter. I have one pamphlet which I will read, because it seems to me [DOT]to indicate the correct situation. This comes to me from Hamilton, from the International Order of Good Templars, which we are informed is the largest temperance organization in the world. I quote this passage;
As every province in the Dominion has shown a desire, by the enacting of provincial laws, to prohibit the liquor traffic to the full extent of their constitutional powers, we believe that the time has now arrived when the expressed will of the people should be enacted into Parliamentary laws, and that at the present Session of Parliament, the "Order in Council" legislation, covering importation, manufacture and interprovincial shipment, should be enacted into Parliamentary legislation.
We think that no further vote of the people is necessary, other than that expressed by the various provinces.
That seems to be sound reasoning. If the various provinces of this Dominion, through their Governments and legislatures, see fit, in their wisdom, to adopt a prohibitory law, and if, as is the fact, they find that, owing to constitutional difficul-

ties, they cannot make that law effective, it is the duty of the Dominion Government and Parliament to give them such supplementary legislation as will make the law effective.
**There was a time years ago when there was a great deal of difficulty over this temperance question. Both the Dominion Parliament and the local legislatures claimed the right to deal with it. We had the Dominion License law. This was one of the things over which those two gladiators, Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Oliver Mowat, fought, with the usual result that Sir Oliver Mowat won and the Dominion License law was declared to be ultra vires. The Dominion courts have established the fact that in respect to importation, exportation and manufacture, the Dominion Parliament will control, but as respects the retail sale the local Parliament will control. Let me give the House an illustration how this works. There is a prohibitory law in the province of Nova Scotia. There are a number of brewers in the province. The Halifax brewer cannot sell his beer to the consumer in Halifax, but he can ship it over to an agent in St. John, and then the Halifax consumer can write to the St. John agent and order it sent back. Thus he can get the Halifax beer if he wants it, but he has to pay the price of the beer and two railway freights in order to get it. The thing is preposterous. Seeing, therefore, that iwe should make prohibition effective, my advice to the Government is this: Do not take the initiative; make our legislation supplementary to the provincial law. I agree with the statement made by the International Order of Good Templars that there is no need for a referendum. I respectfully advise the Government that if there is to be a plebiscite or a referendum, they should leave that to the provinces. I do not believe there is any need for a referendum at all. There is no need for one in my constituency nor in my province. There is no question down there. My constituency stands for prohibition; the province of Nova Scotia stands for prohibition; they do not want any referendum, they do not want any plebiscite. My impression is that if the Government adopt the system of a referendum, they will cause further difficulties. I think it would be sound and safe for them to say that so long as any province, by its legislation, desires to have prohibition and to give the full effect of prohibition which its local constitution will permit, the Dominion Government will supplement that by such

Dominion legislation as will make that prohibition thoroughly effective. That is a policy which is consistent with this demand of the temperance people. It is consistent % with the doctrine of provincial rights to which so many people attach importance, and it is an easier solution of the question than any other method which could be adopted.
I want to speak about three or four other subjects but I am afraid I am occupying too much time, so I will ask your attention to only one or two. We are to have legislation respecting the franchise. I do not know what that means. It is a deplorable fact that every franchise Bill introduced into this House has been the subject of bitter party strife and contention. The impression seems to exist that a Franchise Bill, no matter who introduces it, is always designed to serve the interests of one party or the other and consequently it is always resisted by the people on the other side whether it ba in a provincial legislature or in this House. Why should this be? We all ought to agree that the franchise is something sacred, and we all bught to be willing to agree that every mar. and woman in this country entitled to vote should have his and her name placed on the voters' list. We should not create a condition of affairs which will tempt men to make a struggle not only to get on the lists the names of their friends but to keep off the names of those who might vote the*-other way. There has, unfortunately, been trouble over this question in times past. Why should we have two franchise lists? In most of the provinces, practically all, one might say, there is practically manhood and' womanhood suffrage to-day. A man with any pretence to doing almost anything is entitled to vote, and I am glad to say the women also have that right to-day. Why should we go through the form of making up one list for the provinces and another for the Dominion? The voters have to be the same set of people, and why should there not be co-operation between the Dominion and the Provincial Governments to try and agree upon a common list? This is not a new hope of mine. Thirty-four years ago, in the early days of my premiership of Nova Scotia, I saw the trouble in having two voters' lists, and I ventured to send a telegram to Sir John A. Macdonald suggesting a conference between the Dominion and Provincial Governments in the hope of agreeing on one common list. In those days representatives of the Dominion and Provincial Governments never met

in conference. There always seemed to be friction between them, even when both were of the same political party. I am glad that a better condition has prevailed in later years. The ,Dominion Government has repeatedly invited the premiers of the different provinces to come in consultation, and I commend them for doing so; I think it was a wise thing. Then why should we not bring them together to consider this question of the franchise, and let them meet on common ground without any partisanship at all? I think the offer is worth making at all events, and I earnestly commend that suggestion to the consideration of the Government.
That brings me to another question on which I cannot hope to have my views endorsed generally. I want to agree with those gentlemen who have urged that the Wartime Elections Act be repealed as quickly as possible. It is an amazing thing that men can permit themselves to stand up and support a measure of that kind. We talk sometimes of alien enemies in connection with the franchise. There are no alien enemies in that connection. The men to whom protection should be given, the men who have been unjustly treated, are British subjects, and if they were of foreign birth that is all the more reason why they should be treated justly, because they are guests in our house and a guest is always entitled to protection. How did they come to us in Canada? We sent out agents and literature into the highways and byways of continental Europe, begging men to come to Canada and settle on the land. We pictured an alluring situation where land was open for all. We assured these people of every privilege; we told them the land could be had cheaply, and that if they came here and after a certain time took the oath of allegiance to our gracious Sovereign, they would become Canadian citizens and British subjects. They came and settled here and served their time of probation. They did everything a decent citizen could do. Suddenly they wakened up one day to find that they had lost the highest prize of citizenship-the right to vote. Why? There was no concealment about it, there was no pretense of there being any other reason for disfranchising these people than that the Government believed they would vote against them. Surely, that was no reason at all.
Mr. Speaker, we shall need these men and others like them. There is one great asset of any n-ation, of any people, and of any individual; it is character, reputation, good faith. I made a little tour of the West
Indies a few years ago, and as I went from island to island I was much impressed, as any thoughtful men must have been, by the condition I found there. The population everywhere was black or coloured, except for a handful of white people on each island. In some cases the number of whites would be larger than in others, but in every instance they constituted a small minority. And yet this handful of white men were directing and governing these islands in the midst of peace, progress, and prosperity. I asked a very intelligent coloured man with whom I was conversing how his people got along in such a situation. " Oh," he said,
" it is very simple. These white men are Englishmen." I know he used the word in its broadest sense, not in the narrow sense in which we sometimes use it.
" Englishman " means more than England -" What do they know of England who only England know?" The Scotchman, and the Irishman too, is sometimes offended at the use of the word " Englishman " in its narrow sense, but it was Thomas Campbell, himself a Scotchman, who wrote " Ye mariners of England who guard our native seas." England means more than one part of one little island; it means the Motherland, and sometimes the Empire at large. Well, this coloured man said, " The reason we get along so well is because these white men you speak of are Englishmen, and our people have learned that we can trust the honour and faith and justice of an Englishman." Thank Heaven for that reputation of Englishmen which is the inheritance of Britons everywhere-except in Canada.
A few months ago I heard an address delivered in the Canadian Club of Montreal by a clergyman who had spent much of his life in Eastern countries, particularly in Egypt and amongst the tribes of the desert. He told with much pride and satisfaction of the achievements of Englishmen in that region and of what England was doing to further civilization in the East. iSpeaking of the reputation which Englishmen possessed, he said that among one of the tribes which he knew very well it was a common thing for a man, if he wanted to give you the assurance that he would do a certain thing, to say, " By the word of an Englishman I promise it." A few days ago I heard a statement very much like that by a gentleman from South America. He was telling of the opportunities of trade down there, where we hope to do a large amount of business, and he said that Englishmen are doing a big business there and are going to keep it, " because our people trust the Englishman." And he used the very words of the clergyman, " It is a common thing for a

man if he wants to give you an assurance that he will do a certain thing to say, ' By the word of an Englishman I promise it.' " 'Sir, we ought to be proud of that reputation which Englishmen-and Englishmen means Britons-have won throughout the wide world. Who can say to-day with fairness and justice, " By the word of a Canadian I will do it." The word of a Canadian, tried by the War-time Elections Act, is a word of trickery, a word of deception, the word of a cheat. We shall need immigrants in our country, more backs to bear the heavy burden that is coming. From what countries are we to obtain them? W7e want as many as we can get from Great Britain for the more British people we have in the country the better. No doubt there will be many immigrants from the United States.
No better immigrants come to Canada than those from the western United States But with all that, we are not going to have enough, and shall be compelled to send our agents abroad again. In such an event, I can imagine the agent going to one of the continental towns and talking about emigration to Canada. He has a group of men around him, and one man, who has paid particular attention to all that he has said, declares that he knows all about Canada, his brother having come to this country. The agent will (suggest that perhaps he would like to follow his brother's example. "No," the man will say: "an agent like you came here a few years ago to our house and told precisely the same story you are telling now, about the attractiveness of Canada as a country of great opportunities where land could be obtained very cheaply if not free. I could not go, but my brother went, taking with him his little family. He built a home, settled down, took the oath of allegiance, and did all in his power to become a good citizen. With what result? You robbed him of his franchise. Let us pray, Mr. Speaker, that the time may soon come again when a man may be able to say, "Upon the word of a Canadian I can depend!"
One further thought only will I intrude on the" House. Sir, I want to say in conclusion that I would like to see a strong plea made for a free parliament. "A free parliament?" you say; "have we not a free parliament now?" No! We had not a free parliament last year; and if the same policy of the Government be again adhered to, we are not likely to have a free parliament now. What was the situation at the opening of the first session of the new parliament? My conception of the situation

was this: I felt that on matters relating to the prosecution of the war, the Government ought to be strongly supported, certainly by their friends; and I thought they might even claim support from their opponents. But I believed that on all questions not connected with the war every man in the House of Commons should be at liberty to act according to the dictates of his conscience. Was that an erroneous conception? Was there anything unreasonable in that? I think not. Yet, what happened? Before the session had advanced very far, I discovered that my conception of political freedom, as I have just indicated, was one in which my right lion, friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) did not share. On several occasions, on matters in no way connected with the prosecution of the war, the Whips were used to rally men to the support of a particular question; and then in the conclusion came that extraordinary scene in connection with the question of titles. The question was not important in itself. Whether a man votes for or against titles, is not, to my mind, of very great moment; but the manner in which this Parliament was strangled is unquestionably a matter in which we are gravely concerned. A motion was before the House presented by one supporter of the Government; and there was an amendment by another supporter of the Government. These matters were discussed for days and weeks, and every hon. member thought he had a right to freedom of action. Then one night the Prime Minister announced that if a certain course were not followed he would resign. This, Sir, in the midst of war, and at a very critical stage of it, too ! On such a trifling pretext the Prime Minister of Canada was prepared to precipitate a political crisis that might have thrown the country into the throes of another general election. I ask my hon. friends on both sides of the House to stand up for a free Parliament. In a democratic country such as this, we may not all be able to agree on every question. I know I differ from some of my friends on this as well as the other side of the House; but I always endeavour to respect their views and opinions when I feel that they are acting conscientiously; and I ask them to do the same by me. One thing I do very earnestly a|sk them to do, and that is, to insist on freedom of debate, freedom of speech. We might have seen in England, about the same time, a fine example of a free, as contrasted with a strangled, Parliament. The Government had an important Bill before Parliament. An amendment

was made by the House of Lords-rather an important amendment-and when it came down to the House of Commons there was displayed the true spirit of 9 p.m. British parliamentary liberty; for the Government said on this question of the amendment: We do not regard it as vital, and we leave it.to the very open judgment of the House. And the amendment which the House of Lords desired to make to the Government Franchise Bill was rejected. There, Sir, you have an example of a free parliament as compared with the parliament which we had in Canada. I trust that both Grit and Tory:-if there are such people-will hereafter have the satisfaction of knowing that above everything else hon. members will stand for a free parliament representing a free people.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted to preface my remarks with a reference to the distinguished statesman who has so recently passed away, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. From the time I took any interest in political affairs he was a dominating figure in Canadian public life. Although not his follower politically, I always gave to him a large measure of admiration and respect. I admired him for his rare gift of oratory, for his outstanding ability, for his commanding figure, and for his courtly presence. He carved his name enduringly on the period in which he lived. Full of years and honours, in the evening of manhood's day, when the thread of life was growing thin he passed away. Already he is like a fragrant flower that has faded and gone. His passing marks the close of a period in Canadian history. We are now writing the title page of a new epoch in our national life, an epoch full of great promise and pregnant with the most wonderful possibilities. I feel I voice the sentiments, irrespective of their political affiliations, of the people of the county. I represent in this House when I express their appreciation of the great service which Sir Wilfrid Laurier rendered to the State. I also feel that I voice the unanimous sentiment of the citizens of the county of Halton when I extend to the widow of the departed state-man their deepest, their most profound sympathy.
I was somewhat nervous in rising to follow so eminent a gentleman as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). I must confess, however, that the hon. member is a puzzle to me, and I am sure he is a puzzle to the hon. members of the Opposition. During the first
part of his speech he received considerable applause from the Opposition benches. Hon. members on that side were prepared to rejoice more at the return of one sinner than over the ninety and nine who had no need of repentance. Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. gentleman was going to step off the fence, but I see he is still in the same position he occupied at the last session of this Parliament. I heartily concur in the remarks which he made during the latter part of his speech, but there are some inconsistencies in the first part of it. He asked the question, what business had Canada at the Peace Conference? For answer to that question I would refer him to the speech of the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). The hon. gentleman claims that Canada has no right to representation at the Conference. Now, his attitude is rather inconsistent in view of the fact that he upheld the Union Government in the prosecution of the war. He approved of the sending of soldiers to France and Belgium, and if we took part in the conflict, is it not reasonable that we should have a right to have some say at the Conference? Surely the hon. gentleman will not contend that although we sent soldiers to fight the enemy we should have no voice in the discussion of the peace terms.
The hon. member said that Canada bad not gained one cubit. It is not one cubit but many cubits that this country has gained because of the glorious action of our soldiers in establishing this country in such a prominent position among the nations of the earth, a position which it would not have attained otherwise in fifty years. That is one of the results of our taking part in the European conflict. In regard to our taking part in the Peace Conference the hon. gentleman made mention of the boundaries of the nations of Europe, but he thinks that we should not have any interest in that conference because we have no interest in these various boundaries. I would submit to him that disputes over the boundaries of Europe have been the cause of deluging that continent for a thousand years with blood. If by going into this conference and assisting in bringing about a certain measure of satisfaction with the boundaries that are established we can in the future prevent wars, we shall have done a great deal not only for the Dominion of Canada but for the whole world.
I should like to compliment the hon. gentlemen who moved and seconded the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. I compliment them on the very

eloquent and efficient manner in which they performed that very responsible duty. Their remarks were most happy and reflected great credit upon themselves and upon the administration for making the selection. Their sentiments in regard to our gallant soldiers will find an answering echo in the hearts of all true Canadians. The heroism, sacrifice and glorious achievements of our citizen soldiers is a theme to inspire some Canadian poet to perpetuate their memory in immortal verse. But, our soldiers do not want to be immortalized. They want to be repatriated in the most effective and speedy manner possible. The Union (Government was elected for that purpose. In their wisdom the people of Canada chose this Government to perform that duty. There is no lack of (Confidence amongst the members of this side of the House in the ability of the Government to live up to the expectations of the people. Liberal Unionists and Conservative Unionists alike gave up their party affiliation in order to come together on common ground in support of a coalition Government. We did that in the stress and turmoil of a great war brought together by a common interest, a common bond and a common danger that raised us far above the petty issues of political strife.
There is not any doubt that in the estimation of the people of Canada a non-partisan government is the best form of government to settle the many vexed questions which will come up for settlement during the reconstruction period. The tariff issue, that bone of contention between the Bast and the West, can undoubtedly be settled better by a cabinet which is representative of the two great political parties in this country than by any other form of government. If a non-partisan government cannot settle that question to the satisfaction of the people no partisan government can. If the members of this House will view that question with reference to what is in the best interests of Canada as a whole, and not from the point of view of any sectional interest, the path of the Government will be strewn with roses instead of thorns.
The hon. member for Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. J. Read)-and I give the hon. gentleman credit for stating many plain truths in his own inimitable way

expressed a wish for a commission to inquire into the tariff and bring in a policy that would be satisfactory to all political parties. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he is not satisfied with the present Government composed, as it is, of the leading members

of those political parties. Surely, that ought to be satisfactory to any man, even the most exacting.
Possibly the hon. gentleman meant a commission representative of the Opposition in this House, but I reply that the Opposition in this House is not representative of true Liberalism. It is the personal following of the late, lamented leader whose vacant chair so eloquently reminds us that he is no more. It is a striking tribute to his great worth and personal charm that so many gave to him their undivided allegiance. I would like to tell the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) whilst congratulating him on his elevation to that honourable post, that he cannot expect to lead a National Liberal party on a provincial policy dominated by a single province. It is a significant fact that the dividing line between the parties in this House is the defence of our common country. The light is in the window indeed, but it is sadly dimmed by the mists of political prejudice and narrow provincialism. Under such circumstances it becomes the red light of danger giving due warning to all true Liberals to seek congenial companionship elsewhere.
In this country we have quite a large number of defaulters, conscientious objectors and deserters. I have classed the conscientious objector along with the others because a great many of the conscientious objectors were not aware of their objections until the passing of the Military Service Act. The sincere conscientious objector whose objection to military service is based upon his religious faith is entitled to some consideration, and I believe the Government have given that class of man certain consideration. I think- it may be laid down as a principle that he who receives and accepts the protection due to a British subject has placed upon him the obligation to defend those institutions that give him protection. Those institutions are founded on the ballot; by (force of arms they have survived. They have descended to us from preceding generations and are consecrated in the blood of a long line of noble ancestors. Their defence is the common duty of all. The conscientious objector or defaulter who refuses to defend his country in time of war has no right to the exercise of the legislative function in time of peace. The vote is essentially a legislative act. By it laws are enacted and laws are repealed. He who

refuses 'to defend this fundamental principle of democracy has no right to the exercise of its privileges.
I would therefore suggest to the Government that since the war is over the imprisonment of the conscientious objector, the defaulter and deserter is expensive and ineffective. The system of meting out punishment by means of a fine has more to commend it. But I think, Mr. Speaker, that, taking everything into consideration, the best punishment is disfranchisement for life and I would recommend that respectfully to the consideration of the Government. I would make a plea also for more uniformity in the punishment of the defaulter. It is not very edifying to see a defaulter in the province of Ontario given a large fine or a long term of imprisonment when a defaulter in the province of Quebec, equally guilty, is let off with a nominal fine or a few hours imprisonment. In this connection I would cite a case that occurred in Hull just a few days ago. This is from an Ottawa paper, I think the edition of Wednesday:
Twelve absentees under the Military Service Act who came before Magistrate Goyette in the Hull Police Court yesterday escaped with the exceedingly light penalty of six hours in jail each.
In view of the recent passage of an Order in Council which provides a minimum penalty for this class of offender of $250 or three months in jail, the presiding magistrate was asked for an explanation.
"These twelve men were brought before me over two weeks ago," stated Magistrate Goyette, "but for various reasons their cases were not ready to be disposed of until this morning. In view of these circumstances I did not deem it would be fair to impose a new penalty on them, when, if their cases had been disposed of when they were first arrested, they would have gotten off with the usual line of $50 or $75.
"I therefore imposed a term of six hours in jail on each of them, without the option of a fine. You must remember that even one hour in jail, to any one with any self respect, is as big a punishment as a longer term. In future, absentees and defaulters coming before me will be treated under the new Order in Council."
'I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the average defaulter and deserter has not very much self-respect, and a punishment in the shape of six hours in jail is altogether inadequate for his offence. I would call the attention of the Government to the fact that the Orders in Council which have been passed for the purpose of dealing with this inequality of punishment do not meet the case. I have not seen any Order in Council providing for a minimum punishment of three months in jail. There was an Order in Council modifying the first Order
issued in December, 1917, with regard to defaulters, which was amended on the 12th February, and later on the 24th of February. If any other Orders in Council have been promulgated since that date, I have not seen any copy of the Canada Gazette which contains them. The last Order in Council provides for a minimum fine of $250, and a maximum fine of $5,000. The term of imprisonment is to be up to two years. Now, Mr. 'Speaker, I submit that that leaves entirely too much to the discretion of the magistrate, and there consequently is too much room for discrimination in the punishment of defaulters in different parts of the Dominion.
With regard to aliens within our country, there are something like two thousand in internment camps. I am in accord with the policy of the Government that these men shall be returned to their native land at the first opportunity. But I would go further, and possibly the Government intends to do so; I would confiscate the property of those aliens, and even their earnings, leaving them only sufficient to start in a small way in their native land. There are other foreigners, however, in our country who are not enemy aliens, and these men, when they measure up to the standard of Canadian citizenship, should be given a chance; but in every instance, where their interests conflict wita the interests of the returned soldier, they should give way to him.
I am pleased to compliment the Government on bringing in a Bill providing for a new franchise, and giving the women the full right to vote. But I am not in accord with hon. gentlemen on the opposite side when they claim that enemy aliens should be given a vote as before. I hope to see it provided that the enemy aliens, whether they are in this country now or come here later, shall not, get the vote for at least a generation. With regard to foreigners who are not enemy aliens, I think they should be given the vote after a certain time, but not until after seven or ten years' residence in this country, and that an educational test should be applied to them; they should be required to write and read the English language and to have some knowledge of our institutions, to comprehend what - the flag stands for and to understand the responsibility of Canadian citizenship. If they cannot master these things in ten years they certainly are unfit for Canadian citizenship.
The pensions -which are given to our soldiers at the present time, particularly the



pensions to the totally disabled soldier, are entirely inadequate, with the cost of living as we have it to-day. It is possible, Mr. Speaker, that when this country has got back to more stable conditions of peace that	indadequacy	may	disappear. I thinkif there is one	very	definite	thing inthis	country it	is the fact	that thepeople, the members of Parliament and the	Government	are	desirous	that the
Canadian soldier shall receive the highest amount of pension compatible with his disability. I think the people of this country intend to be generous in this respect, and they are desirous that the totally disabled soldier shall receive a pension sufficient to keep him well above want during the remainder of his life. A pension of $600 is certainly not sufficient for that purpose under the present scale of living.
I would like to draw the attention of the Government to the attitude of the Pensions Board toward the average soldier who comes before them for a pension. The returned soldier claims that the attitude of the Pensions Board toward him is to keep the pension down as low as possible compatible with his disability. That is rather a parsimonious attitude. That is not the intention of the Government, ilt is possible that the returned soldier mistakes the attitude of the Pensions Board, but I bring this matter to the attention of the Government in. order that they may inquire into it if they deem it necessary. I believe that it is better the Pensions IBoard should err on the side of generosity than that any soldier should be unfairly treated.
The soldier suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis is in a class by himself. In discussing that question I shall approach it from the viewpoint of the physician. I have seen something of the terrible ravages of this disease on the human organism. I know something of its deceptive character, its tendency to become latent, and its tendency to recur. The contention of the soldier is that the Pensions Board rather treats these cases from a mathematical viewpoint. The tubercle bacilli attack the lung and cause a certain part of it to die and slough off. If the patient is strong enough to resist the sloughing process the lung heals by a process of cicatrization and contraction. This places more work on the heart and causes a lessened power of areation of the blood. The soldier is not as strong as he was before, and is liable to break down under strain. The Pensions Board, after this disease has become latent, measures the disability of the soldier by the amount 
of cicatrization of the lung. I contend that the disability is not always in proportion to the amount of cicatrization of the lung, because in some instances the soldier may be more liable to other diseases; he may not have a strong constitution, and so will break down more easily under strain, and will show more constitutional effects from the same amount of cicatrization of the lung than another person. These soldiers are first treated in a sanatorium, and when the disease becomes latent are sent up before the Pensions Board, and given temporary pensions for six months.
That, I believe, has latterly been extended to one year. At the end of that time, if they remain healthy, they again come before the Pensions Board and are re-examined. The condition of the lung is then stated and the amount of permanent pension apportioned accordingly. If they again have an attack of the disease they are entitled to go to a sanatorium for free treatment, receiving during the period of their treatment pay and allowances the same as if they were on active service. When they are finally cured there is no readjustment of the pension. I think there should be a readjustment of the pension after .each attack, because the lung is in a worse condition after each attack than it was at first. I bring this point to the attention of the Government in the hope that they will look into these statements and see whether they are accurate. They are given to me by the tubercular soldiers themselves.
Up to 31st March, 1918, 3,648 soldiers had been treated for tuberculosis, and at that time there were under treatment 1,619 men, distributed all over Canada in 21 sanatoria.
The Civil Service Commission has been attacked by the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) and has been defended by an hon. minister (Hon. A. K. Maclean). At the last session of this Parliament an Act was passed under which the Civil Service Commission was given charge of appointments to the Outside Service. In passing that Act Parliament's, express purpose was to do away with the evils of patronage. It was expected that these duties would be carried out by the Civil Service Commission efficiently, expeditiously, without suspicion of wrongdoing. In my opinion, the placing of appointments in the hands of a Civil Ser-' vice Commission does not entirely do away with patronage; we simply centralize it in Ottawa. The work of many is put into the hands of the few. It does not require the mind of a statesman to understand that if this work is not carried on in a proper and honest manner the gravest abuses may re-

suit. An army of something like 50,000 men and women are under the control of the Civil Service Commission at Ottawa. This commission is composed of three members, who are supposed to do all that work. I submit that the number of members of the' commission should be increased. They have a secretary, who is not a member of the commission, but its servant. The secretary should have nothing whatever to do with appointments made under the commission; I assume that he has nothing to do with them. If the commission delegate their authority to him or to any one else, then there is no need for the commission and they should be removed from office.
The members of Parliament have some interest in this commission. They created the machinery under which it is operating, and if there is anything wrong with it they should be taken into the confidence of the Government in regard to the matter. The charges that were made by the member for West Toronto were replied to by the minister, but not all of them were refuted; the gravest charge of all, that with regard to the sale of examination papers to prospective candidates, has been admitted. At the trial in Ottawa a few days ago the person who was responsible for the sale of these particular papers was convicted and fined $100. I must say that it was a surprise to me to see that the commission or the Government were not represented at that trial. It is reported in the press that Mr. Foran, the secretary of the commission, expressed surprise at the verdict; apparently he did not know that the trial was taking place. I should think it was his duty and the duty of the commission, to have known and to have been represented there by a lawyer who would see that all the facts were brought out. For the sale of these examination papers the commission is directly responsible. The sale of examination papers is certainly a very reprehensible act, and it is the duty of the commission to make every effort to discover how the leakage came about and who the guilty party is. Parliament demands that the truth be known. No one will be hurt by the truth except the guilty party, and he should be exposed and punished.
I compliment the Government upon its intention to institute a Federal Department of Health. The member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) placed the matter so well before the House that there is not much for me to say. I should like to associate myself, however, with the remarks of that hon. gentleman on this subject, and to impress upon the Government the advisability of having this department placed under a qualified medical man. Many medical men may be found in Canada who are eminently qualified to fill that position with satisfaction to themselves and with credit to the Government.
While on this subject I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the wonderful advance of medical science all over the world. Great advance has been made in other branches of science, particularly in the manufacture of destructive agencies of war-the only marvel is that flesh and blood could stand up against these great engines of destruction. Great advance has been made in the science of transportation, both on water and in the air. But, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the advances in medical, surgical and sanitary sciences have been equal to those made in any other branch of science. This war could not have taken place successfully on the western front had it not been for the wonderful advance in preventive medicine. By virtue of the discoveries in that branch, almost all kinds of infectious disease, such as typhoid fever, smallpox, diphtheria, and so on, have been eliminated from the armies. The deaths on the battle front from disease have been remarkably small; our returning * soldiers who are casualties suffer principally from the effects of wounds, and very little from the effects of disease.
Mr. Speaker, I should be scarcely doing my duty if I did not give some little voice to my feelings with regard to our gallant Canadian soldiers. The day after England declared war on Germany the young men of Canada commenced their steady tramp, to the recruiting offices all over the country; from the east to the west, from the north to the south, they came offering their services in defence of the Empire. It was the most inspiring spectacle ever presented to the world by the colonial possessions of any country ; it was a wonderful concrete evidence of the mighty colonizing power of England. For a thousand years the sons of Britain have been going out from her shores to the farthermost corners of the earth, carrying with them the principles of truth, justice and liberty; carrying with them the tenets of the Christian faith and the foundation principles of democracy; until now, in the twentieth century, at the call of the motherland, the descendants of these adventurous Britishers rushed to her defence in the most stupendous conflict of history. Five hundred thousand of the sons of Canada answered that call, and fighting side by side with the soldiers

of the British Isles, gallantly upheld the best traditions of British arms. _ Sixty thousand of those sons of Canada, in the dawn of their manhood, gave up their all, in order that democracy might live. They are sleeping the sleep that knows no waking on the vine-clad slopes of northern France, and the blood-sodden fields of Belgium, a silent army whose memory will remain green in the hearts of the Canadian people iso long as we cherish British ideals. It is the duty of the Canadian people so to live and act as to be worthy of the great sacrifices they have made. It is our duty to divest ourselves of political prejudices and selfish motives and stand solidly behind the Government in its efforts to do all that is possible for these returning heroes. It is our duty to restrain fanaticism and war-time hysteria and stand steady and firm in support of the Allied Conference now holding its sessions in Paris; so to support their hand against enemy aggression that the glorious victory which our soldiers have won in the field may be followed by a diplomatic victory commensurate with the sacrifices they have made. Unless we do that, we shall be unworthy of those splendid men now returning to their native land, secure in their confidence of a duty well performed, and with a fond expectation in their hearts which we at home fail to understand.
Mr. DUNCAN CAMPBELL ROSS (West Middlesex); Mr. Speaker, at this hour it is not my intention to weary the House with a long speech. I intend to cut my remarks as short as I possibly can, consistently with what I consider my duty to my people.
