He has performed for me a task which I had intended to perform and has done it much better than I could possibly do it myself. He has military knowledge from which to gather his conclusions. He has knowledge which comes from being present almost when these occurrences which are spoken of in this House happened, and he
[Mr. Anderson.!
is here as a representative of the people, and trying, and I have no doubt successfully trying, to do his duty by his brother officers who have carried themselves so nobly in this great struggle. As a Canadian I was very sorry to hear aspersions cast on officers of the Canadian Expeditionary Force by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House in this debate. These men are not here to defend themselves. It is very easy to cast aspersions or to put blame on any person, and it is very hard to overtake these aspersions once they have gone amongst the public. The hon. member for Skeena took up the defence of my fellow-countryman, Sir Arthur Currie, and I think there is no doubt in the mind of any hon. member in this House, nor do I think there will be any doubt in the mind of any man in this country, in regard to his action, his gallantry, his courage, his solicitude for his men, after hearing the remarks that fell from the lips of the hon. member for Skeena. The hon. member spoke of Sir Arthur Currie as a soldier; I have known him for years; I can speak of him as a man. The insinuation was made that Sir Arthur Currie wantonly sacrificed the lives of Canadian soldiers for his own glorification and to satisfy his own ambition. As an intimate acquaintance of that gallant gentleman I resent any such insinuation. Sir Arthur Currie is the last man in the British Empire who would be guilty of such conduct. I know him well, almost from boyhood. There is not a gentleman with a more kindly heart in this great land. That is the last thing he would do. As a matter of fact I know from eye-witnesses, who have been with Sir Arthur Currie after the victorious onslaught of our Canadian boys, who have seen him viewing the death and devastation that onslaught has occasioned, and I can say with confidence, believing it is true, that that general who is blamed here to-day for being heartless in regard to the use of his men, was so affected by the sights he saw, by the lives of Canadians that had been sacrificed, that he could not suppress his grief and openly burst into tears. Selfish ambition and self-glorification are made of sterner and coarser stuff than that. I believe, if a public investigation is held, or if this matter is further discussed in this House, Sir Arthur Currie will be absolutely cleared of all these suspicions, and I believe he deserves nothing but praise and thanks from this great Canadian people. It would be a strange thing if this; gallant soldier, who has been honoured, not only by Britain but by France and Italy with the highest

military distinctions that have been given, should not have been worthy of those honours. Casualties may have happened amongst the Canadian troops. We know they did happen. You cannot win a great victory without such things happening. But we must not forget, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Skeena this afternoon, that Sir Arthur Currie was only a cog in the big machine; that he had not charge of the forces of the Allies; that he was not the generalissimo; that he was only a sub-general; that he had to take his orders and had to obey them, just as he had to give orders and they had to be obeyed. I contend, with a considerable feeling of resentment, that, it is not fair, in the absence of this man, who has covered himself with glory, to have attacks made on him in this House.
The Address speaks of our duty to our soldiers. The appreciation and gratitude of the nations cannot be too earnestly and sincerely expressed to the gallant members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. 1 wish to join with the members of the House who have tried well and successfully to express their gratification at the honour and glory the Canadian soldiers have brought to this country of ours. The glory has been not only the glory of the officers, but the glory of the soldiers. Some one has said that this war was a war of lieutenants, and it is true that these gallant, heroic young Canadian officers have paid an immense toll in order that liberty may prevail in the world and in order that Canada may be a free nation.
But the glory of winning this war is not due to them alone; it is not due solely to the officers nor to Sir Arthur Currie. I quite agree with what was said by the hon. member who seconded the Address (Mr. Manion) that the greater part of the glory for winning this war belongs to the infantryman in the ranks-the man who went over the top and grappled with the Germans in no man's land, and after taking the Hun trenches marched on to his objective, the German front. He is the man who suffered most, who underwent the greatest hardships, who risked most, and it is to him the greater part of the glory for winning this war should go.
We cannot do our duty by merely expressing our gratitude and appreciation ol the services of these men. The men themselves and the people of this country want deeds, not words, in dealing with our returned soldiers, and one thing which the soldiers want and which the people of this country want is their return to the shores
of Canada as quickly as possible. The soldiers are quite right in wanting to get back home as quickly as possible. I appreciate as keenly as any hon. member in this House the difficulties in the way due to the shortage of shipping, for instance. I appreciate the necessity of other troops also getting home, and I appreciate trade necessities in connection with this problem. But "what I say is this, and I feel I shall be backed up by the whole country: It is a strange thing that during the four or five months since the armistice was signed only about one hundred thousand men have been , brought back to Canada whereas, if I am, correctly informed, the American Government has been successful in bringing back from the front about a million of her men. We have been engaged for almost five years in this struggle. Some of our boys have been over there ever since the war began; many of them have been there two or three years. The Americans only went into the war on the 6th of April, 1917, and have therefore been at the front a comparatively short time. They have not been subjected to the hardships our boys have undergone,, nor played the part our noble boys have played, and I say it is the bounden duty of this Government to make efforts much more vigorous than they have made up to-now to see that our soldiers are returned to this country and to civil life at the very earliest opportunity. It should not need a mutiny in a camp with disastrous results to life and limb to wake up the Overseas, Minister of Militia in regard to this matter: As the speech from the Throne intimated' the Government had known for some time that an armistice would be declared so they had plenty of time in which to prepare for the return of our soldiers. I attribute the lack of speed in this matter to the absence of unity of command in our military affairs. I think that if the return of the troops had been handled by the Minister of Militia in Canada instead of by these gentlemen overseas the men would have been returned much more quickly. I fear the reports we read in the papers are only too true, that the knights we send over to England to look after our officers as High Commissioner and as Overseas Minister of Militia are likely more concerned, as Canadians going over there are apt to become, with pink teas, social functions, dinners at the Mansion House, and their own self-glorification, than, attending to the duties they are sent there.-to perform.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Car-vell) the other day made the startling statement that in -the coming year this country

would have a deficit of $100,000,000. It this Government wants to save money I -can conceive of no better way than by getting our boys back from overseas at the *earliest possible date. That is one reason why they should be brought back more speedily. For the 250,000 or 300,000 of our men it is costing this country $3 a day each which amounts to an expenditure of from half to three-quar: ters of a million dollars a day. Every day that brings their discharge nearer is going to save this country anywhere from a quarter to three-quarters of a million dollars a day, according to the number of men demobilized. With the finances of the country in the state described by the Minister of Public Works, it seems to me that is one good reason why demobilization should be speeded up.
In the second place, it will mean contentment among the men. They want to get home and continue their education or go back to their ordinary vocations, and it is desirable that they should be allowed to do so at the earliest possible date.
In-the third place, the earlier we get these men back the earlier they will get to work. There is going to be a great call in this country in the coming spring for men not only for the farms, but for all the building ttades. Once these men are back they will be able to help build up the country instead of being an expense to it.
For these three reasons I humbly submit that the Government should do everything in their power to expedite the demobilization of these men, and I would say further, that if they have to charter ships at most exorbitant rates it will pay them financially to do so.
I am heartily in favour of vocational training for the soldiers. Any man who has fought our battles abroad and been injured so that he cannot carry on the occupation he was engaged in before the war should receive ample assistance from the Government to enable him to learn some other vocation, so that he will not be handicapped in the race of life. Vocational training is the very least this country can do for our boys.
I am also in favour of adequate pensions, and I am glad to see that the Government is not treating the matter this session with the same indifference they showed last year. The committee on pensions, I am glad to see, has already got to work, and I am sure they will go thoroughly into the matter and discuss it from all points of view. While I know that the pensions granted to Canadian soldiers to-day are the highest in the

world, )I feel that the members of this House and the country generally will back the Government and see that absolutely adequate pensions are paid. I am glad also that the committee on pensions is considering the cost of living in relation to pensions, and if they report to the House that the scale of pensions is not high enough I am sure the House will back up the Government in any legislation providing for adequate pensions. Furthermore, I would urge that the committee's report be presented to the House in sufficient time to allow7 of a free and open discussion of the whole matter, in order that the men who have served this country so faithfully and well may have justice done to them.
I am also in favour of land settlement for the soldiers, or, rather, for such of them as are qualified to go on the land and desire to do so. I do not think that every soldier who has a notion that he would like to settle on the land should be encouraged to do so unless he is fit and has some knowledge of farming, or is given some practical education in agriculture. But if these pre-requisites are carried out, I think it is in the interest of the country that soldiers should, under these circumstances, be placed on the land. I believe that it is the duty of the Government to take radical steps, and to take them at once, to see that all land held by railway companies, held by speculators, and held for grazing leases, especially near railroads, shall be expropriated at reasonable rates in order that these men may have suitable farms. I suggest that they go further if they really want to help the soldiers. If they wish to make them successful farmers, they should do what they did a year or so ago in connection with the farming industry, when they were, endeavouring to promote greater production. At that time they bought for the farmers, as I am informed, a thousand tractors, and brought them into the country free of duty. It was a very laudable action on their part, and one that resulted in considerable benefit in increasing production. Now, I would suggest to the Government that if they are going to put soldiers on the land, it is only fair to them, and it is in tire interests of the country, that they should take the duty off such agricultural implements as the soldiers require in order to work the land, if it is not their intention to remove the duty from these implements for all classes of the community. I think the Government should make these implements as cheap to these men as it is possible to make them, so that they wrill not be handicapped in their start in a new7 life-work.

In regard to the franchise question, I am glad to note that a new measure 10 p.m. is being introduced. I wish to associate myself with the exMinister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in his views in regard to the War-time Elections Act. I do not know of any legislation in any British country which was more iniquitous. I say that, not because I was particularly injured by it myself, but I know of other members oir candidates at the last election who were certainly subjected to the gravest injustice by reason of that Act. It was not British, and it was condemned not only on this side of the House. I remember distinctly what the bon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) said in reference to the War-time Election Act, when he was on this side; and I remember also the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) rising in his place-I was next to him-and addressing the Chair when the Act was introduced, deploring the measure ana asking the indulgence of the Chair in the remarks he was then about to make. He said he was ashamed of the fact that he came from the same part of the Dominion of Canada as the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) because of the iniquity of the Act. It is incomprehensible to me what the Government is thinking of, or what the Liberals who joined the Government are thinking of, if they allow that Act to remain on the statute-book.
I welcome the extension of the franchise to women. They have earned it, for they have been the civil soldiers of the war. They have done as nobly at home as the men did abroad, and I think they should have been given the franchise in 1917. At any rate, they deserved it just as much then as they do now; and I believe that at the first opportunity which is given them to register their votes they will indicate in no uncertain way the sentiments which at the present time rankle in their breasts against the action of the Government in 1917, the unfair manner in which they were treated in regard to the franchise at that time. If we are to have a new Franchise Act, I appeal to this Government to make it a fair, an honest, and a just measure. Upon the franchise all our liberties are based. As the franchise has been extended since the Reform Bill of 1832, our liberties have grown. There is only one fair franchise system, as far as I can see, and that is a system such as is followed in the province of Ontario. This was pointed out by the hon. ex-Minister of Finance. I refer to the municipal system. The franchise is based primarily on the voters' list; and if that list is fair and
equitable, the representation will be fair.
I appeal to the Government to adopt that system. The municipal list in the province of Ontario is prepared by the assessor in the first place, revised by the clerk, posted for thirty days, and appeals are heard by the county court judge. None of these officials are politicians; they are non-partisans. The clerk understands who are entitled to vote. He is neither a Liberal nor a Conservative. If he were either he would not long hold office. The result is that the voters' list is fairly prepared, and every one who is entitled to vote, if he desires to have his name on the list, can rest assured that his name will be on it. This is the fair, the British method. On the other hand, the method adopted at the last election was anything but fair or British. How were matters conducted? A host of enumerators were appointed, many of them Conservative ward heelers, who had only one interest at heart, namely to see that voters were on the list who were favourable to the Union Government, while those who were favourable to the Liberal party were excluded. These enumerators were supposed to be recommended by both parties. But what is the practice? We all know what happens. These people are all human; candidates are human, governments are human, enumerators are very human and sometimes very wicked. What happened in my own riding, for instance? I do not wish to be local, but I dare say the same thing happened elsewhere. We heard the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) make the deliberate statement that he would have a fair election. The War-time Elections Act, he said, would'be fair; the enumerators would be non-partisan, each candidate having the privilege of naming half, so that politics would be eliminated. That statement was not only made by the Prime Minister, but ministers of the Crown assured me that such would be the case. What happened, however? There were sixty-nine polling subdivisions in the riding of West Middlesex. Now, I had a right to believe the statement of the Prime Minister made publicly in this country, and to expect that he would keep his word; and I had a right to believe that a minister of the Crown making that promise would keep his word. I repeat the question, what happened, and what will happen again, if this system is allowed to continue? I was never consulted; no member of the Liberal party was consulted. A Tory was appointed and he in turn appointed sixty-nine, or at least sixty-six, Tory partisans. Did they carry out the law justly

and put on the voters' list all who should have been put on? Not at all. Some were fair, but by all means the majority were not; and on election day, instead of attending the polls, as was their duty, to put new voters on that had been left off, these men in some cases were out bringing in voters in Conservative rigs to vote against the Liberals. That is not the kind of thing that will appeal to the Canadian people and inspire them with confidence in their representation in Parliament; and that is certainly not the way in which a Parliament may be made free and honest.
Now, just one remark in reference to the Dominion Health Department. For my own part, I do not believe in it. I think it is an unnecessary duplication of office and will only entail additional expense. Everybody knows we have a sufficiency of cabinet officers at the present time, and a Civil Service that is giving enough trouble. I do not see that any good will be attained through it, and I think it is an encroachment on provincial rights. The followers of this Government will get berths and places, while the public healtn will not be benefited one particle. I am absolutely opposed to it. I believe it is an unnecessary and extravagant encroachment on the rights of the provinces.
There are one or two matters to which I wish to call the attention of the Govern-, ment in regard to my part of the province of Ontario. Some of them may seem parochial, but most of them will affect the Dominion at large. At the present time there is a great wave of unrest all over this country. It prevails among the labouring people and the agricultural community. It prevails particularly amongst these two classes and it appears to me that it is more than justified. One thing I regret, Mr. Speaker, is that in the speech from the Throne, apart from a mention of land settlement which, to say the least, is very illusory, and apart from the assistance which the Government ipromise towards good roads, there is not one particle of encouragement held out to the great agricultural community. We, on this side, have listened until we almost doubt the sincerity of the hon. gentlemen on the other side about the great basic industry of the country, about the importance of agriculture, how our prosperity and the future depend upon its succcess, how it must be fostered, and how the agriculturist must be helped. But we do not see any evidence of putting these high-sounding platitudes into operation and there is nothing in the 
speech from the Throne to lead us to believe that at this session the Government intend to give any relief to the agriculturist.
Some people in the big cities of the country would have us believe that the farmer is a profiteer, that he is getting wealthy, that he is making untold money out of the consumers and the men in the cities. Only recently a report was published by the Ontario Minister of Agriculture. He is a lawyer. I think he is a pietty consistent Tory. I do not think he would have any prejudice in favour of the agricultural community. I have no doubt that his report is absolutely accurate. And what does he find in regard to agriculture in Ontario and in regard to its fortunemaking opportunities? He tells us that there are a million men engaged in agriculture in Ontario. He estimates, after a very careful inquiry into all their resources, an income of $250,000,000 divided among them. In other words, for each man, woman and child there is an income of $250 per year; or for a family of four you would have $1,000 or, to make a generous allowance $1,200. Thus, a farmer with a family of four makes $1,200, and this calculation is based on the returns during the years 1914-1917. The farmer has $1,200 to support his family of four. He buys his farm implements, repairs them, puts in his crops, buys clothes and shoes at the exorbitant prices at which they are selling to-day, pays his taxes, educates his family and incurs all the other expenses incident to domestic life on $1,200 or $1,000 a year. Yet he is claimed to be a profiteer and to be making millions out of the people of the country. After the labouring man, the farmer gets less attention than any other class of the community. As a matter of honesty and frankness I feel compelled to say that the labouring man gets less attention than any other class of the community from the Government at Ottawa. I think he deserves more. But, what have the Government done for the farmer? How have they helped him? It is true that during the war he got larger prices than ever before but we know that this is the first time since the Crimean war that the farmer ever had prices such as he has to-day and this is the first time he ever got prices that came within any proportion of the .cost of producing the things he had to sell.
Did this Government help him? Not a bit of it. This Government said: You are making too much money; we will have to check you and put the hobbles on you.

What did they do to him? When you have any grain to sell you must sell it at so much a bushel, and no more. Did they say that to the miller, the munitions maker, the bacon king or the banker? On the contrary they allowed all these classes to run riot. The miller has made his millions. My hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) proved that conclusively the other night in regard to the big millers, and, as a matter of fact, I know that the smaller millers in this country never made as much money in their history as in the last two years. They made more money out of the bread of the people in the last two years than in the fifty years preceding. We know that the shoe manufacturers are making large profits, with the result that it is almost impossible for a poor man to supply his family with shoes. The same condition exists with regard to clothes. We know what the munition manufacturers have made. They were not interfered with; in fact, they were helped and given capital with which to start their business. But when the farmer seeks to get the price that the demand for his produce would entitle it to, he is immediately cheeked up and a maximum price of $2.24 or something like that is placed upon his product. It is not fair to this man representing as he does a part of the community upon whose prosperity the welfare of the country so largely depends.
There are several things that the agriculturist at the present time is insisting upon getting, which he says he deserves and which I think this Government will be obliged to give him. If this Government does not give it to him, another Government will be placed in power that will be obliged to do so, The first thing that the farmer is asking in my part of the country may appear somewhat petty, but I think he knows his business as well as any other man, and it is that the daylight saving farce of last year shall not again be put into operation. We consult other men in regard to what they want for the carrying on of their business to the best advantage. I do not see why the farmers, representing sixty per cent of the people of Canada, should not be consulted in regard to this matter. In the wester^ part of Ontario they are determined, as far as they can effect their purpose, that this system shall not be in vogue again. The farmers in the United States are of the same opinion, as are also the farmers in Manitoba and the
West. This daylight saving scheme of last year interfered with many things on the farm. It interfered with their work, it interfered with the transaction of their business in town, it interfered with their children's going to school, and it interfered with the hired help of the farmers; and did no good. It is true that it may have been of some advantage to the man who wanted to go out in the afternoon and play a game of golf, or tennis, or run out into the country in his motor car, but we should consider business first rather than pleasure and the farmer's interest should be taken into account in regard to the daylight saving measure.
There is one argument against the position which the farmers take in regard to daylight saving. We are being told that the people of the United States have adopted it again and we must therefore do so. I protest against any such philosophy. It seems to me illogical and unnational. In the olden days when we tried to have reciprocity with the United States-and some of our friends across the way were not wise enough to vote for it but are clamouring for it now-we were told that if we had trade relations with the United States we were going to become an adjunct of that country, going to be its back-yard. That was not true. We were going, by reciprocity, to put ourselves right on the front street. But it seems to me that If we have to follow them in regard to the daylight saving system, and if we cannot regulate that matter for ourselves, we are certainly becoming an adjunct of the United States and are going to be their badk-yard. Is it more important that the railway time tables in this country should not be reprinted, and the railways be put to a little expense, or that the farmer should be able to carry on his great agricultural operations without the embarrassment which this matter brings to him? It seems to me that the whole thing has come down to that, and I for one, coming from the agricultural part of the province of Ontario, protest against any continuation of the foolish system in question.
There is another thing to which I call the attention of the Government. In the western and central parts of the province of Ontario, there is a pressing and most insistent demand from the agriculturists for an interior terminal elevator for their grain. Not so very long ago the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, Mr. Henry; the president of the United Farmers of Ontario, Mr. COMMONS
Halbert; and the president of the United Farmers Co-operative Company, Mr. Burnaby, and other gentlemen, experts in the grain trade and in farming, sent a memorial, I believe, to this Government asking for the establishment of an interior terminal elevator. They asked that such an elevator should be built at some place in the province which would give a central location, and they urged the necessity of this on various grounds, being guided by the experience of the West in connection with terminal elevators. They had evidently studied this matter, they "were men of eminence in the agricultural world, and must know that what they were asking was in the interests of the farming community, and they pointed out that in Ontario, unlike the West, there was no elevator where the grain of the province could be collected, where it could be weighed, where it could be cleaned, and where it would get an official stamp, and they urged the need of this elevator in the interest of the farmers of the province. From their representations I would judge that there are about two hundred million bushels of grain grown in Ontario. A great part of this is used in the feeding of stock, but much of it could be used for interprovincial trade, for local trade, and for export trade, and they urged these reasons for the terminal elevator. The advantages may be summarized under the following heads:
It would provide facilities for the storing, cleaning and grading of different kinds of seed and in this regard, would1 foe of great advantage to the farmers of the province particularly with reference to grass and clover seeds.
It would he of much advantage to the livestock industry of the province by facilitating the distribution of feeding stuffs from one section to another ift the case of short crops in the local districts in the province as a whole.
It would be able to perform a distinct service in preventing the deterioration of certain crops in the province in the years of too much moisture, as is illustrated in the bean crop in recent years. The crop of buckwheat this year has had to be dried because of the wet weather which prevailed at the time of harvesting.
Special emphasis is laid on the fact that such an elevator would be a public elevator and certificates issued would be official Government certificates, both of which are advantages affording great protection to the public and not available in the same sense from private enterprise.
No\v, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that these men know what is in the interest of the farming community of Ontario, and that their request is very reasonable. They point out, moreover, that although this grain elevator may not pay as a commercial enterprise from the start, later on it would pay and consequently in that regard there would be no loss to the Dominion. They point

out another thing which is very important in view of the observations recently made by the Minister of Public Works,

that the erection of this grain elevator, which would mean a considerable outlay, would provide employment to a great many men which the Government at the present time think is so desirable. The Minister of Public Works announced that he is erecting certain Custom House buildings in certain cities for the purpose of employing labour. It seems to me that this one form of construction will be more useful than the erection of Custom House buildings which he may be able to dispense with before long. It is one form of enterprise in which labour can be advantageously employed. I leave the suggestion to the Government and hope they will give it their most serious consideration.
There is one thing in the West that the farmers are clamouring for and that is rural credits. The farmers of Ontario, I know, would also like to see rural credits established. They feel the monopolistic tendencies of our banks, and that they would be assisted by the establishment of rural credits throughout the farming district. I have only to recall to the House that in 1913 the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) brought down a proposition in regard to rural credits which was not only accepted by the Finance Minister as a sound financial propqsition, but also received the approval of the House. I think the Government might very well at this time take into consideration the establishment of rural credits throughout the West and in the province of Ontario.
But after all, Mr. Speaker, the vital question to-day is the tariff. I am not going to discuss it at length to-night because we shall have other opportunities of doing so. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) has said that there is a cleavage between the East and the West in regard to this question. For my own part I do not wish to contradict the hon. gentleman, but I believe he is making a mistake which he will find out before many months go by,
I believe there is no longer a cleavage between the East and the West in regard to the tariff question. At one time it was thought that we might say that "East is East and West is West, and never the twain shall meet" in regard to the tariff. But that day has gone by. The people of Nova Scotia and the people of Alberta are joining hands in regard to this question. The people of Quebec and the people of Saskatchewan are also joining hands; and in the province of Ontario the people are

meeting on common ground. The consumer on the farm, and the consumer in the town to-day are in favour of tariff reduction; and in this connection I know that we are going to have the support, and the farmers are going to have the support, of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) who has just taken his seat, because I remember that hon. gentleman in 1911 advocating in this House, in the skilful way that only he possesses, and analysing with that clean cut analytical mind of his,, the policy of relieving the farmers of Canada of the duty on agricultural implements. Upon that occasion I think the hon. gentleman convinced the House, and almost convinced his own side. I maintain that the farmers and the consumers to-day are one on this question, whether they come from the East or from the West. There is no cleavage in Canada as between the East and the West in regard to the tariff, but there is a cleavage between the people of Canada as a whole-between the consumers on the one side and the great protected privileged interests living in the great cities on the other side. That cleavage has got to be bridged, or partially bridged, by this Government, or the people of Canada will put another Government in power that will do the bridging. These cities seem to think that they occupy the position of old Imperial Rome, and that the whole country should pay tribute to them.
They seem to think that on the clothes on the labourer, on his foodstuffs, on his building material, on everything he uses, tribute should be paid to the manufacturer, to the monopolist, to the combinester, in order to let him live in luxury and plenty. That conviction will be shattered before very long. (I for one-and I have always been in favour of this: it is no new advocacy on my part; it is no new faith that I am expressing-I for one am in favour of a considerable reduction of the tariff. I want to see free farm implements for the agriculturist. He is entitled to them, and I believe that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) thinks that he is entitled to them. I want to see what the farmer needs for his out-buildings-building material brought in free. I want to see cement, fertilizers, lubricating and fuel oil brought in free. As a matter of fact, I am heart and soul in favour of that resolution which was moved in the last Parliament by Hon. Frank Oliver and so ably seconded by the present Minister of Public Works (Hon. F. B. Car-veil). The people are looking for some relief from the burdens of taxation imposed upon them by the tariff. There is a great
outcry as to where we shall get our revenue. It does not seem to me to be well founded.
I do not believe a prohibitive tariff of 42J per cent is going to bring in a great revenue.
I believe that a more reasonable tariff will bring in a larger revenue; that is the history of tariff changes. It is due to the consumer that the Government bestir itself and bring down such a tariff policy as the people are calling for.
It was brought out by the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) that there is a certain amount of stagnation in manufacturing enterprises because the Government has not the courage to move in connection with the tariff. The manufacturers know that there is a cry for a change. They know that the Government does not know what to do. They know that they are badgered on the right by their friends the monopolists and on the left their friends the people from the West. They are standing still, afraid to take the plunge. Capital is unsettled; business men do not know what orders to place. L6t the Government come out in the open and do something. Let them announce a policy; let them convince the manufactui-ers and the business people of Canada that they have some courage in this matter, and let business get settled in the land.
As a word of warning to the Government, I quote the following from an address recently delivered by President Wilson in the United States:
Any man who resists the present tides that run in the world will And himself thrown upon a shore so high and barren that it will seem as if he had been separated from his human kind forever.
This tide of tariff is running so high that these words of the President can be very properly applied to any Government that resists it.
The Minister of Immigration and Colonization speaks also of the cleavage in this country caused by the variety of the races and religions therein; and this he deplores. I say to him in all sincerity that such words from him do not have the right ring. Hardly more than a year has elapsed since the party which he Is now supporting and then supported did everything in my province not only that men could do, but that perverse men could do, to make the cleavage between the races and religions of this country as wide and as impossible of healing as could be done. No Liberal following the Grand Old Chieftain in my part of the country was a loyal British subject; he was branded as a traitor and a pro-German, and classed as being unfit to take

speechtext:
1 desire to read the following cable which I have received from the Overseas Minister of Militia (Sir Edward Kemp) respecting the Kinmel Park disturbance:
Answering your inquiry further information Kinmel Park disturbance, my cable March 7th should be read in conjunction with this, covers the ground pending thorough inquiry which is being carried on. Difficulties have been encountered but discipline amongst Canadians has been considered at least equal to that of best Imperial troops. Unrest in Canadian Camps is accounted for by fact that the men have been away from their homes in 'Canada for periods ranging up to four years or more, have suffered great privations and are thoroughly homesick, a fact which is fully appreciated. It will be easily understood that men who have endured such hardships and monotony would when they reached Kinmel Park, the last stage in England 'before embarkation, if held owing to shipping difficulties, become impatient. Everything possible is done to interest the soldiers while they are waiting to be repatriated. Information on this point will follow. Armistice came at beginning of one of most severe winters England has experienced. Weather has been continually cold and wet with absolute lack of sunshine. Had we been fortunate enough to have been able to proceed with demobilization under more favourable weather conditions there would have been less cause for complaint. There has been general shortage of fuel which has added discomfort. Men have lived in camps, for most part in huts, which is only accommodation. Non-combatant troops coming from different parts of France, also lines of communication troops, have
fMr. Fortier. 1
doubted'ly suffered hardships owing to unavoidable and uncomfortable transportation to England, resulting in colds and in many cases influenza. Discomforts which soldier is willing to put up with when engaged in fighting assume different aspect now that war is over. Labour troubles and general unrest in British Isles and on continent have had some effect upon men. In my cable to you February 25th I pointed out that we were short nine thousand in our shipment of troops to Canada for first fifteen days of February. This was caused by MinisterShipping not being able to deliver ships -which had been specifically promised for certain dates. In some cases ships offered were upon examination refused by us because they were not suitable for carrying troops. In other cases sailings of ships have been postponed four, five and six times and such postponements or cancellations of sailings causing vast amount of extra work in re-forming of sailing parties and re-opening of documents and correction of nominal rolls, etc. Delays and cancellations also lead to rearrangement of flow of troops as far back as Belgium. Men who have been over here for long periods but who have served in corps were embarked for Canada in large numbers before March first. It was not until this date that any corps troops were embarked. Men who have served in corps who are casualties in England so far as possible are collected .and drafted into units of corps which go to Canada according to dispersal areas. Difficulties arise in connection with maintaining permanent cadres owing to specially trained or technical personnel desiring to be returned to Canada in their order of priority and their replacement by efficient personnel causes great difficulty. Too much cannot be said on behalf of men engaged in this work as well as staffs in general, including clerks all descriptions who though anxious to get home and in many cases as much entitled as any one to return, are loyally and patriotically supporting me in endeavour to get troops back. I cannot speak too highly of men who are patiently and patriotically carrying on necessary work to demobilize and embark soldiers for Canada, many of whom have served for long periods and in many cases will be last to be demobilized. This work has been greatly hampered by influenza epidemic. Also work of demobilization has been interfered with through demands of Imperial authorities for necessary accommodation in order to carry out their demobilization, many Canadian reserve units in England having had to be moved at same time under great difficulties in the carrying out of their functions of demobilization. Staff difficulties are also very heavy on account of vast amount of documentation requiring to be carried out in England to meet wishes of authorities in Canada. More men have to be provided for in England than at any time since beginning of the war. Necessity of inaugurating a special system for dealing with corps troops and educating of staffs in accordance with systems prevailing in England. There are also difficulties in carrying out two forms of demobilization side by side, this being unavoidable. Disposition of surplus war material in France and England, horses, etc., is big task in itself. Never since war began has there been such an amount of work to be done in so short a period. Took some time to reverse machine which had been in operation for four and a half years and set it going in opposite direction back to Canada. All practical suggestions for improvements to assist in camp life are readily adopted. Notwithstanding all difficulties with

which we are faced we Will have succeeded by end of this month in moving from Prance to England eighty-five thousand soldiers and from England to Canada not less than one hundred thousand, which is considered here at any rate a remarkable achievement considering all circumstances.
I cabled recently to the Overseas Minister of Militia with respect to certain press reports which had reached Canada alleging that the girls' quarters at Kinmel Camp had been attacked by the men. Sir Edward Kemp replied to my cable as follows:
Cannot anticipate findings of Court Inquiry. Times, however, on March 8th stated with respect to girls employed in camp as follows: " The manageress responsible for girls declares that not the slightest attempt was made to interfere with any of them."
Lloyd's paper, March 9th, says : " No attempt was made by the rioters to interfere with them. The girls were treated with the utmost chivalry." The Telegraph, March 8 th, says: " The girls' camp was not attacked, and as a matter of fact the girls were treated with the utmost chivalry." There is indignation here among all Canadians at exaggerations which appeared particularly in earlier reports in British press. I have expressed indignation of Canadians to newspapers privately and publicly. Some have apologized. No Canadian, however, believed that Canadian soldiers would be guilty of conduct as reported in press respecting girls working in canteens with which they were charged. Cannot say at moment when findings Court Inquiry will be ready. Do not want to create impression that haste is of primary importance. What is required is thorough inquiry.
Kemp.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. D. L. Redman (Calgary East), for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session resumed from Friday, March 14.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. 'Speaker, the definite object I have in rising is to endeavour to make reply to some features of the address delivered in this House on Friday last by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). Since the conclusion of that speech, however, the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) has delivered a very well phrased and well condensed speech on various subjects that have been under review. His remarks consisted mainly in a pilgrimage into problems of tariff, a pilgrimage in which I shall not venture to follow him at present, preferring rather to pursue the advice so often given by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) when he was Minister of Finance, and refrain, as a member of the Government, from a discussion of questions of tariff until the Budget is brought down.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ross), however, indulged in the practice which is somewhat frequently pursued in this Parliament, of referring to an address I had the honour to make and a resolution I had the honour to move in this House in the early months of 1911. The resolution asked the House for a substantial reduction in the duties on implements. The remark I wish to make is this: that the hon. gentleman, in his efforts to criticise what 1 said at that time and myself now in relation to it, followed the habit of making a summary, or rather a very rough and hasty interpretation of what I said at that time instead of quoting my remarks as they were uttered. All I ask of him is: that whenever again he seeks to found any argument upon that speech or that resolution, he be good enough to give the text of the remarks I made or the text of the resolution, because I can assure him now that though something over eight years have gone by there is not a paragraph of that speech by whose principles I am not prepared to abide. The hon. gentleman appears to be at the present time a convert to the arguments I then adduced. I am very glad to know that. I cannot recall, however, that I got much assistance from him then when he was supporting the Government in office. He is an example of the very numerous class of men who are much easier of conversion and much more receptive to new platforms and new policies while enjoying the freedom of opposition and of private life than they are when confronted with the responsibilities of Government.
I am sure that the members of this House Sir, both to your right and to your left, will share with me in congratulating the

hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) on the vigour both of mind and body, of which he gave such ample evidence in his speech of last Friday. It is a matter of encouragement to us all, and indeed of inspiration, that a man of his years and of his long register of public service, a man who when very many around him now were in their cradles was Prime Minister of his province, can at this time rise to as high a level of controversial skill as at any period of his career.
There are many positions in the long range of subjects over which he traversed with which I do not care to take issue. Indeed, with much that he said I am in substantial accord, and my references this afternoon will be rather to contentions he brought forward and positions he took up in respect of which it may be said that the skill with which they were defended was very much better than the care with which they were selected.
First of all; in the latter part of his address, he took the ground that this was no longer a free Parliament; that this was a strangled and shackled Parliament and he ventured to appeal to hon. members to shake off the shackles and restore the pristine freedom of this House. Well, any hon. member or any one looking down from the gallery who has watched the proceedings of this Parliament for the past ten years during which I have been a member, or, indeed, for any ten years preceding, and noted the healthy atmosphere of independence and freedom and the extraordinary latitude of criticism exercised by hon. members on both sides, will have some difficulty in conceiving how any reflective -mind could come to the conclusion that this Parliament, of all parliaments, is shackled.
In attempting to establish his case the Ex-Minister of Finance enunciated certain precepts as to what should be the duty of the supporter of a party, and particularly of a supporter of a government, under the constitutional conditions of parliamentary government under which we live. With the principles he enunciated I want to take issue-and indeed the sharpest possible issue. He proclaims himself an adherent of the party system. Generally speaking, I have no fault to find with that position. I am not able to conceive how our parliamentary government can possibly be continued save under some form of the party system. A party system necessarily involves the concession of individual opinion to the will of the majority. It necessarily involves the tempering of individual aspira-
33i
tions to the average will of the entire body, with the result that though the final policy to which the party man eventually adheres may not meet the individual opinions of many, it will at all events fairly represent the average opinion of all. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), while supporting the general principle of party support, states that it must be confined to one class of subjects only, and that a wholly different relationship exists between the members of a party and the Government in office, or the members of the opposite party and the leader of the Opposition, in another class of subjects. These are his words:
I felt that on matters relating to the prosecution of the war the Government ought to be strongly supported, certainly by their friends, and I thought they might have claimed support from their opponents even in matters relating to the prosecution of the war. But I believe that on all questions not connected with the war every man in the House of Commons should be at liberty to act according to the dictates of his conscience. Was that an erroneous conception? Was there anything unreasonable in that?
There is just this much unreasonable in that. I should like to inquire why the operation of conscience should be excluded from ,the consideration of subjects connected with the prosecution of the war? Why should conscience reign only in the sphere of the ' trivial and the secondary, and be wholly excluded when it comes to the sphere of the important and the vital? If an hon. member of this House is asked to support some article of policy relating to the prosecution of the war which he believes to be not serving the interests of the country at all, which he believes will be a dishonour to his country and result, in part at all events, in disaster to his country, is he to be told that his conscience must not be allowed to speak or to affect his vote, and that on all such matters of great and imperious concern he must bow to the party will and support the Government in office? And is he at the same time to be told that in matters wholly secondary and trivial and inconsequential to the State, in order that his conscience may be kept alive, he is to be allowed to give it free play and to vote just as he like's?
I have stated, in plain language, I am sure, the principles which the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's deems to be sound. Those principles need only to be stated to be condemned as wholly unsound and wrong.
I said a few moments ago that the very existence of party, necessary as it is to the continuity of governmental authority and

to the efficiency of government as government, necessarily involved unity of action and support by party, save in certain extraordinary circumstances. But it would appear to me that the time when a member might see his way not to support the Government in office which he was elected to support would be an occasion, not of minor, but of major consequence-an occasion when the most vital interests of the State were concerned, and when he would determine that rather than support a policy of far-reaching consequence that he deems to be wrong, he would prefer that the Government of the day should change, or that there should be an appeal to the higher court of public opinion. On many such occasions hon. members of this House have seen fit to break from party and take a place by themselves, voting against the Government which generally they were desirous to support. That is a statement of the principle as it has operated and as it is recognized both in the Old Land and in this.
The hon. member, however, went on to give a special instance, and he said in that special instance a grave error was made which resulted in the shackling of this House by the Prime Minister of Canada. I wish to refer to that instance. It was on the occasion of the titles debate of last session. On that occasion the Prime Minister, in the name of the Government of this country moved a certain amendment to a resolution that was before this House. The circumstances were these: The subject of titles had engaged a very large share of public attention for some time and had been under discussion in the press of Canada. In view of that volume of public attention, and in view also, and particularly, of the fact that the question, important or unimportant though it might be in itself, involved our relationship with the Crown and with the Imperial authorities, the Government of this country felt it its duty to come to a definite decision of policy with regard thereto. They came to that decision, and embodied it in an Order in Council; and, more than that, communicated their decision with regard to this subject to the Government of Great Britain
In that position the Government found itself when the question came under discussion in this House, and in such circumstances the Government was bound to take its place as a government, where it had taken it in the Order in Council, and as thus communicated to the Imperial authorities. Now, I know of no case in British history, or in our own history, where a 
government, having finally taken up a position and having communicated that position to the authorities to whom it had to be communicated under the circumstances, could permit that policy to which they were committed to be overthrown by parliament, and thereafter continue to carry on the government of the country. There must be a consideration on the part of Government, as regards each individual case, of its general bearing on the whole body of public legislation. That consideration a government is bound to give, and the Government having given that consideration and come to its decision, were it to be overthrown, the authority necessary to its efficiency is impaired-and a long series of British precedents has taught us that a government in that position serves the public interests best by retiring from office and giving place to those who better represent the people in Parliament. It is not that a government is afraid to carry on, nor that it seeks anything for itself. It is merely in deference to the well-established rule-established through a thousand years of experience- that a government whose authority is so challenged or impaired cannot with advantage legislate in the public interests. Furthermore, there existed this circumstance in connection with the Titles situation; the Government of Great Britain, after communication of the position assumed by the Government of Canada, had, in the most respectful and urgent terms, asked this Government to defer further consideration of the subject, pending a conference upon it in England in the summer of 1918, and in view of that special communication, the stand taken by the Prime Minister in this House was inevitable and necessary. So that the Prime Minister-whether our stand previously had been right or wrong-in speaking as he did in Parliament on that night, was not making anything of a threat to Parliament; he was merely laying down a constitutional principle, by which constitutional principle he deemed himself 'to be bound.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) referred to an Act, passed not by this Government, but by the Government which preceded it, known as the War-time Elections Act. The language which he applied to that legislation was by far the strongest language which he used in the course of his address-language which later I shall quote, and for which he will have to take full responsibility. He made the attack knowing, as he well knew and as no one knew better, that on the subject of

the merits of that Bill on the merits of the legislation which that Bill put into effect, there was necessarily a difference of opinion on the part of ministers who now compose the Government of Canada. He approved of the principle of those men coming together and uniting for another and a higher purpose, and he knew as well, in making his attack upon it, that that Bill of itself goes out of existence automatically on de* mobilization, and that the Government of the day has no contemplation of its being exercised before demobilization. Consequently there would not appear to be very much practical object to be served by the stand he took.
Inasmuch as the attack which he made was certainly of an extraordinary character, and placed, at all events half of the members of this Government in a position that justifies vigorous defence, I wish to offer a little serious comment from the point of view of a member of this House, and of the late Administration, and in no way affecting to speak on behalf of the Government as constitued now. The hon. member stated that under the Wartime Elections Act, a class of the population of this country was disfranchised. That is true. He stated that these disfranchised persons would have voted against the Government of the day had they not been disfranchised, or would as a rule have voted against it. That also I do not deny. I believed that to be true then, and I believe it to be true now. But he went on to say that the only reason given for their disfranchisement was the fact that they would vote against the Administration. Now, I introduced that Bill myself-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I prepared that Bill myself.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear my work approved by hon. gentlemen opposite. I stated the grounds of that Bill to the House. Many other hon. members of this House, both in the Government and out of the Government, stated the principle behind that Bill and the reasons for it; and no one of them-myself or any other [DOT]-ever stated, as the hon. gentleman claims we stated, that the reason for that Bill was the fact that, the persons disfranchised would otherwise vote against the Government. It is one thing to believe they would; it is wholly another thing to base a Bill on that belief. The fact that
they would would be no reason whatever for such legislation. The reason they were disfranchised, as has a hundred times been repeated-be that reason sufficient or be it not-was that these men, bound as they were by ties of blood and kin, and by ties of a very freshly severed citizenship to the enemies of this country were not in a position, freely as Canadian citizens, to decide an issue that involved the conduct of war with the nation from which they came. That, briefly stated, was the reason given; that, briefly stated, was the reason behind the Bill. It was either sufficient or it was not. In my judgment it was good; in my judgment any other course would have been wholly unjustifiable.
But more than that: the hon. member states that the honour of the British name, the honour of the Canadian name, suffered a very serious defamation by the passing of that Act. I will quote his words. He went through a prolonged homily on the value of reputation and of character; on the value of the British name throughout the world, and he proceeded to say:
"Who can say to-day, with fairness and justice, " By the word of a Canadian I will do it " ? The word of a Canadian, tried by the War-time Elections Act, is a word of trickery, a word of deception, and the word of a cheat.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Now, hon. gentlemen venture to " hear, hear " again. It may just be possible that that invective, bitter as it is, extraordinary as it is, may in a few seconds be brought back and laid at the door of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's himself. Is it to be argued that because a person is given the rights of a British subject he is guaranteed forever the franchise? Is it to be argued that an alien coming to this country and acquiring the status of a British subject thereby enjoys a higher guarantee of citizenship than a British-born subject? Nobody would venture either assertion. It cannot be supported. It is not contended by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, or even suggested. He enjoys the same securities as the British subject born, no more and no less. But it is argued that to disfranchise British subjects born, or to disfranchise these others, is to indulge in trickery, deception and cheating. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was for a long time Premier of the province of Nova Scotia. He came into office about the year 1883, and while he was a member of the Government of the

province he introduced a Bill into the legislature of Nova Scotia by which Bill he would disfranchise within that province British subjects in the persons of all within the confines of Nova Scotia who were in the employment of the Government of Canada. That was a clause which was in the Act before, and when he brought it into the Legislature of Nova Scotia and pleaded for its reintroduction into law a motion was made by a member urging that the clause providing for disfranchisement of all these employees of the railways, post offices, inland revenue offices, lighthouses and other services of the Dominion Government in that province, should be struck out. That motion in amendment was resisted by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's,- his resistance prevailed and the clause was retained. That clause reads as follows:
It shall not be lawful for any person to vote at any election for a member or members to represent the people in the general assembly of this Province, who at any time within fifteen days before the day of election, was an employee, or in the receipt of wages or emolument of any kind1 as such employee, in the Post Office, the Custom House, the Inland Revenue Department, the Lighthouse service, on the Government railroads, in the Crown Land Office, or the Local Public Works and Mines.
Then it, goes on to except those who are merely supplying material and the actual postmaster .and mail courier himself. And the class of men disfranchised, born British subjects, bore just about as large a proportion of the electorate of the province as those disfranchised by the War-time Elections Act bore to the electorate of Canada. He himself reaped the fruits of this disfranchisement during five provincial elections in that province.
I am not arguing that the disfranchisement was wrong. I am not questioning it. It is not necessary for my contention to argue that the disfranchisement was wrong. It was put upon the ground that these persons, being employees of the Federal authorities, would be under the influence of their employers and would not be free voters in the contest. It is a little difficult to understand why that argument would not equally aoply to any person in the service of any other employer in the province of Nova Scotia. But, assuming that the argument is good and putting it on the highest plane you can, what is it? It is that by reason of external influence these British subjects were not free in the determination of questions appertaining to the province of Nova Scotia. Will anybody tell me that the influence, the stress, the power of the ties of blood and kin; the groanings
[Mr. Meighen.l
and tears of brothers overseas fighting against this country would not be a thousand times more powerful than would he an influence of that kind? If British honour, if the British name, if the Canadian name has suffered a catastrophe in this country by reason of the exercise of the power of disfranchisement, that catastrophe is a whole lot older than the War-time Elections Act, and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was himself a participant in the wreck.

I am not sure about the date of the Act to which the hon. gentleman refers. Is the introduction of this not very much older than the coming in as Premier of Nova Scotia of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I stated so. It was introduced in 1871, three or four years after Confederation, but does the hon. gentleman argue that if men had been wrongfully disfranchised for thirteen years the continuation of the wrong is justified?

The Liberals repealed
the Act in Nova Scotia and it is out of date long ago.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They repealed the Act
in 1909 long after the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's had ceased to be interested in Nova Scotia politics. If the Wartimes Elections Act is absolutely wrong;- though passed only for one election-how could the legislature of Nova Scotia support an Act and keep it on the statute-book for 38 years as the law of that province, founded on the same principle but on a far weaker case?
Now, I come to that feature of the address of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's in which he criticised the representation of this country at the Peace Conference now in session at Paris. The argument of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was that there were no subjects under discussion at this Peace Conference in which Canada had any special concern or in which Canada had any interest distinct from the interests of the British Islands, and that our representation there should be merged in the representation selected by the British Parliament. His line of thought first of all was that unless we had subjects under discussion there in which we had a purely Canadian interest, as distinct from the interest of Great Britain, we had no right to representation and he said that President Wilson was sound and logical when he resisted representation on the part of Canada. It is very difficult for me to com-

prehend how an hon. gentleman of the long experience of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) could possibly do justice to his intellect and come to the conclusion that there were no subjects under discussion in which we had a very distinct and very vital interest.
We do not fully know what is taking place; that is to say we know nothing more than is communicated to us through the regular channels. The deliberations will subsequently be made public to the extent that the conference decides, and then we will know what has been under discussion. But it seems to me that we can come to a conclusion as to the subjects that are probably under review. First of all there are the fourteen point of President Wilson on the basis of which the terms of -settlement are finally to rest. There are those points -that will be under discussion, and what is one of them? One of them says something about an economic arrangement as to trade between the powers of the world. That must be under discussion. I would not like to undertake to define what was in the President's mind but I presume the-re was something, and will anybody venture to suggest that this Dominion should not be represented and that we have no distinct interest, aside altogether from the interest of the British Islands, in the determination of the question of an economic arrangement as to trade between the Powers?
Furthermore there is under discussion there the question of the purchase, the transportation, and the disposition of food stuffs as between Allied and enemy countries. Will any one suggest that our interests with regard to that are identical with the interests of Great Britain? Our interests are by no means identical; they are distinct, and the problem for us is wholly a Canadian problem. And there could be nothing more vital, and nothing more important, than that representatives of this Dominion of high standing and authority should be there to safeguard the interests of Canada. There is nothing that bears more on the prosperity of this country at this time than- the share of trade obtained by this country in the reconstruction of the .desolated parts of Europe, and the share of purchases made by this country for foodstuffs and for other supplies for Allied and enemy lands. It is all right to have a trade commission, but the principles that bear on these problems are under discussion at the Peace Conference, and in the determination of these principles it is essential to this Dominion that it should be represented.
Then there is the matter of transportation, pending, at all events, the conclusion of the terms of peace. Will any one suggest that the problem of transportation is the same for Canada as it is for Great Britain? It is a different problem altogether, and it is Canadians who must have a say in the solution of that problem so far as we are concerned. I could pass from subject to subject, but there will scarcely be a matter wi-thin the deliberations of thait conference in which we have not an interest, and a distinctive interest. But assuming again that on no single topic have we any concern or any special interest that -may be separated from and made distinct from th-e interest of Great Britain, I affirm here -as a -Canadian citizen that -as -a distinct entity within the British Empire, and as a distinct self-governing entity, we are entitled to a voice in the attitude assumed by Great Britain in the disposal of every question that pertains to the terms of peace.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) referred to the fact that only on one occasion was the representative of Canada seated at the inner council of Ten which, he states, and rightly states, is so powerful in the determination of the problems of the Conference. He made some fun of the reference in the despatch to the fact that the subject under discussion at that meeting was the fixing of the boundaries of Serbia, and intimated to this House that the determination of that question should be left to cleiks in the Foreign Office in England, and that in it we had no concern whatever. Well, sixty thousand soldiers of this country have come to early graves as a result of this war, and you do not trace very far back the causes that led to the war until you come to the boundaries of Serbia. Bosnia, and Herzegovina filched from Serbian control! the Serajevo massacre ! the flame that lighted the world. And on the proper solution of the boundaries of Serbia, as of every power, on the certainty that those boundaries will be delimited in accordance with rightful principles of race and nationality and of selfdetermination, on the certainty that they will be based on the general consent of nations and in fundamental -equity as between nations-on that depends the peace and prosperity of mankind for generations to come.
It is no flattery to the Prime Minister of Canada, no flattery to the Government of Canada, to say that Sir Robert Borden at

this time, removed as he is from local or European prejudices, wholly divorced as he is from the tie3 and understandings that may have bound countries in days gone by, and possessed as he is, of lofty judicial temperament, high legal endowment and strong personality and will-it is no flattery to him to say that his services may be inestimable in the determination of the question of the boundaries of Europe.
Let me .assure Parliament-it needs no assurance I hope-that the Prime Minister did not go over to take part in that Conference, and in the negotiations that led to the 'Conference and that decided its constitution, he did not go over merely as a matter of his own convenience, or to satisfy his pride; he went over there on the earnest and repeated solicitation of the Prime Minister of Great Britain himself, on his earnest and repeated .appeal-praying him to come not at the end of November, or at the
4 p. m. beginning of the Conference, but praying Sir Robert to come and give his services early, not to great Britain, not to Canada, but to the whole Empire, in the determination of the constitution of the Conference, in the determination of all the arrangements leading to it, and in all the problems with which the Government and the Empire were confronted leading to and before that Conference.
I do not think that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was doing quite jusr tice to this Dominion when he pictured the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the President of the United States as feeding out candy to this country, endeavouring to flatter us, and, as it were, to tickle the vanity of Canada in deciding whether we should have representation or not. He even went so far as to say that President Wilson was sound and logical in his position when he took the ground, as in fancy he pictured him taking it, that we had no more right to separate representation than had the state of New York over and above the representation of the United States. Could a more preposterous thought be addressed to a deliberative assembly. Has the state of New York no say in the determination or the government of the United States? Has it no voice in the selection of the delegates of the United States? Has the state of New York any option as to whether or not it goes to war if the United States goes to war? Now let me read the words of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. He says that he can conceive of an anomaly-he can

conceive of something that would be wholly inconceivable and intolerable, and this is what it would be:
True, there is an anomaly in the position. I grant you at once that if we had been obliged to take part in the war, having no voice in the making of it, the condition would be inconceivable and intolerable.
Well, there may be a sense in which, on a declaration of war by Britain, we have a constitutional right to determine whether we will take part in the conflict or not, there may be a constitutional sense in which we have a right to say whether we will take part in the conflict or not; but assuming there is, assuming the hon. member is right-that it would be inconceivable and intolerable that we should be bound by Britain's decision to go to war if we have no say as to whether she goes or not-then I want to put to him this question: are we not to be bound by the Treaty of Peace? Is the Treaty of Peace that binds the British Empire not to bind this country? Yes. we will surely be bound by every line and letter of that treaty that affects the Empire of Britain. And, if such be true, then on what principle under Heaven are we not to have any representation or any say in the making of the Treaty of Peace? If therefore it is inconceivable and intolerable that we should have to go to war on the declaration of war by Great Britain because we have no voice in the declaration, surely it is inconceivable and intolerable that we should be bound by the Treaty of Peace if we have no voice or say in the terms of the treaty at all.
Now it is quite true that the Council of Ten is the principal body, and very likely the initiating body of the conference. And it is very likely true as well that only on rare occasions can Canada have her actual representatives sitting at that council. But what I contend is this : It is absolutely vital that in the determination of the position that the representatives of this Empire shall take at the conference, be they Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Balfour or anybody else, the representatives of this country must sit on the British delegation and have their voice. It is true that, those representatives cannot be dominant on the British panel. It is just as true that the representatives of Nova Scotia or of my province in this Parliament cannot possibly dominate this Parliament; but here they are represented and can make their influence felt, and so long as they can do that, they have their rights. Similarly, we must be represented on the British delegation in order

that the influence and the opinion of this country may be reflected in the action taken by the delegates of the Empire in the Council of Ten.
I do not know by what title the member for Shelburne and Queen's ('Mr. Fielding) describes his new faith. It certainly is not the old Liberalism; it is certainly not anything to which this Union Government can possibly subscribe. The idea that our representation in the concerns of Empire must be merged in representatives selected by the Parliament and Government of Britain and that we can have no say outside of that-surely that is not the Liberalism of to-day. The member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) shakes his head, but I think I heard him applaud and I heard a great many hon. members opposite applaud when the member for Shelburne and Queen's was enunciating these extraordinary theories.
Oh, no.
Not at that juncture.

Mr. Lemieux) observed a discreet silence; he did not like the new dogmas that were being placed before him by the member for Shelburne and Queen's. If the attitude of the member for Shelburne and Queen's with relation to our representation at the conference-a compound of colonization and imperialism gone mad-is to be taken as an indication on his part of a return to the lighted chamber of Liberalism, he emphatically has taken to heart the advice of the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) and has taken his provisions with him. I say this to hon. members who so vigorously applauded the remarks of the member for Shelburne and Queen's on this subject; after they go out from under the magic of his eloquence and mingle with their own peoples, they will not hear many plaudits of heresy like this, especially in the strongholds of their faith.
Hear, hear.
