In this we have the imprimatur of the member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) and so we may take it for granted that hereafter Canada will be conceded to be properly represented in the councils of the Empire and that we shall no longer hear it suggested that the Prime Minister and his colleagues should return to Canada and not continue their work-a work they have so far performed so well in the greatest conference of all time.
A word more, and I have done. I have heard it stated more than once during the progress of this debate, that the Government is seeking shelter from criticism under the shadow of war and that the freedom of criticism of the old days is denied. Well, there was a time, when the war was in progress, when the fate of this country was in peril, that we did ask from hon, gentlemen greater care in the attacks they levelled against the Administration and greater efforts at unity in this House than are ordinarily made under the party system. That was not for the protection or for the good of the Government; it was, as we deemed it, in the vital interests of the country. We felt that the advantages of union were greater than the advantages, however important they were, of the full and free play of party criticism in Parliament. We felt it was important that there should not be an encouragement of disunion in the country by unnecessary disunion in Parliament. But the war is over now-at all events, the peril is passed-we want no favours; we ask for no quarter; we seek no shelter. If the opponents of this Government have any batteries in reserve, let the heavy artillery come on. We shall exhaust every effort to learn and to understand our duty, and by the courage and the efficiency of its performance, we are quite prepared to be judged.
Mr. JULES EDOUARD PREVOST (Terrebonne) Translation) : Mr. Speaker, whoever in this House rises to take part in this debate, cannot help noticing with deep sorrow the vacant seat once occupied by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Hon. members who preceded me were anxious to lay their tribute of sweet remembrance and praise on the grave of that illustrious Canadian. As the days pass away, we realize more and more that a great voice has lapsed into silence, but within these precincts we can still hear the echo of the golden words with which Laurier used to express the great Liberal principles which always guided his life and illuminated Canadian politics.
Just as the stars project their rays over the boundless space long after their fires are extinct, the splendor cast on our national life by Laurier i,s not about to fade away and will be continued for a long time in our history. He iis istill alive, first in our heart then in the Libeiral policy which was his own and which cannot die. We do not see him among us and his pleasant smile and intelligent eyes shine no more in this House, but his spirit is still present, I mean the vivid inspiration which created.

maintained and developed in hi.s mind the wise political doctrines of the golden mean, the only one that may apply to this country.
Some people have disdainfully called that policy opportunism. Truly, it was opportunism, but the right kind of opportunism. There are two sorts of opportunism; one, woeful and vile, which consists of changing heart and soul according to the time -and chances of personal benefit; the other, a well comprehensive policy, which leads you to accept unavoidable but honest compromises in order to go as far as possible toward the -end in view which it would be difficult to accomplish all of a sudden.
Laurier's science of conceding was always guided by the -most sincere Liberalism. His idea of Liberalism hovered always very high; it was most attractive because it appealed to all indiscriminately -and solicited the support of -every man in the heart of whom, as he so w-ell described, are enshrined the principles of -eternal truth and unalterable justice.
It was Liberalism in its most extensive form, that which Lauri-er advooaited and practiced, opposing action to reaction, the reasonable emancipation of the mind to its bondage, progress to stagnancy, education to ignorance, and including claims for all legitimate liberties, tolerance, war on fanaticism and the firm respect of the rights of mankind.
Thus placed at th-e apex, Laurier's idiea of Liberalism prevailed over the races, 'the creeds and even the parties. That is why he had so many supporters and -explains how h-e leaves so many sincere admirer,s on all -sides, in all groups. But he believed, and we believe with him, that the Liberal party is the political organization which is most capable to carry out the ideal of Liberalism.
W-e are the trustees of Laurier's doctrine. It is our duty, as much as our best claim to glory, to work for the triumph of that ideal of Canadian Liberalism. The whole of Canada is proud of Lauri-er and surrounds his memory with pr-ai-se and regrets as a halo the brightness of which nothing can ever impair.
But we, his adepts, his political followers, have greater cause than any others to pride ourselves on such a leader and to mourn his death. Should. Laurier comeback in our midst now I believe he would s-ay to us, in pleasant and fervid tones: "My friends, men amount to Ixtt1;; what counts is the ideal. The ideal -of Canadian Liberalism did not disappear with me and

when I bequeathed it to you, I gave vou the best of myself."
By the light of our late lamented leader's political doctrine, allow me to consider for a few moments the -policy, or rather ihe lack of policy of this Government. It is a well known fact that this Union Government has been the greatest enemy of union in Canada. Unionism has divided the country, the souls and hearts of its people, the Liberal as well as the Conservative parties, and the Government to which it gave birth is divided against itself. The Union Government will destroy itself like the scorpion which bites off its own tail. That party whose policy was embodied in the one cry: "Win the War," has not even succeeded in administering safely the affairs of this country in the actual interest of the war.
The sensational disclosures made in this House, a few days ago, by the hon. member for Victoria, ex Minister of Militia, are adding to the substantial evidence already secured.	.
Those whose mission it is to wash the Government of all impurity may reply that the hon. member for Victoria did not go in the trenches and, therefore, is not well acquainted with what was going on at the front; they may also say that he was relieved from his duties of Minister by Sir Robert Borden and that his criticism is inspired by per-sonal grudge. But another arraignment still more formidable than the charges laid by the ex-Minister of Militia, has just been made against the military administration of this -Government which is alleged to have been created for the *purpose of "winning the war." I am referring to the statements made in the legislature of Quebec, last Friday, by General Smart, Conservative member for Westmount.
In a forceful -speech. Gene-rial Smart, who returned from overseas recently, where he secured an important command and remarkable promotions after four years of active service, denounced the medical service and the general administration of the Canadian army in Great Britain and in Canada.
What will be the answer of this Government to the charges laid by the general, who -makes 'the following -solemn -declaration :
Before I left -England, I was refluested by several officers to call the attention of the Canadian, people upon certain conditions which obtained there for a long time and which the officers could not bring to light.
Unfortunately they can do nothing for those who are dead, except perpetuate their memory and extend protection to their families; but there are many officers and men who are going

to be the wards of the Government- during the next -2'0 or 30 *years, and' it is in their own interest that I should bring forth the following facts: I say, without "any fear of being contradicted by any unbiased authority, that the medical administration Overseas was bad. It showed itself dull and careless and should have been much improved. Personally, after a stay of four years overseas, I have no confidence in those who carry on the administration in Great Britain.
General Smart sharply criticized the heads of the Army Medical Corps and particularly Sir George iPerley who, according to his statement, caused much harm and trouble which he set forth and condemned. In the course of his violent denunciation, General Smart cited facts and names; his facts were quite specific. For instance he charged the beads of the Army Medical 'Corps with having caused the death of General Steele and through their inefficiency and carelessness, and with rendering incurable a great number of soldiers.
The dealings of 'Sir George Perley, General Turner and Sir Edward Kemp are closely scrutinized by that gallant officer. He positively states that the troubles at Rhyl, as well as those which occurred at Shorncliffe, at Witney and at Bramshott, were the outcome of the resentment inspired by the treatment to which the men had been subjected for a long time' past. He denounced some of the Orders in Council passed by this Government and wondered whether this Government were composed of men still possessed of common sense.
After having re-asserted that the overseas administration was 'bad and had been so for the last two years, General Smart moved the following resolution which was adopted unanimously:
That in the opinion of this House, the Federal Government should supply the people with all the information relative to the treatment meted out to officers and men of the Canadian Expeditionary Force recruited in this province, who have returned from overseas sick or wounded and are still under treatment in the hospitals.
Mr. Gault another Conservative of long standing, whose name I have already mentioned, seconded general Smart's motion.
In view of these facts, the "win the war" Government find themselves in a queer position. Such is the work accomplished by the Government, who juggled away the election in 1917, by proclaiming that they want first of all to organize the Canadian army in order to win the war. Such is the record of this Union Government, who persist in saying- that their task is not yet completed and that their existence is absolutely necessary for the welfare of the country. The
. more we go, the more we realize the harm which they are doing, as evidenced by the returning officers and soldiers. General Smart exclaimed in the Quebec Legislature: "I do not want imperialism, if it must be at the cost of the soldiers suffering". These words which fall as a whip's lash on the face of the Government are expressing my own opinion, and I may add that the "win-the-war" cry, with which the Unionists were able to smother the free and true expression of public opinion in 1917, is no longer strong -enough to drown the loud denunciations and the hitter complaints of those who fell the victims of the carelessness, incompetence and favoritism of this Government. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, since the tragedy on the battlefield is over, why should they keep up at home this joke of unionism which has not even a pretence to justify its existence?
Let us see what the Government has accomplished. In establishing conscription, they satisfied nobody, and, less of all, the western farmers; they broke the harmony, so essential to the efficiency of our common endeavour during the terrible war in which we were taking part. Under that useless legislation, they succeed in securing only a few hundred soldiers more than they would have done under the voluntary system, had the latter been properly organized. It is easy to prove- it, and I will do so on another occasion during this session, should I be given an opportunity to do so.
The speech from the Throne contains no reference to the most serious problems which Canada is facing to-day. The country is indebted to the extent of $2,000,000,-' 000. Each year we shall require several hundred millions to meet our most unavoidable obligations. One of the ministers told this House -a few days ago 'that he *expected -a deficit of one hundred millions for the next fiscal year. However, the speech from the Throne does not mention any way by which the Government can secure the revenue which they require.
There is no mention of the cost of living in the speech from the Throne, though it is a difficult problem which requires a prompt solution. Who -does not know of, or has not suffered from the effects of the increased cost of living: unjustified penury and hardship for the great majority of the people, distress for many, evident social unrest, agitation among certain sections of the proletariat, strikes or threat to strike, ever swelling budgets on account of the increases in salary, pensions and bonuses which we must provide for

1899, they were charging 16.17 per cent on all dutiable and free goods, that is 3.49 per cent less on the value of the goods imported for home consumption. For every $100 collected in 1879, we were charging only $83 in 1899. And the Liberal party kept on lowering the tariff from year to year. However when they came into power, the expenses of the country exceeded the receipts by two millions, and this did not prevent them from lowering the tariff. Therefore the Liberals have first reduced the duties to the extent of $17 per $100, and then they did away with high protection duties on all staple commodities.
For instance, cotton and linen and linen goods had to pay a specific duty of from one to two cents per square yard and an ad valorem duty of 15 per cent; the Liberal Administration abolished the specific duty and made a big cut in the ad valorem duty. The consumer was benefited for, when you come down to it, it is the consumer who has to pay the customs duties on all the goods we import into this country.
Some other examples: There was a duty of 71 cents per gallon on petrol; the Liberals reduced this to 5 cents. Under the Tories molasses paid an ad valorem duty of 15 per cent; the Liberals cut this down to li cents a gallon. Under the Conservative Administration ready-made clothing paid 10 cents a pound plus ah ad valorem duty of 35 per cent; under the Liberals the 10 cents per pound duty was abolished and the ad valorem reduced by 10 per cent.
The Liberal Government followed the same policy with regard to woollens; under the Conservatives these goods paid a specific duty of 74 cents and 20 per cent ad valorem; the Liberals, abolished the specific duty.
So that it may be said in very truth that the Liberals instituted a tariff for revenue only; and they adopted a policy of reciprocity with the United iStates in natural products.
We are told that a downward revision of the tariff at the present time would deprive the country of revenue which is badly needed. That sort of argument does not put the question on the proper plane. The tariff may be lowered in such a way as to protect the consumer and nevertheless still maintain and even increase the country's revenue. What must be done is to change the incidence of taxation. Let us note that in Canada about 10 per cent of our revenue is derived from excess profits and from the income tax, while 90 per cent is derived from customs duties and excise, which

latter affect the pockets of the consumer. In England 82 per cent of the revenue is derived from excess profits and from the income tax while customs and excise furnish only 18 per cent. In England the burden is on the rich; here it is chiefly the poor man who pays. In France, besides the income tax there is a tax on excess profits. Starting at 50 per cent this tax has risen to 60 per cent on all profits above 500,000 francs. 1 believe this tax has been still further increased. If I be correct, 60 percent is levied on profits beyond 100,000 francs, 70 per cent above 200,000 and, as in England, 80 per cent on all profits over and above 500,000 francs. In Canada the Union Government which always protects the big fellow .at the expense of those who are least .able to bear it, instead of increasing the excess profits tax so as to hear more heavily on the higher profits, has done just the opposite. I'll prove this to you: the income tax passed at the session of 1917 falls on the salaried workers and, on the other hand, exempts in unbelievable proportions the profits of the big enterprises which have fattened on the war; the same is true of big busimests which, through its tremendous capital, puts an abnormal strain on the resources of the country.
Let us compare the amounts contributed, in proportion to their profits, by the companies with a capital of $100,000, first through the war profits tax which lapsed on December 31, 1918, and then through the income tax.
A company making 10 per cent profit paid into the Treasury, under the business profits tax, $750; under the income tax that company pays only $280. A profit of 15 per cent brought $2,000; with the new tax all we get is $480. A 20 per cent profit gave $4,500; now it gives only $680; a 25 per cent profit used to give $8,250; all it gives now is $880. A profit of 30 per cent which used to bring $12,000 now merely brings in $1,080. A profit of 50 per cent contributed, under the old tax $27,000; under the income tax, the Treasury receives only $1,880. A 100 per cent profit used to give $64,500 in taxes; now it gives but $3,000; while a profit of 200 per cent which was formerly taxed to the tune oE $139,500 is now asked to pay a paltry $7,880.
Would we like to get a better understanding of how it is that the companies which are making very big profits are exempt, fnm the tremendous burden of taxation while those with small salaries are being constantly called upon to pay a great deal more

than they can afford? Let us cite a few instances of this and, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me to be perhaps a bit tiresome so as to make clear what I have to say and prove my case with substantial facts and figures
Let us suppose that the companies I am about to speak of made the same profits in
1916,	1917 and 1918, and then let u.s compare what they formerly paid, and what they pay to-day, into the Public Treasury. Let us take the O^ilvie Company, for instance: in 1916 its revenue on a capital investment of $5,622,486, warranted the payment, under the business profits tax, of $280,886. In
1917,	if we suppose the company's revenue to be the same as in 1916, the tax on its profits .should have amounted to $547,478, but with the income tax all the company has to pay on its 1919 profits is $60,564.
Another company, one which is not unknown, is the Wm. Davies Co.; in 1916 they paid an excess profits tax of $223,063. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1917, they should pay $1,380,000; but for 1919 all the income tax demands from them is $55,200.
The net profits of the Nova Scotia Steel Co. in 1916 were $2,104,478 and the excess profits tax brought $237,2150; but their income tax for 1919 is only $84,056.
Take Canada Foundry: net profits in 1916, $653,852; war tax, $222,368. The income tax has reduced this amount to $26,152.
.The Ford Motor Co., with an .invested capital of $5,909,000, cleared profits amounting to $3,303,678, or '54.2 per cent, in 1916. Under the old tax this company contributed to the Treasury $697,328. In 1917 its taxes amounted to $1,782,095, but with the income tax this will be cut down to $127,987.
The Northern Aluminium Co., with a capital investment of $3,860,000 cleared $1,636,600 profits in 1916, or 42.4 per cent; tax in 1916, $341,679; tax in 1917, $822,332. With the new income tax this company has to pay a mere tax of $65,565.
The Canada Forging Co., with an investment of $1,455,526 cleared $991,359 profits in 1916, let us say 68.11 per cent, and this brought a tax of $222,368; in 1917 this eom-.pany paid into the Treasury $590,689; while in 1919 all they will pay will be $39,524.
The Steel Co. of Canada, with an investment of $13,963,000, cleared in 1916 a profit of $2,210,343, or 15.83 per cent; hence its tax amounted to $308,240; in 1917 the company paid taxes to the tune of $337,056; the income tax will bring only $88,293.
The Imperial Oil Co., capital, $27,161,000, cleared in 1916, $4,837,364 or 17.81 per cent;
war tax, $734,046; 1917, $924,849. The tax under the new order will be only $193,374.
The Fairbanks-Morse Co., capital, $3,686,500, cleared $669,100, in 1916 a percentage of 18.15 per cent; war tax $102,748; 1917, $135,767. The income tax will be satisfied with $26,640,
These figures go to show how lightly the income tax bears on the companies that are making the heaviest profits. And we must not lose sight of the fact that a great many of them are. manufacturing articles of universal use, the prices of which have increased enormously since the declaration of war.
It is evident that these millionaire companies are not paying a sufficient share of the taxes which burden our Canadian people. Even when their share of the taxes was higher than it is today they were still paying less than they would have paid in Australia for instance.
Thus, in 1916, Stanfield Limited, instead of paying $14,297, would have paid $54,844 in Australia; in 1917 they would have paid $82,266. The Consolidated Rubber Co., would have paid to the Australian Treasury, in 1916, $458,750 instead of $154,687; and in 1917 they would have paid $680,625 instead of $247,500. In Australia, in 1916, the Dominion 'Ganners would have paid $278,425 taxes instead of the $79,125 they paid Canada; in 1917, their taxes would have been $417,637 instead of $177,120.
The Government, far from looking to these millionaire corporations lor ian increase in our revenue at a time when the war which brought them colossal fortunes is putting a huge debt on this country, asks them for less than ever and lightens their burden.
If the Government had adopted a more enlightened policy, as has been done in Australia, they could abolish the duty on every single one of the prime necessaries of life and still increase the country's revenue.
The Union Government has neglected, and continues to neglect the alarming difficulties which the nation are vitally interested in seeing solved. If this Union Government insists on staying on despite the march of events which to-day fail to justify its existence, at least it should not reveal itself as a union against one race, against a minority that, within the fold of Confederation possesses, by virtue of our Constitution and of the most elementary justice, the same rights as the majority.
Oligarchy has been precisely defined: "A small group of citizens who undertake to

govern to the exclusion of the other citizens" (such was Canada from 1791 to 1840) "or a numerous class who exercise a monopoly of political power to the exclusion of the other citizens" (such is Canada since 1917, that is since the spontaneous generation of Union Government.)
We must regard a government of that kind as one of the enemies of freedom.
The present Government systematically neglects the French Canadian element and refuses to grant these people the share they are entitled to in the administration and the reconstruction of the country.
The Government is not justified in giving as its reason the fact that the province of Quebec went solid against those in power at the time of the 1917 elections. To begin with, the French Canadian element has plenty of company: the Opposition group in this House represents 800,000 Canadian voters of whom 519,940 are outside the province of Quebec; and this figure of 519,940 is one half of the vote polled by the Government throughout the entire Dominion.
Besides, has the Government any right to indulge such a narrow-minded grudge when it has proclaimed itself so often and so loudly the champion of democracy, justice and freedom? Nevertheless the Union Government, instead of striving to bring about the union of all races, the harmonious concord of all minds and hearts in a common national undertaking, without distinction of nationality, creed or opinion, seems determined to organize a union against the French Canadian Catholics, and thus comes under the head of the definition I gave a moment ago: a class who exercise a monopoly of political power to the exclusion of other citizens.
I find one proof of this, one out of a hundred, in the fact that we barely find two French Canadians on the numerous commissions appointed by the Government during the war; so much so that the Montreal district Chambre de Commerce was moved to protest, and with good reason, against this ostracism of French Canadians on the commissions appointed by the Union Government, especially on the commission sent to represent Canada in France and Belgium. In this connection the Government's fanaticism brought about the result, which n.)t only is ridiculous but will work harm to our country's interests, that commissioners who have not the slightest knowledge of the French language represent Canada in France and Belgium in an endeavour to promote our commercial interests after the

war! After that we can hardly feel astonished that the said commission is not meeting with any great success.
I find another proof of this deplorable spirit that seems to animate the Government, which styles itself a Union Government, in the list of physicians recently appointed by the Repatriation committee. Out of fifty doctors appointed how7 many are French Canadian? Not a single one!
If we but watch a bit these governmental appointments and the distribution of federal funds w7e are soon convinced, and the conviction strengthens the further we go, that w.e French Canadians are being systematically robbed. We are being deprived of our share of the profits accruing to us 'as partners in Confederation. The element which supports Union Government comprises only 54 per cent of the population and still they 'wish to treat the French Canadians as a conquered and ransomed people. What we contribute to the Pubhc Treasury and what comes back to us in the form of public expenditure shows clearly the supremely unjust manner in which the Government of National Discord treats a race that is inferior to no other and that holds imprescriptible rights to representation whether in the councils of the nation, in the public service or in honours and in the distribution of State moneys.
Can it be that the Union Government is the official representative of that Anglo-Canadian clique defined and upbraided by William Moore in his fine book "The Clash" in which he, a Protestant and an Anglo-Canadian acknowledges and proves that his compatriots are meting out to the French Canadians -exactly the same treatment as that which characterized the deportment of the Germans towards the people of Alsace-Lorraine, the Poles and the Danes.
I am asking for no favour or privilege for the French Canadian all I wish for iis the recognition of that right for which the Great Pow7ers of the Entente have just won a glorious victory. Have not the French Canadians the same right to national liberty and to justice as the Czecho-Slovaks, the Poles and the other nationalities within the muscovite empire? After the war which has just come to a close and which was heralded as humanity's crusade for the triumph of right let us hope that never again will any people be forced to hear the yoke of a tyrannical majority. Let -them well understand and harken to what I say, those Unionists who are plotting the de-

gradation of the French 'Canadians, those jingoes and Tories who persecute us in our language and in our faith wherever they meet us.
We must never lose sight of the fact, and particularly the Union Government should always bear in mind, that the British Empire is not founded on violence, on force, on oligarchy, but on moral principles, on the principles of liberty and equality.
I claim for all those whose country occupies the first place in their hearts, and who want to see this country rise to prosperity and greatness in the full enjoyment of peace and harmony, I claim for both races in Canada the same political reciprocity that King Albert promised the Walloons and the Flemish on his return to Belgium last November.
'Let the Union Government which insists on surviving the war at least accomplish deeds of life and not of death. Let the Government beware of dishonouring the name of Canada by depriving citizens of foreign extraction, whom we ourselves brought here at great expense, of rights which were promised and given them. Let us clean, or rather let us disinfect our statutes of that iniquitous measure the War Time Elections Act, and not show more severity than France or the United States towards citizens of enemy origin. So long as these folks remain peaceful citizens, respectable, industrious and law-abiding we cannot, without forfeiting our honour, repudiate the rights we granted them when we admitted them to British citizenship.
Let the Union Government give millions to the provinces for the building of great national highways, for the development of technical education, which forms the backbone of our industrial progress and our commercial expansion, for organizing hygiene and sanitation throughout the country, for agriculture; I am in favour of all that; but these grants should be made on a just basis, on the basis of population, and the distribution of the grants should be left to the autonomous government of each province.
Let the Government think of the people and stop being the protector of our millionaires, and this latter to .such an extent that one of the Government's own friends was able to say that it belonged to Mr. Flavelle.
Let the Government see to it that the consumer is protected and this can be done without working any harm to our industries, if the tariff is lowered on all the necessaries of life and prices are fixed in such a way as to prevent the profiteers from piling up fortunes out of all reason.
Let the Government proceed to make a more equitable distribution of the taxes, so that the rich man and not the poor man will pay most. Let it show the greatest solicitude for our glorious soldiers who have emblazoned the name of Canada on the battlefields of Europe, let it show as much interest in the humblest of them as in the officers; let. it shelter from misery our wounded and their families and furnish steady employment to the others, by reinstating them in their old positions, by settling them on the land or by utilizing their labour on works of national importance.
Let the Government be generous and just to all military defaulters; most of them are farmers who had been promised exemption and were shamefully deceived by the Government. Let the Government forgive; it has itself so much to be forgiven.
I fear, Mr. Speaker, that ail this cannot be accomplished under the present Government which instead of giving its attention to matters of what we term reconstruction, seems to be entirely preoccupied with holding together its own structure which threatens to fall apart. We perceive the outer sign which permits us to force the tumbling into a heap of this patched up edifice. That is what is causing such great anxiety to the Government and that is what makes us feel hopeful; for the sooner this mongrel union, which will go down in history under the mocking title of "unionism," has been sundered, the better it will be for the people of this country who will then choose administrators and legislators more respectful of our Constitution, more jealous of the rights of all our citizens, and more devoted to the real interest of this dear land of ours.
Mr. JOHN A. MAHARG (Maple Creek): Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the discussion on the question that is now before the House, I would like, on behalf of the interests that I largely represent, as well as on my own behalf, to say a word or two in regard to the passing of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We in the West owe very much to our departed friend, much more than I would attempt at this time to enumerate. About the time of his taking up the reins of office here in 1896, the West was in a very bad condition, the agriculturists of Western Canada being, in so far as the marketing of their products was concerned, almost entirely in the hands of possibly one of the largest and most gigantic combines. I refer to the grain combine. It is not necessary to go into the details; suffice it to say that we had to take just



what they saw fit to give us. As there was no machinery whatever of a Federal character to deal with such conditions, we appealed to the late Prime Minister for redress, and we received it in a very great measure. Whatever else there may be on which we may differ, there is at least one warm spot that will always remain for Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the hearts of the agriculturists of Western Canada. We feel that he was indeed a great and noble person; his aim in life was to relieve the oppressed, and I think I can say with all sincerity that the life of our departed friend was largely devoted to this sublime object. If the words of the Master be true,- as I believe,-then, I am sure that the dead Liberal chieftain's cup has been an overflowing one in this world and Will continue as such in the great beyond.
Before touching on the speech from the Throne, I would like to refer to one or two of the remarks made by the hon. member
for iShelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in this House.
I am sorry the hon. gentleman (Mr, Fielding) is not in his seat, not that I have any very serious criticism to make, for with a great deal that he said I am thoroughly in accord; but there are one or two points I should like to touch on, and the first point is with reference to the presence overseas of certain ministers of the Crown. I am not in a position to say whether it is necessary for them all to be there at the present time, but I have no hesitation whatever in saying that, so far as the presence overseas of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Boiden) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is concerned, there never was a time in the history of Canada when they were more required over there than now. I had the pleasure of being in England a couple of months ago, and conditions there and on the Continent are such that unless we have the very best possible representation overseas conditions in Canada within twelve months will be very far from favourable. I will refer to this matter later when dealing with the chief product of Western Canada -our grain.
I also wish to criticise the remarks of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's , with reference to the "word of a Canadian'' not standing for very much when certain legislation passed by this Parliament some time ago is taken into consideration. With all due respect for his opinion, I can cite a case where we would have suffered much greater humiliation by breaking our word
[Mr. Maharg'.l
than on the occasion my hon. friend had in mind. Ever since our boys have been going to the war, what promise have we made to them? From one end of Canada to the other the parting word has been: "We will see you through boys, we will back you up to the last man and the last dollar.'' As to that there was no division of opinion throughout this country. And I ask, what value would be placed on our word now if we in this House had said, as some have said: "Canada has done enough for the present; let other countries who have not done their share have their way for a while." If this Parliament had said that, the word of a Canadian, the word of the Canadian people might truly have been lightly thought of; if we had not taken the stand we did I shudder to think of the criticism that would have been levelled at us by the few Canadian soldiers who would have returned. I for one would have hung my head in shame when they came back, and I am sure many others would have done the same.
The hon. member (Mr. Fielding) also gave some advice to the farmers of Western Canada. He advised them to join up with one or the other of the two great political parties in this country, but he would not undertake to say which party they should join. Surely, the hon. member, with his long political experience, was a little unreasonable in leaving the selection to agriculturists without any political experience whatever, especially seeing that for the time being he had decided to stay in a position from which he could jump to one side of the fence or the other. For his information and for the information of the House I might say that the farmers of Western Canada have absolutely no intention,-and I doubt if they will have for some considerable time-of tying themselves up to either one of the two great political parties we knew in this country in the past. Neither do I think they are going to tie themselves up definitely to the Unionist party, at this particular time. They do not wish to fetter themselves in any way; they are determined to have absolute freedom so far as action in this House is concerned.
A representative of . the press has described it as a case of choosing between the sheep and the goats. That should be an easy decision to make under ordinary circumstances, for certainly the western farmers do not want to link themselves up with the goats whichever they may be. and as the Good Book tells us to beware of

wolves in sheep's clothing, we do not like to tie ourselves up with the sheep, even supposing we were able to distinguish them from the goats at the present time.
With the greater portion of the speech of His Excellency the Governor General, and particularly with that part referring to the war having been brought to a successful conclusion, I am in hearty accord. But with other parts of the speech I do not entirely agree. I think the first legislation mentioned is the new Franchise Act that will be brought down. I do not know just what is in the minds of the Government, but I will say this much: unless the new Act makes radical changes in the Act on which the last election was fought, it will be severely criticised so far as Western Canada is concerned. I do not say that I disapprove entirely of the War-time Elections Act, but it has certain features which the West did not like, and I trust the Government will give due consideration to that.
With regard to highways, although I should undoubtedly like to see good highways, I am thoroughly convinced that there are other things which We need more at this moment than highways, or what might be termed automobile roads. A national highway has been spoken of. To attempt to build such a highway at this time would in my opinion be utter folly, and I am convinced that there are many other works which should first be undertaken, and which would prove much more valuable and provide an equal amount of employment, and perhaps more congenial employment. Take, for instance, our railways. The amount of money which the Government purposes setting aside for distribution, over a number of years, in the building of highways, would go a long way towards giving relief in the way of railway facilities to certain districts in Western Canada which have been waiting patiently for it for the last seven or eight, and, in some cases, ten or even twelve years.
The next matter referred to in the Address is the question of housing. Now, if it is the intention of the Government to confine the proposed assistance to returned men, I have nothing whatever to say in opposition to it. I entirely agree with any proposal that aims at assisting those who are now seeking homes, and who have been married overseas. I think we should give such men every possible assistance in securing homes. But if it is the intention that this assistance shall be general, for any and every one in the country, then I would certainly object very seriously. I do
m
not think that such a thing would be proper. We, in Canada, should surely be in sufficiently good circumstances to be able to look after our domestic wants,-that is, those of us who have remained at home during the war. Employment has been abundant, wages have been, to say the least, fair, and in some cases more than fair; and it seems to me that those desiring accommodation should be in a position to obtain their own requirements, if they have not been overseas. The matter of assisting the returned soldier is one that, in my opinion, should be given special consideration. The plan under which the Gov-" ernment are now working is in some respects very good. In other respects I do not think it goes far enough. Some three or four years ago I outlined what I thought to be a better plan, and the Government has adopted my suggestion practically in its entirety, but with this exception, that they are leaving the returned soldier entirely at the mercy of the land speculator, at least so far as Western Canada is concerned. As far as I can ascertain, there is no provision made for dealing with those who purchased land in that part of the country years and years ago, who gave for it a mere pittance, and who are now holding it at what, to my mind, are exorbitant and unreasonable prices; at all events when it is offered to the returned soldiers. This Government might very well indeed devote its attention to some measure whereby the present Soldiers' Settlement Board, or some other board, could step in when they considered prices were exorbitant, and act as arbitrator between the returned soldiers and those holding the land.
Now, I come to the question of prohibition. I do not' think we need worry very much about that. I feel that the Government must surely be convinced that the people of Canada have intimated very unequivocally to them their opinion on this matter. There is one argument,-indeed,
I might term it a campaign,-that is being used to defeat the interests of prohibition in Canada. This argument came to my notice on different occasions. It is an argument which is being urged by those who are anxious to have the prohibition law, as they say, " eased up just a little bit." They contend that the soldiers want beer; that they have been accustomed to getting it overseas and will demand it on their return. Well, were I a returned soldier 1 would regard such a statement in the light of an insult. I cannot for one moment think that the boys who have been "over there" fighting all this time for our protection,

will come back and lend their assistance to any attempt that may be made to restore in this country a demon which no less a personage that the Prime Minister of Great Britain said was a greater enemy to England than the Germans themselves. I repeat, Sir, I cannot for one moment think that those boys have anything like that in their minds at all.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I shall mention some of the things that are not contained in the Address of His Excellency, and which are of considerable interest, at least so far as our part of the Dominion is concerned. I have learned much since coming here, and I have discovered that the gulf that existed between the East and the West is now in some respects very largely bridged; and that there is a feeling, which is apparently steadily growing, in favour of a greater degree of freedom in relation to matters of fiscal policy. We discern it on all sides. It appears in very unexpected quarters; and personally I think that this Government would be wise to heed it. At the present time, owing to some misconceptions as to what the Western agriculturists, as well as those of Eastern Canada, have been asking for, I would request the privilege of placing on Hansard the entire platform as propounded by the Canadian Council of Agriculture. It has never before been placed in Hansard. The first section of our platform is this:
1.	-A League of Nations as an international organization to give permanence to the world's peace by removing old causes of conflict.
2.	-We believe that the further development of the British Empire should be sought along the lines of partnership between nations free and equal, under the present governmental system of British constitutional authority. We are strongly opposed to any attempt to centralize imperial control. Any attempt to set up an independent authority with power to bind the Dominions, whether this authority be termed parliament, council or cabinet, would hamper the growth of responsible and informed democracy in the Dominions.
The Tariff.
3.	-Whereas Canada is now confronted with a huge national war debt and other greatly increased financial obligations, which can be most readily and effectively reduced by the development of our natural resources, chief of which is agricultural lands;
And whereas it is desirable that an agricultural career should be made attractive to our returned soldiers and the large anticipated immigration, and owing to the fact that this can best be accomplished by the development of a national policy which will reduce to a minimum the cost of living and the cost of production;
And whereas the war has revealed the amazing financial strength of Great Britain, which has enabled her to finance, not only her own part in the struggle, but also to assist

in financing her Allies to the extent of hundreds of millions of pounds, this enviable position being due to the free trade policy which has enabled her to draw her supplies freely from every quarter of the globe and consequently to undersell her competitors on the world's markets, and because this policy has not only been profitable to Great Britain, but has greatly strengthened the bonds of Empire by facilitating trade between the Motherland and her overseas dominions-we believe that the best interests of the Empire and of Canada would be served by reciprocal action on the part of Canada through gradual reductions of the tariff on British imports, having for its object closer union and a better understanding between Canada and the Motherland and at the same time bring about a great reduction in the cost of living to our Canadian people.
Posters Combines.
And whereas the Protective Tariff has fostered combines, trusts, and "gentlemen's agreements'' in almost every line of Canadian industrial enterprise, by means of which the people of Canada-both urban and rural-have been shamefully exploited through the elimination of competition, the ruination of many of our smaller industries and the advancement of prices on practically all manufactured goods to the full extent permitted by the tariff;
And whereas agriculture-the basic industry upon which the success of all other industries primarily depends:-is unduly handicapped throughout Canada as shown by the declining rural population in both Eastern and Western Canada, due largely to the greatly increased cost of agricultural implements and machinery, clothing, boots and shoes, building material and practically everything the farmer has to buy, caused by the Protective Tariff, so that it is becoming impossible for farmers generally, under normal conditions, to carry on farming operations profitably;
And whereas the Protective Tariff is the most wasteful and costly method ever designed for raising national revenue, because for every dollar obtained thereby for the public treasury at least three dollars pass into the pockets of the protected interests, thereby building up a privileged class at the expense of the masses, thus making the rich richer and the poor poorer;
And whereas the Protective Tariff has been and is a chief corrupting influence in our national life because the protected interests in order to maintain their unjust privileges have contributed lavishly to political and campaign funds, thus encouraging both political parties to look to them for support, thereby lowering the standard of public morality.
Definite Tariff Demands.
Therefore be it resolved that the Canadian Council of Agriculture, representing the organized farmers of Canada, urges that, as a means of remedying these evils and bringing about much needed social and economic reforms, our tariff laws should be amended as follows:-
(a)	By an immediate and substantial allround reduction of the customs- tariff.
(b)	By reducing the customs duty on goods imported from Great Britain to one-half the rates charged under the general tariff, and that further gradual, uniform reductions be made in the remaining tariff on British imports that will ensure complete Free Trade

between Great Britain and Canada in five years.
(c)	That the Reciprocity Agreement of 1911, which still remains on the United State statute books, be accepted by the Parliament of Canada.
(d)	That all foodstuff not included in the Reciprocity Agreement be placed on the free list.
(e)	That agricultural implements, farm machinery, vehicles, fertilizers, coal, lumber, cement, illuminating fuel and lubricating oils be placed on the free list, and that all raw materials and machinery used in their manufacture also be placed on the free list.
(f)	That all tariff concessions granted to other countries be immediately extended to Great Britain.
(g)	That all corporations engaged in the manufacture of products protected by the customs tariff be obliged to publish annually comprehensive and accurate statements of their earnings.
(h)	That every claim for tariff protection by any industry should be heard publicly before a special committee of Parliament.
Taxation Proposals.
4.	-As these tariff reductions may very considerably reduce the national revenue from that source, the Canadian Council of Agriculture would recommend that, in order to provide the necessary additional revenue for carrying on the Government of the country and for the bearing of the cost of the war, direct taxation be imposed in the following manner:-
(a)	By a direct tax on unimproved land values, including all natural resources.
(b)	By a graduated personal income tax.
(c)	By a graduated inheritance tax on large estates.
(d)	By a graduated income tax on the profits of corporations.
(e)	That in levying and collecting the business profits tax the Dominion Government should insist that it be absolutely upon the basis of the actual cash invested in the business and that no considerations be allowed for what is popularly known as watered stock.
(f)	That no more natural resources be alienated from the Crown, but brought into use only under short-term leases, in which the interests of the public shall be properly safeguarded, such leases to be granted only by public auction.
The Returned Soldier.
5.	-With regard to the returned soldier we urge:-
(a)	That it is the recognized duty of Canada tc exercise all due diligence for the future well-being of the returned soldier and his dependents.
(b)	That demobilization should take place only after return to Canada.
(c)	That first selection for return and demobilization should be made in the order of length of service of those who have definite occupations awaiting them or have other assured means of support, preference being given first to married men and then to the relative need of industries, with care to insure so far as possible the discharge of farmers in time for the opening of spring work upon the land.
(d)	That general demobilization should be gradual, aiming at the discharge of men only as it is found possible to secure steady employment.
(e)	It is highly desirable that if physically fit discharged men should endeavour to return to their former occupation, employers should be urged to reinstate such men in their former positions wherever possible.
(f)	That vocational training should be confined to those who while in the service have become unfitted for their former occupation.
tg) That provision should be made for insurance at the public expense of unpensioned men who have become undesirable insurance risks while in the service.
(h) That facilities should be provided at the public expense that will enable returned soldiers to settle upon farming land when by training or experience they are qualified to do. so.
6.	-We recognize the very serious problem confronting labour in urban industry resulting from the cessation of war, and we urge that every means economically feasible and practicable should be used by federal, provincial and municipal authorities in relieving unemployment in the cities and towns; and, further, recommend the adoption of the principle of co-operation as the guiding spirit in the future relations between employer and employees- between capital and labour.
Land Settlement.
7.	-A land settlement scheme based on a regulating influence in the selling price of land. Owners of idle areas should be obliged to file a selling price on their lands, that price also to be regarded as an assessable value for purposes of taxation.
8.	-Extension of co-operative agencies in agriculture to cover the whole field of marketing, including arrangements with consumers' societies for the supplying of foodstuffs at the lowest rates and with the minimum of middleman handling.
9.	-Public ownership and control of railway, water and aerial transportation, telephone, telegraph and express systems, all projects in the development of natural power, and of the coal mining industry.
Other Democratic Reforms.
10.	-To bring about a greater measure of democracy in government, we recommend:-
(a)	The immediate repeal of the War Time
Elections' Act.	[DOT]
(b)	The discontinuance of the practice of conferring titles upon citizens of Canada.
(c)	The reform of the federal Senate.
(d)	An immediate check upon the growth of government by order in council, and increased responsibility of individual members of parliament in all legislation.
(e)	The complete abolition of the patronage system.
(f)	The publication of contributions and expenditures both before and after election campaigns.
(g)	The removal -of press censorship upon the restoration of peace and the immediate restoration of the rights of free speech.
(h)	The setting forth by daily newspapers and periodical publications, of the facts of their ownership and control.
(i)	Proportional representation.
(j)	The establishment of measures of direct legislation through the initiative referendum and recall.
(k)	The opening of seats in Parliament to women on the same terms as men.

That, Mr. Speaker, in substance is the programme of the Western agriculturist. I might go so far as to say that it is the programme of the agriculturists of Eastern Canada also. I might go even further and say that those who have been the most advanced in the demand for tariff concessions have been the organized agriculturist body of the province of Ontario, and they have gone further in their demands than have the organized agriculturists of Western Canada. Things are moving, and it will be well, indeed, not only for the members of the Government, but for the members of this House to keep their ears very close to the ground. There is a feeling of discontent abroad which is not by any means confined to the agriculturist; the consumer is probably just a little more agitated over present conditions than even the agriculturist. That is being manifested very clearly in a great many quarters, and even from some unexpected directions, so that I think it behooves us all to give serious consideration to this matter during the present session in order that we may possibly avoid serious consequences before Parliament might have an opportunity of meeting again.
I am not at present going to enter into any argument about the tariff, because this is not the proper time to do so-when the Budget is brought down ample opportunity will be afforded for full discussion-but I would just say, for the benefit of those entrusted with the framing of that Budget, that we expect something of a rather generous nature in .so far as the reduction of the tariff is concerned. As intimated last session by myself, we have been keeping close watch on the trend of events, and we have been keeping our ear to the ground. Hon. gentlemen will remember that I stated then that we were prepared to give the Union Government every opportunity to make good.
The reason advanced last session for not interfering with the tariff was the seriousness of the war situation. We agreed with , that to a man. Not a Western member that I know of raised the slightest objection to passing that issue over until another session at least, and possibly until the actual conclusion of the war, that is, the actual fighting. Now the war is over in so far as the fighting is concerned. We expect that within a very short time the peace treaty will have been concluded and signed, so that we shall know where we are at. We have come back again this session, and the request now made is that we leave the tariff question in abeyance during the period of

reconstruction. Mr. Speaker, that is going just a little too far; that is asking just a little too much; the request is entirely too indefinite. There are those who might endeavour

I will not say that they would- to have us believe that reconstruction will be going on when the next session meets. I do not doubt but that it will, for reconstruction will take some considerable time; it depends entirely upon the attitude of the people towards reconstruction work. A Reconstruction Association has been formed in Eastern Canada they were very anxious to get Western Canada linked up with them- and they had their representatives ~out through the West. We attended some of the gatherings, addressed by those gentlemen, and listened to their speeches, but it is the same old method that has been adopted. They, too, according to their spokesmen, have an Eastern and Western method of campaigning. One of their officials-and a very prominent one I may say-when speaking in a manufacturing town in Eastern Canada, the town of Galt, I believe it was, is reported as having said that the tariff was a dead issue, it was as musty as the tombs of Egypt, and should not, under any consideration, be resurrected; it should be left there. That same gentleman came West. He visited my home town and addressed the Canadian Club there. I had the pleasure of listening to his address, but in so far as the tariff was concerned the mustiness had all disappeared-the issue had been resurrected from the tombs of Egypt very hurriedly and had been transplanted to Western Canada, for his words there were that the tariff was quite a live issue and must be dealt with. "But," this gentleman said, "I do not say that there should be an upward revision of the tariff at all;" he took very good care; however, not to intimate that there would be a possibility of a downward revision in so far as they were concerned; he kept that very much under his hat. That kind of talk will not satisfy Western Canada.
Surely we can deal with this tariff issue on its merits, give it the same position in the East as it holds in the West, and talk in exactly the same way to those who may be anxious to have it maintained as to those who are anxious to have it revised downward. And there is another attitude that has been displayed in the House which I deprecate very much. I noticed the other day that when some references were made to the reduction of the tariff, and one Western gentleman was waxing quite eloquent in speaking of the subject, an hon. gentleman from Eastern Canada

jumped up very indignantly and strutted out of the Chamber, using expressions in regard to my friend's arguments that I would not care to use on the floor of the House, as I think they would be pronounced unparliamentary, and you, Mr. Speaker, would be quite within your jurisdiction in asking for a retraction of them. If that is the attitude some people in Eastern Canada are going to take against the arguments of the West, well and good, but we had all hoped there would be a different spirit displayed. Let me say that the West is not one of those com-munitiqs of people that cannot at least attempt, and I think fairly well, to distinguish and appreciate the other man's point of view. We have never taken the attitude that we are absolutely right, that we invariably have got to have exactly what we ask for; but we would like the manufacturers, who have been asking us to postpone tariff reduction from one year to another, to at least give us an idea of what we might expect from them even if we did agree to postpone it for another year.. But they vouchsafe no information; they simply ask us to come back a year later when doubtless we will be alsked to postpone consideration again for some other reason.
How, as I have already stated, in so far as Western Canada is concerned, we have got to the end of our tether, and for the benefit of the manufacturers I want to make a statement to the House, and it is this: I may preface it by stating the position four or five years ago, when this matter came up in the House. There was a strong agitation in the West at that time for tariff reduction, and there was just as strong opposition to it in the East. The press was inflamed with arguments and abuse of the western farmer by eastern interests. Then a movement was started in the West in the way of a campaign to persuade all our western agriculturists to buy only imported articles. Now, that was just at the bursting point, as it were; and a few representatives of agriculture in the West counselled these people at least to stay their hand in that respect, which they did.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was attempting, for the benefit of the Manufacturers' Association, to describe a situation that was almost sure to arise unless something was
done along <the lines -I had suggested in regard to the tariff. I was endeavouring to describe the acute feeling in favour of tariff reduction versus protection that existed in Western Canada some few years ago. I had just started to outline a movement that was taking form there, the result of which would have been that practically no articles of Canadian manufacture would have been purchased throughout Western Canada. As I intimated, some of the leaders in the movement thought this would be unwise and, their counsel prevailing, no action was taken at that time. The matter had come before our organized bodies in a very concrete form, and everything pointed towards definite action being taken, but the feeling was allayed for the time being. Feeling is, however, running a little high again, and I have no doubt that a similar situation will arise in the future. Should that be the case, none of the leaders would be able to stem the tide. I am not saying this for purely selfish reasons. Under present conditions we have to have a revenue, and if the Government decides to maintain the present policy of raising the major proportion of its revenue by indirect taxation by means of a tariff, then there is only one thing for us as patriotic citizens to do, and that is to buy our requirements in such a way that the revenue derived from that source will go into the treasury of the country and not be divided between the treasury and those whom the tariff is protecting. We shall be very sorry to see such a condition of affairs arise. We are just as anxious as the manufacturers themselves that they shall continue to prosper and increase their output. In fact, from the attitude the manufacturers assume, I think we are a little more anxious for them to increase their output than they are themselves. We are supported in our views not only in the West but in the East, and what I have described is the feeling not merely of the agriculturists of the West but of almost the entire population of the West. I do not think there is in Western Canada a newspaper that does not support the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. The Legislature of Saskatchewan, at a recent session, unanimously passed a resolution endorsing these views and asking for tariff reduction. Although that assembly is composed of persons on both sides of politics, there is no division in that regard. Returned soldiers in Western Canada with whom I have been speaking are in favour of those principles. I hold in my hand a letter from a returned soldier who has undergone eight

or ten operations resulting from his wounds, but who has still enough pluck to go back on to the land and endeavour to work out his own destiny. This is a quotation from his letter:
What your association is fighting for will benefit thousands of soldiers who go on the land.
It is the association of farmers to which he refers. This is not class legislation so far as the West is concerned.
The West made Union Government possible. Why did the West support Union Government - almost unanimously? In the province from which I come Union Government could not have received stronger support than it did. Out of seven or eight acclamations of Unionist candidates throughout all of Canada, four came from Saskatchewan. There was not in that province a single Unionist member who did not receive a very large majority, and, taking into consideration the vote polled, Union Government got on the average, in that province, the largest majorities received anywhere in Canada. I may isay further that Saskatchewan returned a complete list of Unionist members. Why did the people of Saskatchewan do that? I suppose we have in that province the largest association of agriculturists in the world, banded together in one body. We have some fourteen or fifteen hundred distinct entities in that one organization, and so far as their actions are concerned they are entirely autonomous. It is probably as educative a body as can foe found anywhere. Any hon, member who has been fortunate enough to attend our conventions at which we have from fifteen hundred to two thousand delegates, will realize that those people are trying at least to inform themselves. They take this attitude: We have listened to promises long enough; we have, if I may use the phrase, seen the buck passed from one side to the other; we have seen in this Parliament, when one side was in power, the other side would immediately bring up something of special interest to Western Canada. The former Liberal Government, for instance, went into power on the distinct promise that they were going to have a tariff for revenue only, and the West expected great things from them. But when a resolution came from the other side of the House asking for radical reductions in the tariff on agricultural implements, our Liberal friends did not see fit to grant them. The same gentleman who moved the resolution has been on the treasury benches now for a considerable time, but he has not gone out
[iMr. Maharg. ]
of his way to bring about that reduction although he has a better opportunity to do so. The West has come to the conclusion that there is no use depending on preelection promises; that there must be something more than that. The reason why the West supported Union Government is because Union Government had been bold enough to do something; they had taken a stand; they said: We are going to furnish sufficient recruits to keep our forces at the front right up to strength. That was doing something that appealed to the people of the West. They said: A Government that has grit enough to take such a stand regardless of consequences is the Government to which we want to give an opportunity to carry on a little further. The Union Government carried out their pledges to the letter, and when the big push came, as it did last August, the forces of Canada were second to none on the Western front. It is recognized that they were the best disciplined, best equipped troops on the field, with every battalion right up to strength, and with a strong reserve, and that they were ready to go into action at any moment.
The Union Government carried out its pledges. That appealed to the West, and the West is prepared to support this Union Government again if it will take the same bold stand in our domestic affairs as it took with regard to our soldiers on the western front. The Government's policy then was no mythical thing floating in the air; it was nailed down in legislation. It is no use for any Government, whether it be Unionist or something else, to appeal to Western Canada again until it has demonstrated its sincerity by taking action.
The West has been spoken of sometimes as unpatriotic, and our schools have been held up to ridicule by some Eastern journals in a very unfair way. I remember that during the last provincial election in Saskatchewan there seemed to be more anxiety in some parts of the East than there was in Saskatchewan itself. A friend of mine in Ontario, for instance, sent me copies of a certain paper which pointed out the condition in which our schools were supposed to be, and told us we were educating our children to be non-Canadians and such stuff as that. Just to show the patriotic feeling amongst the school children of Saskatchewan let me give one illustration-* and I could give several. During the war an organization was formed to raise funds for a patriotic purpose from the school children throughout the entire Dominion. The appeal was made to

probably twenty millions. Now, Serbia has no food of any kind. Her people are merely living from hand to mouth, and must be supplied from extraneous sources. Their producing possibilities are almost nil, as the country has been completedy denuded of all equipment in practically every direction, being destitute of even seed to sow. Rumania is in the same position, while alien countries are in as bad a plight. Germany, with her very large population, was not a considerable importer of wheat. Although she consumes a great deal of cereals, of about 400,000,000 bushels consumed she did not import more than about 70,000,000 bushels of wheat, but she was a large producer of rye, Which took the place of wheat. Now we are given to understand that Germany's producing powers are practically exhausted, so that she may be compelled to import large quantities of grain. With all those countries in that condition, with not only transportation and distribution facilities to be secured, but credits to be provided, I believe that Canada will have to provide credits for a very large amount of her exports to them. Therefore, the people of Canada must arrange matters to meet these circumstances, if they are going to dispose of their products. Possibly we could secure credit elsewhere. We might secure it from the United States, and probably that would be satisfactory; but in view of rumours which are current overseas and in Canada,
I think the safest course for the Dominion to take is to provide those credits herself, so that there may be no possibility of restrictions in any shape or form interfering with the export of her products. I am not in a position to say definitely that then have been restrictions, hut the rumours one hears from time to time might indicate that there has been some difficulty in that direction.
About the beginning of January there was quite a large surplus of wheat in the world. The United States had about 300,000,000 bushels, while India, Argentina, and Australia had probably an equal amount amongst them. But what do we find today? These stocks, so far as the United States is concerned, are going very quickly. At all events, the millers are now offering a premium over the fixed prices to secure this wheat for their mills. That must surely be an indication, that the stocks of wheat, so far at least as the United States is concerned, are in demand; otherwise the millers would not be offering a premium for the wheat. Now, if the European conditions are as I have outlined them, there will be a heavy demand for cereals from this

country. The United States at the beginning of the year was reported as having sown the largest acreage of wheat in its history. Conditions were almost perfect, and it was thought that there would be a tremendous surplus, of wheat on hand when the United States crop should be harvested next year. Well, there may be, but one cannot estimate the crop six months before it is harvested. We might just as well try to figure out the crop of Western. Canada, the seed of which is still in the granaries, as to figure out the crop of fall wheat that has been sown in the fall. So that we do not know, and nobody can tell, just what the situation will be, but personally I am convinced that if a satisfactory peace can be arrived at; if conditions can be restored to anything like normal in those countries that I have just mentioned; if transportation facilities can be provided, with an organized government of some form to carry on the distribution- and if credit is forthcoming, we will find a ready market for all of our wheat and our other agricultural, products as well. But it will be necessary for this Government to exert every effort. I am certain that our representatives overseas are working on that. They were doing so-at least some of them-some months ago, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has no holiday, I can assure you, Sir. He is as busy a man as can be found anywhere. I had not the pleasure of meeting the Prime Minister. He was in Paris at that time, but I met the Minister ol Trade and Commerce on different occasions, and he assuredly will have all he can do for some time to come, and instead of criticisms being directed at those gentlemen, they should be given every encouragement in order that they may assist in an attempt to remedy conditions to permit of a free export of our products into those countries.
This brings me to the question of what is going to be done with the wheat crop of Western Canada. Different suggestions have been made. There is a request from one of the provinces that the price of wheat should be fixed. I will not say at this stage whether that is a proper thing to do or not, but one thing I will say, and that is, that if we are going to have a stabilized business industry in Canada during the next wheat season from August or September on something musit be done.
I have outlined to you the difficulty of disposing of our grain quickly. It is going to take us the entire crop year to dispose of it. We will not be able to rush it out. Storage facilities will not he available for

it should we have a fair average crop. Something will have to be done to stabilize the price which will be paid for that grain. If it is thrown open to the world, and open to speculation, and an assurance of equal treatment is not guaranteed for the entire year, the market will simply be glutted early in the season, the price will be forced down to the lowest level, and after all the storage has been occupied and all the money of the country has been invested in wheat, the price will go up and neither the producer nor the consumer will get a square deal. The consumer will have to pay the high price and the producer will have to* take the low' price. This Government has got to do something; whether it be to fix the price or to absolutely prohibit speculation, something must be done. I think there is only one way to do it and that is by fixing the price. It is a very difficult matter to prevent speculation in the handling of grain. The only successful remedy we have found for it has been the fixing of the price.
With all due respect to the other two provinces, they are not as anxious for a fixed price as we are in Saskatchewan. Their interests differ from ours. They are not the wheat-growing provinces that Saskatchewan is. Our province produces more wheat than all the re^t of Canada combined. Consequently, we are very much interested in what is going to be done with wheat. Manitoba has a more varied production in the matter of coarse grains and stock, while from 75 to 80 per cent of the agriculturists of Saskatchewan produce wheat. Almost the entire balance is divided between oats, wheat, and some stock.
Some arrangement will have to be entered into if you are going to stabilize the industry because its effect will be far reaching and will not be confined to agriculture. It will go all the way down through the line to the consumer in more ways than one. It will have an effect on production in urban centres in the same way 'that it will have throughout the country. If something is not done to stabilize this industry, to give some kind of a guarantee that all who produce wheat are going to receive fair and equal treatment, the area that will be sown to wheat will be decreased to an alarming extent. I have met men-yes, scores of them-who have said that unless something is done to guarantee them a fair return they will not under any circumstances seed anywhere the amount of ground they had prepared for seeding. Seed is very expensive; it costs something to seed in Western Canada and the old saying that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush is going to appeal very forcibly to those people before they are going to spend from ?4 to $5 an acre to provide seed for this land.
I want to go back again to the criticism of the farmers of the West that I have heard since 1 have come down here. I will give one illustration. I have been told: "You fellows come down here to Ottawa with your seal skin coats and your fur-lined coats (and all that kind of stuff); the West must be rolling in wealth." You have only to look at tire blue books which are available to everybody to be able to reckon for yourself what the average income has been for western farmers from Winnipeg to the Rocky Mountains. True, we had a bumper crop in 1915 almost all over the entire West. What was the result with regard to prices? While we had a jumper crop, prices fell on the market and it is doubtful if there was any profit at all in the production of the crop. In 1914 there was practically a crop failure in Western Canada. Eastern industry felt it very keenly.
' Unemployment existed all over the country, soup kitchens were established everywhere and provincial governments were loaning money to different municipalities to provide employment. I remember that in our own little city thousands of dollars were expended in crushing stone in the hope that it might be used some day for pavements just simply to give employment as a consequence of the 1914 crop having been almost an entire failure in Western Canada.
If there was a little profit in the 1915 crop, which there, was, and I am not arguing that there was not, it was largely taken up, and in some cases entirely taken up in meeting the deficit of 1914. What has been the result since 1915?-very moderate crops on the average and in large areas almost total failure. Take Saskatchewan as an illustration. Our entire exportable surplus of wheat from the last crop is about 65,000,000 bushels or, say, 70,000,000 bushels. The proportion of that from Saskatchewan, put it at one-half, would be in the neighbourhood of 35,000,000 bushels. We have in that province roughly speaking 120,000 or 125,000 farmers. We will say that 25,000 farmers were producers of other grain; that is a very liberal estimate. We will take 100,000 was exported. The proceeds of these 35,000,000 bushels of Saskatchewan grain that was exported. The proceeds of those 35,000,000 bushels, providing it was all high

grade grain, none of it less than No. 2, would be $70,000,000, roughly speaking. It might average $2 per bushel but no more provided it was high grade grain. Therefore, you have $70,000,000 distributed amongst 100,000 people. What does that mean? That is the gross amount and you can figure it out for yourself. That would only give each man a gross revenue of $700. Out of that he has to take his entire expenses.
