In the first place he would have in the neighbourhood of $500 or $600 to pay for labour, allowing only one man to each individual farmer, he would have to pay from $60 to $80 and if he employed a married couple he would have to pay from $100 to $125 per month. At the very start he has to pay from $600 to $700 for labour and that would leave him about $900 to take care of all his other expenses. I could go on and give you the actual expenses that this man had to pay, and show you that the average farmer of the province of Saskatchewan did not make one single dollar last year. Indeed, I doubt if he broke even. You have only got to take the actual figures for that statement. You do not need to take my word at all, go to the blue books and find it for yourselves. The Conditions in the two years previous were very little better. So that in so far as the farmers of Western Canada are concerned, they have not been making money out of the war. As far as Eastern Canada is concerned, the representatives of the Eastern agriculturists are more familiar with the situation here, and can deal with it themselves. The condition with respect to the West is this: That up to the outbreak of the war, agriculture in Western Canada was at a very low ebb. The tide was flowing the other way; instead of increasing numbers engaging in agriculture, the population was decreasing. There is no question about that; any man who was in Western Canada and was familiar with the conditions, knows that the number of people living on the land was decreasing-they were moving out of the country right along. The war has helped to hold them. There was the prospect at least of securing a good crop and a good price for their grain. They lived in hopes of securing a good crop, and they are still there and prepared for another trial-at least, practically ninety or ninety-five per cent of them are still there. I do not think more than five or ten per cent had migrated from the land; they are prepared to try it again providing they will get at least some return for what they produce. I have placed these facts before the

Government and the House in order to show that unless something is done in regard to the marketing of our crop next year, the sowing of an increased acreage in Canada next year need not be looked for, but on the contrary, the result will be much the other way.
Is there any remedy to he found in shipping to the United States?
We are prohibited from shipping there now.
But ordinarily the market there is open?
It will be open on one condition, and that is if the production of the United States is below their requirements.
Who shut you out?

The United States Government, on account of the war conditions. Now they have got an abundance of wheat there for themselves, the price of which is guaranteed by the Government, and they are not going to purchase the surplus wheat of Canada, and take a chance of disposing of it again. They have got sufficient wheat of their own to look after, without taking ours.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say in conclusion that Western Canada is watching this Government very closely. It is also watching this House, and individual members of the House very closely, and unless something is done,-I want to be very clear and emphatic in this statement,-to attempt to remedy conditions in so far as the West is concerned, you will at least have a number of by-elections on your hands before this House meets again next session.

Mr. Speaker, a born citizen of Quebec city cannot let the occasion pass without paying a last tribute to the memory of our late leader, the member for the electoral division of Quebec East, J3ir Wilfrid Laurier.
To speak on behalf of electors, whose confidence and admiration in Sir Wilfrid Laurier have never faltered, my first impression was to use the French language. It is the language that Sir Wilfrid loved the most; it is the language he spoke at home, it is the language spoken by every one of his former electors. In speaking French I would feel more at ease, hut I realize that in making use of the English language, it may demonstrate that with very little effort and good will, one can be made to speak both languages.

/I have come to the conclusion that in being courteous to the majority in this House, I am but following the example of my revered leader. If, Sir, at this time, the whole country is in mourning, no part of Canada regrets more the loss of this illustrious statesman than the electoral division of Quebec East. Sir Wilfrid began to serve his country as far back as 1871 in the Provincial Legislature of Quebec. A few years later he had already reached distinction as a statesman both in the Parliament of Canada and outside, to such an extent that he was offered, and accepted, a portfolio in Mackenzie's Cabinet. An election had to take place and the newly chosen minister had to go before his constituents of Arthabaska to have this choice ratified, but Arfhabaska turned him down. In an instant, a nomination paper was prepared in St. Roch and St. Sauveur, and a delegation succeeded in bringing to Quebec East the then down-hearted and disappointed young minister. From that time this constituency has enjoyed the honour and privilege of having been faithful to one of the very best public servants this country has ever had. Of him it may well be said:
In youth a student, and in old age a sage,
Lover of freedom, of mankind a friend,
Noble in aim from childhood to the end,
Great is thy mark upon historic page.
Among those who then affixed their signature to the nomination paper for the election of Quebec East very few are alive today. Their names were given lately in the press, and I shall quote them in the order in which they were published: S. N. Parent, Chas. A. Parent, M. Coleman, J. B. Laliberte, Jos. Gauthier, J. E. Martineau. It is	these men	who
jointly with the members of the district of Quebec have been claiming the right to bury their distinguished compatriot in Quebec city where a reverent population could come and pray by his grave. Their desire was a true expression of their love and devotedness, but when they realized how painful, not to say cruel, it would have been to impose a second separation upon Lady Laurier, the accomplished and beloved wife who for over fifty years had been the best companion of her husband, the claim was given up.
It is not my intention to make a full review of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's career. Laurier will sleep forever in a cemetery of the province of Ontario and, to use the expression of Archbishop Mathieu, of Regina, he lies as a connecting link between Ontario and Quebec, the two large provinces which during a lifetime he has tried to see
united in perfect harmony. Unfortunately, Sir, his teachings have not been successful in the province of Ontario, and he died at a time when the racial and religious prejudices have in that very province reached possibly the limit. Let us hope that a reaction will soon occur for the general benefit of the community.
We find, from the speeches delivered by members in this House and from expressions that have lately appeared in the press, that a reaction is certainly taking place. No province would more gladly welcome a change than the province of Quebec. Educated by Laurier and following the broad principles for which he stood, it will gladly join with those who have at heart a sincere desire that the Dominion shall enter upon an era of progressive reconstruction and readjustment.
These two words, Sir, cover a great deal of ground; they involve a consideration of various problems connected with the situation created by the war. I shall glance rapidly over a very few of the most important of those which I find mentioned in the speech from the Throne.
The consensus of opinion is that nothing is too good for the soldier, especially the returned soldier, and that steps should be taken at once to enable him to enter into civil life under the best possible circumstances. I need not say that every policy having such an aim in view should meet with unrestricted support. I am not very conversant with things pertaining to militia or military matters, but I have heard remarks made to justify the assertion that unless a distinction be made between officers and men who remained in Canada and officers and men who have actually gone to the front, troubles will surely arise. It may be true that certain officers knew so much about certain things that their services were more valuable at home than they would be abroad. Unfortunately, the soldiers who have been overseas do not seem to think so. What this Government, therefore, ought to do, is give to returned men positions that have been filled by men who have done no actual fighting. In various departments, not only in Ottawa but in many cities all over Canada, the very best situations have been held during the last four years or more by men who did not-so far as we can judge, at any rate - make what could be called a real sacrifice in connection with the war. It was said that their services were so valuable that they could not be dispensed with-that was always the excuse given when it was desired to keep a man in a job of some son.

But as soon as the soldier; return from the front, the very first thing they say when they see an officer who has not been overseas, is: "This man will soon disappear; we will see that he disappears and that we take his place." If you want to facilitate the re-establishment of the returned soldiers into civil life, one of the first things to be done is to replace by returned soldiers men who have remained in the country during the last four years. The soldiers want it, and I believe they are entitled to it. Of course, this may not meet with all views; it may not be in line with all purposes. Evidently the Government, however, has realized some of the necessities of the situation, because in the speech from the Throne certain things are mentioned, the carrying out of which will likely have the effect of helping the soldier to re-enter civil life. Among these are two which I have specially noticed: the construction of highways and the provision for better housing conditions.
I have heard some criticism of the proposal for the construction of highways. I have heard men say that to some extent this is an infringement upon provincial rights; that whatever moneys go from the Dominion Government for this purpose should be handed directly to and be spent by the provinces themselves. There may be a good deal in that suggestion, but from the resolution as it appears on the Order Paper-of course, the resolution has not yet been moved-it seems to me that there is not much danger to be apprehended in this connection. I am much inclined to congratulate the Government upon inaugurating this policy for the construction of highways. I know of no other province where the policy of improving roads and highways has been so well developed as- it has been in the province of Quebec, from which I come. That being the case, 9 p.m. I am interested in supporting a policy of that kind. Although in Quebec that policy has produced good results, there is yet something lacking. We find in certain places that our highways are disconnected because of the absence of bridges. It would be a good thing if some of that federal money could be spent on the building of bridges at certain places, for instance to complete a break in the road connecting Ontario and Quebec by building a bridge at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, so that the people of the twc provinces may pass back and forth in automobiles instead of by train, and so that they may not be separated as they have

been in the past. I suggest that if some of that money be spent in that way, much good will result. Besides, we find that throughout the country, industries which were formerly engaged in the manufacture of munitions have now stopped work. If bridge building is carried on these industries will have something to do, soldiers and ordinary labourers will find employment, and one more step will be taken towards re-establishing the soldier in civil life.
Then, the speech from the Throne mentioned some steps to be taken to provide better housing conditions. I have heard a good deal of criticism of that from gentlemen on the other side of the House, but in itself the policy is not so very bad if it is properly applied. Of course, we cannot discuss it very well at this stage because we do not know what the Bill will contain. But although we have not the Bill, in a certain little booklet that the Government has spread all over the country, called "Conservation," certain photographs are published. It appears from these that the houses recommended for the labouring classes are to be built in rows, one house touching the other, without any extra land at all. It seems to me that if any moneys are to be spent in that direction, a fair quantity of land ought to be provided for each house to be occupied by labouring men. That would be much better for him and for his family, and would go far towards preventing the bad feeling which may exist among labouring classes who live under such condition's that they have no chance of taking a little fresh air.
Other things are mentioned in the speech from the Throne; I shall not refer to them all. But I believe that the Government should not stop with the proposals mentioned in the speech from the Thrdne. I think that money devoted to the development of our natural resources would be well spent; and in this respect I share the views of a few hon. gentlemen who have referred to this matter during the course of this debate.
Part of the Northwest is altogether unknown, and in Quebec there is a territory which is unknown and which is said to be probably the wealthiest section of Canada so far as minerals of all kinds are concerned. I am speaking of new Quebec, or Ungava. The iron beds of Ungava are said to be the very best in the world. According to the report made by Professor Low some years ago, there is in that territory immense wealth in reserve for the people of

Canada. It is said that the water-powers of the Hamilton river of Ungava will produce as many million horse-power as imagination can conceive.
We have been told -that the returned soldiers have been so much in the open air that many of them will not care to return to office work. Here is an opportunity for them. Let survey parties be formed and sent into the Ungava district. There are hundreds of returned soldiers who have experience in connection with aeroplanes, who will be glad to take up this work, and the time is not far distant when aeroplanes will be used for this purpose. His Excellency the Governor General recently made a speech in which he said:-
Obviously, it is not for me, in my position, to attempt to lay down either rules of policy or rules of conduct. But certainly I may say that my experience here-very short but if I may be allowed to say so, my very happy experience in Canada-teaches me that far greater attention ought to be paid than is paid at the present moment to research work and to the development of the natural resources of the country. And I cannot help thinking that, in facing the great problems which lie in front of us those who are responsible for the administration and the conduct of affairs should proceed on these lines. Whatever money is required to be spent that money should only be considered as an investment, and a very safe investment, I believe it will be. Canada provides a very fruitful field for both research work and development. It is almost commonplace to say that the Dominion's resources have only been scratched. Thus we have unlimited opportunities for the future, and it is for all, whether we belong to great institutions like yours, or whether we are engaged in other affairs, to do everything which lies in our power to develop on sound, scientific, and practical lines, the knowledge which we already possess of these great resources.
So much for the mineral and other resources of Ungava. I think the Government will do well also to inquire into the fishing industry in the province of Quebec. The Labrador coast, the Baie des Chaleurs and the Gulf of St. Lawrence can provide the whole of Canada with the best fish in the world, but up to now the industry has been altogether ignored. Strange to say, there was given, a short time ago before the Quebec Board of Trade, a splendid address by a prominent Englishman, Mr. H. C. Thomson, in which he showed the people of Quebec what could be done as regards the fishing industry in that province. To embody what he said, I will put on Hansard the resolution passed by the Board of Trade following the speech delivered by Mr. Thomson:-
Resolved:-That the thanks of this general meeting of the members of the Quebec Board of Trade be expressed to Mr. Harry Cranfuird
Thomson, of London, for his most interesting address upon the extent and wealth of the deep sea fisheries of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the Baie des Chaleurs and the coasts of New Found-land and Labrador, and that the Board desires to express its conviction of the inestimable value of these fisheries as a source of cheap food for the people of Canada and the United States, made so urgent by the present high prices of all other food. That the experience of Aberdeen, Grimsby, and other fishing ports of the United Kingdom whence thousands of tons of fresh fish have of late years been sent daily in chilled cars to all the cities of England and Scotland, and also that of Gloucester, Mass., whence similar shipments are made to United States centres, and where fish preserving and curing in all its shapes is now being carried on, would seem to point to the advisability of more attention being paid in Canada to the exploitation of this source of cheap food. There would seem to be no reason why Quebec should not become, like Aberdeen or Grimsby, a distributing point for fresh fish brought in by properly equipped iced fish carriers from Baie des Chaleurs and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, destined to all points in Canada and the United States, provided a suitable iced warehouse were erected on the Louise Dock alongside both railway tracks and deep water.
If the Government will take these remarks into consideration and also the requests made by many hon. members to develop the natural resources of Canada, I have no doubt that such a policy will meet with general approval.
With regard to the situation created by the war, I have been very much impressed by the speech that was delivered by the Minister c.f Public Works (Mr. Carvell). I think he stated that the debt this country is facing to-day is over $2,000,000,000, and that our expenses cannot be less than $300,000,000 per annum. He stated that our revenue is not expected to be more than $195,000,000, so that we are short $105,000,000, and the Government at last puts this question: Where are we going to find the money? I must congratulate the Minister of Public Works for having boldly put the facts and the situation as it is before the country. I have also been impressed by the speech delivered by the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), in which he made certain statements, and I said to myself: Perhaps the Minister of Public Works could find in that speech a hint as to where he could get a little of the money for which he is looking. I was amazed to hear falling from the lips of an ex-minister of the Crown (Sir Sam Hughes), who was responsible for some of the expenses of the war, the following words:-
We had bad financial conditions in Canada- but of these I do not speak now. At that time, I regret to say certain distinguished members of the Government were not moderate in their

views or in their actions. Why, I have had ministers of the Crown bombard me on behalf of different interests and in order to keep this business, that business and the other business from failing, from going to pieces, I was asked to buy a few hundred yards of cloth here, and a few hundred there. The Dominion of Canada was down to such a state in financial matters that we had to practically dole the contracts out, to give some business here, some there, and some elsewhere and this became a very serious drawback.
Let me read a little further. The ex-Minister of Militia and Defence tells us that in the very midst of the war, when the lives of our soldiers were at stake, there were grafters around trying to get money out of him. The hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) stated the other day that for every dollar spent on the soldier another dollar has gone in graft, and it begins to look as if that statement were true To continue the words of the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir 'Sam Hughes):
Sir Joseph Flavelle became head of the Munitions Board, this work having been transferred from the War Department in England to the Munitions Department. Then, following that, we find a certain distinguished citizen obtaining large contracts both in Canada and tire United States for the supply of meats and meat products. We have had some evidence in Canada about meat profits, but we have only touched the fringe of it yet, and we have not got anything about what was going on in the United States. I am informed on very reliable authority that upwards of $5,000,000 monthly was handed1 over in the last three or four years in the United States under contracts with the British Government and other governments to this gentleman, by reason of the position which he held as head of the Munitions Board, which gave him the prestige that enabled him to get all these things into his own hands, little by little, until the whole affair was brought in as an appendage to the business interests run by this Toronto organization. Its estimated profits will he upwards of $100,000,000 in the last four years on theste commodities alone.
Bir, if we are short of money, as w'e are told by the Minister of Public Works, one of the first steps we should take is to get back the money that has been pocketed by these people. There are other ways, perhaps more interesting to the city of Quebec in particular, in which money could be saved by this Government. It is no secret that for a good many years past the province of Quebec has been deliberately isolated by the Government of the day. Still, Quebec is alive just the same, and will probably continue to live. Although we are not receiving any favours from the Government, there are citizens among us who wanted to help on the war and do something for the soldiers. Mr. G. G. Stuart, K.C., a lawyer well known all over Canada, a considerable time ago bequeathed

to the Government his beautiful estate of about three hundred acres, to be used for hospital purposes for the Canadian soldiers. The property is situated on the St. Foy road, overlooking the St. Lawrence river, occupying as fine a site as could be imagined. Although this property was bequeathed to the Government over a year ago, the Government has done nothing towards providing a hospital, and not a cent has been spent on the property for the benefit of the returned soldier. On the contrary, the Government has been renting hospital accommodation elsewhere. The Government, for instance, rented Kent House, which is situated on the Quebec Railway, Light & Power Company line, which company is very friendly to the Government, while all the time the property bequeathed by Mr. Stuart was lying idle. Another instance of how the Government is favouring this company is the fact that it has given the company a contract for lighting all the public buildings of Quebec-the post office, the Customs Department, the Revenue Department and the Militia Department buildings-without calling for tenders, and the contract is good for five years. There are other competing companies in the city of Quebec, but they were not given a chance to tender. This was simply another case of throwing away money.
I wish to refer to the Siberian expedition and to correct a statement made by the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn) the other day. I understood him to say that all members of the Siberian Force had left this country voluntarily. That is not correct, because I know quite a few young men who, though willing to go and fight in France, deliberately refused to sign any papers for Siberia. And yet those men have been sent. I was very glad to hear the Minister say they would all soon be back. The province of Quebec badly needs these men, and they should certainly be back in Canada for the beginning of the summer. In Siberia, they aTe of no use to this country or to anybody else, unless, as wras suggested by the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Kennedy), they are there trying to collect loans made by capitalists of Europe.
I was very much interested in the speech of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck), and particularly in his defence of Sir Arthur Currie; and one thing which he said in connection with that matter impressed me considerably. He said that when the troops were going through places infested with Germans the natural feeling at the moment
MARCH 17, my
was to crash the enemy, paying them back in their own coin. But he said the policy of revenge was not worth a man's life. These words struck me as being very eloquent and compelled a thought which I shall now express, in regard to the last Order in Council passed by the Government that the fathers-for that is what it amounts to-of defaulters under the Military Service Act should be fined at least $250. I do not know what the intention of the Government is; but if it is intended that defaulters should go to jail, I would say, let that Order in Council stand as it is, because with such a fine as that at least eighty per cent of the defaulters would have to go to jail. Now, if the policy of revenge is not worth a man's life, it should not, I think, be worth a man's liberty; and I think that if the Government persists in enforcing such heavy fines it is nothing but revenge. It is ungenerous; and the result will be that a good many young men who were not as guilty as some people believe them to be will be sent to prison. Every one expresses a desire for harmony now. Well, if the Government have the same desire, I suggest that one of the first things they should do is to repeal that Order in Council and leave the whole matter to the discretion of the judges. Our judges have proven themselves capable and honourable throughout the whole history of Canada, and I do not see why they should now be incapable of dealing with this matter. They are familiar with local conditions and should be the best judges under the circumstances-at least better judges than the Government.
In conclusion I will say this: Quebec is not as bad as it has been represented to be. Quebec-is well disposed toward the rest of Canada, and will gladly unite with those who have the best interests of the country at heart. It stands for order as against the forces that would make for revolutionary change. Its devotion to Canada's cherished institutions and to the highest interest will continue in the years to come.
Mr. JOHN A. CURRIE (North Simcoe): Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the House and the country must be getting tired of this prolonged debate on the Address. I am one of the old members of the House and I have not yet seen an Address discussed at such length. However, it is just as well, perhaps, that the Government should have the views of its followers and the hon. members of the Opposition upon questions of public policy, so that it may frame its legislation in accordance with such views.
It would be quite impossible for me to offer any tribute as touching or as graceful as those tributes which have so far been offered to the memory of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier who has passed away from his place in this House, and whose face and figure I am sure all of us miss a great deal.
I have known him for a great many years, and I always had considerable admiration for him-personally unbounded admiration; although I confess I could not see my way clear to follow him in some of his policies. He had that magnetic quality which endeared him to his followers, and he had filled the place in the public life of this country with dignity, with courage and address; and even his bitterest enemies cannot deny that though he may have erred in his policies, he erred believing that he was doing his best for the country.
Now, it is always painful for a speaker- especially so is it for me-to refer to personal matters; but possibly it might be just as well for me to dispose of these questions at the beginning of my address. Unfortunately, in his speech the other day, the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) made a reference to myself which was calculated to reflect upon .Sir Arthur Currie, the leader of the Canadian army in Flanders. In that speech the hon. member left it to be inferred that an injustice had been done to me by Sir Arthur Currie. He said that I was blamed for something for which Sir Arthur Currie was to blame, and that no effort had been made to vindicate me. Now, I am very much obliged to the hon. member for his endeavour to help me fight my battles; although my friends and intimates will admit, I believe, that I am generally quite capable of attending to my own affairs. The circumstance to which he alluded was this. In the second battle of Ypres >1 had the great honour to be senior officer at Grafenstafel Ridge, and that point, which was farthest east in the enemy's line was held by my battalion, the 15th Battalion, 48th Highlanders, of Toronto. When the war broke out I wag in command of that battalion in the city of Toronto. It was considered one of the crack battalions of Canada, and was then 985 men strong which was greater than the number of men in any other single battalion in the country. It was fully armed, had complete field equipment, and was ready to take the field, and when the call to this war came, as a member of this House, and for the dignity of the House, I considered it my duty to leave all personal affairs and go; so that it should not be said by the people of this country that when the call to the war



came no member of the House of Commons was willing to go, and that we were all a lot of " safety-firstcrs." I went to the war, and I do not regret it. I will say further, that from the very moment I landed in England, I felt that there was being made an effort-to use the vernacular-to " can " me. But I behaved myself with becoming dignity, avoided controversies of every kind, kept out of politics, and attended to my own business. I complained only once. When my men were up to their knees in mud and their tents were down, and there was no place for them to warm themselves, or dry themselves, il did write to Headquarters. I told them I thought that in Canada we did better for hogs, than they were doing by the men over there. Nothing was said about that; I was forgiven. The reason I did say it then, or make a kick, was simply because the Canadian battalions had given details of men to build huts for themselves, they had built them, the huts had been unoccupied for nearly three weeks and we should have been allowed to go into them. When I went to France I still felt that I was under observation and that there was some hidden hand behind, I do not know whose, seeking to destroy me in some way or other. I was not mistaken. When we were at Fleurbaix my battalion was very well-behaved and we did not have a crime oftener than once in four or five days. Then commissioners came down from army headquarters to investigate and I was virtually deprived of my command. They wanted to inspect my battalion and they inspected it. They told me that my battalion had been shielding crime amongst the men. They inspected every company and every man, and if the inspecting officer found an " i " that was not dotted, or a " t " that was not crossed, and if every man was not clean shaved and in his proper order and place, I knew what was going to happen to me. Fortunately, the battalion was well-behaved and the commissioners, after they had been around, came and complimented me and said that they were in error, that they did not consider it possible that a Canadian battalion could have such good behaviour, such fine discipline and such clean, well-behaved men as mine. I was permitted to carry on. They could not have found anything else because the men who were with me were amongst the finest boys to be found in the city of Toronto, all well-behaved lads, not such a class as you would expect to be guilty of any crimes.

At the battle of Ypres I was placed in a peculiar position. I was the commandant or senior officer on Gravenstafel ridge. That ridge was held by my own battalion together with the Montreal Highlanders; and the 7th were dug in on our left, this being the battalion to which the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Cooper) was attached. The 7th was dug in on the road between St. Julien and Gravenstafel ridge. It was on the morning of the 24th that the Germans attacked my battalion. Early in the morning the gas attack came and my battalion was gassed and it seemed as if every gun in the German army was turned upcn us. We were attacked about fifty to one and they flattened our front line trenches, killing and wounding a great many of my men.
I might here say as a matter of explanation that when I came back to Canada I was told by some high military officers that I should have withdrawn my battalion rather than remain in such a dangerous place. If I had had my own way I would have withdrawn to the crest of Gravenstafel ridge and dug in. But we had no option in the matter. On the night before the grand attack word was sent out to every individual company commander by telephone that he was not to move until help came next day. If I had withdrawn my battalion or any of my men before orders came to move, I would have been courtmartialled, and I would have deserved it, because it would have been disobedience of orders. In the morning, however, when the attack came, I was there. The attack occurred about four o'clock in the morning. My men had nothing to do but fight and die in their places or be taken. They could not get out. Three-quarters of my battalion fell, but they sold their lives dearly. Between six and seven o'clock the grand attack was virtually over. My second in command, Major Marshall, had been posted on my left in a reserve trench, with my adjutant, now Col. Dansereau of Montreal, with a machine gun and a platoon of men. At daylight a German Albatross flying machine came over and dropped green flares over them. In a little while several batteries of eight or nine-inch guns began firing into their trench, blowing it to pieces and killing every man in it except seven or eight. I saw Major Marshall emerge between my men and the line of the 7th with half a dozen men and walk in the direction of the dressing station, and I went down to see him in order to ascertain what had hap-

pened to the rest of the command. I had seen them bombarded about 350 yards away and I wanted to know what had happened to my adjutant. He told me that my adjutant was killed- Fortunately that did not turn out to be true; he was badly wounded on the top of the head but he managed to crawl out afterwards. At that time the commanding officer of the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Cooper) came over to me. He was a young man, Major Odium, now Brigadier-General Odium and one of the famous Canadian officers. His commanding officer had been killed the evening before near Kaiserleer when they went out to reconnoitre the German line. I refer to Col. Hart Maharg. Major Odium came and asked me if I felt he would be justified in remaining in his position. I asked him what he thought he ought to do, and he said that he thought he ought to stick it. I told him to carry on. He did stick it and the 7th died in their trenches almost to a man. They were dug in between St. Julien and Kaiserleer. The hon. member for South Vancouver says he saw me that day and spoke to me. He said he had seen General Sir Arthur Currie also. If he saw, and spoke to me, it would be at the dressing station and if so he was out of his position or a casualty because he otherwise should have been with his men on the road. I do not recollect seeing him that morning, but if he did speak to me it was at the crossroads in the rear of Kaiserleer at the dressing station. I do remember that scattered units of men had carried wounded men to the dressing station. I ordered them back to the trenches on the reverse slope of Gravenstafel ridge as senior officer and it may be that I did sometimes use language rather more forcible than polite. I believe that one man did write home that I told him and his chum to get into the trenches and that if he moved out without orders he would have his blooming head shot off, or something of that kind. However, that is where I was that morning, and I did not leave that position that morning.
With regard to Sir Arthur Currie, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) has' placed this question quite clearly before the House already, and as far as he (Gen. Currie) was concerned, there was nothing discreditable either to me or to himself, as far as I can see, in the whole transaction. He was at Fortuin his headquarters immediately south of St. Julien. Our brigade was on his left, and on our
left were the French. He had given us the 10th and the 7th to help us out the evening of the day when the battle opened. The 10th battalion was badly cut up that night. That battalion w^s formed of troops from Saskatoon and Moosejaw. The 16th battalion, the Highlanders from Vancouver, which the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) had the honour to command and the 10th were lined up immediately to the west of St. Julien. They were in reserve and they were lined up on Thursday night after the gas attack on the French. They formed line with fixed bayonets and went forward to meet the Germans at St. Julien wood. There never wat a braver bayonet charge than that in the whole war, They drove the Germans back half a mile and established themselves, and their losses were tremendous. On Saturday morning the 10th Battalion was withdrawn, or at least the remnant of it, consisting of about one hundred and fifty men under Major Ormond. It was sent down to our assistance in the terrible salient, that tract we were in, at Gravenstafel Ridge. Major Ormond reported to me that morning-and his report is in the archives of the Militia Department-to that effect. Sir Arthur Currie was at his quarters in Fortuin. We all expected that reinforcements would have arrived at daylight in the morning, but they did not. The reinforcements did not arrive until hours afterwards, until after noon, or rather late in the afternoon, when the Durham Light Infantry came into that sector. Sir Arthur Currie got tired of calling on the telephone for help, and walked down from Fortuin to Wiltchz, about a mile and a half away, and he had a "-head-on" collision with the British commander, General Snow-at least I was so informed, I do not know personally. He w anted to know why they were not sending help to us. I wish to say that if I had not been in the position, the honoui-able position, that I was in on Gravenstafel Ridge, I would just as soon have been in his position, because there was nothing dishonourable about it, and I think when his report is brought before this House it will establish that fact. Now, as far as the point is concerned where I was located, and the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Cooper), if there was one little spot in the whole world at that moment that the German Emperor wanted, it was that very place, Gravenstafel Ridge. If he had captured it that morning many believe the history of the world would have been changed. We held that ridge, and what is more we did not give it up. The ridge

was turned over to English troops, the Durham Light Infantry, who fought and went into action that morning right fresh from England, never having seen a trench before, not knowing the difference between a hedge and a trench. They fought for nearly two weeks in those trenches at the cross-roads, where I had previously been, and held the place. Nobody can cast any reflections upon any of those officers and men in my hearing with my consent. This war has seen a great deal of sacrifice, and it is most unfortunate that some people at home have done nothing but scandalize and slander the living and the dead. Why should I say anything against Sir Arthur Currie? I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that he is a wonder, and the fact that he managed to come through with all the intrigue that I saw going on-not amongst the soldiers, mind you, but there was intrigue going on-the fact that he, a civilian soldier, * like myself, a militiaman, came through with the highest honours and led the Canadians to victory, I think is a marvel. It should encourage every other citizen in this country to perfect himself in the study of arms, so that should the time ever come when their country is in danger they will be able, as the old Greeks said, to take their place in the ranks.
Now', Mr. Speaker, I have covered that phase of the matter. I do not know, Sir, but I trust that we have heard the last of all this talk. I agree with the hon. minister, who suggested that some substantial recognition should be granted to Sir Arthur Currie. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the very first thing this House should have done- and I regret there wras nothing at all pertaining to this matter in the speech from the Throne-was, after offering thanks to Almighty God for saving us, \vas to tender the thanks of this young nation to the officers and the men who have fought so bravely for us in those foreign fields in this great war, and w'ritten the name of Canada with victory and with glory. There is no man living in the Canadian forces that I can feel in my heart for one minute would do anything wrong, or anything that might injure his country. If he did wrong -and after all we are only human-it would be with the motive of doing good; and if a man makes a mistake in war when he is trying to do good. I think our forgiveness should be extended to him. But I cannot recall a single case of the kind.
The Canadians have had great losses. The living are coming home, many of them to find their homes virtually desolate, their

business gone, and hardly knowing which way to turn. To them we should offer every encouragement. It should not be our part to seek in any possible way to minimize their employment. They fought for this country, and they did so, not because they expected that Canada was'going to get any territory added to its already broad acres, or that it was going to have any wrongs righted; they fought because they were fighting for humanity, and making the future of this country sure, making sure that Canada would never become an adjunct or an appendage to any other country in the world. That is the feeling they had, and that is why they went overseas and sacrificed their lives. To these officers and men the thanks of this House are due, and I hope that the leader of the Government will take the earliest opportunity to have the House pass a unanimous vote of thanks to our army, such as the British nation always does after its army is victorious in a great war.
Attempts are made right and left to set the men against the officers, and I have heard remarks in this House, and read statements in the Canadian press, trying to disparage the officers, and saying -that the pensions of the men should be the same as the officers, or that the officers should not get more than the men. In my view there is nothing too good for the men, but you must bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the officers of the Canadian army that went overseas in the first place-it is true their pay has been increased a trifle-on the basis of the same pay as the English officers; in fact their pay was less than that of English officers, while our men received four times the pay of the English private. I do not begrudge our men four times the pay of the English Tommy-they were always willing, if necessary, to do four times the fighting of any other man in the field. But as far as the officers were concerned a lieutenant-colonel, occupying the same position as I occupied, in the British army received a dollar a day more pay than I did. And those young men who led the troops over the top, the bravest of the brave, our subalterns, our lieutenants, what did they get? They did not get enough to maintain their wives on, they did not get as much money, Mr. Speaker, as the armourer corporals in the Canadian Forces got in pay. And still there is talk about the big pay of the officers! I trust that this House will not hear any more talk about the difference in pay or pension between the officers and the men. They all

did their duty, and they all did it very well. In peace they will be united.
As far as I am personally concerned, it is not very comfortable or pleasant for me to speak of my own affairs, but I will say this: I am not sorry that I took part in the war, it will always be a pleasure to me, even though I got no honour or glory out of it. You would think to hear some people talk that I had made a million out of the war over there, that I had received a peerage, or title, a V.C., and all that sort of thing. I got nothing, I did not want anything, and I do not want anything. The fact that I have the honour and affection of my men, the fact that the "Original" men of the First Division, last year asked me to lead them in the parade on Yonge street, Toronto, on St. Julien day, does not show there is any great reflection on me. I did not seek glory of any kind; I trust, therefore, that the House has heard the last of that and that no further reference will be made to it.
I want to compliment the member for Skeena (Mr. Peck, V.C.) on being in this House and on having secured meritorious recognition; also the other young men on this side of the House who have fought in the war and have been in the actual zones of combat. I am sorry that more of my old colleagues in the House cannot say that they were in the actual zone of conflict. A great many of them volunteered, put on khaki, raised regiments and took them overseas, and just as they got as far as the front received the same kind of telegram to come home that I got. I do not think that I should have ever got to the field of battle unless by some accident.
Two other members of tire House of Commons got to the actual zone of combat. One was Colonel Baker-blessed be his memory. He died in action; no finer man ever wore khaki. I trust that some spot in the new buildings will Ire found where a monument may be placed to remind future generations of parliamentarians that there were men of red blood in the House of Commons in the days of the Great War.
Then, the member for Ontario, Colonel Sharpe, went to the trenches and would not leave them until his health broke down and he was a complete wreck. He died in Montreal-no wonder, when he spent two years and a half constantly within the sound of the guns, constantly in the midst of that great carnage. It was with great difficulty that he got as far as the front, but he was determined that nothing short of illness or death would take him away, because h^ like every other member of this
House, knew that if he did come back, he would-having my case in mind-" have it thrown into him " for all time to come by those who had stayed at home. But he has gone to his reward, and I trust that a place will be found to erect some monument to his memory. No finer comrade in arms could any man have than the late Colonel Sharpe.
I would like to say a word about those young men who have given their lives for their country. They died in order that Canada might be a great country, and here a responsibility rests upon members on both sides of the House. The responsibility is upon us of making this country great; of avoiding selfishness; of seeking to further not our own personal interests, but the interests of our country. These men have died gloriously in the cause of the Empire and, as Rudyard Kipling has said, quoting Ecclesiasticus, " Their names and their memories shall live forevermore." They have died in a great cause. It is a matter of deep regret that matters should be brought up which will cause the heartstrings of their parents and relatives at home to be wrung again. I know what that means, because for two days my own family lived in apprehension, having been informed after the battle of St. Julien that I was missing, that I had been killed.
We should not offer these parents condolence, because the young men of Canada died doing their duty. We may offer our consolation. They will always have the feeling that their sons did their duty and that of all the people of Canada they stand nearer to the heart-strings of our country than any others. Many of these people will send sons to this House; many will come to this House who have served in the war. You may rest assured that these men will do good service for their King and country and that Canada will never suffer by them.
I have heard it said that the'country is afraid of the returned soldier. Mr. Speaker, people do not understand the returned soldier. References of a disgraceful character have been made in the press to the riots at this town in Wales. I am not surprised at riots if conditions were such as described to me in a letter from a fi'iend. I know what it is to be up to the knees in mud, I know what it is to be without coal and to have to buy coal and coal oil out of my own pocket in order to keep my men warm. I know what it is to have the sleet and rain beating down and to hear the men coughing, their physical resistance breaking down, so that one could not sleep at night. There are several hundred dead Canadians in the

Netherhaven cemetery who perished from cold and exposure on Salisbury Plains. These men at Rhyl Camp must have been undergoing the same kind of exposure or they would not have rioted. The riot is to be regretted. I trust that the country will forgive them; the only thing I cannot forgive is the; loss of life in connection with those riots. Somebody is responsible for that, and sooner or later, when the proper time comes, unquestionably this House will fix that responsibility.
I have dealt with some personal matters to the satisfaction, I hope, of everybody in the House. I trust that this recrimination will cease. We should all be satisfied that every officer and man of all the forces has done his duty to the best of his ability. Many of our boys gave up their lives in the performance of their duty. There are fathers on both sides of this House who have given sons to the great cause. These boys may have died trying to do the impossible, but it was because we did the impossible that the name of Canada is on the map in connection with this war.
I wish to deal at some length with fiscal questions. It is now ten o'clock, and I would ask the indulgence of the House in permitting me to move the adjournment of the debate.

MEWBURN (Minister of Militia): With your permission, Sir, I would like, as a matter of courtesy to the members of this House, to remind them that the Princess Patricia Canadian Light Infantry is expeoted to arrive in Ottawa to-morrow morning. They will then proceed by Besserer, Nicholas and Rideau streets to Connaught Square in front of the Chateau Laurier, where a platform is being erected, and it is hoped as many members of the Parliament as possible will be present there. Consideration of the motion of Mr. D. L. Redman (Calgary East), for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the Session, resumed from Monday, March 17.
Mr. JOHN A. CURRIE (North Simcoe): Mr. Speaker, yesterday evening when the House so kindly granted my request for adjournment, I stated that it was my intention to-day to deal with the question of the tariff and the economic condition of this country. The great war in which our soldiers have been engaged is over, and this country like every other country, is now confronted with the weighty problem of reconstruction. Very few people, when they speak of reorganization and reconstruction, realize the vital importance of those matters to Canada. Such a war as this was an unheard of thing before. In the whole history of the world, nothing like it had ever before occurred. It has swept away old traditions. It has destroyed old institutions, and many preconceived notions. In fact, all the old ideas of public men and of the people generally have undergone a change. This was brought very strongly to my mind the other day as I listened to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), discussing, in the same old tone, in the same old words, old policies and old matters that do not count at all to-day amidst the vital issues that confront us. His speech reminded me very much of J. M. Barrie's play "the Mollusc," which I had the pleasure of seeing not long ago. As J. M. Barrie's plays always contain a moral, this play contained a moral for the politicians as well as for others. According to the play, a mollusc is a shell-fish that attaches itself to a rock or some other object, and that never moves. When I heard the hon. gentleman quoting from the speech of President Wilson about the waves and the tides moving on and sweeping things before them, the idea of the mollusc naturally occurred to me. As a mollusc attaches itself to a rock and never moves from that spot, so, many public men holding certain views, are determined to stick to them; never to change their policies; to carry on consistently forever with the same old politics, living entirely in the past. When I heard him speaking of free trade, and also my good old friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), whom I love to listen to, speaking
about free trade, at this present moment, knowing the actual condition of the economic affairs of the world, the idea of the mollusc instinctively occurred to me, and I realize that no wave, even of war, pestilence and famine, will move those people one inch from the same old ideas.
Listening to these speeches, one would think for the moment that the whole world had stood still during the war and was starting on from 1914 as if nothing had occurred in the meantime. What are the facts confronting the people of this country? The whole world is, at the present time, engaged, not in a war of arms, but in an economic war. We find that England has slammed the door shut with embargoes on every country; that the United States has closed its doors and embargoed everything; that France has embargoed the foodstuffs and manufactures of the whole world. In fact, there is, at the present moment, no country discussing or even mentioning the words "free trade" except this country of Canada. These are facts. England will never go back to the former state of affairs, so Lloyd George says. England, at the present time, is in exactly the same position as she was in the time of Cromwell. She has Navigation Laws as she had then and Protection as she had then, and that Protection is even more effective now. You cannot get a dollar's worth of your manufactured goods into England, and England has decided that the manufacturers of Germany, the United States, or any other country, can no longer dump their goods into England to the detriment and injury of the English workingman. Not only is that the condition, but the agricultural situation has entirely changed. We listened with a great deal of pleasure to the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Maliarg) who, last evening, gave the story of the West-and a very fine story it was. If I did not know the actual conditions I should be very much inclined to agree with his view.
Let us first consider the conditions confronting the agriculturists of this country, and then see whether free trade (or in other words economic destruction) is going to assist them. A significant statement was made in this House a day or so ago by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). He is fully aware of the principle of cabinet responsibility, anc\ therefore his statement that he stood for the total abolition of the tariff on agricultural implements, as he did in 1908-1909, was very significant. The manufacturers and working men, of the

East are forced to the conclusion that this Government stands on that very ground. What are the conditions affecting the agricultural interests of this country? Mr. Lloyd George in one of his great speeches during the last election-I think it was at Manchester-said that in the year preceding the war Great Britain had raised only twelve weeks' supply of her own food, but that last year she had raised forty-two weeks' supply. That was a significant statement. He further stated that Great Britain would never again be dependent upon the outside world for her foodstuffs as she was before the war, and that legislation already existed and further provision would be made guaranteeing the agriculturists of Great Britain protection and a fair price for their product. Can we,' therefore, look for a market in England? Can we look for a market in Europe? Russia has been mentioned. Nobody in his senses would propose to sell anything to Russia at the present moment, because she has repudiated her national debt. In fact, all those countries of Central Europe to which it is intimated we are going to sell vast quantities of cereals are seething with Bolshevism, a doctrine, which is founded on the repudiation of national debts. If we sell anything to those countries, can we be sure that we will receive payment unless Great Britain or one of the other big powers guarantees payment? Conditions the whole world over have changed. Every elevator in this country, through the failure of the Government to put an embargo on foreign wheat, is jam full of American wheat and other grains. The result has been that we have not been able to move our own grain from the West, although the people of this country have provided the money to purchase it. Owing to the Government giving way, as a matter of policy, to the cry in the West for free wheat, we now have free trade in wheat with the United States, so far as our laws and treaties provide. But have we really got free wheat? The hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) told us that we could not ship a pound of wheat or cereals now to the United States. How is that, when the treaty provided for reciprocal privileges? The reason is because the United Slates is protecting its own people. It has a protective policy, just as Great Britain has at the present time, and will have, according to present indications, for many years to come. The policy of Prance, of Italy, and of every other country except Canada is also a protective policy. We are supposed to have 
free wheat with the United States, but the door of the United States has been slammed shut on our farmers, and I am satisfied that she will have an embargo against our wheat just as long as free wheat between the two countries is on the programme. But free wheat has not prevented the United States from selling us their wheat. According to the returns for 1918 the United States sold us half a million dollars worth of wheat, while we sold none to them. Last year we sold no cereals to the United States, as was admitted last night, but the United States sold us between seven and eight million dollars worth of corn to be used for human food in this country, and we were forced to eat it as a substitute for our own wheat. The result is that to-day every grocer in this country has his shelves loaded down with corn flour and is unable to sell it. It will mean a great loss to those who have bought these wheat substitutes from the United States. What is the use of treaties and reciprocity which are not observed.
I have read all the authorities on free trade and know my Adam Smith possibly as well as the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I also know something of Jean Baptiste Say, who, according to the French-speaking members of this House, was an apostle of Adam Smith. He certainly was the apostle Paul of Adam Smith, because he cleared up many things on which Adam Smith himself was not so clear; Now, according to old economic doctrines preached before the war, a great war such as we have had was impossible. It was said that no great power could live in a condition of war with another great power for more than two or three weeks. Nevertheless the great war came and lasted four-years, exploding all the fallacies propounded by Norman Angell and others who talked of peace, and whose work we now know was simply a form of German propaganda intended to render us defenceless so that we could be struck down by not being prepared.
Will any hon. gentleman tell me what country wants free trade at the present moment? Germany to-day has all her factories intact; not a wheel has been hurt, and they are ready now to flood this country with cheap manufactures if free trade is extended to them. Therefore, I ask this House and the people of this country soberly to consider exactly what our situation is. Is it not a fact that those who have the interests of this country at heart and our legislators, who know how delicate the situation is at home in our cities and towns,

should unite and forget all this ancient babble about free trade? Is it not in the interests of Canada to ask the Government to initiate a policy of embargoes against every country, so that when the economic conference sits in Paris, as it will immediately after the Peace Conference has concluded its labours, Canada will have at least a jack-knife to trade? To my mind, that is the sensible policy. I am fully conscious how difficult it is for me, a manufacturer, to address a gathering of any kind on any question pertaining to the industries of this country. We all know how unfairly the manufacturers of this country are constantly being attacked. The press of this country is fanning the flame of class hatred, so that the manufacturer appears to be a man full of plans of spoliation of treason, strategem and spoils, whose whole aim and object in life is to destroy society and pocket as much money as possible himself.	.
To give you an idea of the unfair way in which the manufacturers are attacked, I need refer only to my own case. A few weeks ago I addressed a gathering of Liberal Conservatives in the city of Toronto, and at that time the Toronto Globe was preaching far and wide all over this country that Canada had a forty-two and one-half per cent tariff. Now everybody knows that that is not so. If you turn up the pages of the customs returns, you will find a page devoted there to the percentage of the tariff of this country on goods entered for consumption. You will find, on that page, that the percentage is only 16.7, if I remember rightly, for last year. In view of that fact, why should the Globe talk about 42J per cent? The Globe for forty years has been menacing the industries of the country constantly, in season and out of season, at a cost to the people of millions of dollars. As the leader of this Government at one time said in the city of Toronto, we are living constantly on suspended sentence. That is the chief reason why Canada has not achieved a success equal to that of the United States. If we had not been going around with one arm tied behind our backs, this country of ours would have a population to-day of at least 25,000,000 or 30,000,000. But this constant agitation, I pointed out, had injured' the country. I challenged the accuracy of the Globe statement that the tariff was 42£ per cent. As a matter of fact on the goods consumed in Canada that are subject to tariff the duty amounts to something like 27J per cent, which includes 71 per cent war tax. We must bear in mind also, Mr. Speaker- and I would like all
hon. members of the House to remember this-that the foreign manufacturer exporting into Canada is allowed, whether rightly or wrongly, to reduce the price of his goods below the regular market price in his own country by 5 per cent; so that this country and the manufacturers of this country lose exactly 5 per cent thereby. Now, take 71 per cent from 271 per cent and you have 20 per cent; from that take 5 per cent again, and the total protection that this country really has on the goods that are entered for home consumption is only something like 15 per cent. Surely that is not a very high tariff. I replied to the Globe to that effect. The Globe reported me to the extent of a small paragraph, but came out later with a column and a half of a reply. It began by stating that I was president of, or was connected with, a concern engaged in the manufacture of wire; and said by inference that I was virtually a member of a wire or nail combine. Now, I am connected with the Imperial iSteel Company of Collingwood, and for two years we have not manufactured and sold in Canada products to the extent of 20 tons. We went into the foreign market and tried to sell goods wdiere the Germans had sold before-in South Africa, India, Ceylon, Java, and other foreign countries. That concern last year sold goods to foreign countries to the value of over $850,000 worth, and paid out over a quarter of a million in wages in the town of Collingwood. I do not think, therefore, that it owes any apologies to the Globe. Furthermore, the Globe stated that a case had been tried in the courts in which a suit had been brought by a dealer in eastern Ontario against a manufacturer of wire, and that the judge, in giving judgment, said that the goods were sold with the understanding that the jobber who purchased them would maintain the " association " price. Therefore, the judge and the Globe said: " You are a combine; you belong to a combine; an association; you are characterized by the courts as being an illegal combine." Now, if the Globe had gone into the facts, it would have discovered that the " association " price was not an association price of the manufacturers at all, because no combination exists, nor has existed for very many years, among the makers of wire nails or wire, nor has there been any gentleman's agreement. The association price referred to was the price of the jobbers' association, and not of the manufacturers. Nor do I belong to any association that is involved in any combine, for that is a very poor argument to put for-

ward, after all is said and done, as the United States is now discussing the necessity of permitting its manufacturers to form committees of trade to deal with the sale of United States goods in foreign countries. Why should such unfair argument be raised? I challenge the 'Globe to show that I belong or have belonged to the association which has been referred to,, and I make that challenge openly and publicly. I do not belong to the Manufacturers' Association, because if I did I would be challenged on that ground also. Ever since I went into public life I have kept out of the Manufacturers' Association. So that, as far as all these things are concerned, I hope the hon. gentlemen who are listening to me will realize that I am not speaking on behalf of any interest of the kind. I am trying to put the industrial side of this question, for the workmen as well as the manufacturers.
Now, the problem before the people of this country at the present time is the demobilization of the soldiers, and the remobilization of our industries. The question of our taxes, which have been added to enormously through the war, also confronts us. On the question of demobilization I do not quite agree with the programme of the Government. Two years ago 1 expressed my views in one of the local papers here-I said that the soldiers should be returned by units and that the Headquarters of the units should be established in brigade areas here, and that the men should be allowed to have working furlough, and should be kept under pay for six months or a year after they return. I expressed the opinion that when a man returned he should be given a working furlough so that he might obtain a position, and if he did not like it he could go back and drill for a while, and when he became tired of drilling he could go and get a job again. In that way he would be able to find the position that suited him best and in which he could be most useful, because the men who are discharged are in an unsettled state of mind. They are not in their old frame of mind, and when they get a position they do not always realize how good it is, and after a few weeks it becomes irksome, and they give it up and walk around the streets, acquiring habits of idleness. Now, if it is unavoidable that they should be idle at any time, it would be better for them to spend the interval with their unit, where they would be under discipline for the time being. If such were the case the country would not see the sad spectacle of some of these men peddling shoe-laces. The soldier has had very little fMr. Currie. 1
out of the war. If he was kept a year in this way. he would not be getting as much out of it as the man who stayed at home working on munitions. The question is, what are we to do with the soldiers? A programme of land settlement is proposed. The soldier must go into some industry, either in the manufacturing industry or in the industry of agriculture. A few years ago-not ten years, or even eight years ago-we had millions of acres of idle land in the West. We have Colonization Ministers, and Bureaus of 'Colonization and all that sort of thing, but strange to say, when the soldier returns and a little piece of land is wanted for 'him, there is no land left. A programme is proposed, a copy of which I have here, which provides that the soldier can purchase a farm costing up to $5,000, the Government assisting him, and that he can borrow $2,000 more for his house, and farm implements. Then he is expected to begin life as a farmer on a hundred, or hundred and fifty acres of land, with a mortgage of $7,000 tied round his neck. I do not approve of that, Mr. Speaker. I think that the returned soldier who has fought in the war is entitled to just exactly as fair and generous treatment as a soldier who fought in South Africa, or those who fought in the Fenian Raid, and I say that adequate justice must be done these men. They should not be allowed to be the dupes of a lot of real estate dealers. The returned soldier is at the mercy of real estate men, and, indeed, at the mercy of everybody. He never will be able to raise his head above water if you put a debt of that kind upon his shoulders. *
We know there are millions of acres of land in the West standing idle. Great corporations control between 22,000,000 and 25,000,000 acres of the finest land in the West along the railways that never had a plough in it and never a man settled upon it. It would be much better to take that land over at a fair price and give the returned soldier his land free. Give him assistance,, if need be, to help him along; supply him with seed wheat, give him a start and do not allow him to become the victim of the real estate sharks. This country surely is not run by real estate sharks. I never saw them do any good to any country anywhere, much less to Canada.
How about the returned soldier in urban districts? I want to tell this House and this Government that if you are going to start closing the industries, if you are going to adopt the policy of reducing the industrial life of the country, if you are going to

deprive the present factories of the small amount of protection that they now have, you are going to take away from the Soldier the opportunity of employment. As the conditions are now, there is not a manufacturer in this country who will invest a dollar in any industry. Every dollar they have and the employment of their men is menaced by this movement to wipe out protection and to have free implements, and free this, and free that. That means that the United States will be the country that will be manufacturing those things for us, and the workmen that are at the present time employed in the industries of Canada will have to go to the United States.
In the name of God is that going to give employment to our returned soldiers? Not in this country. That, Sir, is directly the opposite of the view we should take in regard to these matters.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) made use of an argument that is constantly employed against the manufacturers. He said that if he purchased a foreign article on which there was a duty of $2 he would pay that $2 into the treasury of this country. Quite right. But if he purchased an article of Canadian manufacture, the Canadian manufacturer would put the $2 into his pocket. Would the Canadian manufacturer put the -$2 in his pocket? Go a little beyond that and see how much of that $2 the Canadian manufacturer would actually put in his pocket. The Canadian manufacturer does not earn five per cent on his turnover. The balance of the $2 would really go into the pockets of the men, women and children who were employed in his factory. And they are doing what? They are eating the products of those men in the West who are so much opposed to them.
Let me put the argument to you .in another way. There is one thing that the farmer in the West needs, and that is greater markets. He is not only producing far more in the way of cereals than this country, or the United States, or Great Britain, or any other country, will for the moment need. He needs greater markets. He thought that he was going to get a greater market in the United States. Did he get it? Bang! The Americans shut the door in his face in spite of treaties and everything else. That is just in line with what I and other hon. members on the floor of the House said they would do, when we were discussing the reciprocity question. We said that it did hot matter what we did in connection with reciprocity; the very
moment the United States got it they would slam the door in our face, while at the same time shoving their goods into our country.
The elevators of this country are filled with United States wheat, and it is the duty of this Government to embargo their wheat and grain unless they want this country flooded with their products at any price in the next two or three months, resulting in the price of our wheat being reduced to forty or fifty cents a bushel. They will be willing to take several million dollars loss on last year's crop, and on this year's crop, if they can get rid of it and control this market. That would stop their farmers coming to Canada.
Suppose I were a.farmer in the West, and I bought a tractor in Canada and paid a dollar or so more for it because it was a Canadian product-is there not such a thing as nationalism, as love of country? Has all that feeling been taken out of our breasts entirely? I know too much to believe that. But, supposing you do buy an American tractor-every pound of the food that the men who built that tractor in the United States consume is supplied by the growers of American products and you do not supply anything in exchange for the money that you have paid for that tractor. But if you built that tractor in Canada, every dollar that went into its manufacture would go to the men here who were providing a greater market for the men in the West, by consuming their wheat and beef in Canada and God knows we want greater markets.
We want to help the West. The East has never tried, and never will try to injure the West, even in spite of all those new trenches and wire entanglements that they are setting up, and all their threats about what is going to happen to us in the East. We are men of red blood, we are the fathers and brothers of the men who carried Vimy Ridge, took Cambrai, and destroyed the finest units in the German army. You cannot scare us. We never get scared.
My hon. friend the Minister of Colonization and Immigration (Mr. Calder) said that the greatest danger in this country was the politician who was appealing to the soldier. I say that the man who is the most dangerous to the people of this country is the man who is preaching class hatred. The press of the West, with very few exceptions, have been preaching class hatred against the East for a number of years. They have been constantly threatening us and calling upon their people to unite against the East.

What has the East done to the West? The time came when not a pound of western grain could -be sent to Europe. Great Britain, with all her boasted resources, had no money to buy grain or flour two years ago. We have heard a great deal about what free trade has done for Great Britain, but free trade had not increased English industry during the twenty years before the war one-quarter as much as protection had increased the industry of Germany, France and other countries. Great Britain was without any money; she was at the end of her resources and the western crop could not be moved. Where was the West to get its wider markets then? There was no money in Europe to purchase grain. The United States slammed its doors tight. In that situation, did the people of this country stand idly by and do nothing to help? The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) asked the people of Canada to buy Victory bonds in order that the crop should be moved from the West and in order that we might provide Great Britain with the credit that was necessary for the movement of that crop. Was there any demur from the people of the East? They went down in their pockets and bought Victory bonds. The men in the factories that the western people want to close up bought Victory bonds. The little girls working in the factories in the east went without winter clothing to buy bonds in order that the people of England might have food, and that the people of the West might get good prices for their wheat. Is it becoming of the West to come down here, threaten these people and say: We want to close up this factory and that factory because they want ten or fifteen per cent protection; we will send the people employed in those factories over to the United States? We want to buy foreign goods, not Canadian made goods.
And I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that as a matter of fact within the next year the people of this country will have to go down into their pockets to buy another crop in the West. Now would it be well for any manufacturer in the East to go round saying to our workingmen, " I would boycott the West, I would not buy any western flour or any western oatmeal, I would not buy Victory bonds to pay for their wheat or do anything of that kind because those people in the West want to close our factories?" That is exactly the kind of class hatred that some of these men in the West are preaching against the East, though there are hon. gentlemen in this House, representing the Grain Growers' in the West, who are big enough and broad-minded enough not to

take that stand. But it is exceedingly difficult for them to do so:	they are bombarded night and day by telegrams from a lot of men in the West, headed by a man named Wood, who is known to be an avowed annexationist.
I ask the hon. gentleman to prove his statement in regard to Mr. Wood?

It is well known that Mr. Wood and his crowd are the people who have been raising such a row because the Germans in the West lost their votes. We have had hon. gentlemen talk in that way here. The German schools in the West, and the Germanizing of the West rests at their door. They are responsible.
