We know exactly where all this clamour comes from, and we know there is a small clique of these men in the West, so-called leaders of the farmers, there, who are trying to induce them to form Soviets1, and councils of agriculture, [DOT]and this, that, and the other thing which will have the effect of destroying industry and dividing this country. Now I do not pretend, and I do not wish to be so understood to be preaching class hatred of any kind. We have had a little bit of that class, of race hatred between Quebec and Ontario, and nothing has come of it, only perhaps a broken head or two; but the kind of class hatred to which I am alluding touches the life of everybody-it touches the pocket and the employment of all. It is going to tear this country to pieces and destroy its industries-that is exactly what is going to happen. Let me ask hon. gentlemen a question-and I would like them, and the people of this country to ponder well over it-how are you going to get additional employment for the returned soldier in factories if you are going to close those factories? I cannot see how it is going to be done; and to my mind it is disgraceful that there can be found in this Dominion people going about the country preaching class hatred of that kind. I know exactly what I am talking about. Up in my riding ia year ago there was a gathering of farmers, and they sent for me to>
come and direct them. We weire taking council together to find out how they could best increase production for that particular township for the coming year to help in the war. I went there and we had the finest meeting possible. Talk about a class meeting, or a religious meeting-there was nothing at all of the kind that could equal it. When the meeting was over and the assembled farmers had decided that they were going to add five or ten acres of wheat each, so many cattle and hogs, and what they were going to do to make up for

the boys that were away (they were going to help one another anti exchange their labour with each other and do all the good they could) about half past nine a man came in with a grip under his arm and asked if he could be allowed to talk. We said " yes " we were quite willing, and he got up and started in preaching this Bolshevism. First, he wanted to destroy the commercial- travellers because he said they were eating up $500,000,000 a year of the money of this country. Then the lawyers came in for criticism. They were the worst of the lot, they were parasites, the names he called them were something awful. Then he started after the other professions and the manufacturers, and the legislators, and it was only a tirade and torrent of abuse. He had been going along in this way for about half an hour when a farmer rose and objected. He said to me, " Are we going to listen to all this nonsense? Where does this man come from? Is he a pro-German?" I said, "I do not know." Then the farmer asked the man himself, "Where dot you come from?" The man replied that he came from some place in western Ontario. The farmer then said to him, "How do you come to be here preaching this kind of stuff to us, who pays you for coming here?" The man's reply was, "The United Farmers of Alberta sent down a thousand dollars to carry on this propaganda." There is the whole story. Then a farmer said, "You are not preaching Canadian propaganda-you are a disloyal subject and a pro-German," and four or five of the audience made a rush for him and he had to get out of the meeting. That is the kind of propaganda that is being carried on all over the country, and we might as well face the issue now squarely and fairly, we might as well look it fairly in the face and ask ourselves the question, "Are we going to be subjected constantly to these class hatred programmes, or are we going to listen to such trash for the moment in the presence of our dead, or going to try and build Canada into a great country and be a united people.
Now let us look at the question from another aspect. I saw this programme of the Council of Agriculture. It was very nicely and skilfully drawn up, and a man in my riding, a farmer, said to me, "Did you read that platform?" I said, "Yes, I did." "Well, you know," he said, "it reminds me of the dress my old lady wears in the summer." I inquired, "What is that?" He said, "It is a Mother Hubbard." I inquired, "Why is it like a Mother Hub-oard dress?" "Because," he said, "it
covers everything." This programme covers everything. There are only two things left out of it that I can discover, the Ouija Board and the Twentieth Plane, nothing else. Very well, let us examine it. What are the tariff propojsals? I have dealt with those and I have told the House plainly that if you are going to remove the protection that we have we shaill be destroyed industrially. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) put a very pertinent question, and placed his finger on the sore spot when he asked, "Why cannot Canada compete?	That is the whole thing.
I say that in the markets of the world we have had to go out and seek business in competition with the Americans during the last few years. In one export business the manufacture of wire, Canadian manufacturers have increased the business from nothing to $9,000,000 last year in competition with the United States and foreign countries. Why can we not compete at home? That is the question. The reason that iwe cannot compete is because the L mted States will not allow us a free exchange with them.- If we had a free exchange of commodities, of all kinds of manufactured products, with the United States, there is not a manufacturer in the Dominion but would be willing to compete and be very glad to do so. But what has occurred? They never allow us to compete on fair terms. As a matter of fact a great many of the leading manufacturers in Canada to-day have within the last three or four years built factories in the United States, so that when their line of business is wiped out by the western propaganda they can take their workmen over there and find them employment. The United States will welcome them, and protect them with a high tariff. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is that fair to our working men? Is that building up this country? Can we compete under such circumstances? Is there any line of business that we can compete in? Can the grain growers in the West compete with United States at the present moment in the article of wheat?
Yes.
See where you are at the present moment.
There is no doubt we can compete.
You will know inside oi six months whether you can compete or not. You know that to-day you cannot compete to the extent of a bushel of wheat in the foreign markets against American wheat.
We are willing to try.

Unless, as an hon. member said last night, the Government fixes a price for you in your local market you cannot compete and you have to submit
to a loss on the wheat you export for the Americans are going to take a big loss which their government will pay. Who will pay your loss?
What about seed?

I do not say anything about that. We bought seed for the West and I was very pleased to support that^ proposal in Parliament. That is one of the greatest examples of the benefits of a national policy.
Oh, oh.

Wait a moment until I get through. I say that was one of the greatest examples of the benefits of the national policy that I have yet seen, when we bought that seed wheat for the West and especially for Saskatchewan. We bought that wheat and gave it to the farmers, and inside of a year or two it resulted in the addition of over a million bushels yearly to the crop of this country. That was national protection. Now, suppose we had adopted the policy of "do nothing" which these gentlemen teach; what- would have happened then to the West? I am quite in agreement with the hon. member for Maple Creek when he says that we should fix a price for the wheat of the West. That is in line with the National Policy.
May I make a correction? The hon. gentleman has made the straight assertion that I asked this Government to fix the price of wheat.

No, I am wrong there. The grain growers of the hon. gentleman s province asked that, and I will support my hon. friend in this House on that proposal- if he will be a good National Policy man and go in for protection. You cannot blow hot and cold in this matter. You cannot get all your manufactured goods free and then ask the rest of the country to fix a price for your products. That is impossible. We should stand together on all these questions. Having regard to the tremendous production of cereals in the United States, it is a question whether we should go in for cereals as strongly this year as we might.
The hon. gentleman painted a lurid picture last night of what was to happen to the farmers of his province. He said that

the farmers of a community of 100,000 received only something like 370,000,000, or $700 each, from the sale of their exported grain. But only a few days ago the Minister of Agriculture for Saskatchewan was telling the assembled farmers there that that province had marketed over $370,000,000 worth of farm products and that the average income from this source of every farmer in the province was over $3,700. Now, who are we to believe? I believe that the people there are not so badly off. I am inclined to accept Mr. Dunning s statement in preference to that of the member for Maple Creek' (Mr. Maharg), although I have great regard for that hon. gentleman. I think, however, that in the statement which the hon. member for Maple Creek made, he had reference only to wheat, not to other cereals.
Now, I have given you a picture of what is going to happen. You may say: "What are you going to do about it?" I am going to point out the actual facts of the case.
I am going to ask hon. members of this House to forget all this class talk, to remember there are two sides to every question. I sat at the feet of Macdonald and Tupper and other great statesmen. I listened to their arguments, and I became a firm protectionist. I made up my mind that protection does not mean high tariff. It means the assisting of every person in this country when he is in need; it means an effort to build up our country and make it greater to give it a place in the sun. It is not a question of high taxation or low taxation. I am going to deal with the matter of taxes in a few minutes. But let me ask this: Is there anything in the policy of this Council of Agriculture, when you examine it from end to end, which can convince you that the community which adopted that platform has shown any desire to assist in paying the taxes which have been brought about by the great war? The figures will be here in a few days, and I am satisfied that it will then be shown that the people of Toronto are paying more income tax-a form of taxation which all the western members are strongly in favour of

into the Dominion treasury than all the Prairie Provinces are paying. The member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) laughs. He is taking great consolation to himself because the Governments of the United States and of Canada have adopted the income tax. But income tax is only a form of taxation whereby a government raises revenue for its purposes. Various methods of taxation were em-

ployed before the income tax was adopted. In South Africa they have a hut tax; a man pays so much on his hut. In England the tax on window-glass was abolished years ago; people did not dare put window-glass in their houses without being taxed for doing so. Then, there were taxes on the wheels of the carts, so that it was found advisable to have carts with two wheels instead of four. Previous to the war Great Britain did not raise the bulk of its taxation by an income tax. Income tax did not amount to fifty per cent of the taxes raised by Great Britain. She now has a large income tax because there was no other way in which the money of the wealthy people could be got at. The leader of this Government was not careful in his provision for an income tax on the people of this country; he did not distinguish between the people who earn their income by personal exertion and those who derive their income from estates that have been left to them or investments. That distinction is made in Great Britain. For instance, a lawyer like the Minister of Public Works (Hon. F. B. Carvell) has, we will say, an income of $6,000 or $7,000; he is taxed on a certain amount of that, while a farmer alongside of him whose income is the same, if not larger, escapes the income tax entirely by saying: "My income is in the nature of wages; I have worked hard with my hands for my income. What I have spent on my family should be deducted and therefore I do not have to pay any taxes." This man is let off, while the hon. member is taxed. That is not fair.
The income tax is very unjust in many ways. Income tax is a field which is or should be reserved entirely for municipalities. In Toronto I pay an income tax of 3J per cent on the little salary which I get -"indemnity," we call it-from the House of Commons; and other members from Toronto do the same. Then we have to turn around and pay an added tax to the Bomin-ion Government on that same amount. In adopting the system of income tax, the Dominion Government, rightly or wrongly, entered a sphere of taxation which had been reserved for the municipalities. Having done that, it must now go further into it and get after the land sooner or later; then where will our friends the agriculturists come in? The platform of the Council of Agriculture states that tnere should be a tax on land that is not used. Well, go ahead and do that, and in a few years there will be no land that is not used; then where will you get your taxes? The next step will
then be the placing of a tax on the farm. After the great Napoleonic War there was a land tax in England of eight shillings on every acre of farm land. Considering the direct tax you would have to put on the farmers of this country if you abolish custom duties, as compared with that imposed upon other classes, two dollars an acre would be a fair amount to impose on farm lands. Every farmer in this country would, therefore, if you are going to adopt the system of directly taxing their property, have to pay two dollars an acre as his share of that taxation. What Government would carry out that idea and live? If you are going to wipe out the industries that are now supplying $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 of this taxation by taxing their output, where will you then go to get your money? The declarations of the Council of Agriculture are revolutionary; they include many of the platforms of the Soviets. If you put the tax all on one thing and thus wipe out that thing altogether, then, of course you wipe out the taxation. How can you get an income out of the factory in the East if you take steps which cause the factory to be closed and it has moved to the United States?
I warn every man, woman and child in this country who earns his living by industry to beware of agitations of this kind. I ask every man, woman or child who owns a Victory Bond: What is going to be it? value if this policy is carried out? If the leader of the Government intends to adopt this policy of cutting down protection, to whom is he going to appeal when he again wants to sell Victory Bonds? What will be the result of such a policy? Can he sell his bonds to the Council of Agriculture? This country has only a small population. It comprises a number of provinces and those provinces have many divergent interests. Let me briefly sketch the condition of affairs in each province, and then let me ask the people of those provinces whether they are prepared to adopt an agrarian policy as against an industrial policy?
Let me first consider 'that province down by the sea which is represented by the leader of the Opposition . (Mr. McKenzie). He could tell me that at the present time hundreds of workingmen are walking the streets of the towns of 'that province, waiting to see what the action of the Government is going to be in the matter of protection of industries. At the present moment in Canada, -all industry is paralysed, standing still. Gentlemen will have to ex-

cuse me for using such strong language, because I am not accustomed 'to doing so; but I am a good patriot-at least I hope so; indeed, I hope we are all good patriots and when some one introduces such an antinational policy at such a critical time, it is like a bugler sounding the retreat to our army when the Germans are upon them. That is the position we are in. In my hon. friend's province down by the sea there is a vast quantity of coal; but owing to the policy that has been adopted of taking away the ships from this country and using them elsewhere, the coal industry of Nova Scotia lias languished, and instead of Canada supplying South America, Central America and part of Europe with coal, as She could have done if we bad been allowed to use our own ships, our ships are taken away from us, no effort is made to replace them, and the collieries are virtually idle. The coal industry >and the steel industry of Nova Scotia are great industries and the steel industry will, if it is properly developed, be one of the greatest industries in the world. If is far greater than that of Germany because Germany has lost her iron fields, whereas Canada has her iron and her coal fields there. What can a policy of agriculture to offer to the province of Nova Scotia? It means that if you remove the taxes, the manufacture of agricultural and other implements will fall into the bands of United States manufacturers and there will be less iron and coal needed from Nova Scotia. The result will be that many of 'those brave Nova Scotians-and in Nova Scotia is to be found the finest class of industrial people on the continent-will start the same old exodus of twenty years ago into the New England States. It is these people who went into these States in the old days who have made itheir industries what they are. At the present time, if you go into one of the manufacturing concerns in the New England States an'd ask to see the skilled mechanic, Who is running the plant, the master-mechanic, the man who does the designing, you will find What? That he is a Nova Scotian. Eecently, I had occasion to go to Pittsburg to consult one of the greatest metallurgists in the world. After we had talked for a while, he said: " You will be surprised to know that I am a Scotch Canadian." I said: "Are you?" " Yes," he said, " 'my father moved to the New England States when I was a small boy, and I was born in Nova Scotia." Nova Scotia has never had a proper opportunity; it has never bad a 'tin roof put on its in-
dustries. Some people, even amongst Nova Scotians, are continually preaching against the industries of that province. What has Nova Scotia to expect out of grain farming? Nothing at all. The country is, to a certain extent, rough, and is not adapted to agriculture; it would barely feed its own population. Nevertheless, Nova Scotia, with all its wealth of coal and iron, can easily sustain an industrial population of 20 000,000. Its coal and iron, is on the sea-board, where it should compete with the world.
Let me come now to New Brunswick, and we find similar conditions in its forests and mines. Nothing is being done to develop its fisheries, although there are great fisheries there. If this country had taken the proper stand, so far as the fisheries of that province are concerned, it would have provided cold storage facilities, so that the fisheries oi New Brunswick-and the same may be said of Nova Scotia-would have been supplying frozen fish to Europe in competition with the whole world. But they cannot compete. Why? Because they have not the money to provide themselves with the necessary transportation to put their products on the markets of the world. Assistance from the Government is necessary, and a national policy is a policy that would provide them with ships and cold storage and would see that their fish were put on the markets of the world.
In Quebec there are great water-powers, vast iron fields, great forests and large industries. The finest workers to he found in Canada are from Quebec. The people of Quebec are an industrial people, and there is no reason why, with her cheap power, Quebec should not be the Manchester of the whole of North America. In textiles, in manufactures that require power and skilled workmen, she has made tremendous strides. Does the man or woman who works in a factory in Quebec want to have that factory closed? The manufacturers can always, in some way or another, escape disaster; he will cash in, and move to the United States, but the workingman, when the factory is closed, cannot cash in. He has to give up his house, losing what he invested in it. He will have to leave his own parish, losing everything, and go to the United States in order to carry on business there. For many years, while we were fighting for industries in this country, many of the people of Quebec were unfortunately compelled to go to foreign factories in order to earn a livelihood. When the National Policy was endorsed by that great leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose seat is now vacant,

when he refused to destroy the industries of the country at the behest of some of his followers-and he was a greater protectionist than many so-called protectionists, because they did not practise what they preached- his province began to develop its industries on a greater scale, the workers came back, and emigration ceased. These people did great service in this war in manufacturing munitions. If Quebec had not an industrial population it could not do that. If it had not cheap power it could not do that. It has all that is necessary to make a country great industrially. Is there anything for Quebec in a policy that destroys the factory and fosters nothing but agriculture; that wipes out all those great factories and turns them into turnip fields?
I wag almost forgetting that little green island called Prince Edward, down by the sea. It is an agricultural island, but still it is a model of thrift, and its cities and towns are gradually acquiring factories. It has a good, sound, well educated population. It is like Denmark. Denmark has no coal and it is the greatest agricultural country in the world, but still one-third of the population of Denmark is an industrial population, employed in factories.
Let us see what resources Ontario possesses. Ontario and Quebec have the cheapest power in the world. This war has taught us at least one thing, and that is this: Coal is power, water is power. Power is everything. The country that has the cheapest power is the country that is going to dominate the industries of the world, if that country is given the opportunity. Coal will never be a dollar a ton again. I used to buy lots of coal for a dollar a ton, but you cannot buy it at any such figure in the United States now. Coal will never go back to a dollar a ton again, unless, perhaps, in Alberta. We have power in Ontario and power in Quebec. We can harness that power on to the belt of a machine at a price equal to a dollar a ton coal. When we do that we can compete with the world, but we cannot compete with the United States in the way its goods are sold in this country. Let me point out one way in which they have, to my personal knowledge, competed with Canadian manufacturers, and I will ask you if such a course is fair. The Globe, in its discussion of the wire industry, stated that a large quantity of wire products had been sold Vy the United States in western Canada last year. That is true. How does it happen that while we are sending thousands of tons of wire products out of this country in competition with the United States, the United States can com-36
pete with us in the home markets? On that class of goods the tariff is very small. This is the method the United States' manufacturers adopt: During the whole period of the war the base price of nails in Pittsburg was about $3.50 per hundred pounds. That was the price quoted on your order. If you were an American and went to Pittsburg for a car of nails they would say: "The ordered price is $3.50 per hundred weight in car lots." I might say that I wanted a carload of nails to sell in Indiana. They would ask me when I wanted the nails. I might say: "Next week, because there are a lot of farmers there wanting to build farm houses." They would reply, "Very sorry, we will book your order, but we cannot guarantee to deliver until after the war." Then you wotdd be stumped and would have to buy "spot" nails. The price of "spot" nails ranged from $5.00 to $5.50; that was the export price to all foreign countries except Canada. * The conditions were then, that if you were an American and wanted nails for immediate delivery, you had to pay $5.50, but if you were a Canadian you could have the nails delivered next week at $3.50, the ordered price, because they want to put Canadian industries out of business. The Canadian manufacturers sold nine million dollars worth of wire products in competition with American manufacturers in the markets of the world last year, and at the same time the Americans took our market here. They are doing exactly the same thing with wheat, by putting an embargo on it. That is their policy every time-to drive our industries out of business-and they have no more mercy on a Canadian farmer than for any other Canadian manufacturer; and the farmer is the biggest manufacturer Canada has.
We now come to consider the province of Ontario from an industrial standpoint. We have the largest amount of developed water-power, and we have a thrifty population. Toronto is a great city. Some people call it "Hogtown," but its heart beats true to the people, and industries of this country, no matter where they are located. It has just as soft a spot in its heart for the men of the West as for any other people in the world. Why, most of the people now living in the West originally came from Ontario. Manitoba is peopled almost entirely by people from this province, and I know the heart of the West responds to the heartbeats of Ontario. Ontario's policy is to build up everything in this country, so that one day Canada will have her place in the sun with other na-



tions. The province is rich in iron. It has no coal, except white coal, hut where in the world can you find more silver than in Ontario, where can you find gold mines greater or better developed than in our province? The Hollinger mine is the greatest gold mine in the world.
I want to tell the House something about the iron mines of Ontario. We have great fields of iron which have never been touched, but there is not a workable area of iron ore in the province an acre in extent that has not been staked out and owned by the alien. In the United States millions of dollars are invested in the iron business; there is more money involved in that business than the value of the whole resources of Canada. These corporations are not interested in opening up iron mines in Ontario. To show how they operate, there are great deposits of iron in Minnesota. A new range had recently been discovered known as the Cayuna range. Some poor men owned that range at first, but later an option was taken on the property by a great iron corporation in the United States, which put in two years diamond drilling on. the range. When they got through they said to the owners: "We are very sorry, hut we cannot exercise our option as (here is no ore there " That is the kind of stunner the people of Canada get Who are interested in iron areas, after they are examined by American corporations, unless the property should be of proved value, when it might be taken over and shut down. As it happened, there were men of money on that Cayuna Range and they, the owners, proceeded to develop it with their own money, and last year the range turned out to be one of the great iron areas of the United States. That shows that the iron corporation which had an option on the property was only interested in keeping the iron out of the market. That is what these people would do with the iron deposits of Ontario, just to keep the iron out of our markets. I hope that fresh discoveries of iron will be made in the province of Ontario and, as a good National Policy man, I trust the Government will do something to assist the iron mining industry of this country, and then the province of Ontario will take its rightful place as a great producer if iron.
The province of Manitoba is a great graingrowing country. The farmers of that province have become wealthy and have decided to make their homes there. They have beautiful farms, and houses like the chateaux of France. The city of Winnipeg has cheaper power than almost any city in the

world and is destined to be one of our greatest manufacturing cities-greater even than St. Paul or St. Louis. I do not know whether I shall live to see that day, but it will undoubtedly come if the Government adopts the policy I should like to see adopted, because Winnipeg has cheaper power, an active population, and other advantages. The northern part of Manitoba contains untold mineral wealth. In that district is the Mandy mine, one of the greatest copper mines in the world. Rich gold and nickel mines have also been discovered in this province. What is this country doing to assist in the development of those mines? Nothing. I am not one of those who want to see public money thrown away at the present juncture, but I would say that it is the duty of the Government, in the case of mines that have been proved to contain forty to fifty million dollars worth of ore, to build railways to bring out the products of the mines. The late J. J. Hill used to say that one good copper mine in the West was better than a whole wheat county. I do not know whether that is true or not, but if what the best experts in the world say of the mines of northern Manitoba is true we have a wonderful source of wealth there, which will mean a great future for the province of Manitoba and the country as a whole. I hope to see the day when the province of Manitoba will march along with Ontario. Hon. members may be surprised to know that in the particular business in which I am engaged we can buy manufactured goods from the city of Winnipeg and bring them down to Ontario cheaper than we can get those go.ods from our local mills. We ship our product in jute bags, and we bought those bags in the city of Winnipeg cheaper than we could have got them in Ontario or the East. Our staves we buy from New Brunswick. This goes to show that the industries of this country are closely interlinked together and that there is no inter-provincial divisions. We. must all realize that, and not be small and narrow and provincial.
I now come to the province of Saskatchewan. One of the things the people of that province want is the abolition of the duty on cement. Now if there is one business that the AVest is succeeding in, it is the manufacture of cement. Ontario no longer makes any cement for the West. All the cement the West uses, and it uses a great deal, is manufactured in the West. Saskatchewan has rich fields of clay for cement, and great areas of cheap coal to burn that cement, and is destined to be one of the

great cement producing districts in the world.
There is another point. Can any hon. member tell me of any industry involving manual labour and the use of power that has been established in this country without the help of a protective tariff ? We all know, if we read the history of the United States aright, that the greatest industry in that country is cotton, and that the cotton industry was not firmly established in the United States for many years until after a stout protective tariff was put on cotton so as to give their own cotton growers a chance against East Indian cotton. Can anybody point to one single industry established in Canada that has not been protected? In Saskatchewan there are great areas of natural gas and coal, and areas of oil that undoubtedly have not yet been discovered in that great province, which I believe will be one of the greatest manufacturing provinces in the Confederation. There are also great mineral resources, such as asphaltum, in the northern parts of that territory. We have been establishing councils of research to see what industries we can establish. Permit me, Sir, to point out one industry which we could establish by a national policy. There is no duty on pottery coming into Canada. We have no potteries. Consider the millions of dollars worth of china that is brought into Canada, yet, strange to say, the china clay, feldspar and all the materials that go to make pottery in the United States are imported into the United States from Canada, and all the cups and saucers and chinaware used there are manufactured from Canadian materials. Why should we let ourselves be robbed of our natural resources in that way? Why should the pottery industry not be established in Canada? I understand there are great deposits of china clay in Saskatchewan. Now, why should not thousands of soldiers who are engaged in potteries in England not be brought to these provinces so that a great industry might be established in this country? There are also vast areas of glass sand in Canada. We had a small glass industry in Canada, but whisky bottles were all that we made, because that was the only line protected. Window glass to the value of $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 a year,-and up to even $15,000,000 is used in Canada. But we have no window glass industry in this country because there has been no duty on window glass, and you cannot establish an industry under such circumstances. One half of the wire industry of this country is without protection, and if this Government would place a proper 361
protective tariff on it I am confident in saying that a whole division of returned soldiers could be absorbed in that industry alone. We have not these industries simply because there is no duty. There is no better glass sand than is to be found in the West, and we should be making all the glass windows that are needed for our stores, and for the stores of the Empire, and I believe we could secure the trade of Australia and foreign countries if we had such an industry here. But all the people of Saskatchewan do not approve of this agitation and class hatred, and they are looking forward to the day when Saskatoon and Regina and all those fine cities there will see the wheels of industry running, and every village will have its factories. There is no reason why this should not be so, and why the western farmer should not take his automobile in the evening and go into town and meet his boy and girl at the factory and go to the movies. That would be the proper condition in this country, but you cannot live miles from civilization and make yourself believe that that is right. Why, Mr. Speaker, if I were to believe the doctrine that is being preached by alleged representatives of agriculture, I would not think of advising returned soldiers or any body else to go into farming, for they would be nothing more nor less than slaves. You cannot preach that doctrine to the farmer, because he knows better. The farmers of Ontario are thrifty, having in their houses all the modern conveniences of the city home. They are becoming wealthy land-owners, and have all their money in the Ontario factories; and that is why they voted against reciprocity.
If we took the tariff off and reverted to free trade and that policy came before the people of this country again they would reject it. Now, as regards Alberta, the German Empire has 4.5 per cent of the coal of the world. Alberta has 124 per cent. Canada has 174 per cent of the coal of the world, and yet Germany built an Empire on 44 per cent. Now, if we are really Canadians we will not do one single act in this House or elsewhere that would tend to delay the day when Canada will take her proper place as the greatest manufacturing country in the world, with all the resources we have. I have never seen iron in Michigan or 'Minnesota to equal that of Alberta. There is in that province everything that goes to make a country great. It possesses the elements to make it the greatest steel and iron producing section of the whole of North America. " That is all right, Colonel," you say, " but why not let all the coal fields there be used to grow wheat? Never mind

about the coal." Well, when I was a young man, twenty-five years ago, .1 was in Colorado. In that state it was all gold mining, Cripple creek was booming and any one who mentioned the iron industry would be run out. The idea of Colorado competing with Pittsburg in the iron or steel business was considered absurd. But what has happened? To-day Colorado has forgotten about Cripple creek and although it is far away in the Western States it has an iron and steel industry that produces great wealth, and is of considerable importance, and will compare with any steel and iron centre in the world. At that time no mention could ever be made of iron. I hope to see the day -if this country adopts a proper system of protection, when the province of Alberta will put Pittsburg and all those iron regions in the United States in the shade. Its coal resources are far greater than Pennsylvania ever dreamed of, it has iron and gas, and all it needs is a policy of protection to encourage investment there, and the building of railroads to connect the iron with the coal fields, and the coal fields and iron fields with the natural gas resources, and Alberta will have a greater iron industry than the world has ever seen. Yet the farmers of Alberta, headed by a man named Wood, want all the industries of the East destroyed, and would discourage the eastern man who would like to go to develop these resources from going West and investing his dollar there. Has Alberta after all staked its all in agriculture? Has Saskatchewan staked its all in agriculture? Agriculture is only one of the dozen eggs they have in the basket. And Manitoba? Well, it does not follow the programme of the agriculturalists when it comes to voting. And let me turn to ask the province by the sea in the west, British Columbia, with its great areas of coal and iron, and its water-powers beyond the comprehensions of the world. No country in the world has such great hidden wealth as British Columbia. It has a great wealth of minerals, a great wealth of coal, and enormous forest wealth, it is capable of producing tremendous quantities of paper.
As to fisheries, no country can equal it. Well, British Columbia is British Columbia and after all British Columbia is not the "West" British Columbia is the place where the east and west meet. If we are going to have foreign trade one of the great channels oi the country through which that trade will pass will be British Columbia. Our greatest field for foreign trade is the Orient, and Australasia.
Now, you may ask me:	What do you
suggest doing? That is the question, if I IMr. Currie.]
had the doing, I would immediately place an embargo upon the grain and manufactured products of every other country. Talk about the handling of grain! Those men who talk about grain-growing in the West, those men who control the grain of the West, allow a small coterie of Americans to get in ahead of them and to fill our terminal elevators with grain while they have their grain still in the granaries. It is absurd. The time has oome when no alien should be allowed to own any of the granaries or transportation resources of this country. I do not care who he may be, or how friendly he may be. They have now blocked all our elevators with their grain. If the agriculturists of the West had devoted as much of their time to looking after their own interests as far as the elevators are concerned as after the affairs of the eastern manufacturers they would not have allowed their elevators to be stuffed with American grain while their own wheat is still in the fields and granaries.
The hon. member for Maple Creek made reference to the late lamented leader of the Liberal party, and he said that he was the man who first brought the elevators in the West to time. The western elevators are not brought to time. I have in my pocket a report on these western elevators which I might read, but I have no desire to extend my remarks. There are men in this House who are interested in these terminal elevators. Mr. Speaker, will you be surprised when I tell you that last year the overage-that is the amount of grain that was illegally taken from the farmers in the West by the elevators amounted to over $2,000,000. Has there been any kick? Or any row raised about that with the elevators?-No. Why? The -Grain Growers own elevators and I understand the earnings of that company last year were 44J per cent. There is no manufacturing industry in the East that can -compare with that, not even Sir Joseph Fl-avelle's. Let us take the mote out.of our own eye before we remove the beam from any body else's.
What would I do? The situation is very grave. Let us drop all this trade controversy for the moment. Let us assist the Government and back it- up. Let us insist upon the adoption of a policy of embargo similar to that which every other country has adopted so that when we g-o into treaty making we will have a jack knife in a trade we will have -a jimmy that will force some of our products into the markets -of those countries. This is the way to provide foreign markets for our products.
There -is only one way to get those foreign markets and that is by providing pro-

per transportation at sea. There has been a great deal of talk about this 'Government giving contracts for building ships but that is the wisest thing the Government ever did and there is not a ship building on our stocks to-day that could not be sold tomorrow for a great deal more money than it is costing us to Japan or some other nation. That is ia fact that everybody in the business knows. Those ships should be put on those lines of transportation, not between Canada and broken down European countries which have been devastated by the war but between Canada, South and Central America. South Africa, India, China, Japan, Australia and New Zealand. What did the export of our manufactured _ goods last year amount to outside of munitions? It amounted to over half a billion dollars, principally to these countries. If this Government provided lines of transportation So that goods can be transported from Canadian factories to the markets of the world at less than they can be carried from the factories of Germany, France or the United States, we can get the market. We will get them. It will not matter then so much if the Americans come in and sell their stuff here; we can carry on and Canada will become a great manufacturing country and its products will find a market all over the world. The American manufacturers want a market at their door. They are afraid to go abroad in search of markets. It is only the big companies there that seek the foreign markets. The manufacturer in Canada has sought a market for his goods abroad; he has more courage than any other man in the world. When they were asked to make shells the Canadian manufacturers supplied their own money and financed themselves whereas in every other country the manufacturers were financed by the government. If you provide the Canadian manufacturer with transportation they will get the business. You would imagine from listening to those who are trying to stir up class hatred that the Canadian manufacturer is a terrible man. The manufacturer has a heart like any other man. He has a wife and family, he tries to do good in the community. He sometimes goes to church on Sunday. He is not such an awful man as he is pictured. When it comes to the question of patriotism the manufacturer takes no back seat to any grain-grower or any other person in the community. He has given a great deal to the war. What did the manufacturer do when he was asked to make munitions? In England they gave the manufacturer the money with which to put in his
machinery and to finance the payment of his workmen. In this country the manufacturer had to go down on his knees and dig and shovel for himself. He did that and he made munitions cheaper than in any other country in the world. Did he not play his part in this war? You would think that it was not the man fighting in the trenches who won the war but that it was somebody away back on a farm or little village who talked politics. It makes me tired to hear such nonsense as that. Let us take a big view of this question. The manufacturer has done his share. He only asks what is fair and square. He does not want the country to adopt a policy that is _ going to drive his workmen out of his factory and into a foreign country. Nor, does he want to be driven out of the country himself. He wants to be considered a Canadian. His profits have not been as great as those of any other class of the community. I mentioned that the grain growers' profits were 44J per cent. I do not believe that any of these manufacturers have ever made such a profit as that. Let us forget all that and let us be big. Let us adopt the policy of Canada for the Canadians. Let us adopt a policy that will give employment to our soldiers and to every class of the community. We cannot grow up to be a great nation if one foot-the industrial foot-is bound up like the foot of a Chinese lady who goes limping about. We cannot make this a great country unless it is well balanced. The United States is an example to us in that respect. The United States is a great country and under normal conditions it does not care whether it exports its cereals or not. In case of war the United States could live alone. It is a self-contained country. Germany was almost in the same position before the war. It adopted a form of national policy and aspired to national greatness. One hundred years ago Germany was composed of a hundred very small states but they united and Germany became a great industrial country. She was foolish enough to commence this war in the effort to dominate the world industrially. She made a mistake as a result of which her dream of world power has been shattered but not her industries. Her industries will come back again and her -products will seek the markets of the world later on. Are we prepared to give them free trade?
I have put before the House the views of those who look upon this question in the same way as I do. I sat at the feet of the fathers of the National Policy; I have

listened to their arguments. I have nothing to go back upon in that respect. I am a Liberal-Conservative. I believe in the National Policy and I do not believe in giving way one inch to sectionalism, to one part of this country in opposition to the interests of another part. My party is not in any sense represented in this Govern-ernment. We realize that. We were quite willing-
Some lion. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen need not laugh. I am stating facts. The Conservative party could have carried on. It never needed to ask anybody to come in, but when this war was on, in the greatness of their hearts, there was not a single man of the party that was not willing to ask other members of this House or gentlemen outside who were of the same views as we were in regard to carrying on the war, to come in and take a share of the responsibility. But the Conservative party did not have before it, when that question was discussed, the trade issue. We did not have that before us, and we did not invite people into the Government of the day who were going to adopt the policy that would be destructive in its effects on agriculture or the industries of the country. We did not follow the policy that was adopted in Great Britain, the policy of governing by groups whereby the Unionists have their own caucus and their own whips, the Conservatives have their own caucus and their own whips, and the Liberals who went over to the Liberal-Unionist ranks have their own caucus and their own whips. According to that rule, which is an historic one, we, the Conservatives in this House, should have had our own whips and our own caucus, and be represented directly in the Government by our own ministers. We did not do that, we were big and broad enough not to press for that. The Conservatives in this House have not held any caucus, and have not decided, or taken, any ground as far as any of the policies of the country are concerned -we were quite willing to leave that to the Union Government as an Administration. Other groups have caucused. But if there is going to be a change, if there is going to be deviation by the adoption of any policy that violates the principles of the historic Conservative party, there will be, without question, a caucus and a meeting of the Conservative party of this country in convention. It will foregather and we snail see who is going to have the funeral-we shall have a state funeral of some kind.

There is no doubt about -	- can set that
down as being as certain as that the sun rises in the East every day. After all the sacrifices that the members of that party have undergone for the sake of peace and unity and the building up of this country, if the principles which they have fought for to build up this country, and with which we have beaten our opponents again and again-and we can beat them again with the same policies-are going to be violated, and if it is intended to come down to a policy of compromise, all I can say is, "Nothing doing." I come from a race of Covenanters, and we do not compromise. There will be a decision very soon on this matter, and whatever that decision will be. upon it will depend to a large extent the future prosperity of this country. What have our men fought for? What have they died for, for wrhat reason have they written, the name 01 Canada large in the four corners of the whole world, if we are going to adopt a policy of retrogression, if we are going to stand still. It cannot be done. We must march on, and I would ask my friends on both sides in this House, and in all parts of Canada, who are lovers of their country and like to see things moving along, to drop all this piffle about Free Trade that we had before the war when there were no real issues at stake. There is only one great issue before the people of this country at the present moment, there is only one great issue for every man in this House, and that is the future success of Canada. Now that the war is over that is the great subject that confronts us. Let us think of that constantly, let us forget our own personal interest and put the interests of Canada above everything else.
iMr. MICHAEL CLARK (Red Deer): Does not my hon. friend, who has just taken his seat, think it would be wise ro give the evidence of a direct quotation before he makes a statement in this House that a gentleman occupying so important a public position as Mr. Wood-the United Farmers' President in Alberta-is an annexationist?

Unfortunately I have not got the statement here to prove it, but it is well known that during the Reciprocity fight Mr. Wood was trying to preach the doctrine of annexing this country to the United States, or making this country an adjunct of the Republic. He is an American bom, and he thought he had all the Americans in western Canada behind him in that propaganda. Unfortunately for him, when the war broke out, and the Americans were

drawn into the struggle, those settlers of that nationality in the West gave every evidence that they are just as good and loyal Canadians as the rest of the people of Canada. I have not got the quotation, but it is well known in the East and spoken of everywhere, that Mr. Wood was an avowed annexationist-that his object is to annex this country to the United States.
If that is not the case, I am very sorry "to put him in wrong." Until such time, however, as he changes his belief I shall have to adhere to my description of him.
Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIlEUX (Maison-neuve): The House will not expect that in the few observations I have to offer I shall discuss the rival policies of Free Trade and Protection. Opportunity will be afforded during the debate on the Budget to deal with that very important issue; but it strikes me, after having listened to the remarks of my good friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that there is something wrong in his arguments about high protection, and about the future of this country, both of which he has linked together. If I gathered rightly from his remarks, he preached the doctrine of wider markets for Canada, and at the same time advocated a policy of embargo against foreign goods.
I am only a layman, I do not pose as an authority on economics, or to have slept with Adam Smith by my bedside-although I admit some familiarity with the works of that great economist-but it seems to me that the Canadian manufacturer and the Canadian Government would have very poor results indeed if they were to place an embargo on the goods of foreign countries.

I think the hon. gentleman mistakes the purpose of an embargo. There is such a thing as an embargo, and there is also a system of licensing. The embargo would be placed against the goods of foreign countries coming into Canada; the licensing system is applied to goods exported by some countries.
Mr. LEMIlEUX:	I understood my hon.
friend to advocate placing an embargo on goods coming from the United States.
My hon. friend is correct as to that.

At all events it is clear
in my mind from what my friend said that the high protectionists of Canada all want things their own way, and those who do not share their opinions are to be termed Bolshevists.
I have listened to the lecture which my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) has read his colleagues on that side of the House. I am not impertinent enough to desire to intervene in the quarrel	or quarrels that
may exist. All	these rows,	which
have taken place in the House since the beginning of this debate, will,
I am sure, be transferred to-morrow, if I am well informed, to the caucus. We do not see any latch-string at the door ^ for entrance to that caucus, but 1 can offer some advice at least to my good friends-if the worst comes to the worst, let them follow the Queensbury rules.
Mr. Speaker, this debate has lasted long enough, and should soon come to an end.
I do not intend, therefore, to offer any lengthy remarks this afternoon; I shall make them as concise as possible in order to expedite the business of the House.
First of all, I join with members on both sides of the House in tendering my most sincere congratulations to the two young members who moved (Mr. Redman) and seconded (Mr. Manion) the Address. I think it will be agreed that they are an addition to the debating power of the House of Commons.
I wish also to congratulate my friend the member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) upon the great honour which has been conferred upon him in his selection as leader of the Liberal party during the present session. His fidelity to his late leader and his loyalty to his friends and to the principles which they represent have been tested by his clansmen sitting at your left, Mr. Speaker. He was not deterred by clamour or by passion from doing what he conceived to be right. He knew in days gone by how to steer his course; he was not deceived by false lights on the shore; and that explains why he sits where he does to-day.
The member for North Cape Breton and Victoria succeeds, as has been said by several others, a great leader, one of the great Canadians of the age. It seems to me that in the disappearance from public life of the lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier a giant oak has fallen in the forest. I believe that I express the sentiments of the House when I say of him:
The Knight's hones are dust,
And his good sword rust;
Hils soul is with the saints, I trust.
Mr. Speaker, 'Sir Wilfrid Laurier is gone from our midst; but his spirit is still with us. I believe that on both sides of the House we can find inspiration in the noble life and lofty ideals of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Allusion has been made in this House and outside of this House-notably in a

manifesto issued by the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Hon. Mr. Fielding) during the last election, when a division occurred in the ranks of the Liberal party- to the "Quebec situation." I admit that there has been a Quebec situation, unfortunately; but time is a great healer and the clash will not last forever. Already I see signs in and out of this House which indicate that the time is not far distant when the estrangement between the old province of Quebec and the rest of the Dominion will be a thing of the past. I say that the clash cannot last, because there are men of good-will on both sides of politics and amongst all races. The extremists, unfortunately, have had sway of late.; now has struck the hour of moderation and for moderate men. There was a Quebec situation, as was stated by the member for Shelburne and Queen's in his manifesto; but it was not of our making. It was very easy in 1870 for Bismarck to create a French situation by the sending of a false despatch from Ems. So it was easy in 1917 to create a Quebec situation, which, I repeat, was not of her own making.
I read during my leisure hours the speeches of that great Irishman who is acknowledged as foremost amongst English orators. You will notice that when the Irishmen produce a man of genius, John Bull, who looks always after number one, takes him unto himself. I have always been struck with the following phrase from one of Edmund Burke's speeches, which I would like some of my friends to read and to ponder;
It looks to me narrow and pedantic to apply the ordinary ideas of criminal justice to this great public contest. I do not know the method of drawing up an indictment against a whole people.
Mr. Speaker, as I stated a moment ago, there was a Quebec situation during 1917, but it was concocted, it was planned, it was matured, and it was launched, by expert hands. It was engineered by a patriot, Sir Clifford Sifton, aided and abetted by two other knights of equal fame, Sir Joseph Flavelle and Sir William Mackenzie; and it was worked up to a frenzy by a subsidized press. A clear and far-seeing man like my esteemed friend and ex-colleague, the member for Shelburne and Queen's, might have . discovered the eye-wash, the camouflage, because they were of the same creation as those of 1911 which destroyed the policy of my hon. friend, advocated by us during that year. Mr. Speaker, it was given to a plain Scotch "hielander" to discern it. The member for Shelburne and 
__	Queen S'stated the other evening
5 p.m. that gratitude was a scarce commodity. Unfortunately it is, but the Liberals of this Dominion and their representatives in this Parliament have not exhausted their supply of gratitude; and that is why at the opening of this session, on the morrow of the death of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, unanimously and enthusiastically they entrusted their political soul to a Scotch Presbyterian whose head is as cool as the snow-capped mountains of the highlands, and whose heart is as warm as the glens of dear old Scotia.
I do not need to import into this House the domestic affairs of the Liberal party. At the beginning of the session the leader of the Opposition held out the olive.branch to those hon. gentlemen who differed from us on a single issue relating to the war: to accept or reject it, as they might choose. This friendly offer was undoubtedly the extending of a privilege, if they chose to avail themselves of it, to hon. gentlemen to whom it was made. But it has been a surprise to the members to your left, Mr. Speaker, to hear some hon. gentlemen impute motives and intentions on the part of the leader of the Opposition that we know were not entertained by him when he made	this .offer
out of the goodness of his heart.
May I, therefore, be pardoned if I refer briefly to what was said on this score by my old colleague and esteemed friend, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding)? The hon. gentleman gave us a good deal of gratuitous advice in the course of which he coupled up the friendly invitation of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) with the claim said to have been made by some person or persons connected with the Liberal party to the effect that when the upheaval took place in 1917, those who remained true to their leader became the possessors of the Ark of the Covenant of Liberalism. Personally,-and I am pretty well informed on the affairs of the Liberal party-I do not know of any such ' claim having been made. Thank Heaven! in the Liberal party we respect individual opinions; we can differ and yet remain Liberals. I do, however, know that in repelling the persistent attacks of certain newspapers, when they continuously sneered at us and claimed that we were not real Liberals, but mere Laurier Liberals, we were obliged in self defence to direct public attention to certain historic facts; and perhaps it would he well that I should do so again in order to remove any misconception that, may exist in the mind of the hon. member for

Shelburne and Queen's or in that of any other hon. gentleman on this subject.
Estrangements and divisions have taken place before to-day in the Liberal party in Canada and in other countries. It is a common occurrence in the traditions of the Liberal party that at times the members ol that party may differ. Take the history of English Liberalism. In 1886, some Liberals of the Rowellian type differed with Mr. Gladstone. If I mistake not, the Liberals who left Mr. Gladstone on the Home Rule question and who joined the Unionist party of the time, became leaders of the Conservative party of to-day. Has not the same thing occurred at a later date? When Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman was the leader of the Liberal party in 1900 there was again a difference of opinion; and I am told, in fact I know, that the Liberals who left him on that occasion, left him for good, joining the Conservative party, and they are at the present time still within the ranks of that party. On those two occasions, therefore, it is historically true that the custodians of the Ark of the Covenant of Liberalism were those who remained true and faithful to Gladstone and to Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman.

I am sure, knowing my hon. friend's mind, and appreciating as I do that he does not wish to be historically inaccurate, he will permit me to say that in the case of the Liberal-Unionist split, Sir George Trevelyan was one of two Liberal-Unionists who participated in the famous round-table conference for the reunion of the Liberal party. Afterwards, Sir George Trevelyan, on his own initiative, returned to the Liberal party.

I can quote chapter and verse in support of my own opinion. I can tell my hon. friend that Lord Lans-downe was a Liberal until he left Gladstone on the Home Rule question and became one of the leaders of the Tory party in England. Earl Grey, a former Governor General, left Gladstone and became one of the leaders of the Tory party. I may say that Lord Rosebery left Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, and Lord Rosebery is today considered one of the leaders of the Im-peralist party in England. I could give name after name; but it is true, as a matter of history-and my fibn. friend cannot deny it-that those who remained with Gladstone and with Campbell-Bannerman represented the Liberal thought of England.
!So it was in Canada at the time of Confederation. Take the example of George
Brown. In 1885, in 1890, in 1891 and in 1911-on each of these occasions of political disturbance, the Liberal leader and those who remained true to him wei'e regarded as the custodians of the Ark of the Covenant of Canadian Liberalism. Does the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) contend that the upheaval of 1917 must be considered as an exception to the rule, and that because of the personality of this or that gentleman who then broke with the Liberal party, the records of the past and the teachings of history must be ignored? If so, he will find few to agree with him-more particularly when it is borne in mind that by a statute of this Parliament, the leader of the Opposition is officially recognized. I will say this to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's that there is another side to the Indian story which he told the House the other day. The wigwam was not lost; the Indian was lost. The Indian left the primeval forest in the morning; he met some white trash, drank some fire water, and in the evening when he came back into the bush, he could not find the wigwam. I would advise my hon. friend to hold another parley with John, the Indian, and say to him: "John, the wigwam is not lost; the wigwam is just where it always was, but the old chief, against whom we took the war path is dead; and so you might as well put away your tomahawk and scalping knife and come in from the war path and lend a hand to those who are trying to restore a free Parliament in order that they may re-establish the ways of peace."
To be serious, let me say this: The Liberal party is greater than any individual. Further, it is our belief that in the general recognition of this truth by Liberals of all shades of opinion will there be found a rallying place for the forces that make for national harmony and national progress, and that only upon such common ground will it be possible to formulate a policy that will make Liberalism the cure for the-ills against which the masses of the people are now crying out in words of ominous import.
I remember, when I was a boy here at the University, trying to emulate my good friend the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), the professor would ask me to translate from Pope's Essay on Criticism. I remember the first two lines of that Essay:
'Tis with our judgments as our watches, none
Go just alike, yet each believes his own.
Exactly so. My hon. friend and esteemed colleague the member for Shelburne and

Queen's (-Mr. Fielding) believes lie is right in his conception of Liberalism. I believe he is wrong. Our watches do not go just alike. We each believe our own. I will make a bargain with him. Your watch, my friend, is not accurate. Perhaps mine is not accurate. Let us therefore turn to the old grandfather clock and set the time by it.
Mr. Speaker, this awful war is over, and I need not say how proud we all are of the record our soldiers made at the front- proud of the living, and prouder still of the dead. If this victory means anything it means the crushing of militarism, not only in Germany, but the whole world over, Canada included. -Canadians have played their part in this war. For territorial aggrandisement? No. For the securing of indemnity? No. For a voice in the foreign affairs of the British -Empire? No, Mr. -Speaker. The five hundred thousand Canadian soldiers who with unfaltering steps faced the grey lines of Germany fought the battles of this war in order to put an end to all wars in the future, so that there might not perish from the earth what was so w-ell defined by old Lincoln as " Government of the people, hy the people, for the people." What will be the outcome of this welter of blood? We are told that we are to have a Society of Nations, possibly a League of Peace, but call it by whatever name you choose, I proudly hope that this Parliament of Canada. after all the sacrifices that have been made by our boys, will be called upon to ratify the treaty and the covenant of peace.
I know we are not a sovereign power, but, Sir, I remember two occasions' during my parliamentary career when this Parliament -and we were not then a sovereign power- was called upon to ratify foreign treaties- the French treaty and the Japanese treaty. Both these treaties concerned our commercial relations with two foreign countries. Surely, if this Parliament can ratify commercial treaties as a matter of course, it should be called upon, in view of all the sacrifices that have been made by Canada in this war, to ratify the Peace Treaty. We have given unsparingly in men and in money. We mourn the loss of sixty thousand of our bravest, and thousands have come back maimed or wounded. Our country is saddled with a colossal debt, our industries are crippled, and we are facing a future fraught with the gravest perils as a result of our participation in the world wrar. I claim for Canada, my country, the honour of ratifying the Peace Treaty along with the other Allied nations. Canada has won that

distinction. We owe that to the living; we owe it to the dead. True, Mr. Speaker, this may not increase our stature hy one cubit. But it may enlarge our orbit. I have no patience with those who claim to be Liberals and are satisfied with the clerks of the British Foreign Office to represent Canada and do our work eternally.
I said a moment ago that this great war was over. The historic parties are aligned anew. I have listened to several addresses by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House-all my friends-and I heard them repeat one after another their belief that all parties in this country had gone to pieces, that there were no more Liberals and no more Conservatives. True, my hon. friend from North Simeoe (Mr. Currie) declared that the old, historic Conservative party was still in existence.
I turn to my authority. Burke, for his definition of a political party:-
A body of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some political principle in which they are all agreed.
Air. Speaker, the party system has existed in Great Britain for many centuries. We borrow our traditions and our ideals, politically speaking, from the mother of parliaments, and as long as there are two Britishers in the world there will be a party system, and that party system will resolve itself into two groups-a Liberal group and a Conservative group.
What is Liberalism? liberalism is not so much a policy as a habit of mind. It is the disposition of the man who looks upon each of his fellows as of equal worth with himself. Upon class distinctions in society, rank, wealth, race and creed he wages unceasing war. What is Conservatism? The Tory habitually thinks of his fellow creatures, not according to their individuality, but according to their class, the face value of which, regardless of their intrinsic worth, either entitles or disentitles them to his favour. They either belong to his own class or they do not. The real worth of each is not the standard by which he forms his judgment of them. Every act and utterance, every refusal or protest of another person is referred to the artificial connection or distinction, instead of being judged for itself. In a word, the Tory looks down from the institution to the man; the Liberal up from the man to the institution. That, Sir, is the basic distinction between Liberalism and Conservatism; it is the distinction which exists in all liberty-loving countries, such as those under the rule of King George the Fifth.

Party government needs no justification. Men differ widely in their views, but they can co-operate by subordinating some of their ideas to a general policy. What is the function of parties? It is to crystallize public sentiment, to formulate issues. In 1911 my hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) crystallized the policy of the Conservative party in one phrase which he coined in Toronto, " No truck or trade with the Yankees," and my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) crystallized and formulated the policy of the Liberal party-wider markets for Canada.
