Well, these -words have been repeated. I do not know how many sessions we have had since their alleged use, but it gives me great pleasure, indeed, to hear the Acting Piime Minister of this Government state boldly and emphatically that he never used such debasing language in reference to our great ally to the south of us. The people have a direct voice in deciding public questions and in choosing and controlling the Government. Party government, I will go further and say, intensifies popular interest in public affairs, and promotes stability and order in national affairs. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that as long as we follow the British system of government, and British ideals, we shall have the party system. It is true, parties may be temporarily decimated, but they are bound to revive. Iln England a few weeks ago Mr. Asquith was defeated-and it was a great misfortune for the United Kingdom that he was defeated; and the Liberal party was absolutely annihilated. Parties may be annihilated for a time, but, I say, they will revive; and only the day before yesterday in a by-election which took place in England, Mr. Lloyd George suffered the severest blow in his political career. In the province of Ontario the Liberal party was annihilated. We had a so-called leader who made an alliance with the Premier of that province in order to prevent public opinion from pronouncing itself on the public issues of the day. But what has happened? The people have taken into their own hands their salvation; and in by-elections which have taken place of late, Liberal opinion has asserted itself in the province of Ontario. I dare say if the Government of the day in Canada were to open some of the constituencies-the good Scotch constituency of Glengarry, the constituency of North Ontario, the constituency of Assiniboia, and Quebec East-I dare say my hon. friend would hear 'from the people; and the Government, strong as it is, might perhaps learn something from them. Mr. Speaker, you cannot change human nature. You may tell the people not to mention this, and not to speak of that. You may scientifically muzzle the press and prevent it from conveying to the public the real facts of the case. But you cannot change human nature; and already, Mr. Speaker, there is a clamour in this country against the methods adopted by the present Government. Why, Sir, we have that clamour arising from the ministerial benches. We all heard the speech delivered the other day by my hon. friend the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), and we heard the speech delivered by the prominent Unionist member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). And what do we gather from these two speeches?-to take only two examples. Since the beginning of this debate my sympathies have rather been with my good friend the genial Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White). He has been attacked and badly handled on right and left by his own friends. What did we hear? The hon. member for Victoria-who, I am told, was in his younger days a staunch Grit-he and the editor of the Toronto World one day bore the banners in a procession headed by the late Sir Oliver iMowat. He evidently recalls his younger days, because the other day he was the first to sound that note to the Government: "Restore the rights [DOT] of a free Parliament;" and that note was reechoed by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's. We have been told from both sides of the House-and we have heard it especially from both groups on the other side of the House-'that Orders in Council should be abolished if responsible government is not to be a by-word. Sir, I say that the latest example that this House has had of lack of responsible government

is the Order in Council which came as a bomb the other day in reference to the receivership of the Grand Trunk Pacific. That we should in the year of our Lord, 1919 clamour for responsible government in Canada is indeed a sad commentary on Unionism in Canada. But this is not all. We have been told repeatedly by gentlemen belonging to both groups of the Government, that the iniquitous War-time Elections Act snould be repealed. We have heard that it is a blemish on the statute book of Canada. Oh, it is true, my good friend from Westminster (Mr. Stacey), whom I do not see in his seat at present, said-in order probably to forestall the criticism that might come from this side of the House- that in that election of 1917 the people did not care for the means but were only looking at the end. Mr. Speaker, it is the first time that this doctrine of the end being justified by the means has been proclaimed in the House of Commons of Canada. I have been told-indeed I have read it not once but in practically every issue of the Orange Sentinel-that this doctrine is a sinister Jesuitical one. Mr. Speaker, if that is the policy of the Unionist party as proclaimed by my hon. friend from Westminster (Mr. Stacey), I would ask my good friend, the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) immediately to appoint a delegate-who should be Mr. Hocken himself-and send him to Borne and have him tender .to the General of the Jesuit Order an abject apology on behalf of the Orange party. The end justifies the means, said my hon. friend from Westminster. But what about the charges which were made during the last session? What about the charges that were made, and made so eloquently, by our young friend the hon. member for iChambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) in which it was established beyond a doubt that hundreds of men were induced to swear falsely as to their domicile in Canada? What about the charges made on the other side of the Atlantic? The Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid), a King's Counsel from the province of Nova Scotia, and a certain colonel from London, Ontario, were said to have had their hands in a plot during the last campaign so as to apportion votes to constituencies where ministerial candidates were not safe. What about these charges? Can we ignore them? If the Government has any honour, and its honour is in its own hands, it is in duty bound to probe the charges which have been made and to

investigate every one of them. If the Government does not do it, let it open one or two constituencies even in the province of Ontario and it will learn what the good people of Ontario think of such methods.
The hon. member for Westminster (Mr. Stacey) said that the bond of unity in Canada should be based on honour, truth and toleration. Let me tell him that if the War-time Elections Act is not repealed we cannot speak of honour, truth or toleration in this Parliament. Let me now make a very brief survey of the conditions prevailing in Canada.
The hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) depicted in this House the other day a very roseate outlook. As a result of this great war Canada had participated in the deliberations of the War Cabinet and out of the war there would be evolved a cabinet of governments. He was not very clear as to the constitutional aspect of that change. Then he depicted conditions prevailing in Russia under Bolshevist rule. Sir, I do not think it is necessary for Sir Robert Borden, our Premier, to go to Prinkipo in order to investigate the conditions in Russia under Bolshevism. This Government appointed a friend of their own, Mr. C. H. Cahan, K.C., who was my opponent during the last Dominion election, to investigate the socialistic propaganda in Canada. Of late he has published a pamphlet as to what he found in Canada. He declares that there is in Canada a socialistic and Bolshevist propaganda that in my judgment should be enough to prevent the Prime Minister from running after it in Russia. In the last page of his pamphlet Mr. Cahan says:
I have endeavoured to give you an idea of the milder forms of the propaganda, which has covertly been carried on throughout Canada, with the evident object of weakening the will of the Canadian people to carry on the war to a successful conclusion, and, more recently, to create difficulties and dissensions within Canada so as to hinder the attainment of a satisfactory peace. I say milder forms of propaganda advisedly; for, if I were to quote at length the quantities of obscene, profane and seditious pamphlets which have been circulated throughout Canada by the social revolutionists, it would only serve to excite your bitter animosity, and perhaps lay myself open to the charge of disseminating sedition, though merely repeating it for your information.
Here we have a gentleman appointed by the Government to inquire into the operations of the Bolshevists and socialists in Canada. His report is full of information on this subject of the most serious nature. Yet we are told by the President of the

Privy Council that Bolshevism is operating only in Russia. He did not say it but I suppose the logical conclusion to be arrived at from his speech wa,s that the Prime Minister of Canada was therefore justified in going to Prinkipo. Let us look after our own affairs and let the Bolshevists of Russia look after theirs.
The observations and the ramblings of my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council may be very interesting but we must face, and solve, our own Canadian problems. As the hon. member for Shel-burn and Queen's said, let us attend to our own affairs. What is the true situation to-day? I will not give my own opinion. I will give the opinion expressed by a bosom friend of the President of the Privy Council, a very eminent divine belonging, if I mistake not, to the Methodist church. Dr. Bland addressed a meeting a few evenings ago in Toronto and he used this language as he described the conditions in Canada:
There is no English-speaking country at least so ill prepared for the storm now breaking on the world. Canada is a steamer drifting into the rapids, the crew quarrelling and no captain in sight. We have section pitted against section, race against race, class against class and the soldiers a powerful and unknown factor.
Is that picture too sombre? Is it true that Canada is the image of a steamer drifting into the rapids, is it true that the crew is quarrelling, is there no captain of the ship? Let us look at the situation. That the crew is quarrelling we have no better evidence than what we have had this afternoon, yesterday and indeed ever since the debate started in this House of Commons. That we have no captain is undisputed. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens told us the other day that the captain was in Paris with three of his colleagues and that he was more needed in Ottawa than in Paris.
This session of Parliament has been delayed for nine months. In England, last year, they held two sessions and had a general election. In Canada we have delayed for nine months the meeting of Parliament. The usages of Parliament have been abridged. I have read the Parliamentary and constitutional history of England as interpreted by the best authors. It struck ' me that two years ago when we allowed Sir George Perley and two of the parliamentary secretaries to sit in this Parliament and to receive the emoluments of office without going before the people we were seriously abridging the British and the Canadian constitution. We saw a minister of the Crown (Mr. Blondin) defeated in two constituencies, and yet for months afterwards he continued in office and received emoluments as Portmaster General. He had no seat in this House, but finally he was provided with one in the Senate.
The writs for by-elections, Mr. Speaker, are not issued, as you well know. The national debt of Canada is simply staggering in its figures. We are facing a huge deficit. The Minister of Public Works the other day asked the House to look carefully into the condition of affairs, before the coming financial year was over, with a view of seeing what we are going to do in the future, and to look carefully, from a business standpoint, to the question where we are going to get the extra one hundred millions of revenue which we shall require after the present fiscal year. The adverse balance of trade is growing, and growing abnormally. Here is what I read in The Morning Sun, of New York, of March 11th, speaking of the staunch ally, the opulent customer and near-kin that Canada is to the United States:
In the seven months Canada bought from us a quarter of a billion dollars more than Canada sold us.
This is how the balance of trade stands as between Canada and the United States. And yet for years and years, when my good friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) was the financial pilot of this country the wails of my hon. friends opposite, wails of sorrow and regret, filled the other Chamber. They would speak then only of the adverse balance of trade. Well, Mr. Speaker, this year, after a period of only seven months there is an adverse balance of a quarter of a billion of dollars as between the United States and Canada.
The Civil Service, right here in Ottawa- and if the expression were not a little vulgar, I would say right under the noses of the Prime Minister and the minister responsible for the Civil Service-are up in arms. Labour is arrayed against capital. Unemployment is rife in the large cities. Why, only in the city of Montreal-df I am well informed by my friend the member for Bonavemture (Mr. Marcil) who is one of the city commissioners-there are actually twenty-five thousand men clamouring for work and bread. The railway problem is more entangled than ever. The freight rates have been unduly increased, and perhaps the express rates may be also unduly advanced before long. The cost of living is soaring higher and higher every day, and riots are occurring all over the land. Not

in Quebec you have noticed, Mr. Speaker -we have riots in Quebec only on the eve of a general election when there is a Unionist Government appealing for support, and those riots are concocted and paid for by the Department of Justice. There have been riots in Toronto-actually in the loyal city of Toronto-.and the police of that city, .a splendid body of men, had to defend themselves against the returned soldiers. Restaurants were broken into and .men were bleeding from wounds. Where was the mayor of Toronto in all .that trouble? Alas, investigation does not say. There were riots in Toronto, in Winnipeg, in Halifax, and in Lindsay
That was over a girl.

-There is mutiny in the camps. We have all heard of what has taken place at Rhyl. I was informed the other day that the Third Division had mutinied because they had refused to be used as a police force against their fellow-workers in Great Britain. I cannot say whether it is true, but it has been asserted to me-of course, ithe press would not give out that information. Is the steamer drifting	into	the rapids? Sir, theGovernment has no policy, no pilot, no captain and no head. Its policy is indecision, confusion, humiliation and anarchy. I may be told that, all this is the result of the war. Sir, a Frenchman who came to this country during the war	as a trade	commissionercoined a very good phrase in my presence as he was	delivering a speech in
Montreal. He said: France was taken unawares by war, France must not be taken unawares by peace. I agree, Sir, that all the Allied Governments were taken unawares by war, but this Government was warned repeatedly, during two, three and four sessions, that it should not be taken at a disadvantage and should cut its cloth accordingly. In England, Sir, they provided for peace conditions. Two years ago, according to a report to the British Government,, a Ministry of Reconstruction was created. I shall not waste the time of the House, but we have in that report the evidence that John Bull, as ever, was prudent, was far-seeing, and knew how to conduct his affairs. In Canada we did not know how to be prudent for the future, and the Government has been very derelict in its duty. All we hear is, words, words, and only words- reconstruction, co-operation, Imperialism, and nothing is done. The truth of the 
matter is this so-called Union is nothing but a bombast, a fake, a sham. First of all, there is no union; since the commencement of the session u'e have had that experience. There is no union, there is no Government-eve are ruled by factions. Sir Clifford Sifton is the ruler of this country, and he belongs to a Trinity. My friend from Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) said the other day that the Government was owned by Sir Joseph Flavelle. He stated only part of the truth. The Government is owned mainly and really by Sir William Mackenzie, Sir Joseph Flavelle and Sir Clifford Sifton. They are the masters of this Government, and when I say that there is no government, that we are ruled by faction, I am within the bounds of truth, my statement is borne out by the facts. The speeches delivered by hon. gentlemen supporting the Government are not only warnings, but they constitute, in my judgment, the most serious arraignment that was ever made against a government.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when the House
rose at six o'clock I was directing attention to the fact that the Government was being assailed not so much by its opponents, which is quite natural, as by its own friends. During the course of this debate we have heard not only very grave warnings, but also charges of a most serious character. The charges laid at the door of the Government by the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) are among the gravest ever made against a Government. Sir, let me read to you a few sentences from the speech delivered in this House on March 4, by the member for Victoria. I find the following in a letter which he had addressed to the Prime Minister, and which he read during the course of his remarks:
I have on other occasions drawn your attention to the massacres at Lens, Passchendaele. etc., where the only apparent object was to glorify the General in command, and make it impossible, through butchery, to have a Fifth and Sixth Division and two Army Corps. .	.
I think the time has arrived when you should assert yourself along positive lines, demand the removal of incompetents and have this needless slaughter-for I can call it nothing else-of our Canadian lads stopped. You should secure returns of the losses by brigade and battalions during each year or tenure of command, and what each brigade accomplished, and it will be found that, in many instances, the brigades and

battalions that have accomplished the most have suffered the least.
Bull-head and incompetency are traceable by the horrible casualties rolling up into eight and ten times the total force of a battalion or a brigade.
The hon. member spoke about the attack on Cambrai and the taking of Mons. He said:
I have just this to say about Mons. Were I in authority, the officer who, four hours before the Armistice was signed, although he had been notified beforehand that the Armistice was to begin at eleven o'clock, ordered the attack on Mons, thus needlessly sacrificing the lives of Canadian soldiers, would be tried summarily by court martial and punished so far as the law would allow.
It has been my misfortune to lose my only boy in this war. I would not, as the father of that boy, think for one moment of attacking the General Officer Commanding the Canadian forces. I do not for one moment believe that the charges made by the member for Victoria against Sir Arthur Currie are well founded; it is unbelievable that they should be so. I cannot believe that our boys were caused to be slaughtered and butchered for the sake of a little vainglory on the part of the Commanding Officer. But these charges have been made; they are now public property; they have re-echoed from province to province; indeed they are known throughout the world. The charges are made not by an insignificant person, but by a gentleman who was a member of the Government as Minister of Militia, by a gentleman who more than any one else can claim the credit of having equipped and sent overseas our First Contingent. The charges are made by one who, with all his failings, is known to be a generous-hearted gentleman. Sir, the Prime Minister and his colleagues may deny the charges; brother officers in this House may refute them, and the press may speak of the cruel egotism of the member for Victoria. But there is a sound public opinion in Canada, and whether the charge is well-founded or not, you cannot annul it by a mere denial or a sneer. The fathers and mothers of those who went through the valley of shadow during the great war will not be satisfied by a denial or by a sneer; they will insist, with bleeding hearts, upon an investigation which will probe these charges to the bottom. Indeed, the whole military situation so far as Canada is concerned is but a sad and melancholy tale of the Government's incompetency.
I have spoken of the charges made by the member for'Victoria. What about the specific charges made but a few days ago by Brigadier-General Smart, a gallant officer
if there is one, who has seen four years' service at the front, who does not belong to the Liberal party, who supports the Government in my native province as member for the loyal city of Westmount? Sir, the day of his first appearance in the Quebec Legislature on his return from the front, he deems it his duty to inform the country of what has taken place and of what is taking place yonder. Let me read in a few crisp sentences the charges made by General Smart. I quote from the Toronto Globe's report of his speech:
I feel it is up to me to tell the people of Canada how the Canadian Medical Service blundered overseas; how patronage, influence, pull, went to paralyse the good work of the medical services.
That is not surprising. During the session of 1916-17 the same charges were made from liiis side of the House, but we were debarred from the right of having Dr. Bruce's report laid on the Table. You will remember, Sir, how that genial gentleman who occupied my seat at that time, the Hon. Mr. Pugsley, insisted that that report should be laid on the table of the House. We could, however, never obtain that report. General Smart goes on to say:
I perfectly know who is responsible for this state of things; official Ottawa knows it too; Sir Robert Borden does not ignore it, but no one dares tell. And that is why I feel it is up to me to show all the evil that has been done, to show the abuse, the ill-treatment our wounded and sick received overseas at the hands of the improperly managed medical service. The whole trouble is to be traced to Argyll House.
We have heard, during the last few months, a great deal about slackers and time-servers. The farmer or the farmer's son, who was working on the farm, in order that our soldiers might get food, was not a slacker; but I am told that there were thousands of slackers at Argyll House in London receiving high pay. General Smart continues:
And I may add that personally, after seeing all that I have seen, I have not the slightest confidence in those who administer the affairs in England. Sir George Perley had much to do with the management of our medical service. Who gave him the authority to treat our wounded in such a way, be it even for the cause of Imperialism? Well, gentlemen, I tell you, if Imperialism is to be maintained through such a system, I say it is time that it be destroyed. I am as good an Imperialist as any one, hut I do not care for this Imperialism at such a price; I care not for Imperialism if it is to be built on the sufferings of our wounded heroes.
Let me tell the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) that such severe language was never used by any hon. mem-

bers on this side of the House. General Smart says that Brigadier-General Turner is wealt-armed. He blames him for the recent riotings at Rhyl and other camps, and he traces the matter back to the abuse and ill-treatment of the men.
General Smart said that many Canadian officers in England had asked him to bring these facts to light. Recalling the death of Major-General Steele, in London-
One of the best Canadian soldiers that Canada ever produced,
-he said that the Major General died of a broken heart over these things. He says he will produce correspondence to this effect.
Further he says:
Gentlemen, I tell you, without fear of impartial contradiction, that the medical service overseas was directed in an insensible and neglected way. Our Canadian wounded were afforded a medical service that was absolutely inadequate, and I have seen instances where medical officers, ridiculously inapt to care for the sick and wounded, were put in charge of important hospital units. I have pitied the poor soldiers that were made to travel through the British Isles to far-off hospitals when they passed close to the unit that should have received them for their particular treatment. . . . He stated instances where men medically found unfit in Canada, were, however, sent to England. These men caused hard work and worry to the officers overseas, went through hardships, and are now coming back a charge to the country, for they will be getting pay pension all at the expense of the country. Then General Smart told of what he saw in his own Military District of Shorncliffe. He said he could not criticise the medical officers and nurses. They were up to what he had expected from them, but, he says, I feel I must and do criticise the headquarters of management of this service.
General Smart said that each Canadian hospital had its full stall: of competent doctors and nurses, but outside of these hospitals, there had been organized Voluntary Aid Detachments, made up of people of good-will, but who knew little or nothing of medical care, and he stated instances where soldiers were left for definite treatment in these Voluntary Aid Detachments while cots were empty in the regular hospitals.
He stated that, in cases he knew of, men had lost the use of their eyes because of this practice. When such cases reached the proper hospitals, said General Smart, it was too late for treatment to have any effect.
General Smart then mentioned cases where patronage placed in responsible posts men who had not even diplomas of medical studies, while competent men without the "pull" were kept in England or in posts where their science and experience could not be used to succor our wounded and sick.
Talking of the riot, General Smart said that the Rhyl outbreak was not the first of this kind; there had been outbreaks previously at Shorncliffe, Witley, Bramshott, and even at Rhyl before.
General Smart concludes by vindicating the French Canadian soldiers. I must offer General Smart my sincere thanks for that
[Mr. Lemieux.j
timely vindication. I have noticed that the subsidized press, when the cable despatch telling of those riots reached Canada, assigned the cause of them to the Montreal regiments; but, of course, a denial was immediately forthcoming, and then the subsidized press published another lie in order to cover up the old one. It said that the French Canadians at the Rhyl camp had been seen with Bolshevik flags.
Shame.
Propaganda.

policy. I am not anxious to be quoted unless you think it necessary.
Sincerely yours,
Arthur C. Pratt.
I was rather surprised, Mr. Speaker, to see that letter published in the Toronto Telegram, as I remembered another article published by the Telegram immediately after the famous election of 1917, referring to the frauds during that election in Toronto. The Telegram said, " We should have denounced those frauds before, but our denunciation might have helped Laur-ier; but now we are free to speak." So the *Toronto Telegram can speak of the military frauds that have been perpetrated at the expense of our soldiers on the other side. I say to my hon. friend the Prime Minister that charges of the gravest character are made, not by civilians, not by political opponents, but by generals and colonels returning from the front where they have served their King, their country, their Empire, well and faithfully. They belong by tradition to the Conservative party, and the least that the Government should do-as it is in honour bound to do-is to probe those charges and punish.the guilty. But, Sir, the Government is not only assailed by the military authorities; not only by its opponents, but we have undergone such a revolution during the past few years that the Government is being assailed by one of its own members and can survive the assault!
I am glad to see my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. T. A. Crerar) in his seat. There was held in the city of Winnipeg some time ago a convention of the farmers of the West, but more especially a meeting of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. The platform which was adopted at that meeting was read yesterday by our friend the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) who is, I believe, president of the Grain Growers' Association of Saskatchewan. That platform, Mr. Speaker, contains the tariff policy of the western farmers, and in most of its planks I take great comfort. If it may please my hon. friend, I may tell him that I endorse several of the planks of that platform. As it was read last night, I need not refer to it again; I may, however, add this. I find that besides the tariff question the farmers passed several resolutions on different matters. For instance, they passed resolutions to bring about a greater measure of democracy in government. As democratic reforms, they demand the immediate repeal of the War-time Elections Act, and the discontinuance of the practice of

conferring titles upon citizens of Canada. I have always contended, and I still contend, that titles in this country have been a source of corruption. Let me say this further to my Conservative as well as to my Liberal friends, that if they want to keep in their fold their followers, they should pass at this session the timely resolution which I see on the Order Paper, and which was moved last year. Let us abolish those titles, which are only a lure to the weak-kneed. The leader of the House knows whereof I speak. The Government has been assailed right and left, since the beginning of this war, and before the war, by some wealthy friends who were anxious to be knighted; and many of the rumblings whieh we hear to-day against the Government are no doubt attributable to disappointed knighthood seekers; and I have this confession to make to my Highland leader, that the Liberal party in the old days lost many of its friends because they could not obtain knighthoods from iSir Wilfrid Laurier. I repeat that it is a source of corruption, and I agree entirely with that plank of the farmers platform. But let us proceed. The farmers advocated an immediate reform of the Federal Senate; an immediate check upon the growth of government by order in council; increased responsibility of individual members of Parliament. in all legislation; the complete abolishing of the patronage system; the publication of contributions and expenditures both before and after election campaigns ; the removal of press censorship upon the restoration of peace, and the immediate restoration of the rights of free speech, the setting forth by daily newspapers and periodical publications of the facts, of their ownership and control; proportional representation, etc., etc. Now, Mr. Speaker, that platform is very compact and very substantial. It will play its part whenever the people of this country are called to the polls. But the point I wish to make is this: This is the platform of the farmers of the West; it is a radical platform. Amongst the delegates who drafted the platform and who contributed the material that produced that platform, I find, to my surprise and my astonishment, the name of the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. T. A. Crerar). Yes. I find the name of Hon. T. A. Crerar from Winnipeg, representing the Manitoba farmers; and I am told-my hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong- I am told he presided at the meeting, put the motion to the meeting, and declared it carried.
I must correct the hon. gentleman. I did not go quite that far.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I accept at once the amendment to the statement I made. But, in all earnestness, I will put this one little question: Does he, or does he not, approve of this platform of the western farmers? I will pause for a moment and ask him to answer " yes " or " no."

The hon. gentleman is rather curious this evening. The platform to which he is referring was not drafted at this meeting in Winnipeg of which he speaks. It was drafted two years ago and reaffirmed at that meeting. I have no hesitation in confessing that, with reference to the platform which was drafted two years ago, I was one of those who assisted in drafting it. I thought it was a good platform then, and I think it is a good platform now.
Mr. GiAUVREAU: You will not stay there very long.

I would have no hesitation in enfolding within the Liberal party my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture. I accept his word: Yes, he assisted in drafting this platform. He was for it then; he is for it now. He has only one thing to do; that is to resign from the Government. This is a very serious matter. Here is a Government where gentlemen are united to carry on the affairs of the country. We have on the Government benches two groups of ministers who differ absolutely one from the other, not on secondary issues, but on the issue of the day. I would be very much interested in knowing what the views of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization are on this question. I know where the able young Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) stands. He stands with my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie). I know where my good friend the hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) stands; he stands where he stood in 1911. I know where my hon. friend the Minister of the Civil Service (Mr. Maclean) stands, and I know where my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture stands. He stated it with a plainness and a frankness that I would like to have the other members of the Government practise. Let us, then, test the frankness, the truthfulness, of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration. He said the other evening that he was a Liberal and that nobody could eject him from the Liberal party. He said

that he stood with the farmers whom he represented in this House. Here is the platform of the farmers of the three large Prairie Provinces. We have the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that he stands by that platform. I want to know if the Minister of Immigration is the same gentleman who goes out west and whispers to the farmers that lie is their friend and that their policy will prevail. Let him speak boldly and proudly this evening. Let us see if he will imitate the good sense and judgment of his colleagues. If the hon. gentleman will allow me to pause for a moment I would like him to answer as the Minister of Agriculture has done.
Oh, oh.
Order.
If I may be allowed-

speechtext: The minister has already spoken and it is a reversal of the rule and practice of the House that a member who is speaking should interrogate hon. members who have already spoken and who are in their seast.
By unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are proceeding away beyond the bounds of order in permitting the hon. gentleman to speak.

If I may be allowed just one word, I think that before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) asks me to answer that question he should answer a question himself. He intimated that he agreed with some of the planks of that platform. He has not taken the House into his confidence to the extent of telling it which of the planks in the platform he agrees with. When he asks me the very general question if I agree with every plank in the platform I think he should at least state his own position.
Then I am to understand that that is the plain, unvarnished answer of the Minister of Immigration?

No; the hon. gentleman has no right to interpret my words at all. There will be lots of opportunities during this session to state exactly where I stand on these various questions, and when the proper time comes I will state where I stand. But I do not propose to be moved in that way by him during the course of a debate to state my position in a general way in reference to a great many matters of very general interest.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The House will readily see the very difficulty 1 anticipated when I endeavoured to prevent the minister from replying. The proceeding is unUsual and very irregular, and I would recommend that it be discontinued.
It is a good thing that the Rules of the House should force me to-
Order, order.
I was not blaming the Speaker at all.
Order, order.
What order?
Order in Council.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think that the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) is questioning the ruling of the Chair.
>Mr. LEMIIEUX: I did not question the ruling of the 'Chair. It is an excellent ruling and we had an eloquent but typical answer from the Minister of Immigration. He stands by that answer and the people of the West will judge. In my opinion, he remains true to himself. I was told when he came here that he was a little bit of a trickster and something of a ward politician.
Order, order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is one word that the hon. gentleman should withdraw and which I call upon him to withdraw, namely, that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization is a trickster. That word is certainly far beyond the bounds of Parliamentary language.
I bow to your decision with pleasure.
Withdraw, withdraw.	.

It is most amusing
that we should have such an aggregation before us this evening-two groups of ministers on the vital issues of the day differing absolutely one from the other. Of course, we shall hear more during the session, and some means will be found to test the principles of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization on the tariff. At all events, the House knows this evening where the Minister of Agriculture stands.
He was not afraid, he did not beat about the bush, he said yes. Mr. Speaker, this is a very vital issue, and it has engrossed the attention of the press of western Canada of late. The farmers of the West sent a representative here some days ago,
[Mr. Caldt-r.j
a gentleman by the name of Rice Jones, and I wonder whether he is an annexationist or not. That gentleman canvassed the opinions of the hon. members who represent western constituences, and according to The Manitoba Free Press of March 15th, here is what he reports:
The wire sent to Ottawa and the replies received from some of the Alberta members follow :
Full Board Meeting of United Farmers now sitting at Calgary request that you, while in Ottawa, present farmers' platform to Government, as representing the organized farmers of Alberta in lieu of sending delegates from here with joint deputation from three Prairie Provinces.

Yes, that was the question. I will tell my hon. friend where I stand, order having been restored. I will quote chapter and verse. The last great message of the former leader of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration, was delivered in this city on the 14th of January last, and his platform has been published, just as the platform of the western farmers, as drafted by my friend the Minister of Agriculture, has been published. I may say for the information of the House that this platform, which was unanimously adopted by the Liberals assembled at Ottawa on the 14th of January last, was prepared under the supervision of the late lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier. After having recited the many resolutions concerning the tariff, moved whilst he was in office and leader of the Opposition, the platform thus concludes:
Now therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this Association, not only should the said Tariff increases of 7J per cent and 5 per cent be immediately repealed, hut that there should also be an immediate downward revision of the Tariff in accordance with the above mentioned omnibus resolution moved by the Liberal Opposition in the House of Commons on May 23rd, 1917, in these terms:-
1.	That wheat, wheat flour, and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list.
2.	That farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
3.	That staple foods and food products (other than wheat flour), domestic animals and foods therefor be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty.
4.	That substantial reductions be made in the general Tariff on all articles imported into Canada, excepting luxuries.'
5.	That the British Preference be increased to fifty per cent of the general Tariff.
That, Mr. Speaker, is my platform. I shall have an opportunity during the present session to vote for it, and I invite those westerners who represent the three (Prairie Provinces to support that policy, because 1 can assure my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, who drafted the farmers' platform, and I can assure my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. dark) and those others who are acting in good faith on the tariff issue, that after the caucus of to-morrow they will know they cannot get anything from the present Government so far as tariff reducions are concerned. Here is where I stand, and I am in good company. I also stand for the fair treatment of soldiers and sailors; for generous care for dependents of the fallen; for the gradual democratization of labour; for the abolition of Government by Order in Council; for the abolition of press censorship; for the repeal of the War-Time Elections Act; and for a League of Nations. There may be some slight differences between the farmers' platform and the Liberal platform. I stand by my leader-I follow his fiery cross-and I stand by my party on this tariff issue. I do not beat about the bush as the Minister of Immigration does.
The hon. gentleman has not stated whether or not he agrees with the farmers' platform on the tariff. I would very much like to be informed as to that.
What about you, now?

I stated a moment ago where I stood when I read the platform laid down by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. My hon. friend is hard of understanding this evening. He cannot comprehend a plain statement; he abhors truth. I said that there were differences, but very slight differences, between the farmers' platform and the Liberal platform. I stand by the Liberal platform, and I think that the farmers of
Will my hon. friend be good enough to explain-I do not understand it yet-how our manufactured goods were prevented, by this arrangement, from being sent overseas?
I know they were prevented by this licensing system-
I do not understand it.

-and by the embargo. We have here the sorry, sad, and melancholy comment of such stout Canadians and Britishers as Mr. Lloyd Harris and Mr. Frank Jones. This lis not a new policy. It was the policy of Mr. Chamberlain, the father of that Imperialism; he did not want our manufacturers to compete with the British manufacturers. There is a lesson to be drawn from this last incident. Let us think of Canada, first, last and always. Let us be Canadians inspired by British ideals, but loyal, first, last and always to our native country, Canada.

I was fairly intimate with the policy of the late Rt. Hon. Joseph Chamberlain and I never heard him make such a statement. Will the hon. member be good enough to give an example of where Mr. Chamberlain objected to goods manufactured in Canada coming into Great Britain?

I will give the example of the " hidden list "-the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens will remember it- a list of manufactured goods which in any preferential agreement with the Mother Country should not compete with British goods. I have chapter and verse and I shall be happy, on another occasion, to convey that information to my hon. friend.
Let us be Canadians, inspired always by British ideals, but loyal to our country. I am not advocating the independence of Canada. I am not hinting at any annexation movement. Far be that from my thoughts. I am a Canadian. My ancestors were in this country three hundred years

ago, and I am not going to sell my birthright for a mess of pottage. I am a Canadian and I -am a Britisher, but I say that the time has come, after this great war in which we have made so many sacrifices- that, in the words of Sir John A. Macdonald, " we should think of our country always." I remember a speech delivered by Sir John Thompson, on the occasion of the death of Sir John A. Macdonald, and I find these words in appreciation of the career of that great chieftain:
Sir John's Jove of Canada and his desire to serve her must he put far dn front of all his characteristics. His daily thought might 'be expressed in Webster's words : "Let our one object be our country, our whole country, and nothing hut our country." " Nothing but our country " in the sense that Canada was to be first of all, in every consideration of -public policy or personal action. His true and1 deep Canadiandsm was the " pillar or cloud by day, and the pillar of fire by night," to the hundreds of thousands whom he led as no man oou-ld have led by a mere party banner."
That was the Canadian policy of Sir John A. Macdonald. It was also the policy of Sir Wilfiid Laurier.
We have responsible Government in Canada and we cannot -turn baok to colonialism. I do not share the views of my esteemed friend and colleague the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) that we should fee satisfied	to let the	Colonial Office in
London manage the affairs of Canada.
I have a little more pride than that. We are not a nation of one million or two million, but a nation of eight million people, and some day when good times come back, when a Liberal administration comes into office perhaps we shall have a population of ten or fifteen million. We have won responsible government.	Formerly, England
drafted our tariffs, managed our post office affairs, looked after our public works, involved us in her commercial treaties, and defended Canada with her regulars. But we have outlived that policy, and to revive it now would simply be to ignore our national dignity. For eighty years Canada has been working towards greater efficiency, greater self-reliance, and more complete self-government. In matters of defence, we control not only our land forces, but our naval forces also. As a Canadian-I am speaking only for myself-I stand by the policy of ruling our own country and looking after our own affairs. A nation, like the individual, must go forward-not go backwards, crab-like. We must go forward, and I am looking hopefully forward to the day when there will be, not a colony or even a

dominion of Canada, but a Kingdom of Canada. That was the view held by the fathers of Confederation. Sir, the fathers of Confederation delighted to proclaim that their offspring was to be a nation, and they did not hesitate to assign to Canada prophetically and proudly, its place and order among the nations of the earth. The Hon. Adams G. Archibald, of Nova Scotia, said that the united provinces " would form a nation which in all the elements that constitute real greatness might he ranked as the third or fourth on the face of the globe." Lt.-Col. Gray, of New Brunswick, said that they " wanted a national union, one which would enable them to take an honourable place among the nations of the earth." The Hon. Chas. Fisher, of New Brunswick, said that the federation " would be the fourth maritime power in the world. England, France and the United States would alone be superior to it." Sir George E. Cartier said that the delegates had " met to inquire whether it were possible for the provinces from their present fragmentary and isolated materials, to form a nation or kingdom." Sir John A. Macdonald said that the delegates had in view " the noble object of founding a great British monarchy in connection with the British Empire and under the British Queen." He said:-
I am a subject of a great British-American nation, under the government of Her Majesty, and in connection with the Empire of Great Britain and Ireland.
" Confederation," he added, " would give them the national prowess and strength which would make them at least the fourth nation on the face of the globe." He preferred for the title of the new confederation " The Kingdom of Canada," and he desired an Imperial alliance with the Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with the Crown as the sufficient bond of union. At another time Sir John A. Macdwonald said that the new constitution " was intended to be, as far as circumstances would permit, similar to that of the Imperial Government, and recognizing the Sovereign of Great Britain as its sole and only head."
Sir, I accept the views of the Fathers of Confederation, and notably the noble views of the late Sir John A. Macdonald. The British Empire must assume this grander character and rise to its higher ideal. I claim that there should be not inferiority, hut equality; not subservience, but equi-pollence; not subjection either of Canada to the United Kingdom now, or of the United Kingdom to Canada, but absolute and unreserved brotherhood, making with Australia, South Africa and other great

nations " a galaxy of nations." That phrase was coined by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he spoke in England at the time of the Diamond Jubilee. But in order to attain to the proud position of being a kingdom in the sense that there will be a feeling of brotherhood between all the British Dominions and the Mother Country, we must first of all be a united people. And I think the House will agree with me that the time has come to unite the Canadian people of all creeds, of all races and of all provinces. I remember a great speech delivered by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier in Nova Scotia at an Acadian convention a few years ago. He told his audience that during his visit to the old country he had admired the noble proportions of some of the Gothic cathedrals of England and of France, and he prophesied that Canada too some day would take the form of a Gothic cathedral. "In that wonderful architecture," he said, " there is marble, and it remains marble; there is granite, and it remains granite; there is oak, and it remains oak; but those materials are blended into a harmonious whole." Mr. Speaker, we have in this country the best elements of which to create the great Kingdom of Canada. The very best races of the world are here-the sturdy Scot, the impulsive Frenchman, the warm-hearted Irishman, and the cool and brainy Englishman. Sir, if these races, representing as they do the loftiest ideals and the noblest traditions of Europe, are blended together after this war in which our men have played such a noble and lasting part, we shall then be in a position to build a great Canadian nationality.

I congratulate the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) on the very able manner in which he has held the attention of this House for nearly two hours and three-quarters. I shall not inflict myself upon the House for that length of time. I am sorry the hon. member cannot swallow the organized farmers' platform, but I suppose he is not used to taking pills of that kind unless they are sugar-coated with politics. I understand that my hon. friends came into power in 1896 on a platform as radical in many lines as the present farmers' platform, and it was practically forgotten for fifteen years by my hon. friend and his associates. Now I want to say as a farmer from the prairies that the farmers of the West-I can speak for them-are not as easily caught to-day as they were in 1896; and if my good friend and his associates want to get the farmers' support they will
have to undertake, not as a pre-election promise, but at once, a thorough housecleaning on their side of the House, so that they may say with some degree of truth that they are Liberals indeed.
I wish in passing, Mr. 'Speaker, to refer to some of the statements made by the gallant colonel who represents the constituency of North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). I shall borrow a phrase for the time being from the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). I am of the opinion that we have two prophets in this House. At all events I am sure we have at least one, representing the constituency of North Simcoe. Unfortunately he is a prophet who predicts destruction. He tells us of the great calamities that will befall 'Canada if the tariff is interfered with; and that reminds me, of a statement that was made in the city of Winnipeg some years ago by a secretary of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, when he said that the Manufacturers' Association of Canada was so strongly organized that, if they saw fit, they could cause the grass to grow on the streets of any town or city in the Dominion of Canada. 'Perhaps my friend from Sim-coe is one of that number. He made the statement in regard to the embargo on wheat, endeavouring to make us believe that it was the American Government that _ put on that embargo. If il am correct- and I believe I am-the embargo was put on by the Government of Canada -at the request of the British Government in order that the foodstuffs of Canada might be preserved for Great Britain and her Allies; and even if the embargo had been imposed by the American Government conditions would not compare at all with those of normal times. Then he states that there was a duty on foodstuffs in Canada of 271 per cent, but he failed to tell us how this would enable the labourers or mechanics working in factories in the cities to obtain their foodstuffs cheaper. I think he made a mistake when he quoted that figure of 27J per cent as the average duty on foodstuffs. Next, in dealing with the land policy of the Government he gave some advice as to what the Government should do in regard to the returned soldiers. He said in effect that the Government should give to the soldiers land on the same terms as given to the ISouth African veterans, implying I presume, that they should be issued scrip. Now any one who has been in the West for any length of time knows that very few soldiers who received scrip settled on the land. It was merely a bonanza for the speculators, who bought the scrip at a

trifling figure; and as a result many of the scrip lands to-day lie unotcupied. But while the gallant Colonel'(Mr. Currie) who has had the honour to represent North Sirncoe would like the Government to do well by the returned soldier, I would suggest to him one way in which he might very materially help those returned men who desire to go on the land. I presume he is a member of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Might he not persuade the association at least to give our soldiers who go on the land their implements duty free? That would be a considerable help to those men. The hon. member launched an attack on Mr. H. W. Wood of Alberta, President of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, a man who has been re-elected to that position by acclamation for two or three years. I have known the gentleman myself for a number of years and can say most emphatically that he has a character at which no one can	point a finger;	and	beforeany	hon.	member in this	House
makes any charge against him, he should at least be armed with the proof; and 1 hope that before very long Mr. H. W. Wood will request the hon. member for Sirncoe to prove his words. The hon. member tells us that a concern with which he is connected successfully competed in the foreign market to the tune of $9,000,000. Well, I am glad to know that, Mr. Speaker. The western farmers are glad to know that the Canadian manufacturers are able to compete in the foreign market against any manufacturer in the world, and if they can compete in the foreign market thousands of miles away from home, the query is why can they not compete right at home? He says-in order to scare us, I suppose-that the Canadian manufacturers are commencing to build factories in the United States because there is a fear of the tariff being interfered with. That may be so. I do not doubt the words of any hon. member of this House, but I would like to have the proof of that assertion; and if the manufacturers are doing that, the remedy is quite simple-lower the tariff to the same level as the American tariff, and then our Canadian manufacturers will have access to a field where there are one hundred millions of people, while the American manufacturers will have access to eight millions. I think that the advantages are on the side of the Canadian manufacturers, if they could see it. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) says they cannot see it-but there are none so 
blind as those who will not see. Then the hon. member goes on to say that the farmers of the West are Bolshevists, that they are stirring up strife. Shortly after that, however, he evidently forgets himself, for he says that the farmers in the West mostly all came from Ontario. Now, if his first statement is correct, that the farmers of the West are mostly Bolshevists, then good old Ontario must be a cradle of Bolshevism. The hon. member says he became a convert to high protection when he sat at the feet of the late Sir John A. Macdonald. I am not at all surprised that the hon. member for North Sirncoe became a convert to high protection when he had the great privilege of sitting at the feet of such an illustrious leader; but I am convinced of this that when the late Sir John A. Macdonald was buried, my hon. friend from North Sirncoe buried his intellect in that grave and that he had nothing more to learn in connection with tariff. Another of his prophesies is this: he says that if anything is done to the tariff there will be a state funeral. I understand that the hon. member for North Sirncoe was one of the foremost men-he was indeed a very prominent man-at a banquet in the city of Toronto where seven of the Ginger group were present. Now, Mr. Speaker, he threatens there is going to be a state funeral if the tariff is disturbed, and, Sir, I am of the opinion that the funeral he refers to will be the funeral of the Ginger Group which he represents. I am of the opinion that the Canadian manufacturers represent the situation for trade in a cartoon which appeared in the Grain Growers' Guide about two months ago. This is a farm scene, Mr. Speaker, and you will pardon me for citing it here. The cartoon pictured a calf about two years old and the farmer trying to wean it away from the cow.	It was nip and tuck which
one would win-the farmer or the calf. It is my opinion that the longer we give high protection to our Canadian manufacturers, the longer will they want it to be maintained.
Mr.' McMASTER: Hear, hear.

I am very glad to hear an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House say "Hear, hear." Then the hon. gentleman from Sirncoe told us that the manufacturers did not make a profit of five per cent on their turn over. That statement is just a little misleading. Why did the hon. member for Sirncoe not tell us what interest they made on their capital in-

vesed ? Then we would understand what their profit amounts to. To state that they do not make five per cent on their overturn is very misleading. Perhaps he will inform us later on what interest the manufacturers make on their invested capital and also on their watered stock.
Mr. Speaker, in passing, I wish to add my tribute of praise to the late, beloved and lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and in doing so would simply say "Amen" to all the good things which have been said of him who has crossed the bar. A year ago when this Parliament met for the first time we did so under the great cloud of war, and the victory which has since been achieved was still hanging in the balance, and to many of us it seemed that victory was doubtful or at least a long way off, but to-day, as part of the British Empire, we rejoice with her and-our Allies that victory has come to us, and the whole world breathes easier and our gallant victorious soldiers are now returning home to us. The task of taking care of our men and re-establishing them back in civil life will be equally as large an undertaking as the prosecution of the war and will bring up many new problems for our government to handle. As an independent supporter of Union Government, it is my opinion, Sir, that it is well for Canada that we have a Union Government and not a party Government to grapple with the gigantic problem of reconstruction, and, Mr. Speaker, while the remark has been made by hon. members opposite that our Union Government, and especially the Minister of Immigration, was in a state of unpreparedness when the armistice was signed; even if that is so, Sir, I do not think it is very much to be wondered at, because we know that even the British Government, who were very much nearer the seat of war than we were, were of the opinion, and in fact, had made preparations for continuing the campaign for at least another winter. But, Mr. Speaker, at this late stage of the debate I do not wish to occupy the time of the House very long, but I wish to make a few remarks in passing on some of the problems that immediately confront us.
I would like first to say a word on the land policy of the present iGovernment, which also applies to previous Governments, both Grit and Tory. We are informed, Sir, that there are about 15,000 homesteads available within 15 miles of our railways and that only 2,000 of them are fit for cultivation. I am informed we have over 4,000 soldiers at the present time ready and willing to go on to the land. To ask our returned soliders to go beyond the fifteen mile limit to homestead would be a crime, when we have 31 million acres of alienated, uncultivated and unoccupied land lying within the fifteen mile railway belt. This condition, Mr. Speaker, has not been brought about by this Government or by the policy of this Government but by the policies of past Governments, Liberal and Conservative; and we now find that our Dominion Government have got to go into the open market to buy back the lands which were previously sold for a trifle to speculators and corporations. When I say sold I would perhaps express it better if I said were given away for a trifle, for I understand that from $1 to S3 per acre was about the prevailing price received for our lands years ago.
I will now point out to you, Sir, some of the evils of the unoccupied lands. In the first place our unoccupied lands do not contribute anything towards the cost of construction of our railways other than the trifling amount for which they were sold. Then again, miles of railroads must be built past unoccupied lands to reach the occupied lands. While the occupied lands produce traffic for the road, and the exportable products help to pay the nation's debts, unoccupied lands produce no revenue and create no trade for the benefit of the road and further our unoccupied lands do not contribute anything towards paying the debts of the country; they retard the progress of settlement and in many cases prevent the establishment of schools; in many cases also they are not taxable and do not help to build or maintain public highways.
I would like to point out, Sir, to this Government the evil of selling lands to the individual or corporation without duties of occupancy attached. I would recommend to the careful consideration of this Government the selling of lands only to actual settlers. It is not the price obtained by the State by the sale of lands that enriches the state but rather the products of the soil which feeds the population, creates business and the exportable surplus must help pay the debt of our country. I would like also to point out to you the spirit of the West. When famine stared the British Empire and her Allies in the face, and our Government urged greater production, the West responded with a very large increased acreage put under cultivation. This was brought about partly by the fact that small tractors were brought into the country free of duty, and thereby the price was very materially reduced. But, Sir, the West

The Question of ways and means is so basic in relation to alt other matters that after much consideration would' urge you not to be satisfied with anything less this session than a distinct step toward fiscal programme Canadian Council of Agriculture. If Government balks, let it take the responsibility; the sun will still rise and set.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the West believes that the Union Government will be able to read the handwriting on the wall. This is the ultimatum of organized agriculture. If you do not listen to the members who are here to-day, you certainly will have to deal with the West at no distant date.
I want to say a word with regard to the Canadian manufacturers, particularly the manufacturers of agricultural implements. Why is it, Sir, that our manufacturers will not treat us, the farmers of Canada, the same as they treat farmers in the British Isles, Australia, New Zealand, and European countries, where they sell their machinery in the open market, competing with other manufacturers of the world? I am informed on very reliable authority that the prices at which these implements are sold in Europe, Australia and New Zealand, are very much below the prices at which they are sold to the Canadian farmers. This applies particularly to us in the West. We are Canadians, and we wish to be treated at least the same as farmers are treated in other countries by our Canadian manufacturers. I do not think that is asking too much.
We know, Sir, that our Canadian mechanics are second to none in the world and that our Canadian manufacturers are stronger than many of the manufacturing concerns in the United States. Manufacturers have told us that electrical power in Canada, of which they use a good deal, is dearer than it is in the United States. I have a book issued by a commission in the United States before which Sir Adam Beck gave some very valuable information. I find from it that electrical power on this side of the line is about fifty per cent less than the price in the state of New York.
Organized agriculture does not for a minute want to put the Canadian manufacturer out of business, but we want to see him get down to competition. The wider field for him is the wider market. The necessary change in our tariff laws will open up to the Canadian manufacturer a field where there are 100,000,000 people and enable the American manufacturer to get into a field where there are 8,000,000 people.
The Second Vice-President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Mr. J. S. McKinnon, in an address to one of the clubs 
in Toronto, said that the Grain Growers wanted to escape practically all taxation. That is not so. If you read the platform of the Organized Farmers you will find that we have set forth a system of taxation which we believe would be suitable to conditions in Canada to-day. The Second Vice-President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association is not a strong high protectionist, as some members of this House are. He says:
The present tariff is imperfect. It has many contradictions and imperfections. As it has not been revised since 1907 and as there have been many changes in our national life since that date, especially on account of the war, it is obvious that the present tariff may not be suited to the conditions of the day. We believe that it should be revised, but revised scientifically.
Referring to the first statement made by Mr. McKinnon, the Organized Farmers' platform clearly sets forth the fact that the Grain Growers do not want to escape taxation; that they are willing and anxious to pay their full share. But we do object strenuously to paying taxes to bolster up the manufacturers under the present iniquitous tariff system. We are willing to pay taxes to the Dominion treasury, but not to the coffers of the manufacturers. Then Mr. McKinnon goes on to prophesy the bankruptcy which will come about in Canada if the tariff is removed. He asks whether the soldiers must wait and possibly be prevented from obtaining employment before the tariff laws are changed. I say emphatically, no. The soldier who goes on the land to farm is just as anxious as any other farmer that the tariff be reduced.
It must be distinctly understood that agriculture, being the basic industry of Canada, is the foundation stone upon which all our industries rest, and if that basic industry is not attractive as well as profitable, our industries will all suffer accordingly. The Government of Canada, therefore, must see to it that our basic industry prospers; if it does not, all industries will come to ruin which the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has predicted.
I pray for the indulgence of this House while I read a short extract from some literature which the Canadian Manufacturers' Association have supplied me with. Before doing so, I will read just two paragraphs from a statement made by Mr. Tom Moore, President of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, in an address which he delivered to the Canadian Club in the city of Toronto yesterday:-
I tell you if you are content to wait until revolution has taken place, you will have the upheaval in Canada as well as they had it in

Russia' and everywhere else. So declared Tom Moore, President of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada in an address to the Canadian Club here to-day, speaking on the subject of "industrial unrest of the present day."
He further stated:
Mr. Moore declared it was the duty of the Government to set the example for all employers in placing its own contracts. The Government should base its contracts on the best conditions of wages and employment that exists in the country, and not according to the local conditions, which were often unfavourable.
'Labour forces and many employing forces,' Mr. Moore said, 'believe that a greater measure of nationalization of some of the monopolies of the country should take place.'
Mr. Moore touched on the Tariff question. 'Any industry which needs a protective tariff should be prepared to place its books under Government inspections, and the inspection of its workmen and should show why it needs the tariff,' he declared. 'If you leave it to one side, I'm afraid you will have a hard time convincing the workers that a tariff is neces-sa ry.'
Let me quote just an extract from the Toronto Globe under date of January 30:
The manifesto of the Manufacturers' Association on the tariff leaves no room for doubt as to the attitude of the association towards the removal of the war tax on imported goods. . . . The issue between the high tariff manufacturers, who constitute what is relatively small proportion of the manufacturing interests of the Dominion and the consumer, is put plainly in the manifesto. An indefinite delay in tariff revision is proposed permitting the continuance of a fiscal system under which three-quarters of the taxation of the country is to be drawn from customs and war taxes upon imported goods and raw materials. A system of taxation so one-sided cannot be continued indefinitely. It oppresses the poor and unduly favours the rich, because the taxation is levied most heavily on food, clothing and household utensils which are as necessary in the homes of the poor as of the rich. . . . The conditions admitted by the Manufacturers' Association in its statement, that customs taxation on consumption yields over 75 per cent of all our federal revenue from taxes, ought not to be continued indefinitely. They stifle Canadian enterprise and overload the shoulders of the bread winner in humble circumstances upon whom customs taxation falls relatively far more heavily than the well-to-do.
Then the Ottawa Citizen says in effect:
The statement issued by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association replying to the platform of the organized Canadian Farmers says that the tariff reform policy of the farmers will revolutionize our present fiscal system. There is nothing to be afraid of in this reference to a possible fiscal revolution in Canada. People should be prepared for it, young people especially ; for the time must undoubtedly come when Canada will be again a young man's country, emancipated from the control of the old men who staked everything on a belief in city industries	Whatever the outcome may be,
the organized farmers should press forward with their educational propaganda. There can be nothing to fear from a policy of free trade
with Great Britain in five years, and of the other proposed fiscal reforms in the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, provided that Canada is ready to become a young man's country again.
Then the Beacon, a newspaper published in the city of Stratford, says under date of January 31:
The Manufacturers' Association does not want any disturbance in the trade of the country which would be caused by a discussion on the tariff.
This is from the Montreal Star under date of February 5:
Let us get at the facts, promptly, radically, and in a spirit of justice, make a beginning first with the necessities of agricultural production. Let us work out a new national policy based upon the new national needs and freed from the old shibboleths.
Then the Manitoba Free Press has these words to say:
The statement published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association yesterday in reply to the tariff planks in the Farmers' Platform evinces no desire to find a middle way between high protection and free trade. It admits that a revision of the tariff is due, urges its postponement until after the reconstruction period, and claims that their services to the country and the Allies during the war entitles the manufacturers to a free hand in transforming Canadian industry back again from war to peace conditions. The proposal to postpone even this technical consideration of the tariff until after the period of reconstruction is over shows the manufacturers to be as blind as ever to the real imperfections of the present situation. . . . The complete lack of statesmanlike vision among the manufacturers make more than ever imperative the discovery of it among the political leaders of the country. The farmers have spoken; the manufacturers have replied; and it remains for the Union Government, in its turn, to adumbrate a policy which will by firm reasonableness disarm the potential combatants and enable Canada to turn a united front towards the great task of meeting its obligations while building up a contented and prosperous community.
The Grain Growers' Guide has as usual something to say on the -tariff. It has this article on February 5:
The main argument which the Canadian Manufacturers' Association advances against the tariff demands of the Farmers' Platform is that the present is not a wise nor safe time to lower the tariff. This argument may be accepted as pure camouflage. So far as the manufacturers are concerned, there never was and never will be a time when they will be willing to lower the tariff in any way, shape or form. They want the tariff as high as they can get it and to be kept there as long as it is possible.
I will read just one more extract, and that is from the Morning Leader of Regina, Sask., under date of February 1:
The people of Canada have listened to many a wailing appeal from the manufacturers of

Canada in the years that have elapsed since the Conservative party, away back in the seventies, committed this country to the pernicious policy of high tariff protection. During a period of over forty years every hint or suggestion of a reduction of tariff, no matter how small, or how restricted it may have been to a few items, has been the signal for the manufacturers to put up a poor mouth, and cry like the infants they at such times profess their industries to be. On other occasions, however, they puff themselves and ask admiring people to gaze upon their strength and greatness, and the pre-eminent place they occupy in making Canada a nation and giving to it its present stability and prosperity. Canadian manufacturers are puny, weak infants when they are clamouring for favours, or when anything threatens them; but they are giants, bold and unafraid, when they are in a position to dictate to the Government and the masses of the people. It is questionable, however, if during all these years the manufacturers ever issued such a palpable, dishonest, snivelling disgusted appeal as that handed out this week by the general manager of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association by direction of the executive council of that body. It is worthy of the despicable, unspeakable Hun, who, having plundered, destroyed and mutilated to the limit of his ability, throws up his hands when the hour of retribution comes, and like a coward shrieks "Kamerad! Kamerad!" The present wailing appeal of the manufacturers indicates how thoroughly frightened they have become on account of the rising tide of national indignation against the present high tariff which is robbing the people and draining the very life-blood of the nation into the pocket-book and safety vaults of the big interest magnates.
There are several other quotations that I could read, but I wish merely to show to the House that the press of Canada is fairly equally divided on the issue. In fact, I believe, if the balance were found, that the majority of the press would be on the side of the organized farmers.
