On motion of Hon. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior), Bill No. 4, to amend the Yukon Act, was read the second time, and the House went into 'Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Council reduced from ten members to three,
Perhaps the Minister will give some explanation as to the necessity of this Bill and what its purpose is.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Bill has three clauses. The first clause provides for the reduction of the Yukon Council from ten members to three. The Act of last session empowered the Governor in Council to abolish the Yukon council altogether and establish in its place an appointive body if the Governor in Council saw fit, or an appointive organization of any kind. After conferring with the Yukon Commission, I

have come to the conclusion, with the approval of my colleagues, that it would be better to maintain the elective body, but that there is no necessity for so large a body; and it is therefore intended to reduce it from ten to three. It is also intended by clause 3 of the Bill, which I may refer to now, to reduce the annual indemnity from $600 to $400. This is necessitated by the reduction in the estimates, and justified by the reduction of the population in the Yukon.
Might I ask the minister if it is the desire of the Yukon council that this Bill should be put through, or if any communication has been received from the Yukon council respecting the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No communication has been received from the Yukon council respecting the Bill that I am aware of.

In the early history I stood for an elective council and against the appointive council. I have not changed my views on this important question, and I am glad to see that the elective principle is retained, and that the people will be able to carry on their affairs as they have been accustomed to carry them on, and in accordance with the principles of democracy.

Does it not appear to the hon. Minister that any deliberative body managing the affairs of any territory and consisting of only three persons is very small? It seems to me that it would be almost impossible to carry on the business of any considerable country by a body consisting of only three members. It has to be a miniature assembly. It must have a chairman, or a speaker, and that leaves only two men on the floor; and if one moves a motion and the other refuses to second it, there is a deadlock. It would appear to me that there should be at least five men, as the smallest possible number charged with managing the affairs of any province; and I really think the hon. minister should allow this Bill to stand and have a very serious consultation with the representative from the Yukon with a view to seeing whether it is not advisable to make this body larger than is proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is true the body is not very large; but while the territory over which it would have jurisdiction is large, the population is very small. The population of the Yukon Territory to-day is only the population of a very small town. I have had the privilege and advantage of a conference with the member for the Yukon
on this subject and also with the Yukon Commissioner, who has been for many years associated with the administration of that territory, and I thought it was advisable to reduce the total expenditure to something commensurate with the size of the population; and in doing so I find it necessary to recommend the reduction that is ^contained in the Bill. This reduction meets with the approval of the Commissioner of the Yukon Territory. Regard must also be had to the fact that it is a very circumscribed area of jurisdiction they exercise. A great deal of the administration under the Act is vested in the Minister of the Interior and in the Yukon Branch of that department.
May I ask how the members of the council are elected?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is provided for by another section. They are elected by districts.
Does this include Dawson City?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I might say for the information of the hon. gentleman that it is proposed to have three districts, each electing one member. The city of Dawson will be one district, the gold-producing creeks in the vicinity of Dawson and the Stewart river will be district No. 2, and the country around White Horse will be district No. 3.

What is the jurisdiction
of the Yukon council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is really a question that would require some study of the Act in order to answer, and it would take some time.
Roughly speaking?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They have jurisdiction
analogous to that of a town council. They maintain a sort of municipal organization.

They have roads to deal
with, and I presume they must have something to do with the internal legislation of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not very much.
Have they a Speaker?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it is a council, not a parliament.

It is something in the
form of a commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very much.

And besides the council
there is a regular commissionei ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the regular commissioner is an officer of the Government and performs the active functions of Governor of the Territory. The great bulk of administrative work is on him, and he attends meetings of the council.

Perhaps I can
answer the hon. member. The Yukon council is an advisory body. Any Money Bill must originate with the Commissioner of the Territory who is a direct representative of the Federal Government and through whom all moneys voted by Par liament are expended. Money Bills originate with the Governor and he presents them to the council. No money Bill can originate with the council. The council may meet and make ordinances for the good of the country.
Have they got the power to impose taxation for municipal purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They have a limited power of taxation.

This advisory council was
originally composed of ten members and the minister proposes to reduce it to three. What is the difference between the per capita representation as the council originally stood and as the minister proposes to reduce it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not sure that I know the maximum population which the Yukon reached, but it seems to me that it will bear to the present population not far from the ratio of ten to three. The hon. member for Yukon would perhaps answer that question more accurately than I.
It is very difficult to tell what the population of the Yukon was when it reached its highest poipt. It was estimated at from 25,000 to 40,000.
Was the council of ten formed at the time when the population was at its greatest?

When the population was at its greatest the territory was governed by a council appointed by the Federal Government. Judge Dugas, afterwards the Chief Justice of the Territorial Court, served on that council, as did the Commissioner of the Territory, the Controller, the head of the Northwest Mounted Police and the Gold Commissioner. They were all Federal officials. At first the Government permitted the people of the terri-

tory to elect two representatives. . That was in 1902. In 1904 they were given the right to elect five and at the next election after that they were given the right to elect the whole council of ten. I think that perhaps the population of the territory had reached the apex of the curve by the time the council was made elective.
Will the hon. gentleman state whether this Bill is satisfactory to him as the representative of the Yukon?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I take the responsibility of saying that it is satisfactory to me after having consulted with the Commissioner of the Territory, a number of people in the territory and the Minister of the Interior. Some people in the territory would like to have the council abolished and an appointive council created under this statute, but as I said a moment ago I could not convince myself that that was quite in keeping with the spirit of the times, and I am glad to know that the elective principle is being maintained.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Sections 11 and 12 give power to the Commissioner in Council to impose taxes for any purpose within his jurisdiction; respecting the summoning of juries and the enforcement of the attendance of jurors for the trial of civil and criminal cases; the control and regulation of the sale of and traffic in intoxicating liquor in the territory, which is drawing to its close as no liquor has been allowed in for a time, and the preservation of game in the territory.
On section 2-franchise extended to women for election of council:

speechtext: That extends woman's suffrage to the Yukon Territory.

Representations
have been made to me from the Yukon that the indemnity should be left as it is; that is to say at $600. The minister has already stated that one of the objects of this legislation is to give a more economical legislature for the territory. However, in view of the fact that we are cutting down the number from ten to three, I think the minister would be well advised if he left the indemnity as it is at $600. Do they sit at

Air. A. THOA1PSON: Sometimes they sit at night,

They sit only once a year?
Air. A. THOA1PSON: Once a year, the same as Parliament.

As a general rule, how
long does the session last?
Have they Orders in Council?

How long does the
session last?

I think from ten to fifteen days. Three weeks would be a fairly long session of the council. They sat for four weeks one year but from two to three weeks would be about right.
Air. A1EIGHEN: In answer to the hon. member for Kamouraska (Air. E. Lapointe) I may say that they do legislate by Order
in Council as empowered by the Act of 1908 which hon. gentlemen passed.

On section 1-transportation returns excepted from operation of section 15 respecting secrecy,

Would the minister
be good enough to explain the provisions of this Bill?

Under section 15 of the Statistics Act, which was passed at the last session of Parliament, it is provided that all returns made by any individual or corporation upon the request of the officials of the Statistical Bureau are entitled to secrecy. That is, any information they may give is deemed to be secret, and cannot be made public by any body in the department. Of course if that relates to private affairs it is a very proper provision. Section 28 of the same Act provides that statistics furnished by transportation companies is merely privileged. But section 15 is held to override the provisions of section 28. The result is that under a strict interpretation of the Act, statistics given by transportation companies could not be published. The purpose of this section is merely to restore the provision which existed in the statute law in respect to transportation statistics, prior to the passage of the Act.

I would ask the minister if there have been any steps taken in his department to try and co-ordinate the statistics that go to the different departments, with a view to bringing all statistics under one heading?

The Act passed last session, respecting the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, had in mind the very thing which my hon. friend has mentioned. I cannot,

I am sorry to say, inform the hon. gentleman just how far the transfer has been accomplished. I do know that a great deal of the statistics heretofore published by the Customs Department is being transferred to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and it is expected that the railway statistics will also be transferred to that bureau. Ouir statistical system is being extended, and I think the Act passed last session will have a very beneficial effect in affording to the public a wider ranged and better prepared statistics than we have had heretofore.

Statistics, I might remind the minister, would be more useful under the one heading. For instance, under the Dominion Bureau of Statistics the members of this House, and other persons throughout the Dominion, might have one office to apply to in ordfer to get the statistics relating to any particular subject they may be interested in. At the present moment we might apply to that Bureau for certain statistics, and again be referred by it to perhaps my hon. friend's department, or to *the Railway Department, for certain other statistics.

I might inform my'hon. friend that to-day the Bureau of Statistics will obtain for any hon. gentleman any statistical information he requires, no matter to what department it relates. The railway statistical branch has not yet been transferred to the Statistical Bureau, but I trust they will be very shortly.

I want to say that Mr. Coats is a highly efficient public servant, and I would like to render him that testimony here.
Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR: I presume that the statistics referred to include the information obtained in answer to questions sent to manufacturers. Now manufacturers write to me that they have a great many returns to make in connection with their business, that it is becoming an onerous thing, and that some of them have to employ special clerks to look after the returns that the Government call for. I would like to know what use is made of these statistics after they are forwarded. It will be satisfactory to the people who are incurring this expense in compiling and forwarding these statistics, to know that they are utilized by the department and placed before the people in some shape or other. Will the minister tell us what is done in that direction?

I am quite aware of the fact that during the latter part of the war,

various departments of government were seeking information of one jrind or another, and I fear there was a great deal of overlapping, and in some instances our business men were perhaps unnecessarily put to expense and annoyance to afford statistical information to more than one branch or department of government. For instance, the Canada Food Board required at times certain information. Later it would transpire that the Cost of Living Commissioner of the Labour Department might be wanting statistical information along these same lines, and in consequence my hon. friend is quite correct in saying that many business men have been protesting recently against the vast amount of statistical information demanded of them. However, the intention of the Government, and of the various departments, now is to centre in the Bureau of Statistics all work relating to statistics. The Statistical Bureau is attempting to build up statistical information in reference to our internal trade, which figures were never available in this country before. If the Bureau succeeds in compiling reliable information concerning our internal trade it will be of very great interest and benefit to the public. Of course this will mean that the public must vouchsafe on request certain information, but while it may entail some little additional work on the part of certain members of the community, still it will be in the public interest to have that information. However, I can assure my hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysbor-ough (Mr. Sinclair) that it is the purpose of the Government-in fact that was the intention of the Act passed last session- to centre all statistics in the one branch.
What is the difficulty in the way of getting railway statistics into the Bureau of Statistics?

I cannot answer my
hon. friend exactly. There has been some delay. I am not sure whether the Railway Department are facilitating matters very much; and that might be true of any Department-they naturally wish to hold on to their statistical branches as long as they can. I have not had an opportunity of knowing why the railway statistics have not already been brought under this statistical bureau, but they will be very shortly.

We have been
collecting these statistics now for some time. Is anything being done in the way of utilizing them?
Yes, a great deal of statistical information has already been compiled. I hope that the report of the Bureau will be presented to the House shortly.

The minister is aware of the trouble and expense that business men have been subjected to in providing statistical information [DOT] for different departments of the Government. As he has truly said, the country is sick and tired of it, and this is a good time for the minister to make a reassuring statement to the country that, the *war being over, business men will no longer be required to employ extra labour in the compiling of these statistics. Moreover, when this information comes into Ottawa an army of employees is required to dig it out and put it into shape. Great economy would result, not only to business men throughout Canada but to the Government as well, if a good deal of the statistical information that has been required during the past year could be done away with.

The purpose of
the passing of the Statistical Act of last session was to centre in one branch of the public service the compilation of all statistics. The Bureau created for that purpose should be able to co-ordinate the work and minimize the demands upon the public for information. I think I can very sincerely assure my hon. friend that henceforth demands made upon the public for statistics will be very much less than they have been during the last year or two. Statistics were required from the public for many reasons during the last two years, but with the ending of the war the need for obtaining much of this information has passed away.
Is the Food Board still calling for returns from the business people?
I think not.

What is the
estimated cost of establishing this Bureau?

The Bureau of
Statistics, in a certain form, has been in existence for a long time. The Director of the new Bureau of Statistics was the Census Commissioner.

Prior to that, editor of
the Labour Gazette.
I think so. Last session the Dominion Bureau of Statistics was established, under the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is intended that all statistics shall be compiled in that Bureau.
Do you propose to extend the work of that Bureau?
Yes.
What I want to get is the difference between the cost of the present system and that of the new system which it is proposed to establish.

I shall endeavour to give my hon. friend that information. The expenditures of the Customs Department, for instance, in compiling their statistics will be very much lessened by the work of this Bureau.
Mr. ROBB; The complaint is not that information is sought; it is that there is duplication in this respect, with resulting duplication of expense both on the part of the business men throughout the country and of the Government. The minister has said that the Bureau of Statistics was established with a view to gathering all this information, but since that Act was passed the Government of which he is a member has authorized other departments to seek information and has made the business men of the country liable to penalties if that information is not supplied. That is what we are complaining of; we wish that these penalties be withdrawn.
. Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: Prior to the establishment of the Bureau of Statistics, the Canada Food Board, the War Trade Board and other war organizations were established. Properly or improperly, they thought they required certain statistics and demands were accordingly made upon the public for the information. In the meantime, the Bureau of Statistics was not completely organized; as a matter of fact it is not fully organized yet. When the organization of the Bureau is complete, so far as I know there is no reason why any demands should be made on the public for statistical information except through this one body; therefore duplication should be eliminated.

Do I understand that the statistical information gathered by the officials of the Railway Department-I am taking the Railway Department as an example-is now passed on to this Bureau of Statistics; and that the information thus obtained will appear not in the report of the Railway Department, but in the report of this Bureau of Statistics?

That is the intention. The Railway Department have a Statistical Branch which publishes a blue book of railway and transportation statis-

tics. In a short time that branch will pass over to the Bureau of Statistics, the publication now issuing from the Railway Department will cease, and that information will appear in the general statistical book to be published by the Bureau of Statistics.

In other words, a person requiring information regarding statistics of any character will apply not to the particular department with which that information is connected, but to this Bureau of Statistics?

Yes, for instance, in reference to customs statistics, it is expected that the Bureau of Statistics will have more complete and fuller information Uian is to be found in the customs return I think it is likely that the Customs Department will continue to publish an annual blue book showing the customs duties paid upon importations, but the Bureau of Statistics will take the customs returns and interpret them in a different way and make them more valuable to the public.

What did this Bureau of Statistics cost last year?
Mr. A. IC. MACLEAN: I could not give that information to my hon. friend. That will be made available to him when the estimates relating to the Bureau of Statistics are before Parliament.
Is there a large staff?

I should not like to venture an answer to my hon. friend. The staff is .probably larger now than it was at the close of the last session of Parliament. It shalll likely grow, I cannot say.
Mr. ,1. H. SINCLAIR: Who is at the head of it?
Mr. Coats, who was formerly Commissioner of Census.

I do not want to prevent the minister from getting his Bill through, but he has, I take it, given to the House the assurance that the statistics now going to the Railway Department will in future go to the Bureau of Statistics. Am I right?
Yes.

Without wishing to anticipate any of the work of the session, might I ask if there is not in the Railway Bill that is at the present moment going through the Senate a clause with an amendment* to it to the very effect that that branch of statistics will go to the Railway Department?

I understand that an application will be made to strike those clauses out. They were in the Bill, I understand, as originally introduced, and I think at the last session of Parliament, either in committee or in the House, they were struck out, but the Bill was republished with those clauses incorporated.
They will be struck out?
I hope they will be struck out. I intend to ask that they be struck out.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-dates of making and forwarding transportation returns changed.

The purpose of section 2 is simply to change the year for which transportation statistics may be collected. The year required by the Act as at present is the old Government fiscal year ending on June 30, and it is proposed by this section of the Bill to change it to the calendar year, as this corresponds with the financial year of most transportation companies.

Why not attempt uniformity in the financial statistical years of the Government? Our financial year at present ends with the last day of March. Would it not be very much easier to get information for men who take an interest in such matters, if we had all our years coterminous; that is, if our statistical year, our financial year and all our other years in the business of the Government ended with the same day? It is confusing that one year ends with the last day of March, another ends with the last day of June, and another ends with the last day of December. If they could be co-ordinated and systematized so that when we were talking about a statistical or financial year in Government matters we would all have in mind the same period, it would be much better.

I quite agree with the leader of the Opposition that it would be very desirable to bring about the end he suggests, but that is, of course, impossible. The section of the Bill which we are now considering refers merely to transportation statistics, and as these are always con- . trolled by individuals or private corporations, we must accept their fiscal year; at least it makes it less difficult for them if we adopt the calendar year as the period for which they must furnish the annual statistics. That has been the experience of the Bureau of Statistics. Nearly all the

railway companies have their fiscal year corresponding with the calendar year, and this will promote the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Chateauguay (Mr. Robb), because it will make it feasier for transportation companies to give this information at the end of the calendar year which corresponds usually with their business year.

Section agreed to.
On the preamble.
Have the statistics obtained by the 'Canada Registration Board been transferred to the Bureau of Statistics?
They have been, or will be transferred.
Is the Canada Registration Board still in existence?

I do not know whether that information will be of very much interest hereafter or not, but I remember that Mr. Coats, Director of the Bureau, told me the other day that he could tell, by reason of the information gathered by the Canada Registration Board, how many farmers or how many carpenters there were in any county in Canada. Whether such information will be helpful in the future or not I do not know.

I read the other day in one of the Montreal newspapers that the bachelors of that city were protesting very strongly because the Canada Registration Board had sold to the city or to the commissioners of Montreal, for the sum of $500, or a little more than that, the statistics which they had gathered, in order that the city might collect a tax from the poor, unfortunate bachelors. Is that the case?
That is a case in which the Dominion will be assisting in the assertion of provincial or municipal rights.

On the motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean for the adjournment of the House:

What business shall
we take up to-morrow?

Questions first, and notices of motion next. I assume that will exhaust the day, but if not we shall proceed to Public Bills. The Resolution that will be taken up first will probably be the one standing in the name of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) relating to the Grand Trunk Pacific.

I should like to make a suggestion to the minister who is leading the House, which he might take up with his colleagues. In the British House of Commons, on Thursday of each week, the minister who is leading the House gives a statement of the business for each day of the following week. I think the Government might very well adopt that practice. It would enable members and people throughout the country who are interested in a particular item of legislation to know when it was coming up in Parliament.
I shall be very glad to call the attention of my colleagues to my hon. friend's suggestion as it will appear in Hansard to-morrow.

Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 11.30 p.m.
Wednesday, March 19, 1919.
